**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verse 7:**

﴿Muhkamat﴾ (the clear, definitive verses), whose wording is made firm (*uhkimat ibaratuha*), [[Mahmud said: "The muhkamat (definitive verses) are those whose wording is made firm... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: This is as I mentioned earlier about his effort to fit the verses to what he believes. I seek refuge in God from making the Qur'an subordinate to personal opinion (*ra'y*). His belief is that seeing God is impossible, based on the claim of the Qadariyya (the rationalist school that affirmed human free will and denied divine decree) that seeing God entails corporeality (*jismiyya*) and direction (*jiha*). So when a decisive text establishing the vision is revealed to them, such as His saying ﴿Looking at their Lord﴾, they incline to classify it as mutashabih (ambiguous), so that they can refer it, by their claim, to the verse whose apparent meaning they think supports their view.

The verse is His saying ﴿No vision can grasp Him﴾. Our purpose now is to show the necessity of reconciling the two verses in the correct way. We say:

The meaning of ﴿No vision can grasp Him﴾ applies to the life of this world. The meaning of seeing applies to the Hereafter, reconciling the evidences. Or we say:

Although *al-absar* (the visions/eyes) has an apparently general sense, what is intended is a specific group, namely that the visions of the disbelievers cannot grasp Him, as in His saying ﴿Nay, indeed they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾. We also say: there is no contradiction between the two verses, so we place each of them in its proper position. The explanation: *al-absar* is general through the definite article *al-* of the genus (*al-jinsiyya*). The aim of the Qadariyya, by their own claim, is only achieved by agreeing to its generality. In that case, generality is equivalent to the use of *kull* (all), because both the definite article and the generic form indicate totality and comprehensiveness. Once this is established, negation falls on the totality. The established rules hold that negating totality is, linguistically and rationally, a partial negation. Do you not see that when someone says: "Do not spend all the dirhams," what is understood is permission to spend some and prohibition of spending others? And rationally, totality is negated by negating some individuals, even one. Accordingly, the implication of the verse is negation of seeing from some visions and affirmation of it for some visions, and this is exactly the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni community), for they affirm it for the monotheists and deny it for the disbelievers, as indicated by His saying ﴿Nay, indeed they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾. It is thus established that this verse either is interpreted as affirming the vision, or remains on its apparent meaning as evidence for its affirmation in accordance with the Sunna. It cannot be said that the difference has been established between *kull* entering a definite noun of the genus and its not entering. Do you not see that they say that our saying "Man is a writer" is indefinite in effect, meaning particular, and that our saying "Every man is an animal" is universal, not particular? We say: we only went along with the Qadariyya in what binds them to agree with it. They have agreed that *al-absar* includes each and every individual of the genus. Had it not been so, their objective would not be achieved, and we would have been spared the burden of discussing this. This degree of universality agreed upon by both parties does not establish what the people of that discipline called indefinite; rather, this is what is universal according to them. And God is the Granter of success. As for the two other verses, one of which is His saying ﴿Indeed God does not command indecency﴾ and the other His saying ﴿We commanded its affluent ones, and they committed sin therein﴾, al-Zamakhshari does not dispute using them as examples of the muhkam and the mutashabih.]] by being protected (*hufizat*) from possibility and confusion, ﴿mutashabihat﴾ (ambiguous verses), which are confusing and open to multiple meanings, ﴿they are the mother of the Book﴾, meaning the root of the Book, to which the mutashabihat are referred and returned. An example of this is ﴿No vision can grasp Him﴾, ﴿Looking at their Lord﴾, ﴿He does not command indecency﴾, ﴿We commanded its affluent ones﴾.

If you ask: why was the whole Qur'an not muhkam? I answer: if the whole Qur'an were muhkam, people would have attached themselves to it because its meaning is easy to grasp, and they would have turned away from what requires investigation and reflection, through reasoning and inference. Had they done that, they would have abandoned the path by which knowledge of God and His unity can be reached only. Also, the mutashabih involves a test and distinguishes between those who stand firm upon the truth and those who waver in it. Also, there is in the scholars' disputes and their exertion in deriving its meanings and referring them back to the muhkam great benefit, lofty knowledge, and attainment of ranks with God. Also, the believer who holds that there is no contradiction or discrepancy in God's speech, when he sees in it something that appears contradictory, his concern becomes seeking what reconciles it and puts it on one consistent course. He reflects, reviews himself and others, and God opens for him and makes clear the agreement of the mutashabih with the muhkam; then he gains greater tranquility in his belief and strength in his certainty.

﴿Those in whose hearts is deviation﴾, meaning the people of innovation (*ahl al-bid'a*), ﴿follow what is ambiguous of it﴾, meaning they cling to the mutashabih, which may bear what the innovator inclines toward, not matching the muhkam, and may also bear what matches the speech of the people of truth. ﴿Seeking discord﴾, meaning seeking to tempt people away from their religion and mislead them, ﴿and seeking its interpretation﴾, meaning seeking to interpret it according to what they desire. ﴿And none knows its interpretation except God and those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾, meaning the true interpretation which it must be understood to bear cannot be reached except by God, and by His servants who are firmly rooted in knowledge, that is, who are steadfast in it, established in it, and who grasp it with a firm grip (*'adda fihi bi-dirs qati'*). Some stop at His saying "except God" and begin: "and those firmly rooted in knowledge say..."

They interpret the mutashabih as what God has kept knowledge of to Himself, and as knowing the wisdom in it from His verses, such as the number of the guardians of Hell and the like. The first is the preferred view. They say that it is a new sentence explaining the state of those firmly rooted, meaning: these are the people who know the interpretation. ﴿They say: We believe in it﴾, meaning in the mutashabih, ﴿all of it is from our Lord﴾, meaning each part of it and of the muhkam is from Him. Or, regarding the Book: each of its mutashabih and muhkam is from God, the Wise, whose speech does not contradict itself and whose Book does not differ. ﴿And none takes heed except people of understanding﴾, praise for those firmly rooted, for their focus of mind and fine reflection. It is permissible for ﴿they say﴾ to be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to those firmly rooted. Ibn Mas'ud read: "Indeed its interpretation is only with God." Ubayy read: "And those firmly rooted in knowledge say."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verse 8–9:

Do not let our hearts swerve (lā tuzigh qulūbanā), do not test us with trials in which our hearts would swerve (lā tablunā bi-balāyā tazīgh fīhā qulūbunā). [[Maḥmūd said: "Its meaning is: our Lord, do not test us with trials ... etc." Aḥmad said: As for the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna), they make this supplication without altering it, because they affirm the Oneness of God in its true sense, and they believe that every occurrence, whether guidance or deviation, is created by God, exalted is He. As for the Qadariyya, they hold that deviation is not created by God but is created by the servant for himself, so they make this supplication only with an alteration, diverting it from the meaning intended by it, as the author (al-Muṣannif) interpreted it. Yet we do call upon God, in addition to this supplication, that He not test us and not withhold His gentleness from us, āmīn, because all of it is His act and His creation, and nothing exists except Him and His acts, of which we and our acts are part.]] after You have guided us and given us direction to Your religion (baʿda idh hadaytanā wa-arshadtanā li-dīnika). Or: do not withhold Your gentle kindness from us after You have shown us kindness (aw lā tamnaʿnā alṭāfuka baʿda idh luṭta binā). From Yourself, mercy (min ladunka raḥmatan), i.e., a blessing from You, by way of success (tawfīq) and assistance (maʿūna).

It is recited as "lā tuzigh qulūbanā" with the taʾ and the yāʾ (bi-l-tāʾ wa-l-yāʾ), and with "qulūbu" in the nominative (raf MS: al-qulūb). Jāmiʿu l-nās li-yawmin (the gatherer of mankind for a Day): i.e., You gather them for the reckoning of a day, or for the recompense of a day, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the Day He gathers you for the Day of Gathering﴾. It is also recited "jāmiʿu l-nās" in its original form (ʿalā l-aṣl). ﴿Indeed, God does not fail in His promise﴾; its meaning is that divinity is incompatible with failing in a promise, like your saying: "Indeed, the generous one does not disappoint the one who asks him." Al-mīʿād means al-mawʿid (the promise). ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, recited "lan tughniya" with a sukūn on the yāʾ, and this is among the extreme (jadd) instances of finding the vowel burdensome on the soft letters (ḥurūf al-līn).

The kaf (like) is in the nominative position, its implied sense being: "the habit of these disbelievers is like the habit of those before them, the people of Pharaoh and others." It is also permissible that the position of the kaf be in the accusative, governed by "lan tughni" (will not avail) or by "al-wuqud" (fuel). That is: "They will not avail against them just as they did not avail against those (others), or the fire will be kindled with them as it was kindled with them," as you say: "Indeed you wrong people like the habit (dʾab) of your father," meaning like the wronging of your father and as he used to wrong them; and "Indeed so-and-so is deprived like the habit of his father," meaning as his father was deprived.

﴿They denied Our signs, so God seized them for their sins﴾ is an explanation of their habit, what they did and what was done to them, in the form of an answer to an implied question about their condition.

﴿Say to those who disbelieved﴾: they are the polytheists of Mecca. ﴿You will be overcome﴾: meaning on the day of Badr. It was also said: they are the Jews. They said, "Do not let it deceive you that you met a people who were inexperienced in war and you gained an advantage over them; if you fight us, you will know that we are the (real) people." **Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verse 13:**

﴿There has been a sign for you﴾: the address is to the polytheists of Quraysh. ﴿In the two hosts that met﴾: on the day of Badr. ﴿One fighting in the way of God, and another disbelieving; they saw them as twice their number﴾: the polytheists saw the Muslims as twice the number of the polytheists, roughly two thousand. [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its meaning is that the polytheists saw the Muslims as twice the number of the polytheists… etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: Likewise are the verses on intercession, according to the opinion of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunna).]] Or (they saw) them as twice the number of the Muslims, which was six hundred and some twenty. God showed them the Muslims, despite their small number, as many times more, so that they would be awed by them and shrink from fighting them. That was a reinforcement for them from God, as He reinforced them with the angels. The evidence for this is the reading of Nafi‘: ﴿you see them﴾ with the taa’ (ترونهم), meaning: you see, O polytheists of Quraysh, the Muslims as twice your disbelieving host, or as twice themselves. If you say: this contradicts His words in Surat al-Anfal: ﴿and He makes you seem few in their eyes﴾ (وَيُقَلِّلُكُمْ فِي أَعْيُنِهِمْ), I say: first they made them seem few in their eyes until they dared against them, then when they met them, they seemed numerous in their eyes until they were defeated. So the making-few and the making-many were in two different states. Similar to this, among what is carried upon differing states, is His words: ﴿So on that day no man or jinn will be asked about his sin﴾ and His words: ﴿Stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾. Their being made few at one time and many at another in their eyes is more eloquent in power and in manifesting the sign. It was also said: the Muslims see the polytheists as twice the Muslims. [[(His words resume.) He said: "And it was said: the Muslims see the polytheists as twice the Muslims… etc." Ahmad said: He only said that because, according to Nafi‘'s reading, the address would be to the Muslims, i.e., "you see them, O Muslims," and the pronoun of the two multiples would also refer to the Muslims. But it has come in the third-person form, so it entails a shift in a single sentence from the second person to the third person (iltifat), and although that is permissible and eloquent, it mostly occurs across two sentences. Here the statement is a single sentence, because mithlayhim (مثليهم) is the second object of the verb of seeing. If someone said: "I thought you (sg.) would stand up," using the third-person form after the second person, it would not be proper. This is the aspect by which al-Zamakhshari reconciled Nafi‘'s reading with this interpretation. However, a similar difficulty arises in one of his two earlier interpretations just mentioned, since he said: its meaning according to Nafi‘'s reading is: "you see, O polytheists, the Muslims as twice their number, or as twice your disbelieving host," so on this second aspect there is a shift from address to the third person within the very same sentence, just as he imposed on that aspect. And God knows best.]] upon the arrangement that was imposed on them, namely that one should face two, in His words: ﴿If there are among you a hundred patient ones, they will overcome two hundred﴾, after they had been obligated that one should face ten, in His words: ﴿If there are among you twenty patient ones, they will overcome two hundred﴾. For this reason, their weakness was described as ﴿few﴾ [[His words "for this reason their weakness was described" perhaps refer to His words: ﴿And when He showed them to you, when you met, few in your eyes﴾, meaning the weakness of the Muslims, which was six hundred, was described as few, even though the weakness of a thing is more than it. So reflect. (Ibn al-Munayyir's note.)]], because it is few in comparison with ten times, while the disbelievers were three times their number. Nafi‘'s reading does not support this. Ibn Musarrif read ﴿they see them﴾ (يرونهم) in the passive form, with the yaa’ and taa’ (i.e., the reading being passive), meaning: God shows them that by His power. It was also read: ﴿a host fighting, and another disbelieving﴾ with the genitive (بالجر) as a substitution (بدل) for "two hosts," and with the accusative (بالنصب) as a specification (على الاختصاص), or as a circumstantial clause (على الحال) from the pronoun in ﴿they met﴾. ﴿A clear seeing﴾: meaning an open, manifest vision, free of ambiguity, like any other direct observation. ﴿And God strengthens with His help whom He wills﴾: as He strengthened the people of Badr by making them appear numerous in the eyes of the enemy.

Zuyyina lil-nasi (It has been made attractive to people): the one who makes it attractive is Allah, glorified and exalted be He. [Mahmud said: "The one who makes it attractive is Allah, exalted... etc." Ahmad said: The "making attractive" of desires is used to mean the creation of love for them in hearts, and in this sense it is attributed to Allah exalted in truth, since there is no creator except Him, the Creator of everything, whether substance or accident subsisting in substance, love or otherwise. This is praiseworthy in the Sharia, firstly. And "making attractive" is also used to mean urging and commanding the pursuit of desires; in this sense, from it, only the urging towards some desires explicitly stipulated by the Sharia is attributed to Allah exalted, such as marriage coupled with the intention of procreation, following the Sunnah in it, and what runs along its course. As for forbidden desires, their making attractive in this second sense is attributed to Satan, as a descent of his whispering and his embellishing them to the status of commanding them and urging their pursuit. The statement of al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, is to be understood as referring to making attractive in the second sense, not the first, for he is too far removed from attributing the creation of Allah to other than Allah. Rather, al-Zamakhshari often cites such ambiguous expressions, applying them to the principles of the corrupt Qadariyya, so be alert to this, and absolve the speaker, a pious predecessor, of what al-Zamakhshari claims to transmit from him. And Allah is the one who grants success.] for trial, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them﴾. This is supported by the reading of Mujahid: zuyyina lil-nas (with the verb in the active form, naming the agent). And from al-Hasan: "Satan."

And Allah made it attractive to them, because we do not know anyone who censures it more than its Creator: ḥubb al-shahawat (the love of desires). He made the things he mentioned into desires, as an intensification of their being desired and eagerly sought for enjoyment. [(His words continue) He said: "made attractive ... etc." Ahmad said: He means attaching them to the category of: "a man who fasts and breaks fast," where the meaning is placed in the position of the noun for emphasis.] The purpose is to belittle them, so He calls them desires, because desire is considered base by the wise, and whoever follows it bears witness against himself to animality. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 18–19:

His indication of His oneness is likened to His particular acts, which no one else can perform, and to what He has revealed of His verses that declare His oneness, such as Surat al-Ikhlas and Ayat al-Kursi and others, as the testimony of a witness in clarity and disclosure. Likewise (is the testimony of) the angels and those endowed with knowledge, and their argument for it. ﴿Upholding justice﴾ means establishing justice in what He apportions of provisions and terms of life, in rewarding and punishing, and in what He commands His servants of giving one another their due and dealing equally among themselves.

Its being in the accusative (intisab) is as a emphatic circumstantial qualifier (hal mu'akkida) from Him, like His saying: ﴿And it is the truth, confirming﴾ (2:91).

If you say: Why is it permissible to put it in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier singly, and not in the coordinated nouns that precede it? If you said, "Zayd and 'Amr came to me riding," it would not be permissible?

I say: This is permissible because there is no ambiguity, just as it is permissible in His saying: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift﴾ (21:72), where "nafila" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier referring to Jacob. If you said, "Zayd and Hind came to me riding," it would be permissible because (the masculine participle) distinguishes it by its masculinity, or (it is accusative) by way of praise.

If you say: Is it not required that what is in the accusative by way of praise be definite, as in your saying, "Praise belongs to God, the Praiseworthy"? (The Prophet (ﷺ) said:) "We, the company of prophets, do not leave inheritance." [[Ahmad narrated it: Waki' narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu al-Zinad, from al-A'raj, from Abu Hurayra, raised (to the Prophet) with this. And al-Nasa'i narrated it in al-Kubra, from the narration of Ibn 'Uyayna, from al-Zuhri, from Malik ibn Aws ibn al-Hadathan, who said: Umar said to 'Abd al-Rahman, Sa'd, 'Uthman, Talha and al-Zubayr: "I adjure you by God, by whom the heavens and the earth stand, did you hear the Prophet (ﷺ) say such-and-such?" and he mentioned it, and in it they said: "O God, yes." And he narrated it in al-Kuna in the biography of Abu Idris, a student of Abu Sulayman, from a narration from 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umar, from Abu Hurayra, the like of it. Its origin is agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim), from the hadith of 'A'isha with the wording: "We do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity."]] Or (is it not required in) "We are the Banu Nahshal; we do not claim a father"?

I say: It has come indefinite just as it has come definite. Sibawayh cited, among what came indefinite, the verse of the Hudhali:

"And he returns to women bare (of adornment), and disheveled, emaciated ones like the sa'ali (ghouls)."

[[The Hudhali describes a man who hunts and returns to his wife and daughters, who are bare, naked of jewelry and clothing. "Shu'than" (disheveled) is in the accusative as a dispraise, meaning "and I dispraise disheveled ones," that is, with faces dusty from hunger. "Al-'Utul" is the plural of "'atila." "Shu'th" is the plural of "sha'tha'," like "sud" and "sawda'." "Maradi'" is the plural of "mirda'" by analogy, or "mirda'" by usage, meaning they nurse their children. "Sa'alī" is the plural of "sa'lah," which is the female of the demons, meaning ugly in appearance like the ghouls. And it is the most hideous thing among the Arabs.]]

If you say: Is it permissible for it to be a qualifier of the negated noun, as if it were said: "There is no god standing by justice except Him"? I say: It is not far-fetched, for we have seen them extend the separation between the qualifier and the qualified.

If you say: You have made it a circumstantial qualifier of the subject of "shahida (bore witness)." Is it valid for it to be in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of "huwa" in: ﴿There is no god but He﴾? I say: Yes, because it is an emphatic circumstantial qualifier, and an emphatic circumstantial qualifier does not require that the clause in which it is an added benefit contain a governing element, as in your saying, "I am a servant of God, brave." Likewise if you said: "There is no man but a servant of God, brave." And this is more appropriate than its being in the accusative from the subject of "shahida." Likewise its being in the accusative by way of praise.

If you say: Has His standing by justice entered into the ruling of the testimony of God, the angels and those endowed with knowledge, just as the oneness did? I say: Yes, if you make it a circumstantial qualifier of "He," or an accusative of praise from Him, or a qualifier of the negated noun, as if it were said: "God, the angels and those endowed with knowledge bore witness that there is no god but He, and that He stands by justice."

'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read: ﴿the standing by justice﴾, making it a substitute for "He" or the predicate of an omitted subject. Abu Hanifa read: ﴿upright by justice﴾. ﴿The Almighty, the Wise﴾ are two qualifiers confirming what He described His essence with, of oneness and justice, meaning that He is the Almighty whom no other god can overpower, the Wise who does not deviate from justice in His acts.

If you say: What is meant by "those endowed with knowledge," whom He honored with this honor by joining them with Himself and the angels in testifying to His oneness and justice? I say: They are those who establish His oneness and justice by clear proofs and decisive arguments, and they are the scholars of justice [[His saying "and decisive arguments, and they are the scholars of justice" is an allusion to the Mu'tazila, who called themselves "the people of justice and monotheism" (ahl al-'adl wa-l-tawhid). But fairness requires generality, so that it includes Ahl al-Sunna wa-l-Jama'a (the people of the Sunna and the community). (ʿ)]] and of monotheism. It is read (with) "anna" (that) with a fatha and "inna al-din" (indeed the religion) with a kasra, so that the verb falls on "that He," meaning "God bore witness that He," or "that." His saying: ﴿Indeed the religion with God is Islam﴾ is a resumptive clause emphasizing the first clause.

If you say: What is the benefit of this emphasis? I say: Its benefit is that His saying "there is no god but He" is monotheism, and His saying "standing by justice" is equity. When it is followed by His saying "indeed the religion with God is Islam," it indicates that Islam is justice [[His saying "it indicates that Islam is justice" is a forced interpretation that the noble wording does not require, but partisanship prompted it. And his saying "and in it is that whoever holds to" etc. is a thrust against Ahl al-Sunna built upon that, and its verification is in the science of tawhid. In sum, justice and monotheism are not confined to the Mu'tazila's school. (ʿ)]] and monotheism, and it is the religion with God, and whatever else is not in any way part of the religion with Him. In it is that whoever goes to anthropomorphism, or to what leads to it, such as permitting the vision (of God), or goes to determinism (jabr), which is pure injustice, is not upon the religion of God, which is Islam. This is clear and manifest, as you see.

It is read with both (words) with a fatha, on the basis that the second is a substitute for the first, as if it were said: "God bore witness that the religion with God is Islam." The substitute is the substituted in meaning, so it is an explicit clarification, because the religion of God is monotheism and justice. The first is read with a kasra and the second with a fatha, on the basis that the verb falls on "inna," and what lies between them is a confirming parenthetical [[His saying "the verb falls on inna" means on "inna al-din..." etc. (ʿ)]]. This too is evidence that the religion of Islam is justice and monotheism, so all the readings are mutually supportive in this.

'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read: ﴿That there is no god but He.﴾ Ubayy read: ﴿Indeed the religion with God is for Islam,﴾ and this strengthens the reading of the one who opens the first and breaks the second.

It is read: "shuhada' Allah" (witnesses for God), in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of those mentioned before it, and in the nominative as "they are the witnesses of God." If you say: On what is this reading coordinated: ﴿and the angels and those endowed with knowledge﴾? I say: On the pronoun in "shuhada'," and it is permissible because of the intervening separation.

If you say: Why did He repeat His saying: ﴿There is no god but He﴾? [[Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you say: What is the benefit of repeating 'there is no god but He' ... etc.?" Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: This repetition is for what I mentioned in its counterpart, of what the speech opened with, when its distance became long. That is because the speech opened with monotheism, then followed the monotheism with an enumeration of those who testify to it, then His saying "standing by justice," which is transcendence, so the speech lengthened with that, and so He renewed the monotheism after the transcendence in order to connect to His saying "indeed the religion with God is Islam." Had this renewal not been there, the earlier monotheism would have been cut off in understanding from what was intended to be connected to it, and God knows best. He said: "And in it is that whoever goes to anthropomorphism ... etc." Ahmad said: This is an allusion, and indeed an explicit statement, to the expulsion of Ahl al-Sunna from the bond of Islam. What they are blamed for is only that they affirmed the promise God made to His honored servants through the tongue of their noble Prophet (ﷺ), that they will see their Lord as one sees the moon on the night of the full moon, without being harmed in seeing Him. And because they affirmed God's oneness in its true sense, they bore witness that there is no god but He, and that there is no creator of them or of their acts but He. They confined themselves to attributing to themselves a power that accompanies their act, which has no creation nor effect except distinguishing between their voluntary and involuntary acts, and this is what is called in the Law "acquisition" (kasb), as in His saying: ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾ (42:30). This is the faith and monotheism of these people, unlike a people who alter the faces of the texts and deny the vision, whose denial of it appears to be a cause of their deprivation of it, and who make their base selves partners with God in His creatures, claiming that they create for themselves whatever acts they wish, against the will of their Lord, in opposition and defiance of God in His dominion. Then after that they conceal themselves by naming themselves "the people of justice and monotheism." And God knows best who is pious. Compulsion (jabr) is better than association (ishrak). If Ahl al-Sunna are "compellers," then I am the first of the compellers. If you, O Zamakhshari, looked with an eye of fairness at the ignorance and error of the Qadariyya, you would have moved toward the gardens of the Sunna and its shade, and you would have left the slippery paths and places of innovation. But God disliked their rising, and you would have known which of the two groups is more deserving of safety and more fitting to enter among "those endowed with knowledge," who are linked with monotheism alongside the angels, honored by being joined with the Name of God, Mighty and Majestic. O God, inspire us to follow the Sunna, and to thank You, and do not make us feel secure from Your plotting, for none feels secure from God's plotting except the losing people. There is no escape from fear except by fear. And God is the guardian of success.]] I say: He mentioned it first to indicate its exclusivity to oneness, and that there is no god but that distinguished Essence. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 18–19:

His indication of His oneness is likened to His particular acts, which no one else can perform, and to what He has revealed of His verses that declare His oneness, such as Surat al-Ikhlas and Ayat al-Kursi and others, as the testimony of a witness in clarity and disclosure. Likewise (is the testimony of) the angels and those endowed with knowledge, and their argument for it. ﴿Upholding justice﴾ means establishing justice in what He apportions of provisions and terms of life, in rewarding and punishing, and in what He commands His servants of giving one another their due and dealing equally among themselves.

Its being in the accusative (intisab) is as a emphatic circumstantial qualifier (hal mu'akkida) from Him, like His saying: ﴿And it is the truth, confirming﴾ (2:91).

If you say: Why is it permissible to put it in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier singly, and not in the coordinated nouns that precede it? If you said, "Zayd and 'Amr came to me riding," it would not be permissible?

I say: This is permissible because there is no ambiguity, just as it is permissible in His saying: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift﴾ (21:72), where "nafila" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier referring to Jacob. If you said, "Zayd and Hind came to me riding," it would be permissible because (the masculine participle) distinguishes it by its masculinity, or (it is accusative) by way of praise.

If you say: Is it not required that what is in the accusative by way of praise be definite, as in your saying, "Praise belongs to God, the Praiseworthy"? (The Prophet (ﷺ) said:) "We, the company of prophets, do not leave inheritance." [[Ahmad narrated it: Waki' narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu al-Zinad, from al-A'raj, from Abu Hurayra, raised (to the Prophet) with this. And al-Nasa'i narrated it in al-Kubra, from the narration of Ibn 'Uyayna, from al-Zuhri, from Malik ibn Aws ibn al-Hadathan, who said: Umar said to 'Abd al-Rahman, Sa'd, 'Uthman, Talha and al-Zubayr: "I adjure you by God, by whom the heavens and the earth stand, did you hear the Prophet (ﷺ) say such-and-such?" and he mentioned it, and in it they said: "O God, yes." And he narrated it in al-Kuna in the biography of Abu Idris, a student of Abu Sulayman, from a narration from 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umar, from Abu Hurayra, the like of it. Its origin is agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim), from the hadith of 'A'isha with the wording: "We do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity."]] Or (is it not required in) "We are the Banu Nahshal; we do not claim a father"?

I say: It has come indefinite just as it has come definite. Sibawayh cited, among what came indefinite, the verse of the Hudhali:

"And he returns to women bare (of adornment), and disheveled, emaciated ones like the sa'ali (ghouls)."

[[The Hudhali describes a man who hunts and returns to his wife and daughters, who are bare, naked of jewelry and clothing. "Shu'than" (disheveled) is in the accusative as a dispraise, meaning "and I dispraise disheveled ones," that is, with faces dusty from hunger. "Al-'Utul" is the plural of "'atila." "Shu'th" is the plural of "sha'tha'," like "sud" and "sawda'." "Maradi'" is the plural of "mirda'" by analogy, or "mirda'" by usage, meaning they nurse their children. "Sa'alī" is the plural of "sa'lah," which is the female of the demons, meaning ugly in appearance like the ghouls. And it is the most hideous thing among the Arabs.]]

If you say: Is it permissible for it to be a qualifier of the negated noun, as if it were said: "There is no god standing by justice except Him"? I say: It is not far-fetched, for we have seen them extend the separation between the qualifier and the qualified.

If you say: You have made it a circumstantial qualifier of the subject of "shahida (bore witness)." Is it valid for it to be in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of "huwa" in: ﴿There is no god but He﴾? I say: Yes, because it is an emphatic circumstantial qualifier, and an emphatic circumstantial qualifier does not require that the clause in which it is an added benefit contain a governing element, as in your saying, "I am a servant of God, brave." Likewise if you said: "There is no man but a servant of God, brave." And this is more appropriate than its being in the accusative from the subject of "shahida." Likewise its being in the accusative by way of praise.

If you say: Has His standing by justice entered into the ruling of the testimony of God, the angels and those endowed with knowledge, just as the oneness did? I say: Yes, if you make it a circumstantial qualifier of "He," or an accusative of praise from Him, or a qualifier of the negated noun, as if it were said: "God, the angels and those endowed with knowledge bore witness that there is no god but He, and that He stands by justice."

'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read: ﴿the standing by justice﴾, making it a substitute for "He" or the predicate of an omitted subject. Abu Hanifa read: ﴿upright by justice﴾. ﴿The Almighty, the Wise﴾ are two qualifiers confirming what He described His essence with, of oneness and justice, meaning that He is the Almighty whom no other god can overpower, the Wise who does not deviate from justice in His acts.

If you say: What is meant by "those endowed with knowledge," whom He honored with this honor by joining them with Himself and the angels in testifying to His oneness and justice? I say: They are those who establish His oneness and justice by clear proofs and decisive arguments, and they are the scholars of justice [[His saying "and decisive arguments, and they are the scholars of justice" is an allusion to the Mu'tazila, who called themselves "the people of justice and monotheism" (ahl al-'adl wa-l-tawhid). But fairness requires generality, so that it includes Ahl al-Sunna wa-l-Jama'a (the people of the Sunna and the community). (ʿ)]] and of monotheism. It is read (with) "anna" (that) with a fatha and "inna al-din" (indeed the religion) with a kasra, so that the verb falls on "that He," meaning "God bore witness that He," or "that." His saying: ﴿Indeed the religion with God is Islam﴾ is a resumptive clause emphasizing the first clause.

If you say: What is the benefit of this emphasis? I say: Its benefit is that His saying "there is no god but He" is monotheism, and His saying "standing by justice" is equity. When it is followed by His saying "indeed the religion with God is Islam," it indicates that Islam is justice [[His saying "it indicates that Islam is justice" is a forced interpretation that the noble wording does not require, but partisanship prompted it. And his saying "and in it is that whoever holds to" etc. is a thrust against Ahl al-Sunna built upon that, and its verification is in the science of tawhid. In sum, justice and monotheism are not confined to the Mu'tazila's school. (ʿ)]] and monotheism, and it is the religion with God, and whatever else is not in any way part of the religion with Him. In it is that whoever goes to anthropomorphism, or to what leads to it, such as permitting the vision (of God), or goes to determinism (jabr), which is pure injustice, is not upon the religion of God, which is Islam. This is clear and manifest, as you see.

It is read with both (words) with a fatha, on the basis that the second is a substitute for the first, as if it were said: "God bore witness that the religion with God is Islam." The substitute is the substituted in meaning, so it is an explicit clarification, because the religion of God is monotheism and justice. The first is read with a kasra and the second with a fatha, on the basis that the verb falls on "inna," and what lies between them is a confirming parenthetical [[His saying "the verb falls on inna" means on "inna al-din..." etc. (ʿ)]]. This too is evidence that the religion of Islam is justice and monotheism, so all the readings are mutually supportive in this.

It is read: "shuhada' Allah" (witnesses for God), in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of those mentioned before it, and in the nominative as "they are the witnesses of God." If you say: On what is this reading coordinated: ﴿and the angels and those endowed with knowledge﴾? I say: On the pronoun in "shuhada'," and it is permissible because of the intervening separation.

If you say: Why did He repeat His saying: ﴿There is no god but He﴾? [[Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "If you say: What is the benefit of repeating 'there is no god but He' ... etc.?" That is because the speech opened with monotheism, then followed the monotheism with an enumeration of those who testify to it, then His saying "standing by justice," which is transcendence, so the speech lengthened with that, and so He renewed the monotheism after the transcendence in order to connect to His saying "indeed the religion with God is Islam." Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verse 20:

﴿Then if they argue with you﴾, that is, if they dispute with you concerning the religion, ﴿say: "I have submitted my face to God"﴾. That is, I have sincerely devoted my self and my whole being to God alone, not associating with Him any partner in it, by worshipping Him and calling upon Him, and not taking any god along with Him. This means that my religion is tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), which is the ancient religion whose soundness is established for you just as it is established for me, and I have brought nothing novel that you should dispute with me about it. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿Say: "O People of the Book, come to a word that is equitable between us and you: that we worship none but God, and that we associate nothing with Him"﴾. This is a rebuttal of the argument, since what he and those who follow him among the believers hold is the certainty of truth, in which there is no ambiguity; so what is the sense of disputing about it? ﴿And whoever follows me﴾ is a conjunction with the "ta'" in "aslamtu" and it is made good by the intervening element. It is also permissible for the waw to mean "with," in which case it is a direct object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ah). ﴿And say to those who were given the Book, and to the unlettered﴾, namely the Jews and Christians, and the unlettered, those who have no Book, from the polytheists of the Arabs: ﴿"Have you submitted?"﴾ That is, clear proofs have come to you which necessitate submission and require its occurrence without fail; so have you submitted, or are you still upon your disbelief? This is like your saying to someone to whom you have explained a matter, leaving no path of clarification and disclosure unexplored: "Have you understood it or not, may you have no mother?" And of the same kind is His saying, exalted and high: ﴿"So will you not desist?"﴾ after He mentioned the deterrents from wine and gambling. In this interrogation there is a belittling [[the saying "in this interrogation there is belittling" means: regarding the addressee as deficient. (Gh.)]] and a reproach for obstinacy and lack of fairness, because the fair-minded person, when the proof becomes clear to him, does not hesitate in submitting to the truth, whereas obstinacy after the proof has become manifest sets up barriers between him and submission [[the saying "sets up barriers" is perhaps "sudad," i.e., veils. (Gh.)]]. Likewise in "Have you understood it?" there is a rebuke for dullness and dimness of intellect. And in ﴿"So will you not desist?"﴾ there is a reproach for holding back from desisting and for the intense eagerness to engage in what has been forbidden. ﴿Then if they submit, they have indeed been guided﴾: they have benefited themselves, since they have come out of error into guidance and out of darkness into light. ﴿But if they turn away﴾, they will not harm you, for you are only a messenger, charged with conveying the message and directing to the path of guidance.

Al-Hasan recited: "yaqtulūna al-nabiyyīn" (they kill the prophets). Hamzah recited: "wa-yuqatilūna alladhīna yamurūna" (and they fight those who enjoin). ʿAbdullāh recited: "wa-qātalū" (and they fought). And Ubayy recited: "yaqtulūna al-nabiyyīn, wa-alladhīna yamurūna." They are the People of the Book. Their forebears killed the prophets, and their followers killed them, while being pleased with what they did. They were intent on killing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, were it not for Allah's protection.

And on the authority of Abu ʿUbaydah ibn al-Jarrah: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, which of people will have the most severe punishment on the Day of Resurrection?" He said: "A man who kills a prophet, or a man who enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong," then he recited it, then he said: "O Abu ʿUbaydah, the Children of Israel killed forty-three prophets at the beginning of the day in a single hour. Then a hundred and twelve men from the worshippers of the Children of Israel stood up and enjoined their killers to do what is right and forbade them from what is wrong, and they were all killed by the end of the day."[[Narrated by al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tha'labi and al-Baghawi from his narration. In its chain is Abu al-Hasan, a client of the Banu Asad, who is unknown (majhul).]]

"In this world and the Hereafter," because for them there is curse and disgrace in this world and punishment in the Hereafter.

If you ask: why did the fa' (fa, "so") enter the predicate of inna? I answer: because its subject contains the meaning of a conditional, as if it were said: "Those who disbelieve, so give them good tidings" in the sense of "whoever disbelieves, so give him good tidings." And inna does not change the meaning of the inception (ibtida', the nominal beginning of the sentence), so its entry is like its non-entry. Had laita ("would that") or laʿalla ("perhaps") been in its place, the entry of the fa' would have been impossible, because they change the meaning of the inception.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 23–25:

﴿Were given a portion of the Scripture﴾. He means the rabbis of the Jews, and that they obtained a large portion of the Torah.

The word "min" (from) is either partitive (*lil-tab'id*) or explanatory (*lil-bayan*). Or they obtained a portion of the kind of books that were sent down, or of the Tablet, the Torah, and that is a great portion. ﴿They are called to the Book of Allah﴾, which is the Torah, ﴿that it may judge between them﴾. This happened because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered their houses of study and invited them. Nu'aym ibn 'Amr and al-Harith ibn Zayd said to him: "What religion are you upon?"

He said: "Upon the religion of Ibrahim." They said: "Ibrahim was a Jew." He said to them: "Between us and you is the Torah, so come to it." But they refused. It is also said that it was revealed concerning stoning (for adultery), and they disputed about it. From al-Hasan and Qatadah: "The Book of Allah" is the Qur'an, because they knew that it was the Book of Allah and did not doubt it.

﴿Then a faction of them turns away﴾: this is an expression of astonishment at their turning away after their knowledge that returning to the Book of Allah is obligatory. ﴿While they are refusing﴾: they are a people for whom aversion is their constant custom.

It was read as (*liyuhkama*) in the passive form. The preferred view is that what is meant is the disagreement and hostility that occurred between those of their rabbis who embraced Islam and those who did not. They were called to the Book of Allah, whose authenticity they do not dispute, which is the Torah, so that it might judge between the one who is right and the one who is wrong among them. Then a faction of them turns away, namely those who did not embrace Islam. This is because His saying "that it may judge between them" requires that the disagreement be among themselves, not between them and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

That turning away and refusal was due to their making light for themselves of the matter of punishment, and their hope of leaving the Fire after a few days, just as the *Mujbira* (Determinists) and the *Hashwiyya* (literalist anthropomorphists) and others hoped regarding their religion, "what they used to invent."

Mahmud said: "That turning away and refusal was due to their hope of leaving the Fire after a few days, just as the Hashwiyya and the Mujbira hoped, and others, regarding their religion, what they used to invent."

Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is also an insinuation against the people of the Sunna (*Ahl al-Sunna*, the Sunni community) in their belief that the pardoning of the major sins of the believing monotheist is entrusted to the will of Allah the Exalted, even if he dies persisting in them, out of faith in His saying: "Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills" (4:48), and out of belief in intercession for the people of major sins. He holds this against them until he makes them a principle by which the Jews who said "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days" are compared to them. So look at how his heart is filled with hatred and hostility toward the people of the Sunna, and how he filled the earth with hypocrisy from these incitements. So praise belongs to Allah, who has enabled His servant, who is poor in needing to rely upon Him, to take vengeance for the Sunna from the people of innovation, and has pierced their hearts with decisive proofs and with the sharp points of spears.

"Just as the Mujbira and the Hashwiyya hoped" is an insinuation against the people of the Sunna, since they hold that believers among the people of major sins who enter the Fire will come out by intercession or by the pardon of Allah, as the hadiths affirm. (Ṭ)

﴿And their deception in their religion, what they used to invent﴾, namely that their forefathers are the prophets who will intercede for them, just as they were deluded by the intercession of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for their major sins. ﴿So how will it be when We gather them﴾, that is, how will they fare? This is an expression of the enormity of what has been prepared for them and of terror for them, and that they will fall into something for which they have no means of averting or escaping, and that what they told themselves and made easy for themselves was a pretext based on falsehood and a hope for what will not occur.

It is related that the first banner raised for the people of the place of standing (on the Day of Judgment) among the banners of the disbelievers will be the banner of the Jews, and Allah will expose them before the assembled witnesses. Then He will order them to the Fire. ﴿And they will not be wronged﴾: this refers back to every soul by meaning, because it has the sense of all people, just as you say "three souls," meaning "three persons."

He holds this against them until he makes them a principle by which the Jews who said "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days" are compared to them. So look at how his heart is filled with hatred and hostility toward the people of the Sunna, and how he filled the earth with hypocrisy from these incitements. So praise belongs to Allah, who has enabled His servant, who is poor in needing to rely upon Him, to take vengeance for the Sunna from the people of innovation, and has pierced their hearts with decisive proofs and with the sharp points of spears.

﴿And their deception in their religion, what they used to invent﴾, namely that their forefathers are the prophets who will intercede for them, just as they were deluded by the intercession of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for their major sins. ﴿So how will it be when We gather them﴾, that is, how will they fare? Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 23–25:

﴿Were given a portion of the Scripture﴾. He means the rabbis of the Jews, and that they obtained a large portion of the Torah.

The word "min" (from) is either partitive (*lil-tab'id*) or explanatory (*lil-bayan*). Or they obtained a portion of the kind of books that were sent down, or of the Tablet, the Torah, and that is a great portion. ﴿They are called to the Book of Allah﴾, which is the Torah, ﴿that it may judge between them﴾. This happened because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered their houses of study and invited them. Nu'aym ibn 'Amr and al-Harith ibn Zayd said to him: "What religion are you upon?"

He said: "Upon the religion of Ibrahim." They said: "Ibrahim was a Jew." He said to them: "Between us and you is the Torah, so come to it." But they refused. It is also said that it was revealed concerning stoning (for adultery), and they disputed about it. From al-Hasan and Qatadah: "The Book of Allah" is the Qur'an, because they knew that it was the Book of Allah and did not doubt it.

﴿Then a faction of them turns away﴾: this is an expression of astonishment at their turning away after their knowledge that returning to the Book of Allah is obligatory. ﴿While they are refusing﴾: they are a people for whom aversion is their constant custom.

It was read as (*liyuhkama*) in the passive form. They were called to the Book of Allah, whose authenticity they do not dispute, which is the Torah, so that it might judge between the one who is right and the one who is wrong among them. Then a faction of them turns away, namely those who did not embrace Islam. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verse 26–27:

The mim in Allahumma is a substitute for "ya" (the vocative particle), and for this reason the two cannot be combined. This is among the peculiarities of this name, just as it is singled out by the taa' (of oath) in swearing, by the entry of the vocative particle upon it, by its containing the definite article (lam al-ta'rif), by the elision of the hamza in "ya Allah", and by other things besides. ﴿Master of the kingdom﴾: that is, you possess the very essence of sovereignty, so that you dispose of it in the manner in which owners dispose of what they own. ﴿You give the kingdom to whom You will﴾: You bestow upon whom You will the portion of sovereignty that Your wisdom has apportioned and required for him. ﴿And You take the kingdom from whom You will﴾: You strip him of the portion of it that You had given him. Thus the first "kingdom" is general and all-encompassing, while the other two are specific, each being a part of the whole.

It is narrated that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, he promised his community the realms of Persia and Rome. The hypocrites and the Jews said: "Far-fetched, far-fetched! How could Muhammad get the realms of Persia and Rome? They are mightier and more inaccessible than that." [[Al-Wahidi mentioned it in his Asbab (on the authority of Ibn Abbas and Anas, may Allah be pleased with them), but I have not found a chain of narration for it.]]

It is also narrated that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dug the trench in the year of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), and marked out forty cubits for every ten men, they began digging. A huge rock like a great mound emerged from the belly of the trench, which the picks could not bite into. They sent Salman to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to inform him. He took the pick from Salman and struck the rock a blow that split it, and a flash of light came out of it that illuminated what lay between its two lava-fields, as if a lamp were in the middle of a dark house. He exclaimed "Allahu akbar," and the Muslims exclaimed "Allahu akbar" too. He said: "The palaces of al-Hirah have been shown to me, looking like the fangs of dogs." Then he struck a second time and said: "The red palaces of the land of Rome have been shown to me." Then he struck a third time and said: "The palaces of Sana'a have been shown to me, and Jibril (peace be upon him) has informed me that my community will prevail over all of them, so rejoice." The hypocrites said: "Do you not marvel? He promises you and gives you false hopes, and tells you that from Yathrib he sees the palaces of al-Hirah and the cities of Kisra, and that they will be opened to you, while you are digging the trench out of fear, unable to stir out!" So this was revealed.

If it is asked: why does He say ﴿In Your hand is the good﴾, mentioning the good without the evil? The answer: because the discourse concerns the good that He brings to the believers, which the disbelievers denied. So He says "In Your hand is the good," granting it to His allies in spite of His enemies. Furthermore, all of Allah's acts, whether beneficial or harmful, proceed from wisdom and public welfare, so they are all good, such as the giving and the taking away of sovereignty. Then He mentioned His overwhelming power by citing the alternation of night and day, and the condition of the living and the dead in bringing one out of the other, and He joined to this His provision "without reckoning," to show that whoever is able to do those great acts that bewilder minds is able to provide without reckoning to whomever He wills of His servants. Thus He is able to strip the non-Arabs of sovereignty and humble them, and to give it to the Arabs and make them mighty.

In some books it is said: "I am Allah, the King of kings; the hearts of kings and their foreheads are in My hand. If the servants obey Me, I make them a mercy for them; and if the servants disobey Me, I make them a punishment upon them. So do not occupy yourselves with reviling the kings, but turn in repentance to Me, and I will incline them toward you." This is the meaning of his (ﷺ) saying: "As you are, so will your rulers be."
[[Narrated by al-Qada'i in Musnad al-Shihab, through al-Mubarak ibn Fadalah from al-Hasan from Abu Bakrah; in its chain to al-Mubarak there are unknown narrators.]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verse 28:

They were forbidden to take the disbelievers as allies (tawalli) because of kinship between them, or friendship before Islam, or other such causes by which people become friends and keep company. This is repeated in the Qur'an: ﴿And whoever of you takes them as allies, then he is indeed one of them﴾, ﴿Do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾, ﴿You will not find a people who believe in God...﴾ and so on. Love for God's sake and hatred for God's sake is a great principle and one of the foundations of faith.

﴿rather than the believers﴾ means: you have an alternative to allying with the disbelievers in allying with the believers, so do not prefer them over the believers. ﴿And whoever does that has nothing to do with God﴾, that is, whoever allies with the disbelievers has no share at all in God's guardianship. It falls under the name of allegiance (wilaya), meaning he has completely withdrawn from God's guardianship. This is a rational matter, for allying with a friend and allying with his enemy are mutually exclusive. The poet said:

"You love my enemy, then you claim that you are my friend,
and folly is not far from you.
So the one who is my brother is not the one who loves me in front of my eyes,
but the one who loves me when I am absent."

Nawk means folly, and 'azib means distant. He says: the true friend is not one who is friendly with the enemy of his friend, and one who keeps brotherhood in the unseen, not in plain sight. It is permissible for "tawaddu" to be read as a rebuking interrogative, presented in the form of a statement for the sake of censure. "Ra'y 'aynihi" is in the accusative as an adverbial of time, meaning "when he saw him with his own eyes." Al-maghayib means the times of absence.

﴿except when you fear a danger from them﴾, that is, except when you fear from them a matter that must be guarded against. It is also read as ﴿taqiyya﴾. The one who guards himself is called "taqat" and "taqiyya," like the saying "the ruler struck his one who is struck." He was granted a concession in allying with them when they fear them. The intended allegiance here is outward dealing and companionship while the heart is at peace in enmity and hatred, awaiting the removal of the obstacle, like stripping the bark from a stick. This is like the saying of Jesus, peace be upon him: "Be moderate and walk on the side."

﴿And God warns you about Himself﴾, so do not expose yourselves to His wrath by allying with His enemies. This is a severe warning. It is also permissible that ﴿tattaqu﴾ be taken to include the meaning of "tahadhdhara" and "takhafu," so it takes "min," and ﴿taqatan﴾ or ﴿taqiyya﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Fear God as He should be feared﴾.

If you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, concerning allegiance to the disbelievers or anything else that Allah does not approve, Allah knows it and it is not hidden from Him. He is the One who knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth; nothing of it is ever hidden from Him, so your secret and your open conduct are not hidden from Him. "And Allah is over all things Competent," so He is able to punish you. This is an explanation of His words, "And Allah warns you of Himself." For His Self, which is His essence distinguished from all other essences, is characterized by an essential knowledge that is not restricted to one object of knowledge over another, so it relates to all objects of knowledge. It is also characterized by an essential power that is not restricted to one object of power over another, so it is able over all objects of power. Therefore it is fitting that you should beware and guard yourselves, so that no one dares to commit an ugly act or falls short of a duty, since that is certainly observed by Him, and so punishment is due to the one who does so. If one of the servants of a sultan (ruler) knew that the sultan wanted to observe his circumstances, and he entrusted his concern to watching what he brings in and sends out, and set spies over him, and dispatched those who search into his inner affairs, he would take his precaution and be vigilant in his matter, and guard against everything that might cause him to be suspected. So what of the one who knows that the Knower of the self, who knows the secret and what is more hidden, is watchful over him, and yet he is secure? [[The statement "so what of the one who knows that the Knower of the self" is the attribution of the descriptive to its subject, like "beautiful of face"; meaning, His knowledge is of His essence, and He knows nothing beyond His essence, such as the knowledge of contingent events. This is the view of the Mu'tazilah. (Ṣ)]] O Allah, we seek refuge in You from being deceived by Your concealment.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verse 30:

"The Day" (yawma) is in the accusative, governed by "wishes" (tawaddu). The pronoun in "between it" (baynahu) refers to the Day, i.e., the Day of Resurrection, when every soul finds its good and its evil present before it, wishing that there were between it and that Day a great distance (amadan baidan). It is permissible for "the Day" (yawma tajidu) to be in the accusative by an implied verb such as "remember" (udhkur), and for the finding (tajidu) to fall only upon "what it has done" (ma 'amilat). [[His saying "and the finding falls only upon what it has done" means: the verb of finding falls upon what it did of good alone. (Ga')]] "And what it has done" (wa ma 'amilat) is in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), with "wishes" (tawaddu) as its predicate, meaning: "and what it has done of evil, it wishes that between it and that there were a great distance."

It is not correct for "what" (ma) to be conditional, because of the nominative of "wishes" (tawaddu). If you say: Is it correct for it to be conditional according to the reading of Abdullah, "wadda-t" (she wished)? I say: there is no dispute about its soundness, but treating it as subject and predicate is more apt in meaning, since it narrates what occurs on that Day, and more firm because it agrees with the reading of the majority (al-'amma). It is also permissible for "and what it has done" (wa ma 'amilat) to be coordinated with "what it has done" (ma 'amilat), and for "wishes" (tawaddu) to be a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: the Day you find its deed present, wishing to be distant between it and the Day, or the evil deed present, as in His saying: "and they will find what they did present" (wa wajadu ma 'amilu hadiran) — meaning written in their scrolls which they read — and similar to His saying: "then He will inform them of what they did; Allah has counted it, and they have forgotten it" (fa-yunabbi'uhum bi-ma 'amilu ahsahu Allahu wa nasuhu). The "distance" (amad) is the span, as in His saying: "Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts" (ya layta bayni wa baynaka bu'da al-mashriqayn). He repeated His saying "and Allah warns you of Himself" so that it would be in their minds, and they would not be heedless of it. "And Allah is Kind to the servants" — meaning: His warning them of Himself and His making known the state of His knowledge and power is among the great compassion toward the servants, for when they know Him as He should be known and beware of Him, that calls them to seek His pleasure and avoid His wrath. It is reported from al-Hasan that among His compassion for them was that He warned them of Himself. It is also permissible that He intends that, although He is to be feared for His knowledge and power, He is to be hoped for because of the vastness of His mercy, as in His saying: "Indeed, your Lord is Forgiving to the people, and also severe in punishment" (inna rabbaka la-dhu maghfiratin wa dhu 'iqabin alim).

Love of the servants for Allah is a metaphor for their wanting to single Him out for worship to the exclusion of others, and their desire for it. Allah's love for His servants means that He is pleased with them and approves of their actions. The meaning is: if you truly intend to worship Allah, then follow me, so that what you claim of wanting to worship Him is confirmed; He will be pleased with you and forgive you.

It is related from al-Hasan: "Some people, in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), claimed that they loved Allah, so He wanted to make their words confirmed by action. Whoever claims to love Him yet opposes the Sunnah of His Messenger is a liar, and the Book of Allah refutes him."

And if you see someone who mentions the love of Allah while clapping his hands during the mention, becoming ecstatic, [[His words "wa-yun'ar wa-yas'aq" (and he makes a nasal cry and falls in a swoon). In al-Sihah: "al-nu'rah" is a sound in the nasal cavity. It is said: "There was no strife except that so-and-so made a nasal cry in it," meaning he rose up. (Editor)]] then do not doubt that he does not know what Allah is, nor does he understand what the love of Allah is. His clapping, ecstasy, nasal crying and swooning are nothing but that he has imagined in his corrupt soul a pleasing, adored image, named it "Allah" out of his ignorance and debauchery, and then clapped, became ecstatic, cried out and swooned over that imagined image. Often you will see that semen has soiled the waistwrap of that lover at the moment of his swoon, while the foolish common folk around him have filled their sleeves with tears out of pity for his condition.

It is read: "tuhibbūna," "yuhibbukum," and "yuhibbukum," from "habbahu yuhibbuhu." The poet said:

I love Abu Tharwan out of love for his dates,
And I know that kindness to the neighbor is kindest.

By Allah, were it not for his dates, I would not have loved him,
And [his sons] Ubayd and Mushriq would not have been nearer to me.

[[These verses are by Ghaylan ibn Shuja' al-Nahshali. He says: I love this man out of love for his dates. It is also narrated as "Abu Marwan." "And I know that kindness to the neighbor is kindest" means it is more kind than to others, i.e., more gentle; he attributed the kindness to himself as hyperbole, like "jadd jaddihi" (his grandfather's grandfather). It is also possible the meaning is that kindness to the neighbor is more fitting or more complete than to others. If it were read "awfaq" with a waw, it would be clear. In it is an appeal to Abu Marwan and a request for kindness from him through the poet. The predominant dialect uses "ahabba" (quadriliteral). "Habbahu yuhibbuhu" with the vowel of the imperfect's first radical being kissed is rare in its coming as a triliteral and in the vowelling of its imperfect. The regular imperfect of a doubled transitive triliteral takes a damma on its first radical, like "yashuddu" and "yaruddu." "Habba yahubbu" also occurs from the pattern "'alima ya'lamu." "Wa-la kana adna" means nearer to me; "Ubayd and Mushriq" are his two sons. There is iqwa' (a defect of rhyme vowel) in the rhyme. Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad narrated in place of the last hemistich: "and 'Iyad was nearer to me from him, and Mushriq," meaning nearer to me than Abu Marwan. In that case there is no iqwa' in it.]]

As for "fa-in tawallaw" (but if they turn away), it may be past tense, or it may be present tense with the meaning "fa-in tatawallaw" (if you turn away), and it enters into what the Messenger says to them.
