"Habbahu yuhibbuhu" with the vowel of the imperfect's first radical being kissed is rare in its coming as a triliteral and in the vowelling of its imperfect. The regular imperfect of a doubled transitive triliteral takes a damma on its first radical, like "yashuddu" and "yaruddu." "Habba yahubbu" also occurs from the pattern "'alima ya'lamu." "Wa-la kana adna" means nearer to me; "Ubayd and Mushriq" are his two sons. There is iqwa' (a defect of rhyme vowel) in the rhyme. Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad narrated in place of the last hemistich: "and 'Iyad was nearer to me from him, and Mushriq," meaning nearer to me than Abu Marwan. In that case there is no iqwa' in it.]]

As for "fa-in tawallaw" (but if they turn away), it may be past tense, or it may be present tense with the meaning "fa-in tatawallaw" (if you turn away), and it enters into what the Messenger says to them.

Ali Ibrahim: Isma'il, Ishaq and their descendants. And the family of Imran: Musa and Harun [[Al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The family of Imran: Musa and Harun..." etc. Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir), may Allah have mercy on him, said: What supports this second view is that the surah is named "The Family of Imran," and it does not narrate the story of Isa and Maryam in a surah more detailed than its narration in this surah. As for Musa and Harun, their story is not mentioned in this surah. This indicates that the Imran mentioned here is the father of Maryam, and Allah knows best.]] the two sons of Imran, son of Yashhar. It is also said: Isa and Maryam daughter of Imran, son of Mathan. Between the two Imrans there are one thousand eight hundred years.

﴿Dhurriyyatan﴾ (offspring) is a substitute for "the family of Ibrahim" and "the family of Imran." ﴿Ba'duha min ba'd﴾ (some of them from others) means that the two families are one continuous lineage, some branching from others: Musa and Harun from Imran, Imran from Yashhar, Yashhar from Fahith, Fahith from Lawi, Lawi from Ya'qub, and Ya'qub from Ishaq. Likewise Isa son of Maryam daughter of Imran son of Mathan son of Sulayman son of Dawud [[His saying "son of Mathan, son of Sulayman, son of Dawud": "son of Sulayman" means from his lineage. And his saying "son of Yahudha" means from his lineage, as al-Fakhr al-Razi explicitly stated. Abu al-Su'ud mentioned that between Mathan and Sulayman there are about fifteen forefathers, and between Ishya and Yahudha nine forefathers. (A)]] son of Ishya son of Yahudha son of Ya'qub son of Ishaq. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered the family of Ibrahim. It is also said that ﹙some of them from others﹚ refers to religion, like His saying ﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another﴾. ﴿And Allah is Hearing, Knowing﴾: He knows who is fit for chosen status, or He knows that some of them are from others in religion, or He is Hearing and Knowing of the statement of the wife of Imran and her intention. ﴿When﴾ is governed by it (the verb "Hearing and Knowing").

It is also said: it is governed by an implied "remember." The wife of Imran is the wife of Imran son of Mathan, the mother of Maryam the virgin, grandmother of Isa, peace be upon him, and her name was Hanna daughter of Faqudh. Her saying ﴿When the wife of Imran said﴾ following "the family of Imran" supports that Imran is Imran son of Mathan, grandfather of Isa. The other view is supported by the fact that Musa is frequently mentioned alongside Ibrahim. If you say: Imran son of Yashhar had a daughter named Maryam, older than Musa and Harun, and Imran son of Mathan had Maryam the virgin; how do you know that this Imran is the father of Maryam the virgin rather than the father of Maryam who was the sister of Musa and Harun? I say: the guardianship of Zakariyya is sufficient proof that he is the father of the virgin, because Zakariyya son of Adhan and Imran son of Mathan lived in the same era, and Zakariyya had married his daughter Ishya, sister of Maryam, so Yahya and Isa were cousins. It is narrated that she (Hanna) was barren and did not bear children until she became old. While she was in the shade of a tree, she saw a bird feeding its chick, and her soul was moved toward having a child and she wished for one. She said: "O Allah, I vow to You a vow of gratitude if You grant me a child: that I will dedicate him to the Temple of Jerusalem so that he will be among its custodians and servants." She then conceived Maryam, and Imran died while she was pregnant. ﴿Muharraran﴾ (dedicated, freed) means freed for the service of the Temple of Jerusalem, with no claim of mine upon him, I will not employ him, nor occupy him with anything; and this kind of vow was lawful among them. It is narrated that they used to make this vow, and when the boy reached maturity he was given the choice between doing it or not. It is also reported from al-Sha'bi that ﴿muharraran﴾ means sincerely devoted to worship, and that liberation was only for boys; she either considered it hypothetically, or she asked to be granted a male child.

﴿So when she gave birth to her﴾: the pronoun refers to "what is in my womb" [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "The pronoun refers back to what is in my womb..." etc. Ahmad said: The pronoun in her saying "she gave birth to her" encompasses the attribution of giving birth and femaleness to her, so the state falls upon her from the general aspect, and that aspect is that she is a thing that was born, not specifically the attribution of femaleness to her. This very discussion was previously raised at His saying: ﴿If they are not two men﴾.]]. It was feminine according to meaning because what was in her womb was female in Allah's knowledge; or according to the interpretation of "pregnancy," "soul," or "offspring." If you say: How is it permissible for ﴿unthā﴾ (female) to be an accusative state from the pronoun in ﴿waḍa'tuhā﴾, when it is like your saying "I gave birth to the female, female"? I say: The original is "I gave birth to him, female," and it was feminized because the state is feminine, since the state and its possessor are one thing, just as the noun was feminized in "what was your mother," for the predicate's feminization. A parallel is His saying ﴿If they are two women﴾. As for the interpretation of "pregnancy" or "offspring," it is clear, as if it were said: "I gave birth to the pregnancy or the offspring as a female." If you say: Why did she say "I gave birth to her as a female," and what did she intend by this statement? I say: she said it in regret [[(Resumption of his speech) He said: "Her saying 'I gave birth to her as a female' was intended as regret and sorrow..." etc. Ahmad said: This interpretation is that it is from the speech of Allah, Exalted, not a quotation from her. The people of tafsir mentioned another interpretation: that this statement is her own speech, which Allah related from her, namely His saying ﴿And the male is not like the female﴾, and her speech is connected to it by His saying ﴿And I have named her Maryam...﴾. They object to this view that if it is her statement, the expected form would be "the female is not like the male," since her intention is to belittle the female in comparison to the male, and the custom in such cases is to negate from the deficient the resemblance to the complete, not the reverse. The matter appears varied in this, and what they said has not been established for me. Do you not see His saying ﴿You are not like any of the women﴾? He negated from the complete the resemblance to the deficient, even though perfection belongs to the wives of the Prophet, peace be upon him, relative to women in general. And on this basis the expression of the wife of Imran came, and Allah knows best. From this also: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create?﴾]] on account of the failure of her hope and the reversal of her expectation. She had hoped and expected to bear a male, and that is why she vowed him dedicated for service. Because she said this with regret and sorrow, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah knows best what she gave birth to﴾, glorifying what she bore and making her ignorant of how much had been granted to her. Its meaning: Allah knows best the thing she bore and what great matters are connected to it, and that He will make him and his son a sign for the worlds, while she was unaware of that and knew nothing of it, therefore she grieved. In the reading of Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿And Allah knows best what you (feminine) have borne﴾, addressed by Allah to her, meaning: you do not know the worth of this granted one, nor how great its affair and lofty its status are in Allah's knowledge. It was also read: "she gave birth" (waḍa'at), meaning: perhaps Allah has a secret and wisdom in it, and perhaps this female is better than a male, as consolation for herself.

If you say: What is the meaning of His saying ﴿And the male is not like the female﴾? I say: It explains what is in His saying ﴿And Allah knows best what she gave birth to﴾ of glorifying the thing born and elevating it. Its meaning: the male you sought is not like the female that was granted to you. The lam in both is for specificity (ʿahd). If you say: On what is His saying ﴿And I have named her Maryam﴾ conjoined? I say: it is conjoined to "I gave birth to her as a female," and what lies between them consists of two intervening clauses, like His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a great oath, if you only knew﴾. If you say: Why did she mention naming her Maryam to her Lord? I say: because Maryam in their language means "the worshipper" [[(Resumption of his speech) He said: "The benefit of her saying ﴿And I have named her Maryam﴾ is that Maryam in their language means the worshipper..." etc. Ahmad said:

As for the hadith, it is mentioned in the authentic collections, agreed upon as sound. There is no escape from it except by nullifying his words, peace be upon him, by loading upon them what they cannot bear, inclining toward a Mu'tazili rationalism derived from a philosophy derived from atheism, with darknesses upon darknesses. I had earlier, at His saying ﴿They do not rise except as one rises whom Satan has struck with madness through touch﴾, presented what is sufficient. I do not see Satan as anything but having pierced the flanks of the Qadariyya until he split them, and nested in their hearts until al-Zamakhshari and his like were led to say in the Book of Allah and the words of His Messenger, peace be upon him, what is merely imagined, as he said in this hadith, then compared it to the imagery of Ibn al-Rumi in his poetry, out of audacity and bad manners. Had the meaning of what he said been correct, this expression would have been obligatory to avoid. And even if the crying were not actually produced by the newborn, it could be possible, from a distance, to be a figurative image. But what is actually witnessed, there is no basis for interpreting it as mere imagery except a meager belief and the pursuit of a grievous desire.]] . So she intended by that to draw near and to petition Him to protect her, so that her action would conform to her name, and that He would fulfill her expectation of her. Do you not see how she followed it with a request for protection for her and her offspring from Satan and his seduction? As for what is narrated in the hadith: "No child is born except that Satan touches him at his birth, so he cries out from the touch of Satan, except Maryam and her son" [[The author said: Allah knows its authenticity; thus he said. The hadith is in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, at its end: Abu Hurayra said: Recite if you wish: ﴿And indeed I seek refuge for her in You, and for her offspring, from the accursed Satan﴾.]]. Allah knows its authenticity. If it is authentic, its meaning is that every newborn is one whom Satan hopes to seduce, except Maryam and her son, for they were protected; and likewise everyone who shares their attribute, as in His saying ﴿I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants﴾. His crying out upon being touched by him is an imagery and depiction of Satan's hope regarding him, as if he touches him, strikes his hand upon him, and says: "This is one I will seduce." Similar to this imagery is the saying of Ibn al-Rumi:

Because of the calamities the world announces,
the crying of the infant at the moment of birth occurs.
Otherwise, what would make him weep from it, when indeed
he is more spacious than he was in it, and more comfortable?
When he sees the world, he cries out, as if
threatening what he will suffer from its harm.

[Ibn al-Rumi says: The crying of the child at birth is only due to what the world signals of its vicissitudes; otherwise, what would make him weep from it, or what would make him weep from it, since the world is... One narration reads: "since he" (i.e., the child) is more spacious in position than the constriction of the womb and more comfortable. Its return to what makes him weep is distant or unsound. It is permissible that it returns to the spaciousness of the world known from context, then he says: when he sees it he cries out, as if threatening with what he will suffer from its harm before it occurs.]

As for the true nature of touching and pricking as the ignorant literalists imagine, no; had Iblis been empowered over people to prick them, the world would be filled with crying and wailing from the affliction of his pricking. ﴿So her Lord accepted her﴾: He was pleased with her as a substitute for the male in the vow, ﴿with a good acceptance﴾. It has two possibilities. First, that "acceptance" (qabūl) is the name of what something is accepted with, like "snuff" and "purgative," for what is snuffed or purged. That is her singling out for standing in place of the male in the vow, and no female was accepted before her in that; or that her mother would hand her over immediately after birth, before she grew up and became fit for service. It is narrated that Hanna, when she gave birth to Maryam, wrapped her in a cloth and carried her to the mosque, and placed her before the rabbis, sons of Harun, who in Jerusalem were like the keepers of the Ka'ba. She said to them: "Take this vowed offering," and they competed for her, because she was the daughter of their leader and the custodian of their offerings. The sons of Mathan were chiefs of the Children of Israel, their rabbis and their kings. Zakariyya said to them: "I have more right to her; her aunt is with me." They said: "No, until we draw lots for her." So they went—and they were twenty-seven—to a river and cast their pens into it. Zakariyya's pen rose above the water, while theirs sank, so he took charge of her. [[Al-Zamakhshari's words "her aunt is with me": he means his wife Ishya, sister of Hanna. But it was previously mentioned that she (Ishya) was the sister of Maryam, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, said about Yahya and Isa that they were cousins (sons of the maternal aunt). Abu al-Su'ud said that it is said in explaining this that "sister" is often applied to the niece, so the hadith follows that usage. It is also said that Ishya was the half-sister of Hanna through the mother, and the full sister of Maryam through the father, in that Imran married Hanna's mother and she bore Ishya, then he married Hanna, his stepdaughter, and she bore Maryam, based on the permissibility of marrying stepdaughters according to them. (A)]]

The second possibility: it is a verbal noun with an omitted modifier, meaning: "accepted her with an acceptance that is good," i.e., with a matter of good acceptance, which is the singling out. It is also permissible that the meaning of "accepted her" is "received her," as in your saying: "he hastened it" means "he asked for its haste," and "he pursued it" means "he sought it out," which is common in their speech, from "receiving the matter" when one takes it at its beginning and freshness. Al-Qatami said:

"The best of matters is what you receive from it,
and it is not that you follow it in pursuit."

[He says: the best of matters is the one you receive and await, taking it at the first coming; and not one whose outcome you endure until it escapes you and passes, then you follow and pursue it to catch it. The "bi" in the predicate of "laysa" is extra, and the predicate is governed by an omitted modifier: "one of pursuit." "Tatabbu'" originally is "tatatabbu'," with one of the taʾs dropped, either the present-tense taʾ, or the taʾ of the reflexive form, or the taʾ that is the root of the verb, the first of them; since each of the first two came with its own meaning. Al-Jawhari said: "The ittiba' is placed in the position of tatabbu'." So it is a verbal noun, or a verbal noun from which some augments were dropped, and the tafa''ul form is more emphatic than the ifti'al form, so its intended sense is decisively meant here, because it is emphatic.]

From this is the proverb: "Take the matter by its foreparts," meaning: she received her at the beginning of her matter, when she was born, with good acceptance. ﴿And He caused her to grow a good growth﴾: a metaphor for good upbringing returning to her with what puts her right in all her circumstances. It was read: "wa-kaffalahā Zakariyyā," in the measure of "wa-ʿamalahā," [[His saying "and the verb is attributed to Allah, Exalted": perhaps "and the verb." (A)]] and "wa-kaffala-hā Zakariyyā" with the stress on the fa' and the accusative on Zakariyya, the verb being attributed to Allah, meaning: He gathered her to Himself and made Zakariyya her guardian and guarantor of her welfare. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "wa-akfilhā," from His saying ﴿Say, "Make him my guardian"﴾. Mujahid read: "fa-taqabbalahā rabbuhā, wa-anbatahā, wa-kaffalahā," in the imperative form for the three verbs, with "rabbuhā" in the accusative as a supplication: "accept her, O her Lord, and make Zakariyya her guardian." It is said Zakariyya built for her a niche (miḥrāb) in the mosque, that is, a chamber to which one ascends by a ladder. It is also said the miḥrāb is the most noble and foremost place of assembly, as if she were placed in the most noble spot of Jerusalem. It is said their mosques were called maḥārīb. It is narrated that no one entered upon her except him alone, and when he left, she was locked in with seven doors. ﴿Every time Zakariyya entered upon her in the niche, he found with her provision﴾: the provision that descended to her from Paradise. She had never nursed from a breast, so he would find with her winter fruit in summer and summer fruit in winter. ﴿He said: "O Maryam, from where is this for you?"﴾: from where do you have this provision, which is unlike the provisions of this world, and which comes out of its season while the doors are locked upon you, with no way for anyone to bring it to you? ﴿She said: "It is from Allah"﴾, so do not find it strange. It is said she spoke while still young, as Isa spoke while in the cradle. It is narrated from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he went hungry in a time of famine, and Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her, gave him two loaves and a piece of meat, which he gave to someone else; then he returned with them to her and said: "Bring them here, my daughter." She uncovered the tray, and behold, it was full of bread and meat. She was amazed and knew it had descended from Allah. He said to her: "From where is this for you?" She said: "It is from Allah; indeed Allah provides whom He wills without reckoning." The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Praise be to Allah who made you resemble the mistress of the women of the Children of Israel." Then the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, gathered 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan, al-Husayn, and all his household, and they ate from it until they were satisfied, and the food remained as it was; so Fatima gave generously to her neighbours. ﴿Indeed Allah provides whom He wills without reckoning﴾: either part of Maryam's speech, or the speech of the Lord of Majesty, the Mighty, the Exalted: "without measure," meaning without measuring out its abundance, or by grace without accounting and recompense according to the deserving of an action.

Ali Ibrahim: Isma'il, Ishaq and their descendants. And the family of Imran: Musa and Harun [[Al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The family of Imran: Musa and Harun..." etc. Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir), may Allah have mercy on him, said: What supports this second view is that the surah is named "The Family of Imran," and it does not narrate the story of Isa and Maryam in a surah more detailed than its narration in this surah. She had hoped and expected to bear a male, and that is why she vowed him dedicated for service. Because she said this with regret and sorrow, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah knows best what she gave birth to﴾, glorifying what she bore and making her ignorant of how much had been granted to her. In the reading of Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿And Allah knows best what you (feminine) have borne﴾, addressed by Allah to her, meaning: you do not know the worth of this granted one, nor how great its affair and lofty its status are in Allah's knowledge. I say: It explains what is in His saying ﴿And Allah knows best what she gave birth to﴾ of glorifying the thing born and elevating it. If you say: Why did she mention naming her Maryam to her Lord? I say: because Maryam in their language means "the worshipper" [[(Resumption of his speech) He said: "The benefit of her saying ﴿And I have named her Maryam﴾ is that Maryam in their language means the worshipper..." etc. Ahmad said:

As for the hadith, it is mentioned in the authentic collections, agreed upon as sound. There is no escape from it except by nullifying his words, peace be upon him, by loading upon them what they cannot bear, inclining toward a Mu'tazili rationalism derived from a philosophy derived from atheism, with darknesses upon darknesses. I had earlier, at His saying ﴿They do not rise except as one rises whom Satan has struck with madness through touch﴾, presented what is sufficient. I do not see Satan as anything but having pierced the flanks of the Qadariyya until he split them, and nested in their hearts until al-Zamakhshari and his like were led to say in the Book of Allah and the words of His Messenger, peace be upon him, what is merely imagined, as he said in this hadith, then compared it to the imagery of Ibn al-Rumi in his poetry, out of audacity and bad manners. Had the meaning of what he said been correct, this expression would have been obligatory to avoid. And even if the crying were not actually produced by the newborn, it could be possible, from a distance, to be a figurative image. But what is actually witnessed, there is no basis for interpreting it as mere imagery except a meager belief and the pursuit of a grievous desire.]] . So she intended by that to draw near and to petition Him to protect her, so that her action would conform to her name, and that He would fulfill her expectation of her. Do you not see how she followed it with a request for protection for her and her offspring from Satan and his seduction? As for what is narrated in the hadith: "No child is born except that Satan touches him at his birth, so he cries out from the touch of Satan, except Maryam and her son" [[The author said: Allah knows its authenticity; thus he said. The hadith is in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, at its end: Abu Hurayra said: Recite if you wish: ﴿And indeed I seek refuge for her in You, and for her offspring, from the accursed Satan﴾.]]. Allah knows its authenticity. If it is authentic, its meaning is that every newborn is one whom Satan hopes to seduce, except Maryam and her son, for they were protected; and likewise everyone who shares their attribute, as in His saying ﴿I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants﴾. His crying out upon being touched by him is an imagery and depiction of Satan's hope regarding him, as if he touches him, strikes his hand upon him, and says: "This is one I will seduce." Similar to this imagery is the saying of Ibn al-Rumi:

Because of the calamities the world announces,
the crying of the infant at the moment of birth occurs.
Otherwise, what would make him weep from it, when indeed
he is more spacious than he was in it, and more comfortable?
When he sees the world, he cries out, as if
threatening what he will suffer from its harm.

[Ibn al-Rumi says: The crying of the child at birth is only due to what the world signals of its vicissitudes; otherwise, what would make him weep from it, or what would make him weep from it, since the world is... One narration reads: "since he" (i.e., the child) is more spacious in position than the constriction of the womb and more comfortable. Its return to what makes him weep is distant or unsound. It is permissible that it returns to the spaciousness of the world known from context, then he says: when he sees it he cries out, as if threatening with what he will suffer from its harm before it occurs.]

As for the true nature of touching and pricking as the ignorant literalists imagine, no; had Iblis been empowered over people to prick them, the world would be filled with crying and wailing from the affliction of his pricking. ﴿So her Lord accepted her﴾: He was pleased with her as a substitute for the male in the vow, ﴿with a good acceptance﴾. It has two possibilities. First, that "acceptance" (qabūl) is the name of what something is accepted with, like "snuff" and "purgative," for what is snuffed or purged. That is her singling out for standing in place of the male in the vow, and no female was accepted before her in that; or that her mother would hand her over immediately after birth, before she grew up and became fit for service. It is narrated that Hanna, when she gave birth to Maryam, wrapped her in a cloth and carried her to the mosque, and placed her before the rabbis, sons of Harun, who in Jerusalem were like the keepers of the Ka'ba. She said to them: "Take this vowed offering," and they competed for her, because she was the daughter of their leader and the custodian of their offerings. The sons of Mathan were chiefs of the Children of Israel, their rabbis and their kings. Zakariyya said to them: "I have more right to her; her aunt is with me." They said: "No, until we draw lots for her." So they went—and they were twenty-seven—to a river and cast their pens into it. Zakariyya's pen rose above the water, while theirs sank, so he took charge of her. [[Al-Zamakhshari's words "her aunt is with me": he means his wife Ishya, sister of Hanna. But it was previously mentioned that she (Ishya) was the sister of Maryam, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, said about Yahya and Isa that they were cousins (sons of the maternal aunt). Abu al-Su'ud said that it is said in explaining this that "sister" is often applied to the niece, so the hadith follows that usage. It is also said that Ishya was the half-sister of Hanna through the mother, and the full sister of Maryam through the father, in that Imran married Hanna's mother and she bore Ishya, then he married Hanna, his stepdaughter, and she bore Maryam, based on the permissibility of marrying stepdaughters according to them. (A)]]

The second possibility: it is a verbal noun with an omitted modifier, meaning: "accepted her with an acceptance that is good," i.e., with a matter of good acceptance, which is the singling out. It is also permissible that the meaning of "accepted her" is "received her," as in your saying: "he hastened it" means "he asked for its haste," and "he pursued it" means "he sought it out," which is common in their speech, from "receiving the matter" when one takes it at its beginning and freshness. Al-Qatami said:

"The best of matters is what you receive from it,
and it is not that you follow it in pursuit."

[He says: the best of matters is the one you receive and await, taking it at the first coming; and not one whose outcome you endure until it escapes you and passes, then you follow and pursue it to catch it. The "bi" in the predicate of "laysa" is extra, and the predicate is governed by an omitted modifier: "one of pursuit." "Tatabbu'" originally is "tatatabbu'," with one of the taʾs dropped, either the present-tense taʾ, or the taʾ of the reflexive form, or the taʾ that is the root of the verb, the first of them; since each of the first two came with its own meaning. Al-Jawhari said: "The ittiba' is placed in the position of tatabbu'." So it is a verbal noun, or a verbal noun from which some augments were dropped, and the tafa''ul form is more emphatic than the ifti'al form, so its intended sense is decisively meant here, because it is emphatic.]

From this is the proverb: "Take the matter by its foreparts," meaning: she received her at the beginning of her matter, when she was born, with good acceptance. ﴿And He caused her to grow a good growth﴾: a metaphor for good upbringing returning to her with what puts her right in all her circumstances. It was read: "wa-kaffalahā Zakariyyā," in the measure of "wa-ʿamalahā," [[His saying "and the verb is attributed to Allah, Exalted": perhaps "and the verb." (A)]] and "wa-kaffala-hā Zakariyyā" with the stress on the fa' and the accusative on Zakariyya, the verb being attributed to Allah, meaning: He gathered her to Himself and made Zakariyya her guardian and guarantor of her welfare. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "wa-akfilhā," from His saying ﴿Say, "Make him my guardian"﴾. Mujahid read: "fa-taqabbalahā rabbuhā, wa-anbatahā, wa-kaffalahā," in the imperative form for the three verbs, with "rabbuhā" in the accusative as a supplication: "accept her, O her Lord, and make Zakariyya her guardian." It is said Zakariyya built for her a niche (miḥrāb) in the mosque, that is, a chamber to which one ascends by a ladder. It is also said the miḥrāb is the most noble and foremost place of assembly, as if she were placed in the most noble spot of Jerusalem. It is said their mosques were called maḥārīb. It is narrated that no one entered upon her except him alone, and when he left, she was locked in with seven doors. ﴿Every time Zakariyya entered upon her in the niche, he found with her provision﴾: the provision that descended to her from Paradise. She had never nursed from a breast, so he would find with her winter fruit in summer and summer fruit in winter. ﴿He said: "O Maryam, from where is this for you?"﴾: from where do you have this provision, which is unlike the provisions of this world, and which comes out of its season while the doors are locked upon you, with no way for anyone to bring it to you? ﴿She said: "It is from Allah"﴾, so do not find it strange. It is said she spoke while still young, as Isa spoke while in the cradle. It is narrated from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he went hungry in a time of famine, and Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her, gave him two loaves and a piece of meat, which he gave to someone else; then he returned with them to her and said: "Bring them here, my daughter." ﴿Dhurriyyatan﴾ (offspring) is a substitute for "the family of Ibrahim" and "the family of Imran." ﴿Ba'duha min ba'd﴾ (some of them from others) means that the two families are one continuous lineage, some branching from others: Musa and Harun from Imran, Imran from Yashhar, Yashhar from Fahith, Fahith from Lawi, Lawi from Ya'qub, and Ya'qub from Ishaq. Likewise Isa son of Maryam daughter of Imran son of Mathan son of Sulayman son of Dawud [[His saying "son of Mathan, son of Sulayman, son of Dawud": "son of Sulayman" means from his lineage. And his saying "son of Yahudha" means from his lineage, as al-Fakhr al-Razi explicitly stated. Abu al-Su'ud mentioned that between Mathan and Sulayman there are about fifteen forefathers, and between Ishya and Yahudha nine forefathers. (A)]] son of Ishya son of Yahudha son of Ya'qub son of Ishaq. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered the family of Ibrahim. It is also said that ﹙some of them from others﹚ refers to religion, like His saying ﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another﴾. ﴿And Allah is Hearing, Knowing﴾: He knows who is fit for chosen status, or He knows that some of them are from others in religion, or He is Hearing and Knowing of the statement of the wife of Imran and her intention. ﴿When﴾ is governed by it (the verb "Hearing and Knowing").

It is also said: it is governed by an implied "remember." The wife of Imran is the wife of Imran son of Mathan, the mother of Maryam the virgin, grandmother of Isa, peace be upon him, and her name was Hanna daughter of Faqudh. Her saying ﴿When the wife of Imran said﴾ following "the family of Imran" supports that Imran is Imran son of Mathan, grandfather of Isa. The other view is supported by the fact that Musa is frequently mentioned alongside Ibrahim. If you say: Imran son of Yashhar had a daughter named Maryam, older than Musa and Harun, and Imran son of Mathan had Maryam the virgin; how do you know that this Imran is the father of Maryam the virgin rather than the father of Maryam who was the sister of Musa and Harun? I say: the guardianship of Zakariyya is sufficient proof that he is the father of the virgin, because Zakariyya son of Adhan and Imran son of Mathan lived in the same era, and Zakariyya had married his daughter Ishya, sister of Maryam, so Yahya and Isa were cousins. It is narrated that she (Hanna) was barren and did not bear children until she became old. While she was in the shade of a tree, she saw a bird feeding its chick, and her soul was moved toward having a child and she wished for one. She said: "O Allah, I vow to You a vow of gratitude if You grant me a child: that I will dedicate him to the Temple of Jerusalem so that he will be among its custodians and servants." She then conceived Maryam, and Imran died while she was pregnant. ﴿Muharraran﴾ (dedicated, freed) means freed for the service of the Temple of Jerusalem, with no claim of mine upon him, I will not employ him, nor occupy him with anything; and this kind of vow was lawful among them. It is narrated that they used to make this vow, and when the boy reached maturity he was given the choice between doing it or not. It is also reported from al-Sha'bi that ﴿muharraran﴾ means sincerely devoted to worship, and that liberation was only for boys; she either considered it hypothetically, or she asked to be granted a male child.

﴿So when she gave birth to her﴾: the pronoun refers to "what is in my womb" [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "The pronoun refers back to what is in my womb..." etc. Ahmad said: The pronoun in her saying "she gave birth to her" encompasses the attribution of giving birth and femaleness to her, so the state falls upon her from the general aspect, and that aspect is that she is a thing that was born, not specifically the attribution of femaleness to her. This very discussion was previously raised at His saying: ﴿If they are not two men﴾.]]. It was feminine according to meaning because what was in her womb was female in Allah's knowledge; or according to the interpretation of "pregnancy," "soul," or "offspring." If you say: How is it permissible for ﴿unthā﴾ (female) to be an accusative state from the pronoun in ﴿waḍa'tuhā﴾, when it is like your saying "I gave birth to the female, female"? I say: The original is "I gave birth to him, female," and it was feminized because the state is feminine, since the state and its possessor are one thing, just as the noun was feminized in "what was your mother," for the predicate's feminization. A parallel is His saying ﴿If they are two women﴾. As for the interpretation of "pregnancy" or "offspring," it is clear, as if it were said: "I gave birth to the pregnancy or the offspring as a female." If you say: Why did she say "I gave birth to her as a female," and what did she intend by this statement? I say: she said it in regret [[(Resumption of his speech) He said: "Her saying 'I gave birth to her as a female' was intended as regret and sorrow..." etc. Ahmad said: This interpretation is that it is from the speech of Allah, Exalted, not a quotation from her. The people of tafsir mentioned another interpretation: that this statement is her own speech, which Allah related from her, namely His saying ﴿And the male is not like the female﴾, and her speech is connected to it by His saying ﴿And I have named her Maryam...﴾. They object to this view that if it is her statement, the expected form would be "the female is not like the male," since her intention is to belittle the female in comparison to the male, and the custom in such cases is to negate from the deficient the resemblance to the complete, not the reverse. The matter appears varied in this, and what they said has not been established for me. Do you not see His saying ﴿You are not like any of the women﴾? He negated from the complete the resemblance to the deficient, even though perfection belongs to the wives of the Prophet, peace be upon him, relative to women in general. And on this basis the expression of the wife of Imran came, and Allah knows best. From this also: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create?﴾]] on account of the failure of her hope and the reversal of her expectation. She had hoped and expected to bear a male, and that is why she vowed him dedicated for service. Because she said this with regret and sorrow, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Allah knows best what she gave birth to﴾, glorifying what she bore and making her ignorant of how much had been granted to her. Its meaning: Allah knows best the thing she bore and what great matters are connected to it, and that He will make him and his son a sign for the worlds, while she was unaware of that and knew nothing of it, therefore she grieved. In the reading of Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿And Allah knows best what you (feminine) have borne﴾, addressed by Allah to her, meaning: you do not know the worth of this granted one, nor how great its affair and lofty its status are in Allah's knowledge. It was also read: "she gave birth" (waḍa'at), meaning: perhaps Allah has a secret and wisdom in it, and perhaps this female is better than a male, as consolation for herself.

If you say: What is the meaning of His saying ﴿And the male is not like the female﴾? I say: It explains what is in His saying ﴿And Allah knows best what she gave birth to﴾ of glorifying the thing born and elevating it. Its meaning: the male you sought is not like the female that was granted to you. The lam in both is for specificity (ʿahd). If you say: On what is His saying ﴿And I have named her Maryam﴾ conjoined? I say: it is conjoined to "I gave birth to her as a female," and what lies between them consists of two intervening clauses, like His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a great oath, if you only knew﴾. If you say: Why did she mention naming her Maryam to her Lord? I say: because Maryam in their language means "the worshipper" [[(Resumption of his speech) He said: "The benefit of her saying ﴿And I have named her Maryam﴾ is that Maryam in their language means the worshipper..." etc. Ahmad said:

As for the hadith, it is mentioned in the authentic collections, agreed upon as sound. There is no escape from it except by nullifying his words, peace be upon him, by loading upon them what they cannot bear, inclining toward a Mu'tazili rationalism derived from a philosophy derived from atheism, with darknesses upon darknesses. I had earlier, at His saying ﴿They do not rise except as one rises whom Satan has struck with madness through touch﴾, presented what is sufficient. I do not see Satan as anything but having pierced the flanks of the Qadariyya until he split them, and nested in their hearts until al-Zamakhshari and his like were led to say in the Book of Allah and the words of His Messenger, peace be upon him, what is merely imagined, as he said in this hadith, then compared it to the imagery of Ibn al-Rumi in his poetry, out of audacity and bad manners. Had the meaning of what he said been correct, this expression would have been obligatory to avoid. And even if the crying were not actually produced by the newborn, it could be possible, from a distance, to be a figurative image. But what is actually witnessed, there is no basis for interpreting it as mere imagery except a meager belief and the pursuit of a grievous desire.]] . So she intended by that to draw near and to petition Him to protect her, so that her action would conform to her name, and that He would fulfill her expectation of her. Do you not see how she followed it with a request for protection for her and her offspring from Satan and his seduction? As for what is narrated in the hadith: "No child is born except that Satan touches him at his birth, so he cries out from the touch of Satan, except Maryam and her son" [[The author said: Allah knows its authenticity; thus he said. The hadith is in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, at its end: Abu Hurayra said: Recite if you wish: ﴿And indeed I seek refuge for her in You, and for her offspring, from the accursed Satan﴾.]]. Allah knows its authenticity. If it is authentic, its meaning is that every newborn is one whom Satan hopes to seduce, except Maryam and her son, for they were protected; and likewise everyone who shares their attribute, as in His saying ﴿I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants﴾. His crying out upon being touched by him is an imagery and depiction of Satan's hope regarding him, as if he touches him, strikes his hand upon him, and says: "This is one I will seduce." Similar to this imagery is the saying of Ibn al-Rumi:

Because of the calamities the world announces,
the crying of the infant at the moment of birth occurs.
Otherwise, what would make him weep from it, when indeed
he is more spacious than he was in it, and more comfortable?
When he sees the world, he cries out, as if
threatening what he will suffer from its harm.

[Ibn al-Rumi says: The crying of the child at birth is only due to what the world signals of its vicissitudes; otherwise, what would make him weep from it, or what would make him weep from it, since the world is... One narration reads: "since he" (i.e., the child) is more spacious in position than the constriction of the womb and more comfortable. Its return to what makes him weep is distant or unsound. It is permissible that it returns to the spaciousness of the world known from context, then he says: when he sees it he cries out, as if threatening with what he will suffer from its harm before it occurs.]

As for the true nature of touching and pricking as the ignorant literalists imagine, no; had Iblis been empowered over people to prick them, the world would be filled with crying and wailing from the affliction of his pricking. ﴿So her Lord accepted her﴾: He was pleased with her as a substitute for the male in the vow, ﴿with a good acceptance﴾. It has two possibilities. First, that "acceptance" (qabūl) is the name of what something is accepted with, like "snuff" and "purgative," for what is snuffed or purged. That is her singling out for standing in place of the male in the vow, and no female was accepted before her in that; or that her mother would hand her over immediately after birth, before she grew up and became fit for service. It is narrated that Hanna, when she gave birth to Maryam, wrapped her in a cloth and carried her to the mosque, and placed her before the rabbis, sons of Harun, who in Jerusalem were like the keepers of the Ka'ba. She said to them: "Take this vowed offering," and they competed for her, because she was the daughter of their leader and the custodian of their offerings. The sons of Mathan were chiefs of the Children of Israel, their rabbis and their kings. Zakariyya said to them: "I have more right to her; her aunt is with me." They said: "No, until we draw lots for her." So they went—and they were twenty-seven—to a river and cast their pens into it. Zakariyya's pen rose above the water, while theirs sank, so he took charge of her. [[Al-Zamakhshari's words "her aunt is with me": he means his wife Ishya, sister of Hanna. But it was previously mentioned that she (Ishya) was the sister of Maryam, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, said about Yahya and Isa that they were cousins (sons of the maternal aunt). Abu al-Su'ud said that it is said in explaining this that "sister" is often applied to the niece, so the hadith follows that usage. It is also said that Ishya was the half-sister of Hanna through the mother, and the full sister of Maryam through the father, in that Imran married Hanna's mother and she bore Ishya, then he married Hanna, his stepdaughter, and she bore Maryam, based on the permissibility of marrying stepdaughters according to them. (A)]]

The second possibility: it is a verbal noun with an omitted modifier, meaning: "accepted her with an acceptance that is good," i.e., with a matter of good acceptance, which is the singling out. It is also permissible that the meaning of "accepted her" is "received her," as in your saying: "he hastened it" means "he asked for its haste," and "he pursued it" means "he sought it out," which is common in their speech, from "receiving the matter" when one takes it at its beginning and freshness. Al-Qatami said:

"The best of matters is what you receive from it,
and it is not that you follow it in pursuit."

[He says: the best of matters is the one you receive and await, taking it at the first coming; and not one whose outcome you endure until it escapes you and passes, then you follow and pursue it to catch it. The "bi" in the predicate of "laysa" is extra, and the predicate is governed by an omitted modifier: "one of pursuit." "Tatabbu'" originally is "tatatabbu'," with one of the taʾs dropped, either the present-tense taʾ, or the taʾ of the reflexive form, or the taʾ that is the root of the verb, the first of them; since each of the first two came with its own meaning. Al-Jawhari said: "The ittiba' is placed in the position of tatabbu'." So it is a verbal noun, or a verbal noun from which some augments were dropped, and the tafa''ul form is more emphatic than the ifti'al form, so its intended sense is decisively meant here, because it is emphatic.]

From this is the proverb: "Take the matter by its foreparts," meaning: she received her at the beginning of her matter, when she was born, with good acceptance. ﴿And He caused her to grow a good growth﴾: a metaphor for good upbringing returning to her with what puts her right in all her circumstances. It was read: "wa-kaffalahā Zakariyyā," in the measure of "wa-ʿamalahā," [[His saying "and the verb is attributed to Allah, Exalted": perhaps "and the verb." (A)]] and "wa-kaffala-hā Zakariyyā" with the stress on the fa' and the accusative on Zakariyya, the verb being attributed to Allah, meaning: He gathered her to Himself and made Zakariyya her guardian and guarantor of her welfare. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "wa-akfilhā," from His saying ﴿Say, "Make him my guardian"﴾. Mujahid read: "fa-taqabbalahā rabbuhā, wa-anbatahā, wa-kaffalahā," in the imperative form for the three verbs, with "rabbuhā" in the accusative as a supplication: "accept her, O her Lord, and make Zakariyya her guardian." It is said Zakariyya built for her a niche (miḥrāb) in the mosque, that is, a chamber to which one ascends by a ladder. It is also said the miḥrāb is the most noble and foremost place of assembly, as if she were placed in the most noble spot of Jerusalem. It is said their mosques were called maḥārīb. It is narrated that no one entered upon her except him alone, and when he left, she was locked in with seven doors. ﴿Every time Zakariyya entered upon her in the niche, he found with her provision﴾: the provision that descended to her from Paradise. She had never nursed from a breast, so he would find with her winter fruit in summer and summer fruit in winter. ﴿He said: "O Maryam, from where is this for you?"﴾: from where do you have this provision, which is unlike the provisions of this world, and which comes out of its season while the doors are locked upon you, with no way for anyone to bring it to you? ﴿She said: "It is from Allah"﴾, so do not find it strange. It is said she spoke while still young, as Isa spoke while in the cradle. It is narrated from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he went hungry in a time of famine, and Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her, gave him two loaves and a piece of meat, which he gave to someone else; then he returned with them to her and said: "Bring them here, my daughter." She uncovered the tray, and behold, it was full of bread and meat. She was amazed and knew it had descended from Allah. He said to her: "From where is this for you?" She said: "It is from Allah; indeed Allah provides whom He wills without reckoning." The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Praise be to Allah who made you resemble the mistress of the women of the Children of Israel." Then the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, gathered 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan, al-Husayn, and all his household, and they ate from it until they were satisfied, and the food remained as it was; so Fatima gave generously to her neighbours. ﴿Indeed Allah provides whom He wills without reckoning﴾: either part of Maryam's speech, or the speech of the Lord of Majesty, the Mighty, the Exalted: "without measure," meaning without measuring out its abundance, or by grace without accounting and recompense according to the deserving of an action.

When he sees the world, he cries out, as if
threatening what he will suffer from its harm.

[Ibn al-Rumi says: The crying of the child at birth is only due to what the world signals of its vicissitudes; otherwise, what would make him weep from it, or what would make him weep from it, since the world is... One narration reads: "since he" (i.e., the child) is more spacious in position than the constriction of the womb and more comfortable. Its return to what makes him weep is distant or unsound. It is permissible that it returns to the spaciousness of the world known from context, then he says: when he sees it he cries out, as if threatening with what he will suffer from its harm before it occurs.]

As for the true nature of touching and pricking as the ignorant literalists imagine, no; had Iblis been empowered over people to prick them, the world would be filled with crying and wailing from the affliction of his pricking. ﴿So her Lord accepted her﴾: He was pleased with her as a substitute for the male in the vow, ﴿with a good acceptance﴾. It has two possibilities. First, that "acceptance" (qabūl) is the name of what something is accepted with, like "snuff" and "purgative," for what is snuffed or purged. That is her singling out for standing in place of the male in the vow, and no female was accepted before her in that; or that her mother would hand her over immediately after birth, before she grew up and became fit for service. It is narrated that Hanna, when she gave birth to Maryam, wrapped her in a cloth and carried her to the mosque, and placed her before the rabbis, sons of Harun, who in Jerusalem were like the keepers of the Ka'ba. She said to them: "Take this vowed offering," and they competed for her, because she was the daughter of their leader and the custodian of their offerings. The sons of Mathan were chiefs of the Children of Israel, their rabbis and their kings. Zakariyya said to them: "I have more right to her; her aunt is with me." They said: "No, until we draw lots for her." So they went—and they were twenty-seven—to a river and cast their pens into it. Zakariyya's pen rose above the water, while theirs sank, so he took charge of her. [[Al-Zamakhshari's words "her aunt is with me": he means his wife Ishya, sister of Hanna. But it was previously mentioned that she (Ishya) was the sister of Maryam, and the Prophet, peace be upon him, said about Yahya and Isa that they were cousins (sons of the maternal aunt). Abu al-Su'ud said that it is said in explaining this that "sister" is often applied to the niece, so the hadith follows that usage. It is also said that Ishya was the half-sister of Hanna through the mother, and the full sister of Maryam through the father, in that Imran married Hanna's mother and she bore Ishya, then he married Hanna, his stepdaughter, and she bore Maryam, based on the permissibility of marrying stepdaughters according to them. (A)]]

The second possibility: it is a verbal noun with an omitted modifier, meaning: "accepted her with an acceptance that is good," i.e., with a matter of good acceptance, which is the singling out. It is also permissible that the meaning of "accepted her" is "received her," as in your saying: "he hastened it" means "he asked for its haste," and "he pursued it" means "he sought it out," which is common in their speech, from "receiving the matter" when one takes it at its beginning and freshness. Al-Qatami said:

"The best of matters is what you receive from it,
and it is not that you follow it in pursuit."

[He says: the best of matters is the one you receive and await, taking it at the first coming; and not one whose outcome you endure until it escapes you and passes, then you follow and pursue it to catch it. The "bi" in the predicate of "laysa" is extra, and the predicate is governed by an omitted modifier: "one of pursuit." "Tatabbu'" originally is "tatatabbu'," with one of the taʾs dropped, either the present-tense taʾ, or the taʾ of the reflexive form, or the taʾ that is the root of the verb, the first of them; since each of the first two came with its own meaning. Al-Jawhari said: "The ittiba' is placed in the position of tatabbu'." So it is a verbal noun, or a verbal noun from which some augments were dropped, and the tafa''ul form is more emphatic than the ifti'al form, so its intended sense is decisively meant here, because it is emphatic.]

From this is the proverb: "Take the matter by its foreparts," meaning: she received her at the beginning of her matter, when she was born, with good acceptance. ﴿And He caused her to grow a good growth﴾: a metaphor for good upbringing returning to her with what puts her right in all her circumstances. It was read: "wa-kaffalahā Zakariyyā," in the measure of "wa-ʿamalahā," [[His saying "and the verb is attributed to Allah, Exalted": perhaps "and the verb." (A)]] and "wa-kaffala-hā Zakariyyā" with the stress on the fa' and the accusative on Zakariyya, the verb being attributed to Allah, meaning: He gathered her to Himself and made Zakariyya her guardian and guarantor of her welfare. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "wa-akfilhā," from His saying ﴿Say, "Make him my guardian"﴾. Mujahid read: "fa-taqabbalahā rabbuhā, wa-anbatahā, wa-kaffalahā," in the imperative form for the three verbs, with "rabbuhā" in the accusative as a supplication: "accept her, O her Lord, and make Zakariyya her guardian." It is said Zakariyya built for her a niche (miḥrāb) in the mosque, that is, a chamber to which one ascends by a ladder. It is also said the miḥrāb is the most noble and foremost place of assembly, as if she were placed in the most noble spot of Jerusalem. It is said their mosques were called maḥārīb. It is narrated that no one entered upon her except him alone, and when he left, she was locked in with seven doors. ﴿Every time Zakariyya entered upon her in the niche, he found with her provision﴾: the provision that descended to her from Paradise. She had never nursed from a breast, so he would find with her winter fruit in summer and summer fruit in winter. ﴿He said: "O Maryam, from where is this for you?"﴾: from where do you have this provision, which is unlike the provisions of this world, and which comes out of its season while the doors are locked upon you, with no way for anyone to bring it to you? ﴿She said: "It is from Allah"﴾, so do not find it strange. It is said she spoke while still young, as Isa spoke while in the cradle. It is narrated from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he went hungry in a time of famine, and Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her, gave him two loaves and a piece of meat, which he gave to someone else; then he returned with them to her and said: "Bring them here, my daughter." She uncovered the tray, and behold, it was full of bread and meat. She was amazed and knew it had descended from Allah. He said to her: "From where is this for you?" She said: "It is from Allah; indeed Allah provides whom He wills without reckoning." The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Praise be to Allah who made you resemble the mistress of the women of the Children of Israel." Then the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, gathered 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan, al-Husayn, and all his household, and they ate from it until they were satisfied, and the food remained as it was; so Fatima gave generously to her neighbours. ﴿Indeed Allah provides whom He wills without reckoning﴾: either part of Maryam's speech, or the speech of the Lord of Majesty, the Mighty, the Exalted: "without measure," meaning without measuring out its abundance, or by grace without accounting and recompense according to the deserving of an action.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (*al-Kashshaf*) on Surah 3, verses 38–41:

﴿There,﴾ that is, in that place, where he was standing beside Maryam in the *mihrab* (the sanctuary niche), or at that time. The word *hunālika* (there) may be used figuratively here, as *thumma* (then) and *ḥaythu* (where) are used for time. [[Mahmud said: "*Hunālika*, *thumma* and *ḥaythu* are used figuratively for time..." etc. Ahmad said: It is not fitting for a prophet to base his knowledge of the possibility of a barren woman giving birth on witnessing the like of it, since reason judges that this is possible within God's power, even if no parallel has occurred. A better and safer way to put it is: When he witnessed this event occurring as a marvel (*karāma*) for Maryam, his hope extended to an event befitting it as a marvel for himself. And God knows best.]] *Thumma* and *ḥaythu* are used for time as well. When he saw Maryam's state of honour before God and her rank, he desired that he too should have, from his wife, a child like the child of her sister Ḥannah in nobility and in honour before God, even though his wife was barren and aged, since her sister had been likewise. It has been said that when he saw summer fruit out of its season, he became aware of the possibility that a barren woman could bear a child. *Dhurriyya* (offspring) applies to one and to many. ﴿He is the Hearer of supplication﴾, the One who answers it.

It is read: ﴿the angels called him﴾. It has been said that it was Gabriel (peace be upon him) who called him, and the plural *al-malā'ika* (the angels) is used in the manner of saying "So-and-so rides horses." ﴿That God gives you good news﴾ is read with *anna* (that) vowelled with a fatḥa, meaning "that God," and with a kasra, implying the sense of "saying." Or because calling (*nidā'*) is a kind of speech.

It is also read *yubashshiruka* and *yubshiruka*, from *basharahu* and *abshara-hu*. [[*Yubashshiruka*]] with a fatḥa on the *yā'* from *bashsharahu*.

*Yaḥyā*: if it is non-Arabic, which is the apparent case, then it is not declined, because of definiteness and foreignness, like Mūsā and ʿĪsā. If it is Arabic, then it is not declined because of definiteness and its being of the form of a verb, like *Ya'mur*. ﴿Confirming a word from God﴾, confirming ʿĪsā, believing in him. It has been said that he was the first to believe in him. ʿĪsā was called "a word" because he came into being only through the word of God alone, which is His saying "Be" (*kun*), without any other cause.

It has also been said: "confirming a word from God" means believing in a Book from Him. The Book was called a word, as *kalima al-Ḥuwaydara* was said of his poem. *Sayyid* (master) is one who rules his people, that is, surpasses them in nobility. Yaḥyā surpassed his people and surpassed all people in that he never committed a sin at all, and what a mastery that is. *Ḥaṣūr* is one who does not approach women, out of restraint for himself, that is, preventing himself from desires. It has been said that he is one who does not take part with people in gambling. Al-Akhṭal said:

*And a drinking companion who buys wine at a profitable price, drinking with me from the cup,*
*Is neither a restrainer (ḥaṣūr) nor one who gives in to drinking.* [[From al-Akhṭal: he says, many a drinker who buys wine at a profitable, extra price, drinking with me from the cup. It is permissible to link it to what precedes: "not a restrainer, preventing himself from joining the people in gambling," and "nor a *sa'ār*" in the form of *fa'āl* for emphasis, meaning leaving a residue (*su'r*) in the cup, that is, a remainder, from *asʾara* when one leaves something behind; it is anomalous, like *jabbār* from *ajbara*. It is also transmitted as *bi-sawwār*, from *al-sawra*, which is leaping and rowdiness; in that case the *fī* is causal, meaning "nor one whose mind is altered by its cause," and it is not coordinated with *muribḥ*. The second is an emphasis, and the *bā'* is superfluous after *kull*. *Nādamanī* is the predicate, so it is permissible to return to description after the predicate.]]

So it is borrowed for one who does not take part in play and amusement. It is narrated that he passed, while still a child, by some boys who invited him to play, and he said: ﴿I was not created for play.﴾ ﴿Of the righteous﴾, being born of the righteous, because he was from the loins of prophets; or being one of the righteous, like God's saying: ﴿and in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾.

﴿How can I have a son,﴾ an expression of astonishment in terms of custom, as Maryam said: ﴿how can I have a child when no man has touched me?﴾ ﴿And old age has truly reached me,﴾ as in the people's saying: "old age overtook him" (*adrakathu al-sinn al-'āliya*). The meaning is that old age affected me and weakened me. He was ninety-nine years old, and his wife was ninety-eight.

﴿Thus﴾, that is, God does what He wills of wondrous acts like that deed, namely creating a child between an aged, decrepit man and a barren old woman. Or, "thus God" is a subject and predicate, meaning that God is in this manner, and ﴿does what He wills﴾ is an explanation of it: He does what He desires of acts that break customary patterns.

﴿He said: "My Lord, give me a sign."﴾ A sign, a token by which I may know the conception, so that I may receive the blessing with thanks. ﴿He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three days."﴾ He specified speaking to people, to let him know that his tongue would be restrained from the ability to speak to them in particular, while his ability to speak in the remembrance of God would remain; and that is why He said: ﴿and remember your Lord much and glorify Him in the evening and the morning﴾, meaning during the days of your inability to speak to people. This is one of the striking signs.

If you ask: why was his tongue restrained from speaking to people? I answer: to free up the time for the remembrance of God, so that his tongue would not be occupied with anything else, out of devotion to fulfilling the duty of this great blessing and giving thanks for it, which was the reason he asked for the sign. It is as if, when he asked for the sign for the sake of thanks, he was told: "Your sign is that you restrain your tongue except for thanks." The best and most fitting answer is that which is derived from the question and drawn out of it.

﴿except by gestures﴾, a signal by hand or head or otherwise. Its root is movement; one says *irtamaza* when something moves; and from it the sea is called *al-rāmūz*. Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb read *illā ramzan* with two ḍammas, as the plural of *rumūz*, like *rasūl* and *rusul*. It is also read *ramzan* with two fatḥas, as the plural of *rāmiz*, like *khādim* and *khadam*. It is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from him and from "the people," meaning in a single moment, in the sense of "gesturing," as the verse says:

*Whenever you meet me alone, your buttocks' fleshy parts will tremble and quiver,*
*And my sword is sharp, held by fingers that are not seen spreading out.* [[These lines are by ʿAntara, addressing ʿUmāra ibn Ziyād al-ʿAbsī, when he said to his people: "I wish I had met him, so I could relieve you of him and let you know that he is a slave." *Al-ist* means the rear; it is the subject (*fā'il*). *Madhrawayhā* is the object. Its analogical form should have been *madhriyān* with a *yā'*, since it is a defective noun with more than three letters, and the analogical dual is likewise; so its coming with a *wāw* is anomalous, and what made it easy is that its dual is notional, since no singular has been heard for it. Abū ʿAmr is reported to have said *madhrā* in the singular, so the dual would be actual, and it is said accordingly. Abū ʿUbayda is reported to have said *madhrā* in the singular and *madhriyān* in the dual with a *yā'*, on analogy; and if *al-ist* is put in the accusative, it is the object, and *madhrawayhā* is an apposition to it. *Al-madhrawān* with a kasra are the two sides of the buttocks and the two horns of the head. It is said: "He came shaking his two sides," meaning strutting and swaggering. And "a bow with a resonating double edge" means the two places where the string is fixed, the upper and lower. That is, their resonance. *Hā anā dhā* originally means *anā hādhā*, and the *hā'* was moved forward to draw attention. Then he says: "whenever I meet you," in a state where we are alone away from others, "your buttocks tremble," so their quivering is a metaphor for fear. *Tastaṭāra* is emphasized with the light *nūn* turned into an *alif*, and the subject is the pronoun of the addressee, as if fear makes you fly. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the *rawānif*, meaning they quiver and spread like a bird. It is narrated as *rawādif*, and the meaning is one.]]

Like one speaking to the deaf and mute by gesture, so they speak to him by gesture. *Al-ʿashiyy* is from the time the sun declines until it sets. *Al-ibkār* is from the break of dawn until the time of forenoon. It is read *wa-l-abkār* with a fatḥa on the *hamza*, as the plural of *bakr*, like *saḥar* and *asḥār*. One says: "I came to him *bakran*," with two fatḥas.

If you ask: gesturing is not of the kind of speech, so how is it excepted from it? I answer: when it performs the function of speech and what is understood from speech is understood from it, it is called speech. It is also permissible that it is a discontinuous exception.

It has been said that it was Gabriel (peace be upon him) who called him, and the plural *al-malā'ika* (the angels) is used in the manner of saying "So-and-so rides horses." ﴿That God gives you good news﴾ is read with *anna* (that) vowelled with a fatḥa, meaning "that God," and with a kasra, implying the sense of "saying." Or because calling (*nidā'*) is a kind of speech.

It is also read *yubashshiruka* and *yubshiruka*, from *basharahu* and *abshara-hu*. [[*Yubashshiruka*]] with a fatḥa on the *yā'* from *bashsharahu*.

*Yaḥyā*: if it is non-Arabic, which is the apparent case, then it is not declined, because of definiteness and foreignness, like Mūsā and ʿĪsā. If it is Arabic, then it is not declined because of definiteness and its being of the form of a verb, like *Ya'mur*. ﴿Confirming a word from God﴾, confirming ʿĪsā, believing in him. It has been said that he was the first to believe in him. ʿĪsā was called "a word" because he came into being only through the word of God alone, which is His saying "Be" (*kun*), without any other cause.

It has also been said: "confirming a word from God" means believing in a Book from Him. The Book was called a word, as *kalima al-Ḥuwaydara* was said of his poem. *Sayyid* (master) is one who rules his people, that is, surpasses them in nobility. Yaḥyā surpassed his people and surpassed all people in that he never committed a sin at all, and what a mastery that is. *Ḥaṣūr* is one who does not approach women, out of restraint for himself, that is, preventing himself from desires. It has been said that he is one who does not take part with people in gambling. Al-Akhṭal said:

*And a drinking companion who buys wine at a profitable price, drinking with me from the cup,*
*Is neither a restrainer (ḥaṣūr) nor one who gives in to drinking.* [[From al-Akhṭal: he says, many a drinker who buys wine at a profitable, extra price, drinking with me from the cup. It is permissible to link it to what precedes: "not a restrainer, preventing himself from joining the people in gambling," and "nor a *sa'ār*" in the form of *fa'āl* for emphasis, meaning leaving a residue (*su'r*) in the cup, that is, a remainder, from *asʾara* when one leaves something behind; it is anomalous, like *jabbār* from *ajbara*. It is also transmitted as *bi-sawwār*, from *al-sawra*, which is leaping and rowdiness; in that case the *fī* is causal, meaning "nor one whose mind is altered by its cause," and it is not coordinated with *muribḥ*. The second is an emphasis, and the *bā'* is superfluous after *kull*. *Nādamanī* is the predicate, so it is permissible to return to description after the predicate.]]

So it is borrowed for one who does not take part in play and amusement. It is narrated that he passed, while still a child, by some boys who invited him to play, and he said: ﴿I was not created for play.﴾ ﴿Of the righteous﴾, being born of the righteous, because he was from the loins of prophets; or being one of the righteous, like God's saying: ﴿and in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾.

﴿How can I have a son,﴾ an expression of astonishment in terms of custom, as Maryam said: ﴿how can I have a child when no man has touched me?﴾ ﴿And old age has truly reached me,﴾ as in the people's saying: "old age overtook him" (*adrakathu al-sinn al-'āliya*). The meaning is that old age affected me and weakened me. He was ninety-nine years old, and his wife was ninety-eight.

﴿Thus﴾, that is, God does what He wills of wondrous acts like that deed, namely creating a child between an aged, decrepit man and a barren old woman. Or, "thus God" is a subject and predicate, meaning that God is in this manner, and ﴿does what He wills﴾ is an explanation of it: He does what He desires of acts that break customary patterns.

﴿He said: "My Lord, give me a sign."﴾ A sign, a token by which I may know the conception, so that I may receive the blessing with thanks. ﴿He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three days."﴾ He specified speaking to people, to let him know that his tongue would be restrained from the ability to speak to them in particular, while his ability to speak in the remembrance of God would remain; and that is why He said: ﴿and remember your Lord much and glorify Him in the evening and the morning﴾, meaning during the days of your inability to speak to people. This is one of the striking signs.

If you ask: why was his tongue restrained from speaking to people? I answer: to free up the time for the remembrance of God, so that his tongue would not be occupied with anything else, out of devotion to fulfilling the duty of this great blessing and giving thanks for it, which was the reason he asked for the sign. It is as if, when he asked for the sign for the sake of thanks, he was told: "Your sign is that you restrain your tongue except for thanks." The best and most fitting answer is that which is derived from the question and drawn out of it.

﴿except by gestures﴾, a signal by hand or head or otherwise. Its root is movement; one says *irtamaza* when something moves; and from it the sea is called *al-rāmūz*. Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb read *illā ramzan* with two ḍammas, as the plural of *rumūz*, like *rasūl* and *rusul*. It is also read *ramzan* with two fatḥas, as the plural of *rāmiz*, like *khādim* and *khadam*. It is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from him and from "the people," meaning in a single moment, in the sense of "gesturing," as the verse says:

*Whenever you meet me alone, your buttocks' fleshy parts will tremble and quiver,*
*And my sword is sharp, held by fingers that are not seen spreading out.* [[These lines are by ʿAntara, addressing ʿUmāra ibn Ziyād al-ʿAbsī, when he said to his people: "I wish I had met him, so I could relieve you of him and let you know that he is a slave." *Al-ist* means the rear; it is the subject (*fā'il*). *Madhrawayhā* is the object. Its analogical form should have been *madhriyān* with a *yā'*, since it is a defective noun with more than three letters, and the analogical dual is likewise; so its coming with a *wāw* is anomalous, and what made it easy is that its dual is notional, since no singular has been heard for it. Abū ʿAmr is reported to have said *madhrā* in the singular, so the dual would be actual, and it is said accordingly. Abū ʿUbayda is reported to have said *madhrā* in the singular and *madhriyān* in the dual with a *yā'*, on analogy; and if *al-ist* is put in the accusative, it is the object, and *madhrawayhā* is an apposition to it. *Al-madhrawān* with a kasra are the two sides of the buttocks and the two horns of the head. It is said: "He came shaking his two sides," meaning strutting and swaggering. And "a bow with a resonating double edge" means the two places where the string is fixed, the upper and lower. That is, their resonance. *Hā anā dhā* originally means *anā hādhā*, and the *hā'* was moved forward to draw attention. Then he says: "whenever I meet you," in a state where we are alone away from others, "your buttocks tremble," so their quivering is a metaphor for fear. *Tastaṭāra* is emphasized with the light *nūn* turned into an *alif*, and the subject is the pronoun of the addressee, as if fear makes you fly. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the *rawānif*, meaning they quiver and spread like a bird. It is narrated as *rawādif*, and the meaning is one.]]

Like one speaking to the deaf and mute by gesture, so they speak to him by gesture. *Al-ʿashiyy* is from the time the sun declines until it sets. *Al-ibkār* is from the break of dawn until the time of forenoon. It is read *wa-l-abkār* with a fatḥa on the *hamza*, as the plural of *bakr*, like *saḥar* and *asḥār*. One says: "I came to him *bakran*," with two fatḥas.

If you ask: gesturing is not of the kind of speech, so how is it excepted from it? I answer: when it performs the function of speech and what is understood from speech is understood from it, it is called speech. It is also permissible that it is a discontinuous exception.
