Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 42–43:

﴿Yā Maryamu﴾ (O Mary). It is narrated that they spoke it aloud (kallamūhā shafāhan), as a miracle for Zakariyya, or as a foreshadowing (irhāṣ) of the prophethood of ʿĪsā. ﴿Iṣṭafāki﴾ (He chose you) first, when He accepted you from your mother, nurtured you, and singled you out with the noble distinction (al-karāma al-sanniyya). ﴿Wa-ṭahharaki﴾ (and purified you) from what is repugnant of deeds, and from what the Jews slandered you with. ﴿Wa-iṣṭafāki﴾ (and chose you) last, ﴿ʿalā nisāʾi l-ʿālamīn﴾ (above the women of the worlds), in that He granted you ʿĪsā without a father, and this was not given to any other woman.

You were commanded to pray, by mentioning qunūt and sujūd, because they are among the forms (hay'āt) and pillars (arkān) of the prayer. Then it was said to her: ﴿Wa-irkaʿī maʿa r-rākiʿīn﴾ (And bow with those who bow), meaning: let your prayer be with those who pray, that is, in congregation; or, align yourself among those who pray, and be counted in their number and not in the number of others.

It is possible that in her time there were people who would stand and prostrate in their prayer but did not bow (rukūʿ), while others did bow. So she was commanded to bow with those who bow, and not to be with those who do not bow.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 42–43:

﴿Yā Maryamu﴾ (O Mary). It is narrated that they spoke it aloud (kallamūhā shafāhan), as a miracle for Zakariyya, or as a foreshadowing (irhāṣ) of the prophethood of ʿĪsā. ﴿Iṣṭafāki﴾ (He chose you) first, when He accepted you from your mother, nurtured you, and singled you out with the noble distinction (al-karāma al-sanniyya). ﴿Wa-ṭahharaki﴾ (and purified you) from what is repugnant of deeds, and from what the Jews slandered you with. ﴿Wa-iṣṭafāki﴾ (and chose you) last, ﴿ʿalā nisāʾi l-ʿālamīn﴾ (above the women of the worlds), in that He granted you ʿĪsā without a father, and this was not given to any other woman.

You were commanded to pray, by mentioning qunūt and sujūd, because they are among the forms (hay'āt) and pillars (arkān) of the prayer. Then it was said to her: ﴿Wa-irkaʿī maʿa r-rākiʿīn﴾ (And bow with those who bow), meaning: let your prayer be with those who pray, that is, in congregation; or, align yourself among those who pray, and be counted in their number and not in the number of others.

It is possible that in her time there were people who would stand and prostrate in their prayer but did not bow (rukūʿ), while others did bow. So she was commanded to bow with those who bow, and not to be with those who do not bow.

This is a reference to the stories of Zakariyya, Yahya, Maryam and ʿIsa, peace be upon them, that were mentioned before. It means that these are among the unseen matters (ghuyub) which you did not know except through revelation.

If you say: Why did he negate witnessing (al-mushahada), when its absence is known without any doubt, and leave out negating hearing the reports from those who memorised them, which is merely presumed? I say: It was known to them with certain knowledge that he was not one who listens or reads, and they were deniers of revelation, so nothing remained but witnessing, which is extremely far-fetched and impossible. So it was negated by way of mockery of those who denied revelation, although they knew that he had neither hearing nor reading. Similar to this are: ﴿And you were not on the western side﴾, ﴿And you were not on the side of the Mount﴾, ﴿And you were not with them when they agreed upon their affair﴾ [with] their arrows (aqlamahum, azlamahum), which are their arrow-shafts that they threw into the river, casting lots. It is also said: they are the pens with which they used to write the Torah, which they chose for the lottery, seeking blessing through them, ﴿when they were disputing over who would be entrusted with her﴾, competing for the honour of her guardianship.

If you say: With what does ﴿whichever of them would take charge of her﴾ connect? I say: It connects with an omitted element indicated by ﴿they cast their pens﴾, as if it were said: they cast them, looking to see which of them would take charge, or so that they might know, or they say.

The Messiah (al-Masih) is one of the honorific epithets (laqab), like al-Siddiq and al-Faruq. Its origin is the Hebrew *meshiha*, meaning "the blessed one," as in His words ﴿and He has made me blessed wherever I may be﴾. Likewise, ʿIsa (Jesus) is an arabicized form of *Yeshua*. Both names are derived from *al-mash* (wiping) and *al-ʿays* (the mingling of water with earth), like one who writes in water.

If you ask: with what does ﴿when she said﴾ connect? I answer: it is a substitute (badl) for ﴿when the angels said﴾. It may also be a substitute for ﴿when they were disputing﴾, on the basis that the disputing and the good tidings occurred over a long period, as when you say, "I met him in such-and-such a year."

If you ask: why is it said "ʿIsa son of Maryam" when the address is to Maryam?

[Mahmud said: "If you ask why it is said 'ʿIsa son of Maryam' while the address is to Maryam... etc." Ahmad said: This answer is confirmed by her saying ﴿How can I have a son when no man has touched me?﴾, for there had not preceded in God's promise to her of a child anything indicating that he would be without a father. Yet when He attributed him to her, this showed that she understood from it that he would be without a father. And God knows best.]

I answer: children are attributed to their fathers, not to their mothers. By attributing him to her, He informed her that he would be born without a father, so he would be attributed only to his mother. By this she was distinguished and chosen above the women of the worlds.

If you ask: why is the pronoun for "word" used? I answer: because the one named by it is masculine.

If you ask: why is it said "his name is the Messiah, ʿIsa son of Maryam," when these are three things: the name is ʿIsa, while the Messiah and "son" are a title and an attribute?

[(His speech resumes.) He said: "If you ask why it is said 'his name is the Messiah, ʿIsa son of Maryam'..." etc. Ahmad said: In this explanation there is a way out of a difficulty that they raise. They say: if "the Messiah" in the verse is taken to mean the name, which is the apparent sense, then what is the place of "ʿIsa son of Maryam"? And a name is not described as a prophet. And if "the Messiah" is taken to mean the one named by this name, it does not fit with "his name." The difficulty is answered by saying that "the Messiah" is the predicate of "his name," and the intended meaning is the name. As for "ʿIsa son of Maryam," it is the predicate of an omitted subject, its sense being: "He is ʿIsa son of Maryam," and the pronoun refers to the one named by the aforementioned name, separated from the words of "the Messiah." What al-Zamakhshari established is not subject to this difficulty, and it is very good. And God knows best.]

I answer: the name is a sign for the named by which it is recognized and distinguished from others. It is as if it were said: that by which he is recognized and distinguished from all others is the combination of these three.

﴿honorable in this world and the Hereafter﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from ﴿a word﴾. Likewise His words ﴿and among those brought near﴾, ﴿and he will speak﴾, and ﴿and among the righteous﴾. That is: He gives you good tidings of him described by these attributes. The accusative of the circumstantial clause from an indefinite noun is valid because it is qualified.

Honor (wajaha) in this world is prophethood and precedence over people. In the Hereafter it is intercession and high rank in Paradise. His being ﴿among those brought near﴾ is His raising him to heaven and his companionship with the angels.

Al-mahd is what is prepared for the child as his bed; it is named by the verbal noun.

﴿in the cradle﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause, and ﴿and as a grown man﴾ is conjoined to it. The meaning is: "he will speak to people as a child and as a grown man."

Its meaning: he will speak to people in these two states with the speech of prophets, with no difference between the state of childhood and the state of maturity in which reason is complete and prophets receive revelation.

Among the strange interpretations (bida al-tafasir) is that her words ﴿My Lord﴾ are an address to Gabriel, peace be upon him, meaning "O my lord." (﴿And teach him﴾) is conjoined to ﴿will give you good tidings﴾, or to ﴿honorable﴾, or to ﴿will create﴾, or it is an independent statement. ʿAsim and Nafiʿ read *wa-yuʿallimuhu* with the yaʾ.

If you ask: on what do you take ﴿and a messenger﴾ and ﴿confirming﴾, from the preceding accusatives, when His words ﴿that I have come to you﴾ and ﴿of what is before me﴾ refuse to take them that way?

I answer: this is one of the difficult points, and there are two views. The first: that "and I have been sent" is implied before it, intending the saying, its sense being: "and He will teach him the Book and the wisdom, and he will say, 'I have been sent as a messenger that I have come to you,' and confirming what is before me." The second: that "messenger" and "confirming" carry the sense of speech, so it is as if it were said: "and speaking that I have come to you, and speaking that I confirm what is before me."

Al-Yazidi read *wa-rasulun* (and a messenger), conjoined to the words ﴿that I have come to you﴾. The original is "I have been sent with the sign that I have come to you," so the preposition was omitted and the verb governed the accusative.

It is related that fifty thousand sick people would often gather around him; whoever could come came to him, and whoever could not, ʿIsa came to. His cure was by supplication alone. ﴿By God's permission﴾ is repeated to repel the thought of one who suspects in him divinity. It is related that he brought back to life Sam son of Noah while they watched, and they said, "This is magic; show us a sign." So he said, "O so-and-so, you ate such-and-such, and O so-and-so, you have stored such-and-such for yourself."

*Tadhkharun* is also read with a dhal and without shadda. ﴿And to make lawful﴾ is a reference back to His words ﴿with a sign from your Lord﴾, meaning: I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, and to make lawful for you. It is also permissible that "confirming" is referred back to likewise, meaning: I have come to you with a sign, and I have come to you confirming.

What God had forbidden to them in the law of Moses: the fats and the thin fat covering the stomach and intestines (al-thurub, explained by al-Sihah), the flesh of camels, fish, and every animal with claws. ʿIsa made lawful for them some of that. It is also permissible that it is a repetition of His words ﴿I have come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾, meaning: I have come to you with one sign after another of what I have mentioned to you: the creation of the bird, the healing, the raising of the dead, the telling of hidden things, and other things, such as my birth without a father, my speech in the cradle, and all the rest of that.

[Mahmud said: "If you ask why it is said 'ʿIsa son of Maryam' while the address is to Maryam... etc." Ahmad said: This answer is confirmed by her saying ﴿How can I have a son when no man has touched me?﴾, for there had not preceded in God's promise to her of a child anything indicating that he would be without a father. I answer: children are attributed to their fathers, not to their mothers. By attributing him to her, He informed her that he would be born without a father, so he would be attributed only to his mother. By this she was distinguished and chosen above the women of the worlds.

It is said there was no blind person in this community except Qatadah ibn Diʿama al-Sadusi, author of the tafsir. It is related that he brought back to life Sam son of Noah while they watched, and they said, "This is magic; show us a sign." What God had forbidden to them in the law of Moses: the fats and the thin fat covering the stomach and intestines (al-thurub, explained by al-Sihah), the flesh of camels, fish, and every animal with claws. ʿIsa made lawful for them some of that. The meaning of the reading of the one who read with a fatḥa is: "and because God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him," like His words ﴿for the accustomed security of Quraysh... so let them worship﴾.

It is also permissible that the meaning is: "and I have come to you with a sign, that God is my Lord and your Lord," and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection.

The Messiah (al-Masih) is one of the honorific epithets (laqab), like al-Siddiq and al-Faruq. Its origin is the Hebrew *meshiha*, meaning "the blessed one," as in His words ﴿and He has made me blessed wherever I may be﴾. Likewise, ʿIsa (Jesus) is an arabicized form of *Yeshua*. Both names are derived from *al-mash* (wiping) and *al-ʿays* (the mingling of water with earth), like one who writes in water.

If you ask: with what does ﴿when she said﴾ connect? I answer: it is a substitute (badl) for ﴿when the angels said﴾. It may also be a substitute for ﴿when they were disputing﴾, on the basis that the disputing and the good tidings occurred over a long period, as when you say, "I met him in such-and-such a year."

If you ask: why is it said "ʿIsa son of Maryam" when the address is to Maryam?

[Mahmud said: "If you ask why it is said 'ʿIsa son of Maryam' while the address is to Maryam... etc." Ahmad said: This answer is confirmed by her saying ﴿How can I have a son when no man has touched me?﴾, for there had not preceded in God's promise to her of a child anything indicating that he would be without a father. Yet when He attributed him to her, this showed that she understood from it that he would be without a father. And God knows best.]

I answer: children are attributed to their fathers, not to their mothers. By attributing him to her, He informed her that he would be born without a father, so he would be attributed only to his mother. By this she was distinguished and chosen above the women of the worlds.

If you ask: why is the pronoun for "word" used? I answer: because the one named by it is masculine.

If you ask: why is it said "his name is the Messiah, ʿIsa son of Maryam," when these are three things: the name is ʿIsa, while the Messiah and "son" are a title and an attribute?

[(His speech resumes.) He said: "If you ask why it is said 'his name is the Messiah, ʿIsa son of Maryam'..." etc. Ahmad said: In this explanation there is a way out of a difficulty that they raise. They say: if "the Messiah" in the verse is taken to mean the name, which is the apparent sense, then what is the place of "ʿIsa son of Maryam"? And a name is not described as a prophet. And if "the Messiah" is taken to mean the one named by this name, it does not fit with "his name." The difficulty is answered by saying that "the Messiah" is the predicate of "his name," and the intended meaning is the name. As for "ʿIsa son of Maryam," it is the predicate of an omitted subject, its sense being: "He is ʿIsa son of Maryam," and the pronoun refers to the one named by the aforementioned name, separated from the words of "the Messiah." What al-Zamakhshari established is not subject to this difficulty, and it is very good. And God knows best.]

I answer: the name is a sign for the named by which it is recognized and distinguished from others. It is as if it were said: that by which he is recognized and distinguished from all others is the combination of these three.

﴿honorable in this world and the Hereafter﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from ﴿a word﴾. Likewise His words ﴿and among those brought near﴾, ﴿and he will speak﴾, and ﴿and among the righteous﴾. That is: He gives you good tidings of him described by these attributes. The accusative of the circumstantial clause from an indefinite noun is valid because it is qualified.

Honor (wajaha) in this world is prophethood and precedence over people. In the Hereafter it is intercession and high rank in Paradise. His being ﴿among those brought near﴾ is His raising him to heaven and his companionship with the angels.

Al-mahd is what is prepared for the child as his bed; it is named by the verbal noun.

﴿in the cradle﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause, and ﴿and as a grown man﴾ is conjoined to it. The meaning is: "he will speak to people as a child and as a grown man."

Its meaning: he will speak to people in these two states with the speech of prophets, with no difference between the state of childhood and the state of maturity in which reason is complete and prophets receive revelation.

Among the strange interpretations (bida al-tafasir) is that her words ﴿My Lord﴾ are an address to Gabriel, peace be upon him, meaning "O my lord." (﴿And teach him﴾) is conjoined to ﴿will give you good tidings﴾, or to ﴿honorable﴾, or to ﴿will create﴾, or it is an independent statement. ʿAsim and Nafiʿ read *wa-yuʿallimuhu* with the yaʾ.

If you ask: on what do you take ﴿and a messenger﴾ and ﴿confirming﴾, from the preceding accusatives, when His words ﴿that I have come to you﴾ and ﴿of what is before me﴾ refuse to take them that way?

I answer: this is one of the difficult points, and there are two views. The first: that "and I have been sent" is implied before it, intending the saying, its sense being: "and He will teach him the Book and the wisdom, and he will say, 'I have been sent as a messenger that I have come to you,' and confirming what is before me." The second: that "messenger" and "confirming" carry the sense of speech, so it is as if it were said: "and speaking that I have come to you, and speaking that I confirm what is before me."

Al-Yazidi read *wa-rasulun* (and a messenger), conjoined to the words ﴿that I have come to you﴾. The original is "I have been sent with the sign that I have come to you," so the preposition was omitted and the verb governed the accusative.

﴿That I create﴾ is in the accusative as a substitute for ﴿that I have come to you﴾, or in the genitive as a substitute for ﴿a sign﴾, or in the nominative: "it is that I create for you." It was also read *inni* with a kasra, as a new sentence, meaning: "I will determine for you something like the form of a bird."

﴿And I breathe into it﴾: the pronoun refers to the *kaf* (the "you" of "I create you" in the sense of that thing), meaning: into that thing resembling the shape of a bird. ﴿So it becomes a bird﴾: it becomes a bird like other birds, alive. ʿAbdullah read: *fa-anfukhuha* (so I breathe into it).

[The poet said:
"Mawla al-rih qarnayhi wa-jabhatahu... kal-hibraqi tanahha yanfukhu al-fahma"
By Nabigha, describing a wild bull that has turned its two horns and forehead toward the wind. He faces it with his head and breathes against it with his mouth, so a sound is heard from him. He is like the *hibraqi* (wazn Jaʿfari and Zabarjī), which is the blacksmith and the goldsmith. It is narrated as *kal-harqi*, meaning the smith, a relation to the burning of the fire. He likened him to one who has withdrawn to a side, blowing on glowing coal with the fire, so that "blowing" is a circumstantial clause interlocked.]

It is said that he created nothing but the bat. ﴿The blind﴾ is the one born blind; it is also said he was the one whose eyes were wiped smooth. It is said there was no blind person in this community except Qatadah ibn Diʿama al-Sadusi, author of the tafsir. It is related that fifty thousand sick people would often gather around him; whoever could come came to him, and whoever could not, ʿIsa came to. His cure was by supplication alone. ﴿By God's permission﴾ is repeated to repel the thought of one who suspects in him divinity. It is related that he brought back to life Sam son of Noah while they watched, and they said, "This is magic; show us a sign." So he said, "O so-and-so, you ate such-and-such, and O so-and-so, you have stored such-and-such for yourself."

*Tadhkharun* is also read with a dhal and without shadda. ﴿And to make lawful﴾ is a reference back to His words ﴿with a sign from your Lord﴾, meaning: I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, and to make lawful for you. It is also permissible that "confirming" is referred back to likewise, meaning: I have come to you with a sign, and I have come to you confirming.

What God had forbidden to them in the law of Moses: the fats and the thin fat covering the stomach and intestines (al-thurub, explained by al-Sihah), the flesh of camels, fish, and every animal with claws. ʿIsa made lawful for them some of that. It is said he made lawful for them fish and birds that have no spur (al-sisiyya, the thorn like that on a rooster's leg, explained by al-Sihah). They differed about his making lawful the Sabbath for them.

﴿Was forbidden to you﴾ is read in the active form, and the subject is either what lies before me of the Torah, or God, the Mighty and Majestic, or Moses, peace be upon him, since mention of the Torah indicates him, and since it was known to them. It is also read *ḥurrima* in the pattern of *kurrima*.

﴿And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾: a witness to the truth of my messengership, namely His words ﴿Indeed God is my Lord and your Lord﴾, because all the messengers held this statement and did not differ about it. It is also read with a fatḥa as a substitute for ﴿a sign﴾.

His words ﴿So fear God and obey me﴾ are a parenthetical interjection.

If you ask: how did he make this statement a sign from his Lord? I answer: because God made it a sign for him by which he is known to be a messenger like the other messengers, since He guided him to consider the evidences of reason and to reason.

It is also permissible that it is a repetition of His words ﴿I have come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾, meaning: I have come to you with one sign after another of what I have mentioned to you: the creation of the bird, the healing, the raising of the dead, the telling of hidden things, and other things, such as my birth without a father, my speech in the cradle, and all the rest of that.

ʿAbdullah read: *wa-jiʾtukum bi-ayatin min rabbikum, fa-ttaqu Allah lima jiʾtukum bihi min al-ayat, wa-ati'uni fima adʿukum ilayhi* (and I have come to you with signs from your Lord; so fear God for what I have brought you of the signs, and obey me in what I call you to). Then he began: "Indeed God is my Lord and your Lord."

The meaning of the reading of the one who read with a fatḥa is: "and because God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him," like His words ﴿for the accustomed security of Quraysh... so let them worship﴾.

It is also permissible that the meaning is: "and I have come to you with a sign, that God is my Lord and your Lord," and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection.

When Jesus sensed disbelief from them, (that is, he knew it with a certainty free of any doubt, like knowledge of what is perceived by the senses), he said: "Who are my helpers in the cause of God?" (The phrase) "to God" (ilā Allāh) is connected to "helpers" (anṣārī), with the sense of addition implied, as if it were said: "Who among those who attribute themselves to God will help me as I am helped?" Or it may be connected to an omitted element as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the "ya" (of my), meaning: "my helpers, going to God, seeking refuge in Him." The disciples said: "We are God's helpers" (anṣār Allāh), that is, helpers of His religion and His Messenger. The ḥawārī (disciple, apostle) of a man is his choice and his pure one. From this comes the term ḥawāriyyāt for urban women, because of the purity of their complexions and their cleanliness. A poet said:

"So say to the ḥawāriyyāt (the city women) to weep for others than us, and let only the barking dogs weep for us."

[The poet, al-Yashkurī, means: say to the urban women, pure of whiteness, to weep for others than us, as a metaphor that we are not among the people of luxury. Then he forbade anyone from weeping for them except the dogs that are driven with them for hunting, or those accustomed to eating their slain in war, or those that bark at them when they approach their companions, as a metaphor that they are of the people of the desert and of raiding.]

Its measure is ḥawārī, and it is also (used for) one who is very resourceful in stratagem. They asked for his testimony to their Islam only as a confirmation of their faith, because the messengers testify on the Day of Resurrection for their peoples and against them. "With the witnesses" (ma'a al-shāhidīn): with the prophets who testify for their nations, or with those who testify to the Oneness (of God). It was also said: "with the community of Muhammad (ﷺ)," because they are witnesses over mankind.

"And they schemed" (wa-makarū): the waw refers to the disbelieving Children of Israel, from whom disbelief was sensed. Their scheme was that they appointed someone to kill him secretly. "And God schemed" (wa-makara Allāh): He raised Jesus to heaven and made his likeness fall upon the one who sought to assassinate him, so that he was killed. "And God is the best of schemers": the most powerful of them in scheming, the most penetrating in plotting, and the most capable of punishment from a direction the one punished does not perceive.

When God said, "O Jesus, I am going to take you and raise you to Me and purify you from those who disbelieve," this clause is either a time reference governing "the best of deceivers" or a time reference governing "God's plotting." ﴿I am going to take you in full﴾ means: I will complete your term, that is, I will make you fulfil your appointed time.[[His words "i.e., completing your term, meaning: I will preserve you" are based on the view that one who is killed dies before his term is completed, which is the view of the Mu'tazilah (rationalist theological school). (ع)]] Its meaning is: I will preserve you from being killed by the disbelievers, and I will postpone you until a term I have decreed for you, and I will cause you to die a natural death, not to be slain at their hands. ﴿And raise you to Me﴾: to My heaven, the abode of My angels. ﴿And purify you from those who disbelieve﴾: from the evil of their company and the corruption of their fellowship.

It is also said: "mutawaffika" means "I will take you from the earth," from the expression "tawaffaytu māli ʿalā fulān," meaning "I took my full due from so-and-so," when one has received it in full. It is also said: "I will cause you to die at your appointed time after you descend from heaven, and raise you now." It is also said: "one who causes you to receive your sleep in full," from His words ﴿And the one who has not died in her sleep﴾ (39:42). "And raise you" refers to raising you while you are asleep, so that no fear reaches you, and you awaken while you are in heaven, safe and near.

﴿Above those who disbelieve﴾ until the Day of Resurrection: they will be superior to them by proof, and in most circumstances by proof and by the sword. "Those who follow him" are the Muslims, because they follow him in the basic principles of Islam even though the sacred laws differ. This excludes those who denied him and lied about him, such as the Jews and Christians. ﴿So I will judge between you﴾: the explanation of the judgment is His words ﴿So I will punish them﴾ ... ﴿and We will pay them their wages in full﴾.[[His words "so I will punish them, then We will pay them" refer to those who disbelieved. His words "then We will pay them..." etc. refer to those who believed. (ع)]] It is also read as ﴿fa-yuwaffīhim﴾ with the letter yā' (third person masculine).

This is the translation of the passage from al-Zamakhshari's al-Kashshaf on Surah Al ʿImran, verse 58:

"That" refers to what has preceded of the account of ʿIsa (Jesus) and others, and it is the subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is "We recite it" (natluhu), and "from the signs" (min al-ayat) is a predicate following a predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf). It is also permissible for "dhalika" to mean "alladhi" (that which), with "natluhu" as its relative clause (silah), and "min al-ayat" as the predicate. It is also permissible for "dhalika" to be in the accusative, governed by an implied verb whose explanation is "natluhu."

"And the Wise Reminder" (wa al-dhikr al-hakim) is the Qur'an, described by an attribute of the one who is its cause (i.e., God, the Wise), or as if it speaks with wisdom because of the abundance of its wisdom (hukm).

The case of Jesus, in his strange condition, is like the case of Adam. His saying "He created him from dust" is an explanatory clause for what made the comparison (the matter for which that comparison was made). That is, Adam was created from dust, with neither father nor mother, and so is the condition of Jesus.

If you say: how is he compared to him when he (Jesus) came into being without a father, and Adam came into being without a father and a mother?

I say: He resembles him in one of the two respects, and his being singled out in the other respect does not prevent the comparison, because likeness is sharing in some attributes. Also, he is compared to him because he came into being in a way outside the constant custom, and the two are alike in that. Also, existence without a father and a mother is more strange and more contrary to custom than existence without a father, so the strange is compared with the stranger, so as to be more decisive against the opponent and to cut off the root of his doubt when he considers something stranger than what he finds strange.

It is related from some scholars that he was taken captive by the Byzantines, and he said to them: "Why do you worship Jesus?" They said: "Because he had no father." He said: "Then Adam is more deserving, for he had neither father nor mother." They said: "He used to raise the dead." He said: "Then Ezekiel is more deserving, for Jesus raised four men, and Ezekiel raised eight thousand." They said: "He used to heal the blind and the leper." He said: "Then Jirjis (George) is more deserving, for he was boiled and burned and then stood up unharmed."

"He created him from dust": He fashioned him as a body from clay. "Then He said to him: Be," meaning He brought him into being as a human, like His saying (Then We brought into being after him another creation) [23:14]. "So he was": this is a narration of a past state.

The Truth is from your Lord: [it is] a predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf), meaning "it is the truth," like the saying of the people of Khaybar: "Muhammad and the army!" [[This is part of a hadith of Anas, agreed upon (in al-Bukhari and Muslim), with the wording: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) attacked the people of Khaybar at dawn, and they had come out with their spades on their shoulders. When they saw him, they said: 'Muhammad and the army!' ... the hadith." It will come later in Surat al-Saffat.]].

His prohibition of doubt, although the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is far too exalted to be one who doubts, is a means of stirring him to greater steadfastness and tranquility, and so that it may serve as a gentle lesson for others.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 3, verse 61:**

﴿فَمَنْ حَاجَّكَ مِنَ النَّصَارَىٰ فِيهِ مِن بَعْدِ مَا جَاءَكَ مِنَ الْعِلْمِ﴾: that is, from the clear proofs that necessitate knowledge. ﴿تَعَالَوْا﴾: come, let us (lit. "hasten"). The intended meaning is coming with resolve and determination, as we say, "Come, let us think about this matter."

﴿نَدْعُ أَبْنَاءَنَا وَأَبْنَاءَكُمْ﴾: that is, each of us and each of you calls his sons, his women, and himself to mubahala (mutual invocation of divine curse, a mutual imprecation before God).

﴿ثُمَّ نَبْتَهِلْ﴾: then we invoke (mutual) cursing, by saying, "May the curse of God (bahlat Allah) be upon the liar among us and among you." Al-bahlah with a fatha or a damma means "curse." "Allah bahalahu" means God cursed him and removed him far from His mercy, from your saying "abhalahu" when one neglects something. "Naqah bahil" means a camel left without its suckling-restraint (its teats tied, so it is not nursed). The root of ibtihal is this, and then it was used for any supplication in which one strives earnestly, even if it does not involve cursing.

It is related that when he invited them to mubahala, they said, "Let us go back and consider." When they withdrew privately, they said to al-'Aqib, who was their leader in judgment, "O Abd al-Masih, what do you think?" He said: "By God, you have known, O assembly of Christians, that Muhammad is a prophet sent, and he has brought you the decisive word concerning your companion's affair. By God, no people have ever invoked mubahala with a prophet and then their elders lived or their young grew up. If you do it, you will surely perish. If you refuse except to cling to your religion and remain upon what you are upon, then make peace with the man and return to your lands." So he came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) having set out in the morning embracing al-Husayn, holding al-Hasan by the hand, with Fatimah walking behind him and 'Ali behind her, and he was saying: "When I supplicate, say 'Amen.'" Then the bishop of Najran said: "O assembly of Christians, I see faces that, if God wished to remove a mountain from its place, He would remove it by them. So do not invoke mubahala, lest you perish and not a Christian remain upon the face of the earth until the Day of Resurrection." They said: "O Abu al-Qasim, our view is that we will not invoke mubahala against you, and that you leave us upon our religion and we remain upon ours." He said: "If you refuse mubahala, then submit to Islam, and you will have what the Muslims have and you will bear what they bear." They refused. He said: "Then I will fight you." They said:

"We have no power to fight the Arabs, but we will make peace with you on condition that you do not attack us, nor frighten us, nor turn us back from our religion, on condition that we pay you every year two thousand garments: one thousand in Safar and one thousand in Rajab, and thirty ancient iron coats of mail." So he made peace with them on that basis.

[Abu Nu'aym transmitted it in Dala'il al-Nubuwwah, through the chain of Muhammad ibn Marwan al-Suddi from al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, at length. Ibn Marwan is abandoned (matruk) and accused of lying. Then Abu Nu'aym transmitted something similar from al-Sha'bi as a mursal report, in which: "If you refuse mubahala, then submit to Islam, and you will have what the Muslims have and bear what they bear. If you refuse, then give us the jizyah (poll tax), as God Most High said." They said: "We own nothing but ourselves." He said: "If you refuse, then I will throw (the treaty) back to you on equal terms." They said: "We have no power to fight the Arabs, but we will pay the jizyah." So he imposed on them every year two thousand garments: one thousand in Safar and one thousand in Rajab. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The bearer of good news has come to me with the destruction of the people of Najran had they carried through with the mutual cursing." Al-Tabari transmitted it through the chain of Abu Ishaq, who said: "Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr related to me concerning His words, ﴿إِنَّ هَٰذَا لَهُوَ الْقَصَصُ الْحَقُّ﴾ [Surely this is the true narrative]," and he mentioned it as a mursal report. In Sunan Abi Dawud, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: "The Prophet (ﷺ) made peace with the people of Najran for two thousand garments, half in Safar and the rest in Rajab, which they would deliver to the Muslims, and lent thirty coats of mail, thirty horses, thirty camels, and thirty of every kind of weapon, with which they would fight, and the Muslims would be guarantors for them until they returned them to them." This is a part of this story.]

And he (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, destruction has already hung over the people of Najran. Had they invoked the curse, they would have been transformed into monkeys and pigs, the valley would have blazed with fire upon them, and God would have uprooted Najran and its people, even the birds upon the treetops, and the year would not have passed over all the Christians before they perished."

It is related from 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out wearing a striped cloak of black wool. Then al-Hasan came and he took him in, then al-Husayn came and he took him in, then Fatimah, then 'Ali, and then he said: [Muslim transmitted it through the chain of Safiyyah bint Shaybah from her. al-Hakim overlooked it and so sought to add it as a supplement (mustadrak).]

﴿إِنَّمَا يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ لِيُذْهِبَ عَنكُمُ الرِّجْسَ أَهْلَ الْبَيْتِ﴾ [God only desires to remove from you the impurity, O People of the House].

If you say: His invitation to mubahala was only so that the liar among him and his opponent might be made clear, and that is a matter specific to him and to whoever disputes with him. So what is the meaning of including the sons and women? I say: That is more emphatic in showing his confidence in his own condition and his certainty of his truthfulness, since he dared to expose his dearest ones and the fruit of his liver (aflidh kabidihi, i.e., his most beloved ones) and the people most beloved to him to this, and did not limit himself to exposing only his own person, and (this showed) his confidence in the lying of his opponent, so that his opponent would perish together with his beloved ones and dear ones by the destruction of annihilation, should the mubahala be carried through. He singled out the sons and women because they are the most precious of family and the closest to the hearts; a man may ransom them with himself and fight in their defense until he is killed. For this reason, they used to drive the camel-litters (zaʿa'in) with themselves into battles, so that they would prevent them from fleeing, and they called those who defended them with their lives "the guardians of the sacred" (hamat al-haqa'iq). He mentioned them before the souls in the wording to draw attention to their exalted place and nearness of status, and to indicate that they are put forward before the souls and are ransomed by them. In this there is an evidence, nothing stronger than it, of the excellence of the People of the Cloak, peace be upon them. And in it there is a clear proof of the truth of the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ), because no one, whether a supporter or an opponent, has reported that they accepted that.

Indeed, this that was related to you of the news of ʿĪsā (Jesus) is ﴿the true narrative﴾. It is recited with the hāʾ vowelled, لَهُوَ (lahuwa), according to the original form, and also with sukūn, لَهْوَ (lahwa). The reason is that the lām takes the place of part of هو (huwa), so it was lightened, as عضد (ʿaḍd) was lightened from عَضُد (ʿaḍud).

The word هو (huwa) is either a faṣl (separating pronoun) between the ism of إن (inna, its subject) and its khabar (predicate), or a mubtada' (subject) whose khabar is القصص الحق (al-qaṣaṣ al-ḥaqq), and the whole clause is the khabar of إن (inna).

If you ask: why is the lām permitted to enter on the faṣl? I say: since it is permitted for it to enter on the khabar, its entry on the faṣl is even more permissible, because the faṣl is closer to the mubtada' than the khabar is, and the original place of this lām is to enter upon the mubtada'.

The من (min) in His words ﴿There is no god but Allah﴾ has the same status as the building upon fatḥa in لا إله إلا الله (lā ilāha illā Allāh) in conveying the meaning of comprehensiveness (istighrāq). The purpose is a refutation of the Christians in their doctrine of the Trinity.

His words ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of the corrupters﴾ are a threat to them of the punishment mentioned in His words ﴿We will increase them in punishment upon punishment for what they used to corrupt﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verse 64–68:

﴿Say: O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you﴾. It is said: they are the people of the two Scriptures (Jews and Christians). It is said: the delegation of Najran. It is said: the Jews of Medina.

﴿Equitable (sawa')﴾ between us and you: level, with nothing in it that the Qur'an, the Torah and the Gospel disagree about. The explanation of the word is His saying: ﴿that we worship none but Allah, and that we associate nothing with Him, and that some of us do not take others as lords besides Allah﴾, meaning: come to it, so that we do not say, "Uzayr is the son of Allah," nor "the Messiah is the son of Allah," because each of them is a human being like us. And [that we do not] obey our rabbis in what they have innovated of prohibition and permission without returning to what Allah has legislated, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah, and [also] the Messiah, son of Mary; yet they were commanded only to worship one God﴾ [9:31].

And on the authority of 'Adi ibn Hatim: "We did not worship them, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Did they not make lawful for you what was unlawful and unlawful what was lawful, and you followed their word?" He said: "Yes." He said: "That is it."

And on the authority of al-Fudayl: "I do not care whether I obey a created being in disobedience to the Creator, or pray facing other than the qibla."

It has been read as "kalima" with the lam sukun (kalimah). Al-Hasan read "sawa'" in the accusative, meaning "they became equal, in equality."

﴿But if they turn away, then say: Bear witness that we are Muslims﴾: that is, the proof has been established against you, so it is obligatory upon you to acknowledge and submit that we are Muslims, not you, just as the victor says to the vanquished in a dispute or a contest or other such matter: "Acknowledge that I am the victor and surrender the victory to me."

It may also be that it is an allusion, and its meaning is: bear witness and acknowledge that you are disbelievers, since you turned away from the truth after it had become manifest.

Each group among the Jews and Christians claimed that Abraham was of them, and they disputed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers concerning this. So it was said to them: Judaism came into being only after the revelation of the Torah, and Christianity after the revelation of the Gospel, and between Abraham and Moses there were a thousand years, and between him and Jesus two thousand. How then could Abraham be upon a religion that did not come into being until long after his time? ﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾ so that you do not argue with such an impossible argument.

﴿Ha, you are these who argued﴾: "ha" is for alerting, and "antum" is the subject and "ha'ulaa'" its predicate. "Hajajtum" is a resumptive clause explaining the first clause: meaning, you are these foolish persons, and the proof of your foolishness and small intellect is that you argued about ﴿what you have knowledge of﴾, that which the Torah and the Gospel spoke of. ﴿Why then do you argue about what you have no knowledge of﴾, and which is not mentioned in your books, concerning the religion of Abraham.

On the authority of al-Akhfash: "ha antum ha'ulaa'" is "a-antum" in interrogative form, and the hamza was changed into ha'. The meaning of the interrogative is wonder at their foolishness. It is also said that "ha'ulaa'" means "alladhina," and "hajajtum" is its relative clause.

﴿And Allah knows﴾, that is, knows fully what you argued about, ﴿and you do not know﴾ it. Then He informed them that He is free of their religion, and that he was only ﴿a upright monotheist, a Muslim﴾, ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾, just as you were not. Or he meant by "the polytheists" the Jews and Christians, for their associating with Him Uzayr and the Messiah.

﴿Indeed, the most worthy of Abraham among mankind﴾, that is, the most particularly devoted to him and nearest to him by way of close kinship (wilaya, which is nearness), ﴿are those who followed him﴾ in his time and after him, ﴿and this Prophet﴾ in particular, ﴿and those who believe﴾ from his community.

It is read "wa-hadha al-nabiyyu" in the accusative, as a conjunction with the pronoun in "ittaba'uhu," meaning: follow him and follow this Prophet. And in the genitive, as a conjunction with "Ibrahim."

﴿Say: O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you﴾. It is said: they are the people of the two Scriptures (Jews and Christians). It is said: the delegation of Najran. It is said: the Jews of Medina.

﴿Equitable (sawa')﴾ between us and you: level, with nothing in it that the Qur'an, the Torah and the Gospel disagree about. The explanation of the word is His saying: ﴿that we worship none but Allah, and that we associate nothing with Him, and that some of us do not take others as lords besides Allah﴾, meaning: come to it, so that we do not say, "Uzayr is the son of Allah," nor "the Messiah is the son of Allah," because each of them is a human being like us. And [that we do not] obey our rabbis in what they have innovated of prohibition and permission without returning to what Allah has legislated, as in His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah, and [also] the Messiah, son of Mary; yet they were commanded only to worship one God﴾ [9:31].

And on the authority of 'Adi ibn Hatim: "We did not worship them, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Did they not make lawful for you what was unlawful and unlawful what was lawful, and you followed their word?" He said: "Yes." He said: "That is it."

And on the authority of al-Fudayl: "I do not care whether I obey a created being in disobedience to the Creator, or pray facing other than the qibla."

It has been read as "kalima" with the lam sukun (kalimah). Al-Hasan read "sawa'" in the accusative, meaning "they became equal, in equality."

﴿But if they turn away, then say: Bear witness that we are Muslims﴾: that is, the proof has been established against you, so it is obligatory upon you to acknowledge and submit that we are Muslims, not you, just as the victor says to the vanquished in a dispute or a contest or other such matter: "Acknowledge that I am the victor and surrender the victory to me."

It may also be that it is an allusion, and its meaning is: bear witness and acknowledge that you are disbelievers, since you turned away from the truth after it had become manifest.

Each group among the Jews and Christians claimed that Abraham was of them, and they disputed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers concerning this. So it was said to them: Judaism came into being only after the revelation of the Torah, and Christianity after the revelation of the Gospel, and between Abraham and Moses there were a thousand years, and between him and Jesus two thousand. How then could Abraham be upon a religion that did not come into being until long after his time? ﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾ so that you do not argue with such an impossible argument.

﴿Ha, you are these who argued﴾: "ha" is for alerting, and "antum" is the subject and "ha'ulaa'" its predicate. "Hajajtum" is a resumptive clause explaining the first clause: meaning, you are these foolish persons, and the proof of your foolishness and small intellect is that you argued about ﴿what you have knowledge of﴾, that which the Torah and the Gospel spoke of. ﴿Why then do you argue about what you have no knowledge of﴾, and which is not mentioned in your books, concerning the religion of Abraham.

On the authority of al-Akhfash: "ha antum ha'ulaa'" is "a-antum" in interrogative form, and the hamza was changed into ha'. The meaning of the interrogative is wonder at their foolishness. It is also said that "ha'ulaa'" means "alladhina," and "hajajtum" is its relative clause.

﴿And Allah knows﴾, that is, knows fully what you argued about, ﴿and you do not know﴾ it. Then He informed them that He is free of their religion, and that he was only ﴿a upright monotheist, a Muslim﴾, ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾, just as you were not. Or he meant by "the polytheists" the Jews and Christians, for their associating with Him Uzayr and the Messiah.

﴿Indeed, the most worthy of Abraham among mankind﴾, that is, the most particularly devoted to him and nearest to him by way of close kinship (wilaya, which is nearness), ﴿are those who followed him﴾ in his time and after him, ﴿and this Prophet﴾ in particular, ﴿and those who believe﴾ from his community.

It is read "wa-hadha al-nabiyyu" in the accusative, as a conjunction with the pronoun in "ittaba'uhu," meaning: follow him and follow this Prophet. And in the genitive, as a conjunction with "Ibrahim."

Surah 3, verses 69–71:

A group of the People of the Book wished to lead you astray. They were the Jews, who invited Hudhayfah, ʿAmmar and Muʿadh to Judaism. *"And they lead none astray but themselves"*: the burden of misguidance falls only upon them, because their punishment is multiplied for their own misguidance and for their misguiding others. Or it means: they are unable to lead the Muslims astray; they only mislead their likes among their followers. *"Concerning the signs of Allah"*: that is, the Torah and the Injil (Gospel). Their disbelief in them is that they do not believe in what they declare concerning the truth of the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and other matters. *"While you bear witness"*: their acknowledgment that they are the signs of Allah. Or: *"Why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah"*, meaning the Qur'an and the indicators of the Messenger's prophethood, *"while you bear witness"* to his description in the two Books. Or: *"Why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah altogether while you know that they are true?"*

The reading *talbisūna* (تَلْبِسُونَ) with doubling (tashdīd) is also recited.

Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb read *talbasūna* (تَلْبَسُونَ) with a fatḥa on the bā', meaning "you mix the truth with falsehood," as in the saying: *"like one who dresses in two garments of falsehood."* And as in the line:

*"Never was there a father and a son like Marwān and his son, when he clothed himself in glory and girded himself with it."*

This is by al-Farazdaq. The word *wa-ibnan* (وَابْنًا) is in the accusative, coordinated with the position of *ab* (أب), and *mithl* (مثل) may be read in the nominative as the predicate of *lā* (لا), or in the accusative as an attribute of *ab wa-ibnan*, with the predicate omitted.

*Wa-ibnihi* refers to ʿAbd al-Malik. *"Idhā huwa"* refers to Marwān, because the glory of the son derives from the glory of the father, not the reverse. The "glory" here means the praiseworthy deeds that renew from him. Then he likened glory to a garment, by the shared quality of protecting each one who wears it, in the manner of the metaphor by allusion (*al-makniyya*). The verbs *irtadā* (ارتدى, "clothed himself") and *ta'azzara* (تأزر, "girded himself") are imaginative (*takhyīl*). It is also possible that he likened the attainment of it outwardly and inwardly to clothing oneself and girding oneself, in the manner of the explicit metaphor (*al-tasrīḥiyya*). It is also permissible that *idhā* here indicates continuous time, not the future alone.

The day's face means its beginning. He said:

*"Whoever is glad at the killing of Malik,
let him come to our women at the face of the day.
He will find them bareheaded, lamenting him,
striking their faces at dawn."*

This is by Rabi' ibn Ziyad, lamenting Malik ibn Zuhayr al-'Absi. "The face of the day" means its beginning. *Hawasir* means those who uncover their faces. The metre was altered (*sarf lil-wazn*). *Nadba* means raising the voice in weeping over the dead. *Asहar* means the front of the upper necks. The *ba'* (in *bi-wajh*) means "with."

It was the custom of the Arabs not to lament a slain man until his blood-vengeance had been taken. So the elegy contains the sense of praise for them and of gloating over their enemy. He said: whoever is pleased by his killing, let him come to our women at the beginning of the day, and he will find them with their faces uncovered, weeping for him with raised voices, striking their faces together with the fronts of their necks. This means that we have avenged him, so it is lawful for our women to weep for him. Ibn al-'Amid criticised his saying "let him come to our women" (*fa-l-ya'ti nisawatana*). But how excellent is Imam al-Marzuqi, who replaced it with "let him come to our courtyard" (*fa-l-ya'ti sahatana*), because this also avoids moving from explicit mention (*izhar*) to the pronominal reference (*idmar*) at that point.

The meaning is: show belief in what was revealed to the Muslims at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve in it at its end, so that perhaps they will doubt their religion and say: "They returned, and they are people of the Book and knowledge, so they would not have returned unless a matter had become clear to them." Then they will return with your return.

It is also said: twelve rabbis of the Jews of Khaybar agreed among themselves, and some of them said to others: enter the religion of Muhammad at the beginning of the day without true conviction, and disbelieve in it at the end of the day, and say: "We examined our books and consulted our scholars, and we found that Muhammad is not the one described in them, and his falsehood and the invalidity of his religion became clear to us." When you do this, his companions will doubt their religion.

It is also said: this concerns the direction of prayer (*qibla*). When it was turned toward the Ka'bah, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf said to his companions: believe in what was revealed to them concerning prayer toward the Ka'bah, and pray toward it at the beginning of the day, then disbelieve in it at its end and pray toward the Rock. Perhaps they will say: "They know more than we do, and they have returned," so they will return.

﴿And do not believe﴾ is connected to the words ﴿that anyone should be given﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*). That is: do not openly display your belief that anyone should be given the like of what you were given, except to the people of your religion and no others. They meant: keep secret your confirmation that the Muslims have been given the like of what you were given from God's books. Do not reveal it except to your own partisans alone, not to the Muslims, lest it increase them in steadfastness, nor to the polytheists, lest it call them to Islam.

﴿Or they will argue with you before your Lord﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with ﴿that anyone should be given﴾.

[Mahmud said: "﴿or they will argue with you﴾ is coordinated with ﴿that anyone should be given﴾... etc." Ahmad said: In this grammatical construction there is a difficulty, which is that ﴿anyone﴾ (*ahad*) occurs in an affirmed (obligatory) context. This is because the interrogative here is one of denial, and an interrogative of denial in such a context is affirmative. Its sum is that he denied and rebuked them for what they had done, namely concealing their belief that prophethood is not restricted to the Children of Israel, for the two reasons mentioned. So it is a confirmed affirmation. It may be said: the form of the interrogative was observed even though the intended meaning is not literal, and so it was proper for ﴿anyone﴾ to fall within its scope. And God knows best.]

The pronoun in ﴿they will argue with you﴾ refers to ﴿anyone﴾ because it has the sense of the plural. [Mahmud said: "the pronoun in ﴿they will argue with you﴾ refers to ﴿anyone﴾ because it has the sense of the plural... etc." Ahmad said: That is, since it is an indefinite noun in a negated context, as He described it with the plural in His words: ﴿there is none among you who could withhold from Him﴾ (69:47).]

The meaning is: do not believe except for your followers, that the Muslims will argue with you on the Day of Resurrection with the truth, and will overcome you before God, Exalted, with proof.

If you say: what is the meaning of the parenthetical insertion? I say: its meaning is that guidance is God's guidance. Whoever He wills to show kindness to, so that he submits to Islam, or whose steadfastness in Islam He wishes to increase, that will happen, and your plotting, your tricks, and your display of confirmation will not benefit you against the Muslims or the polytheists. Likewise is His saying: ﴿Say: indeed, bounty is in God's hand; He gives it to whomever He wills﴾ (3:73), meaning guidance and success.

Or the speech is complete at His words ﴿except for those who follow your religion﴾, meaning: do not believe this outward belief, which is their belief at the beginning of the day, except for those who follow your religion:

except for those among you who were followers of your religion, from among those who had embraced Islam from among you, because their return was more hoped for in their view than the return of others, and because their conversion was more enraging to them.

His saying ﴿that anyone should be given﴾ means: because anyone should be given the like of what you were given, you said that and plotted it, and for no other reason. That is, the envy and insolence within you, that anyone should be given the like of what you were given of the excellence of knowledge and the Book, prompted you to say what you said. The evidence for this is the reading of Ibn Kathir: *a-an yu'ta aḥad*, with an added interrogative hamza for affirmation and rebuke, meaning: "Is it that anyone should be given...?"

If you say: what then is the meaning of His saying ﴿or they will argue with you﴾ according to this reading? I say: its meaning is that you plotted what you plotted because anyone should be given the like of what you were given, and because of what would follow from their arguing with you before your Lord when you disbelieve in it.

It is also permissible that ﴿the guidance of God﴾ is a substitute for ﴿the guidance﴾, and ﴿that anyone should be given﴾ is the predicate of *inna* (indeed), meaning: say, indeed the guidance of God is that anyone should be given the like of what you were given, or that they should argue with you, so that they argue with you before your Lord and expose your falsehood with their truth and refute your proof.

It was also read: *in yu'ta aḥad*, with *in* being the negative particle (*in al-nafiyya*), and it is connected to the speech of the People of the Book. That is: do not believe except for those who follow your religion, and say to them: no one is given the like of what you were given, until they argue with you before your Lord; meaning, they are not given its like, so they will not argue with you.

It is also permissible that ﴿that anyone should be given﴾ is in the accusative by a verb implied by His saying ﴿and do not believe except for those who follow your religion﴾, as if it were said: say, indeed the guidance is God's guidance, so do not deny that anyone should be given the like of what you were given, because their saying ﴿and do not believe except for those who follow your religion﴾ is a denial that anyone should be given the like of what they were given.

It is also said: twelve rabbis of the Jews of Khaybar agreed among themselves, and some of them said to others: enter the religion of Muhammad at the beginning of the day without true conviction, and disbelieve in it at the end of the day, and say: "We examined our books and consulted our scholars, and we found that Muhammad is not the one described in them, and his falsehood and the invalidity of his religion became clear to us." When you do this, his companions will doubt their religion.

It is also said: this concerns the direction of prayer (*qibla*). When it was turned toward the Ka'bah, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf said to his companions: believe in what was revealed to them concerning prayer toward the Ka'bah, and pray toward it at the beginning of the day, then disbelieve in it at its end and pray toward the Rock. Perhaps they will say: "They know more than we do, and they have returned," so they will return.

﴿And do not believe﴾ is connected to the words ﴿that anyone should be given﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*). That is: do not openly display your belief that anyone should be given the like of what you were given, except to the people of your religion and no others. They meant: keep secret your confirmation that the Muslims have been given the like of what you were given from God's books. Do not reveal it except to your own partisans alone, not to the Muslims, lest it increase them in steadfastness, nor to the polytheists, lest it call them to Islam.

﴿Or they will argue with you before your Lord﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with ﴿that anyone should be given﴾.

[Mahmud said: "﴿or they will argue with you﴾ is coordinated with ﴿that anyone should be given﴾... etc." Ahmad said: In this grammatical construction there is a difficulty, which is that ﴿anyone﴾ (*ahad*) occurs in an affirmed (obligatory) context. This is because the interrogative here is one of denial, and an interrogative of denial in such a context is affirmative. Its sum is that he denied and rebuked them for what they had done, namely concealing their belief that prophethood is not restricted to the Children of Israel, for the two reasons mentioned. So it is a confirmed affirmation. It may be said: the form of the interrogative was observed even though the intended meaning is not literal, and so it was proper for ﴿anyone﴾ to fall within its scope. And God knows best.]

The pronoun in ﴿they will argue with you﴾ refers to ﴿anyone﴾ because it has the sense of the plural. [Mahmud said: "the pronoun in ﴿they will argue with you﴾ refers to ﴿anyone﴾ because it has the sense of the plural... etc." Ahmad said: That is, since it is an indefinite noun in a negated context, as He described it with the plural in His words: ﴿there is none among you who could withhold from Him﴾ (69:47).]

The meaning is: do not believe except for your followers, that the Muslims will argue with you on the Day of Resurrection with the truth, and will overcome you before God, Exalted, with proof.

If you say: what is the meaning of the parenthetical insertion? I say: its meaning is that guidance is God's guidance. Whoever He wills to show kindness to, so that he submits to Islam, or whose steadfastness in Islam He wishes to increase, that will happen, and your plotting, your tricks, and your display of confirmation will not benefit you against the Muslims or the polytheists. Likewise is His saying: ﴿Say: indeed, bounty is in God's hand; He gives it to whomever He wills﴾ (3:73), meaning guidance and success.

Or the speech is complete at His words ﴿except for those who follow your religion﴾, meaning: do not believe this outward belief, which is their belief at the beginning of the day, except for those who follow your religion:

except for those among you who were followers of your religion, from among those who had embraced Islam from among you, because their return was more hoped for in their view than the return of others, and because their conversion was more enraging to them.

His saying ﴿that anyone should be given﴾ means: because anyone should be given the like of what you were given, you said that and plotted it, and for no other reason. That is, the envy and insolence within you, that anyone should be given the like of what you were given of the excellence of knowledge and the Book, prompted you to say what you said. The evidence for this is the reading of Ibn Kathir: *a-an yu'ta aḥad*, with an added interrogative hamza for affirmation and rebuke, meaning: "Is it that anyone should be given...?"

If you say: what then is the meaning of His saying ﴿or they will argue with you﴾ according to this reading? I say: its meaning is that you plotted what you plotted because anyone should be given the like of what you were given, and because of what would follow from their arguing with you before your Lord when you disbelieve in it.

It is also permissible that ﴿the guidance of God﴾ is a substitute for ﴿the guidance﴾, and ﴿that anyone should be given﴾ is the predicate of *inna* (indeed), meaning: say, indeed the guidance of God is that anyone should be given the like of what you were given, or that they should argue with you, so that they argue with you before your Lord and expose your falsehood with their truth and refute your proof.

It was also read: *in yu'ta aḥad*, with *in* being the negative particle (*in al-nafiyya*), and it is connected to the speech of the People of the Book. That is: do not believe except for those who follow your religion, and say to them: no one is given the like of what you were given, until they argue with you before your Lord; meaning, they are not given its like, so they will not argue with you.

It is also permissible that ﴿that anyone should be given﴾ is in the accusative by a verb implied by His saying ﴿and do not believe except for those who follow your religion﴾, as if it were said: say, indeed the guidance is God's guidance, so do not deny that anyone should be given the like of what you were given, because their saying ﴿and do not believe except for those who follow your religion﴾ is a denial that anyone should be given the like of what they were given.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 75–76:

From Ibn ʿAbbas: "Among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you" refers to ʿAbdullah ibn Salam. A man from Quraysh deposited with him one thousand two hundred ounces of gold, and he returned it to him. "And among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you" refers to Phinehas ibn ʿAzuraʾ (Finhas ibn ʿAzura). A man from Quraysh deposited a dinar with him, and he denied it and betrayed him.

It is also said: those who are trustworthy with much are the Christians, because trustworthiness predominates among them, and those who are treacherous with little are the Jews, because treachery predominates among them.

"Except while you remain standing over him" means: except for as long as you remain standing over him, O possessor of the right, standing at his head, pressing him for it and rebuking him, or by bringing the matter before the ruler and establishing proof against him. It is read "yuddihi" with a kasra on the hāʾ and with connection (wasl), and with the kasra without connection, and with sukun. Yahya ibn Wathhab read "taʾmanhu" with a kasra on the tāʾ. "Dumta" is with a kasra on the dāl, from dāma yadāmu.

"That" refers to the withholding of payment, which is implied by "he did not return it." That is, their leaving off the return of rights was because of their saying: "There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered (ummiyyin)," meaning: no reproach or censure may attach to us concerning the unlettered, by which they meant those who are not People of the Book, and what we do to them by withholding their property and harming them, because they are not upon our religion. They considered it lawful to wrong those who opposed them, saying: "He has not made for them any sanctity in our Book."

It is also said: the Jews dealt with men of Quraysh, and when they embraced Islam, the Jews demanded their dues, and they said: "You have no right over us, since you abandoned your religion." They claimed that they had found this in their Book.

From the Prophet (ﷺ), when this was revealed, he said: "The enemies of Allah have lied. Nothing from the Jahiliyyah is not under my feet, except trustworthiness, for it is to be rendered to the righteous and the wicked."

[[Narrated by al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim through Yaʿqub ibn al-Nuʿman al-Qummi, from Jaʿfar, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, as a mursal report.]]

From Ibn ʿAbbas: a man asked him, "We obtain in raids from the property of the dhimmis a hen or a sheep." He said: "What do you say?" He said: "We say there is no blame on us in that." He said: "That is like what the People of the Book said: there is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered. When they pay the jizya, it is not lawful for you to take their property except with their willing consent."

[[Narrated by ʿAbd al-Razzaq and al-Tabari through Abu Ishaq, from Saʿsaʿa ibn Muʿawiya, that he asked Ibn ʿAbbas, and he mentioned it.]]

"And they speak falsely against Allah" by their claim that this is in their Book, "while they know" that they are lying.

"Yes" is an affirmation of what they denied, namely that there is a way (blame) against them regarding the unlettered; that is, yes, there is a way against them concerning them.

His saying "Whoever fulfills his covenant and fears Allah" is a new sentence confirming the sentence that "yes" has stood in for. The pronoun in "his covenant" refers to "whoever fulfills." The meaning is that everyone who fulfills what he has covenanted and fears Allah by refraining from treachery and deceit, then Allah loves him.

If you say: this is general, and it suggests that if the People of the Book had fulfilled their covenants and abstained from treachery, they would have gained Allah's love. I say: Indeed, because when they fulfill covenants, they first fulfill the greatest covenant, which was taken from them in their Book: belief in a messenger confirming what is with them. And if they had feared Allah in refraining from treachery, they would have feared Him in refraining from lying against Allah and distorting His words.

It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to Allah Most High, so that everyone who fulfills the covenant of Allah and fears Him, Allah loves him. This includes faith and other righteous deeds, and what must be guarded against of disbelief and evil deeds.

If you say: then where is the pronoun returning from the conditional to "whoever"? I say: the generality of "the God-fearing" stands in place of the returning pronoun.

From Ibn ʿAbbas: it was revealed concerning ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, Bahira the monk, and their counterparts among the Muslim People of the Book.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 77–78:**

*Yashtarūn* (they exchange, sell): they substitute for *ʿahd Allāh* (the covenant of God) what they had pledged to Him regarding faith in the Messenger who confirms what is with them, and for *aymānihim* (their oaths), what they swore by when they said, "By God, we will certainly believe in him and surely support him." *Thamanan qalīlan* (a small price) is the enjoyment of this world: leadership, bribery, and the like.

It is said that it was revealed concerning Abu Rafi', Lubabah ibn Abi al-Huqayq, and Huyayy ibn Akhtab, who distorted the Torah, altered the description of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and took bribes for doing so.

It is also said: A group of Jews came to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf in a year when they were afflicted by famine, seeking provisions. He said to them, "Do you know that this man is the Messenger of God?" They said, "Yes." He said, "I had intended to hand you over (to him) and clothe you, but God has deprived you of much good."

They said, "Perhaps he has been confused for us. Give us time until we meet him." So they went off and wrote a description other than his description, then returned to him and said, "We made a mistake, and he is not the one described to us." He rejoiced and provided for them.

It is narrated from al-Ash'ath ibn Qays: "It was revealed concerning me. There was a dispute between me and a man over a well, and we brought our case before the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He said, 'Your two witnesses, or his oath.' I said, 'Then he will swear and not care.' He said, 'Whoever swears an oath by which he takes property that is not his, will meet God while He is angry with him.'" (Agreed upon from his narration.)

It is also said that it was revealed concerning a man who displayed merchandise in the market and swore that he had been offered for it a price that he had not been offered.

The soundest view is that it was revealed concerning the People of the Book.

God's words, *bi-ʿahd Allāh* (by the covenant of God), strengthen the view that the pronoun in *bi-ʿahdihi* refers back to God.

*Wa-lā yanẓuru ilayhim* (and He will not look at them) is a *majāz* (figurative usage) meaning contempt for them and displeasure with them. One says, "So-and-so does not look at so-and-so," meaning that he does not value him and does not show him kindness. *Wa-lā yuzakkīhim* (nor will He purify them) means nor will He praise them.

If you ask: What is the difference between using it of one who may be looked at and of one who cannot be looked at? I say: Its original sense, concerning one who may be looked at, is a *kināyah* (metonymy), because whoever values a person turns toward him and gives him the look of his eyes. Then it became common until it became an expression for valuing and kindness even when there was no looking. Then it was applied to one who cannot be looked at, purely in the sense of kindness, as a figurative usage of what had been a metonymy for one who can be looked at.

*La-farīqan* (a group): they are Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Malik ibn al-Sayf, Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and others. *Yalwūna alsinatahum bi-l-kitāb* (they twist their tongues with the Book): they bend them, in reciting it, from what is correct to what is distorted.

The people of Madinah read *yalawwūna* with a shadda (doubled letter), like His words, *lawaw ruʾūsahum* (they turned their heads). It is also narrated from Mujahid and Ibn Kathir: *yalūna*.

Its basis is that they changed the *wāw* that bears a *ḍamma* into a hamza, then lightened it by dropping it and transferring its vowel to the consonant before it.

If you ask: To what does the pronoun in *li-tahsabūhu* (that you may think it) refer? I say: To what is indicated by *yalawwūna alsinatahum bi-l-kitāb*, which is the distorted text. It is also possible that it means: they bend their tongues with something resembling the Book, so that you may think that resemblance to be from the Book. It was also read *li-yaḥsabūhu* with the *yāʾ*, meaning: they do this so that the Muslims may think it is from the Book.

*Wa-yaqūlūna huwa min ʿinda Allāh* (and they say, "It is from God") is an emphasis on His words "it is from the Book," an added reproach against them, a recording of their lying, and an indication that they do not evade or conceal, but openly declare that it is thus in the Torah, and that God revealed it to Moses in this form. This is because of their extreme audacity against God, the hardness of their hearts, and their despair of the Hereafter.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "They are the Jews who came to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. They altered the Torah and wrote a book in which they changed the description of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Then Qurayzah took what they had written and mixed it with the book they had."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 79–80:

It is not for a human being that he should be (given) the Book, the wisdom and prophethood, and then say to the people: "Be worshippers of me rather than of Allah." This is a rebuke to whoever believed in the worship of Jesus. It was also said: Abu Rafi' al-Qurazi and al-Sayyid, from the Christians of Najran, said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Do you want us to worship you and take you as a lord?" He said: "I seek refuge in Allah from worshipping other than Allah, or from commanding the worship of other than Allah! It is not for that that He sent me, nor for that did He command me." Then this was revealed.[[Al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and al-Tabari related it through Ibn Ishaq: "Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad related to me: Sa'id ibn Jubayr or Ikrimah related to me from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: 'The Christians of Najran and the Jewish rabbis gathered before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and disputed in his presence. The rabbis said: Abraham was only a Jew. The Christians said: Abraham was only a Christian. So Allah revealed concerning them (O People of the Book, why do you argue about Abraham?) - the verse. Abu Rafi' al-Qurazi and another man from among them, called al-Ra'is, who was the sayyid, said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he had invited them to Islam: "Do you want us, O Muhammad..." and he mentioned it.'" Al-Wahidi also mentioned in al-Asbab, through al-Kalbi and 'Ata' ibn 'Ayyash, that "Abu Rafi' and al-Ra'is, from the Christians of Najran, said: O Muhammad..." and he mentioned it.]]

It was also said: A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, we greet you as some of us greet one another. Should we not prostrate to you?" He said: "It is not fitting that anyone be prostrated to besides Allah. But honour your Prophet and recognise the rights of those who deserve them."[[I have not found a chain of narration for it. Al-Wahidi transmitted it in al-Asbab from al-Hasan al-Basri, that "a man" and he mentioned it.]]

Nor would He command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. Would He command you to disbelieve after you have submitted? (80)

And (it is not for a human being) to command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. Would he command you to disbelieve after you have submitted? Here the pronoun in "and (it is not) to command you" refers to a human being; it was also said it refers to Allah. The hamza in "ayya'murukum" is for denial.

[[The phrase "after you have submitted" is evidence that those addressed were Muslims, and they are the ones who asked his permission to prostrate to him.]]
