[[The phrase "after you have submitted" is evidence that those addressed were Muslims, and they are the ones who asked his permission to prostrate to him.]]

The covenant of the Prophets (﴿the covenant of the Prophets﴾) has several possible readings.

First, it may be taken literally: the covenant was taken from the Prophets themselves to this effect.

Second, the covenant may be attributed to the Prophets in the sense that they are the ones who made the covenant binding, not the ones bound by it, as you say "the covenant of Allah and the pledge of Allah." It is as if it were said: "And when Allah took the covenant which the Prophets affirmed upon their peoples."

Third, what is meant is the covenant of the children of the Prophets, who are the Children of Israel, with the noun elided (ḥadhf al-muḍāf).

Fourth, what is meant is the People of the Book, and the verse is a rebuke addressed to them in mockery, because they used to say: "We are more entitled to prophethood than Muhammad, for we are the People of the Book, and the Prophets came from among us."

The reading of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud supports this: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Book﴾. The lam in ﴿what I have given you﴾ (lamā ātaytukum) is the lam of preparation (lam al-tawṭi'a, the lam that introduces an oath), because taking a covenant has the meaning of making someone swear. [[Al-Zamakhshari says: "The lam in 'what I have given you' is the lam of preparation, because taking the covenant has the meaning of an oath..." Ahmad says: he means that ﴿a messenger﴾ is the subject of "came," since it cannot be without a pronoun; otherwise this statement would be correct on the basis that the subject is a pronoun, and "a messenger" is the predicate of the relative clause. Al-Zamakhshari did not intend anything but the first, which is the apparent meaning of the verse.]]

In ﴿you shall surely believe in him﴾ (latu'minunna), the lam is the answer to the oath. The word "mā" may be a conditional particle, in which case "latu'minunna" serves as the answer to both the oath and the condition together. It may also be a relative pronoun, meaning: "for that which I have given you, you shall surely believe in it."

It has been read as "lamā ātaynākum" (with the first-person plural). Ḥamzah read "lamā ātaytukum" with a kasra on the lam, and its meaning is: "because of My giving you part of the Book and wisdom, and then because of the coming of a messenger confirming what is with you, you shall surely believe in him," where "mā" is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya), and the two verbs with it, "ātaytukum" and "jā'akum," have the sense of verbal nouns. The lam is introduced for causation, meaning: Allah took their covenant that you shall surely believe in the messenger and surely support him, because I gave you wisdom, and because the messenger whom I command you to believe in and support agrees with you and does not oppose you.

It may also be that "mā" is a relative pronoun. If you ask: how is that permissible, given that the conjunction is upon "ātaytukum," and the phrase "then there came to you" (thumma jā'akum) cannot fall under the rule of the attribute, since you do not say "for him who came to you is a messenger confirming what is with you"? I answer: Yes, it is permissible, because "what is with you" has the meaning of "what I have given you," so it is as if it were said: "for that which I have given you and there came to you a messenger confirming it."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "lamā" with a shaddah, meaning "when I gave you part of the Book and wisdom, and then there came to you a messenger confirming it, you were obliged to believe in him and support him."

It has also been said that the original form was "li-man mā," and they found it heavy to have three consecutive m-sounds, namely the two m's and the nūn that had changed into an m by assimilation into the m, so they dropped one of them, and it became "lamā."

Its meaning is: "for the sake of what I have given you, you shall surely believe in him," and this is similar in meaning to the reading of Ḥamzah, and to "iṣrī" meaning "My covenant."

It has been read "aṣrī" with a ḍammah. It is called iṣr because it is that which is bound (yu'ṣar), that is, tied and knotted, and from it comes al-iṣār, the thing by which one is bound. It may also be that the form with the ḍammah is a dialectal variant of "aṣr," like "ʿabr" and "ʿubr," or that it is the plural of "iṣār."

﴿So bear witness﴾ (fa-ashhadū): let some of you bear witness against others by acknowledgment. ﴿And I am with you among the witnesses﴾ (wa-anā ʿalā dhālikum min al-shāhidīn): this is from your acknowledgment and your witnessing. This is an emphasis upon them and a warning against retraction, once they know it by the witness of Allah and the witness of some of them against others.

It has been said that the address is to the angels.

﴿Whoever turns away after that﴾ (fa-man tawallā ba'da dhālika), after the covenant and the emphasis, ﴿those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ (fa-ulā'ika humu al-fāsiqūn), that is, the rebels among the disbelievers. The interrogative hamzah of denial has entered upon the conjunctive fa, linking one sentence to another. The meaning is: "Then those are the defiantly disobedient, so do they seek other than the religion of Allah?" Then the hamzah was placed between the two.

It is also permissible that it be coordinated upon an elided element whose estimate is: "(Do) they turn away, so do they seek other than the religion of Allah?" The object, which is "other than the religion of Allah," has been placed before its verb, because it is more important, in that the denial, which is the meaning of the hamzah, is directed at what is worshipped falsely.

It has been related that the People of the Book brought their dispute to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning what they differed about in the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him), and each of the two groups claimed that it was more entitled to it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Both groups are free of the religion of Abraham." [[I have not found a chain of narration for it. Al-Wahidi also mentioned it in al-Asbab from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.]] They said: "We will not be content with your judgment, nor will we take up your religion." Then it was revealed: ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah?﴾

It has been read "yabghūn" with the yā', and "turja'ūn" with the tā', which is the reading of Abu 'Amr, because "the seekers" are those who turn away, while "those who are returned" is all of mankind. It has also been read with yā' in both, and with tā' in both.

﴿Willingly﴾ (ṭawʿan), through considering the proofs and being fair to oneself; ﴿and unwillingly﴾ (wa-karhan), by the sword, or by witnessing what compels one to Islam, such as the lifting of the mountain over the Children of Israel, the drowning that overtook Pharaoh, and the approach of death. [[His statement "and the approach of death" means the bordering upon it (al-ishrāf), as in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]] ﴿So when they saw Our might, they said: "We believe in Allah alone."﴾ (fa-lammā ra'aw ba'sanā qālū āmannā billāhi waḥdah). "Willingly" and "unwillingly" are in the accusative as circumstantial states, in the sense of "those who obey" and "those who are compelled."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 84–85:

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to inform about himself and those with him of their faith in ﴿Say﴾. For this reason the pronoun in ﴿Say﴾ is singular, while in ﴿We believe﴾ it is plural. It is also permissible that he was commanded to speak about himself alone, as kings speak (using the plural of majesty), out of Allah's honouring of the rank of His Prophet.

If you ask: Why was "anzala" (sent down) in this verse construed with the preposition of elevation (ʿalā, "upon"), while in the similar verses mentioned earlier it was construed with the preposition of terminus (ilā, "to")? I say: this is because both meanings are present together, for revelation descends from above and reaches the Messengers. So it came sometimes with one of the two meanings and sometimes with the other.

As for one who said: "ʿalaynā" (upon us) was used because of His saying ﴿Say﴾, and "ilaynā" (to us) because of His saying ﴿say (plural: "you say")﴾, to distinguish between the Messengers and the believers, because revelation comes to the Messenger by way of elevation, and comes to them by way of terminus, then he has strained (his interpretation). Do you not see His saying ﴿what was sent down to you﴾, ﴿And We sent down to you the Book﴾, and His saying ﴿Believe in what has been sent down to those who believe﴾?

﴿And to Him we are Muslims﴾: monotheists, sincerely devoting ourselves to Him, not making any partner to Him in worship. Then He said: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam﴾, meaning monotheism and submission, ﴿the religion (dīn)﴾ ﴿the face (wajh) turned to Allah, exalted is He﴾, ﴿it will never be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers﴾, from those who have fallen into loss absolutely, without restriction, for generality.

It was also recited: "wa-man yabtaghi ghayra al-Islām" with assimilation (idghām).

How can God guide a people? That is, how can He show them favour (lutf) when they are not among those worthy of His favour? God knew of their determination in disbelief, and this determination is shown by the fact that they disbelieved after their faith, after they had testified that the Messenger is true, and after the proofs had come to them from the Qur'an and the other miracles by which prophethood is established. They were the Jews, who disbelieved in the Prophet (ﷺ) after having believed in him, when they witnessed the clear proofs that strengthened their faith. It is also said: it was revealed concerning a group who had embraced Islam and then apostatised and joined Mecca, among them Ta'mah ibn Ubayriq, Wahwah ibn al-Aslat, and al-Harith ibn Suwayd ibn al-Samit.

[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you say, what is the position of his saying 'even if he ransoms with it'... This "waw" accompanying the condition requires another condition to which the conditional clause attached to it is necessarily coordinated, and the custom in such cases is that the stated element alerts to the unstated one by way of a fortiori (al-awla). All this is an explanation of the motive for the stated estimate. As for applying the verse to it, it is very difficult, so it is better to mention an aspect by which the verse can be applied in the easiest way and nearest derivation, Allah willing. We say:

All this is a recording that there is no escape nor deliverance for them from the threat; otherwise it is known that they are more incapable of ransoming themselves on that Day.

An example of this estimate: one says, "I will not sell you this garment for a thousand dinars, even if you hand them to me in my hand here." Or it may be meant: "then no ransom will be accepted from any of them, the fill of the earth in gold, which he had given in charity; and even if he ransomed with it again, it would not be accepted from him." It was also read: "fa-lan yuqbala min ahadihim mil' al-ard dhahaban," with the verb in the active voice, its subject being Allah, the Mighty and Exalted, and "mil'" in the accusative. And "mil'" and "al-ard" are read with the two hamzas softened.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verse 92:

﴿You will never attain righteousness﴾: you will not reach the reality of righteousness, nor will you become righteous (abrar). It was also said: you will not attain the righteousness (birr) of God, which is His reward, ﴿until you spend of that which you love﴾, until your spending is from your wealth that you love and prefer. This is like His saying: ﴿Spend of the good things you have earned﴾. The salaf (the early generations), may God have mercy on them, when they loved something, would dedicate it to God.

It is related that when this verse was revealed, Abu Talha came and said: "O Messenger of God, the most beloved of my property to me is Bayruha. So place it, O Messenger of God, wherever God shows you." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Bakh bakh, that is profitable wealth (mal rabih), or wealth that brings gain (mal ra'ih). I think you should make it for your relatives (al-aqrabin)." Abu Talha said: "I will do so, O Messenger of God," and he distributed it among his relatives.

Zayd ibn Harithah came with a horse he loved and said: "This is for the cause of God (fi sabil Allah)." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave it to Usama ibn Zayd to ride. Zayd seemed to feel something in himself and said: "I only intended to give it in charity." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed God the Exalted has accepted it from you."

Umar (may God be pleased with him) wrote to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari to buy for him a slave-girl from the captives of Jalula', on the day the cities of Kisra were conquered. When she came, he was pleased with her and said: "Indeed God the Exalted says: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of that which you love﴾," and he freed her.

A guest came to Abu Dharr, and he said to the herdsman: "Bring me the best of my camels." He brought a thin she-camel. Abu Dharr said: "You have cheated me." He said: "I found the best of the camels to be its stallion." Abu Dharr then mentioned the day when you will need it, and said: "Indeed the day I need it is the day I am placed in my grave."

Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) recited: ﴿until you spend some of what you love﴾. This is evidence that "min" in ﴿مِمَّا تُحِبُّونَ﴾ (of that which you love) is partitive (lil-tab'id), and it is like: "I took from the wealth." The "min" in ﴿مِنْ شَيْءٍ﴾ (of anything) is to specify what you spend, meaning: of whatever thing it is, good that you love or bad that you dislike. ﴿Indeed God is Knowing of everything you spend﴾, so He will recompense you according to it.

Every food was lawful (ḥill) to the Children of Israel, except what Israel (i.e., Ya'qub, peace be upon him) made unlawful for himself. The word ḥill (lawfulness) is a verbal noun. It is said: ḥalla al-shay'u ḥillan, like your saying: dhalati al-dābbatu dhullan, and 'azza al-rajulu 'azzan. In the ḥadith of 'Ā'isha, may Allah be pleased with her: "I used to perfume him for his ḥill and ḥurm" [agreed upon from her narration]. For this reason, the masculine and feminine, the singular and plural are equal in being described by it. Allah the Exalted says:

﴿They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them﴾ — [the verse reads: "they are not lawful for them (lahunna ḥillun lahum)"].

And he who made unlawful for himself, Israel (that is Ya'qub, peace be upon him), was the flesh of camels and their milk; and it is said: the veins. He had sciatica (ʿirq al-nasā), so he vowed that if he recovered he would make unlawful for himself the food he loved most, and that was what he loved most, so he made it unlawful. It is also said: the physicians advised him to avoid it, and he did so with permission from Allah, so it is like Allah's prohibition from the outset.

The meaning is that all foods remained lawful for the Children of Israel before the revelation of the Torah, and the prohibition of what was forbidden to them from it came because of their wrongdoing and transgression. Nothing was forbidden of it before that except the single food which their forefather Israel made unlawful for himself, and they followed him in its prohibition. This is a refutation of the Jews and a denial of them, since they wished to clear themselves of what was condemned against them in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things which had been made lawful for them﴾, up to His saying ﴿a painful punishment﴾. And in His saying: ﴿And for those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws, and of cattle and sheep We forbade them their fats﴾, up to His saying: ﴿That We repaid them for their rebellion﴾. And [it is] a denial of what angered them, which they resented and found distasteful, of what the Qur'an declared about the forbidding of good things to them for their rebellion and wrongdoing. So they said: "We are not the first upon whom it has been forbidden, and this is nothing but an ancient prohibition, which was forbidden to Noah, to Abraham, and to those after him from the Children of Israel, and so on, until the prohibition reached us, so it was forbidden to us as it was forbidden to those before us." Their aim was to deny Allah's testimony against them of rebellion, wrongdoing, hindering from the way of Allah, consuming usury, and taking people's wealth falsely, and what He enumerated of their evil deeds, for each time they committed a major sin, a kind of good things was forbidden to them as a punishment.

﴿Say: Bring the Torah and recite it﴾. This is a command to argue with them using their own Book and to rebuke them with what it states: that the prohibition of what was forbidden to them is a prohibition that arose because of their wrongdoing and transgression, not an ancient prohibition as they claim. It is narrated that they did not dare to bring out the Torah, were confounded, and returned humiliated. In this there is a clear proof of the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ), and of the permissibility of abrogation (naskh), which they deny.

﴿So whoever fabricates a lie against Allah after this, [claiming] that it was forbidden to the Children of Israel before the Torah was revealed, after the decisive proof has become binding upon them, those are the wrongdoers﴾ — the obstinate ones who do not do justice to themselves and do not heed the clear proofs.

﴿So whoever fabricates a lie against Allah after this, [claiming] that it was forbidden to the Children of Israel before the Torah was revealed, after the decisive proof has become binding upon them, those are the wrongdoers﴾ — the obstinate ones who do not do justice to themselves and do not heed the clear proofs.

Say, "Allah has spoken the truth." This is an indirect rebuke of their lying, like His saying: ﴿That is the recompense We gave them for their rebellion, and indeed We are truthful﴾ [Qur'an 6:146]. That is, it is established that Allah is truthful in what He has revealed, and you are the liars.

﴿So follow the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf﴾ [Qur'an 3:95]. This is the religion of Islam, upon which Muhammad (ﷺ) and those who believed with him are based, so that you may be freed from Judaism (yahūdiyya), which has plunged you into corruption of your religion and your worldly affairs, since it compelled you to distort the Book of Allah in order to suit your aims, and obliged you to forbid the good things that Allah made lawful for Abraham and for those who followed him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 96–97 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾ is a qualifier of the House, and the one who established it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is indicated by the reading of those who read (wuḍi'a lil-nās) in the passive form with the agent named, which is Allah. The meaning of Allah establishing a House for mankind is that He made it a place of worship for them, as if He had said: "Indeed, the first place of worship for mankind is the Ka'bah." It is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he was asked about the first mosque established for mankind, and he said: "The Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram), then the Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem)." He was asked how far apart they were, and he said: "Forty [[Agreed upon (muttafaqun 'alayh), from the hadith of Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the first mosque established for mankind. He said: The Sacred Mosque. I said: Then which? He said: Bayt al-Maqdis. I said: How far apart are they? He said: Forty years. Then, wherever the prayer overtakes you, pray, for the whole earth is a mosque for you."]] years." It is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that a man said to him: "Is it the first house?" He said: "No, there were houses before it, but it is the first house established for mankind, blessed, containing guidance, mercy and blessing." The first to build it was Ibrahim; then a people of the Arabs, from Jurhum, built it; then it was demolished, and the 'Amalaqah built it; then it was demolished, and Quraysh built it. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: it is the first house to be pilgrimaged to after the Flood. It was said: it is the first house to appear above the surface of the water at the creation of the heavens and the earth; it was created two thousand years before the earth, and it was a white foam upon the water, and the earth was spread out beneath it. It was said: it is the first house Adam built on the earth. It was said: when Adam was sent down, the angels said to him: "Circumambulate this House, for we circumambulated it two thousand years before you." There had been at its place, before Adam, a house called al-Ḍurāḥ, which was raised during the Flood to the fourth heaven, where the angels of the heavens circumambulate it. ﴿At Bakkah﴾: the House that is at Bakkah. Bakkah is a name for the Sacred City, and Makkah and Bakkah are two dialects regarding it, like their saying al-Nabīṭ and al-Numayṭ, as the name of a place in al-Dahnā', and like their saying, from interchange: amr rātib and rātim, and ḥummá maghmaṭah and maghbaṭah [[His words "ḥummá maghmaṭah and maghbaṭah": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: aghmaṭat 'alayhi al-ḥummá, a dialectal form of aghbaṭat, meaning it persisted. (ʿ)]]. It was said: Makkah is the city, and Bakkah is the place of the mosque. It was said: its derivation is from "bakka," meaning to crowd, because of the crowding of people in it. It is narrated from Qatadah: "People crush one another (yabukku), men and women, and some pray in front of others; this is not suitable except in Makkah, as it was named Bakkah, which means crowding." He said:

"When the drinking companion is seized by ill temper (al-akkah), leave him until he is pressed (yabukka bakkah)."

[[He means: when the "akkah," which is bad temper, seizes the drinking companion who drinks with you, or who waters his camels with you, as if it has possessed him and taken hold of him; "leave him" means let him be, until he takes a portion of water, or until he crowds with his camels at the water once, from crowding. This is an exhortation to noble character, forbearance at anger, and generosity.]]

It was also said: it crushes the necks of tyrants, i.e., it breaks them. No tyrant intended it except that Allah, exalted, struck him down. ﴿Blessed﴾, abundant in good for what is gained by those who make pilgrimage to it, perform the 'umrah, remain devoted at it, and circumambulate it, of reward and expiation of sins. Its being in the accusative is as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from the pronoun concealed in the adverbial phrase, since the estimate is "the one who is at Bakkah is," and the governing element in it is the implied verb of stability (fi'l al-istiqrār) in the adverbial phrase. ﴿And a guidance for the worlds﴾, because it is their qiblah and place of worship. ﴿The station of Ibrahim﴾ is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to His saying ﴿clear signs﴾.

If you say: how is the explanation of a plural by a singular valid? I say: there are two aspects. The first is that he is made, alone, equivalent to many signs, because of the prominence of his matter and the strength of his indication of Allah's power and of Ibrahim's prophethood, from the impression of his foot on hard rock, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed Ibrahim was a nation﴾. The second is that it comprises signs: the impression of the foot in the solid rock is a sign; its sinking into it up to the ankles is a sign; the softening of some of the rock and not the rest is a sign; its preservation, apart from the other signs of the prophets, peace be upon them, is a sign specific to Ibrahim; and its preservation, despite the great number of his enemies among the polytheists, the People of the Book, and the heretics, for thousands of years, is a sign. It is also permissible that what is meant is: in it are clear signs: the station of Ibrahim, and the security of whoever enters it, for two is a kind of plurality like three and four. It is also permissible that these two signs are mentioned and the mention of others is omitted, to indicate the abundance of signs, as if it were said: in it are clear signs: the station of Ibrahim, and the security of whoever enters it, and many others besides them. A similar omission is in the verse of Jarir:

"Ḥanīfah were divided into thirds: a third of them were slaves, and a third were their clients."

[[Jarir says: this tribe was divided into thirds; a third of it were slaves, and a third were freedmen of the tribe or freedmen of the slaves. Accordingly the idafah is in the sense of "min" (of), and the third part is not mentioned, because it is known that only the noble chiefs remained, by the evidence of the division into thirds and the progression from slaves to freedmen. This may imply dispraise, that only a third of the tribe are noble and the rest base; and it may imply praise, that their servants among the slaves are many.]]

From this is his peace be upon him saying: "Three of your worldly things have been made dear to me: perfume, women, and the coolness of my eye in prayer [[It has been mentioned earlier, at His saying ﴿and indeed it is heavy except upon the humble﴾, in abridged form. It was earlier noted that al-Nasa'i transmitted it through the route of Sayyar ibn Hatim from Ja'far ibn Sulayman, and through the route of Salam ibn Miskin, both from Thabit from Anas.
Through the route of Sayyar, it was related by Ahmad in al-Zuhd and by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak. Through the route of Salam, Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Sa'd, al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la, and Ibn 'Adi in al-Kamil transmitted it, and he gave it a defect; and al-'Uqayli in al-Du'afa' likewise. al-Daraqutni said in his 'Ilal: it was related by Abu al-Mundhir Salam, Salam ibn Abi al-Ṣahbā' and Ja'far ibn Sulayman, who related it from Thabit from Anas, but Hammad ibn Zayd opposed them, relating it from Thabit as a mursal. Likewise Muhammad ibn Thabit al-Basri related it. The mursal is closer to correct. 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad related it in the additions to al-Zuhd from other than his father, through the route of Yusuf ibn 'Atiyyah, from Thabit as a mursal too, and Yusuf is weak. It has another route, defective, in al-Tabarani's al-Awsat, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Hadrami, from Yahya ibn 'Uthman al-Harbi, from al-Haqal ibn Ziyad, from al-Awza'i, from Ishaq ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Talhah, from Anas, the like of it. I say: in none of its routes is the word "three"; rather, its beginning in all of them is "Women have been made dear to me of your worldly things," and the addition of "three" corrupts the meaning. However, the Imam Abu Bakr ibn Furak explained it in a separate treatise with its inclusion, and likewise al-Ghazali cited it in the Ihya', and it became widespread on people's tongues.]]."

Ibn 'Abbas, Ubayy, Mujahid, and Abu Ja'far al-Madani in the transmission of Qutaybah read: ﴿clear sign﴾, in the singular. In this there is evidence that the station of Ibrahim is itself an explicative apposition. If you say: how did you permit the station of Ibrahim and the security to be an explicative apposition of the signs, when His saying ﴿and whoever enters it is secure﴾ is a new independent sentence, either initial or conditional? I say: I permitted it from the standpoint of meaning, because His saying ﴿and whoever enters it is secure﴾ indicates the security of the one who enters; so it is as if it were said: in it are clear signs: the station of Ibrahim and the security of its entrant. Do you not see that if you said: in it is a clear sign, whoever enters it is secure, it would be correct, since it has the meaning of your saying: in it is a clear sign, the security of whoever enters it.

If you say: how was the cause of this impression? I say: there are two views. The first is that when the building of the Ka'bah rose and Ibrahim was too weak to lift the stones, he stood on this stone, and his feet sank into it. It was also said: he came visiting from Syria to Makkah, and Ismail's wife said to him: "Descend so that your head may be washed," but he did not descend; so she brought him this stone and placed it under his right side, and he placed his foot upon it until one side of his head was washed; then she moved it to his left side until the other side was washed, and the impression of his feet remained on it.

The meaning of ﴿and whoever enters it is secure﴾ is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a sanctuary secure, while people are snatched away from around them?﴾ and that was by the supplication of Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿My Lord, make this city secure﴾. A man who committed every crime and then took refuge in the Sanctuary was not pursued. It is narrated from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Even if I found the slayer of al-Khattab in it, I would not touch him until he came out of it." [[Narrated by 'Abd al-Razzaq in the Book of Hajj of his Musannaf, and Abu al-Walid al-Azraqi in the History of Makkah through his route from Ibn Jurayj, who heard Ibn Abi Husayn from 'Ikrimah ibn Khalid, who said: 'Umar said this. This report is disconnected (munqati').]] According to Abu Hanifah: whoever is liable to be killed outside the Sanctuary, for retaliation, apostasy, or fornication, and takes refuge in the Sanctuary, is not molested, except that he is not sheltered, fed, given drink, or sold to until he is compelled to leave.

It was also said: secure from the Fire. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever dies in either of the two sanctuaries will be raised on the Day of Resurrection secure." [[Ishaq said: 'Isa ibn Yunus told us, Thawr ibn Yazid told us, a shaykh told me, from Anas, with it. al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related it through Ibn Abi Fudayk from Sulayman ibn Yazid al-Ka'bi from Anas, with it, and added: "Whoever visits me in Madinah seeking reward, will be in my neighbourhood on the Day of Resurrection." Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi related it in full from the hadith of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, with a weak chain, in which there is an unknown narrator. 'Abd al-Razzaq said in his Musannaf: Yahya ibn al-'Ala' and others told us, and Ghalib ibn 'Ubayd Allah raised it, and he mentioned it. Yahya and Ghalib are extremely weak. al-Daraqutni related it from the narration of Harun ibn Abi Qaza'ah, from a man of the family of Hatib, from Hatib in full, and it is defective. al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and al-Saghir related it by two routes from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mu'ammal, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, without the addition. Ibn 'Adi mentioned it in the biography of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mu'ammal. al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab and al-Tabarani related it from the hadith of 'Abd al-Ghafur ibn Sa'id al-Ansari, from Abu Hashim al-Rummani, from Zadhan, from Salman. al-Bayhaqi said: 'Abd al-Ghafur is weak, and it has been related with a better chain than this one, then he mentioned the route of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mu'ammal. Ibn al-Jawzi included it in al-Mawdu'at through the route of 'Abd al-Ghafur, and cited Ibn Hibban as saying: he used to fabricate hadith. I say: this is an error of Ibn al-Jawzi in his handling, for it is not restricted to 'Abd al-Ghafur.]] secure."

And from him, peace be upon him: "Al-Hajun and al-Baqi' are taken by their edges and scattered into Paradise [[I have not found it.]]," and they are the two cemeteries of Makkah and Madinah. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood at the ridge of al-Hajun, and there was no cemetery there at that time, and he said: "Allah will raise from this spot and from this whole Sanctuary seventy thousand whose faces are like the full moon, who will enter Paradise without reckoning, and each of them will intercede for seventy thousand, whose faces are like the full moon [[I have not found it.]]." And it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever endures the heat of Makkah for an hour of a day, Hell will be removed from him the distance of two hundred [[Thus Abu al-Walid al-Azraqi mentioned it in the History of Makkah, but without a chain. Al-'Uqayli related it in al-Du'afa' in the biography of al-Hasan ibn Rashid from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, raised: "Whoever endures the heat of Makkah for an hour, Allah will remove from him Hell by seventy autumns." He said: this is false, without basis, and al-Hasan ibn Rashid transmits strange reports. Abu Shuja' cited it in al-Firdaws from the hadith of Anas, with the wording: "Hell will be removed from him the distance of a hundred years, and Paradise will draw near to him a hundred years."]] years."

﴿Whoever is able﴾ (man istaṭā'a) is a substitution from "people." It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained "ability" as provision and mount. This is also related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar, and most scholars hold it. It is narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr: it is according to the measure of strength. The school of Malik holds that if a man trusts his strength, it is binding on him. And from him: it is according to the measure of capacity; one may find provision and mount and yet be unable to travel, and one may be able to travel without provision or mount. From al-Dahhak: if one is able to hire himself out, he is able. He was asked about this and said: If some of them had an inheritance in Makkah, would he leave it? Rather, he would set out for it even crawling; so likewise the Hajj is obligatory upon him. The pronoun in ﴿to it﴾ refers either to the House or to the Hajj. Every means of reaching a thing is a path to it. In this statement there are kinds of emphasis and intensification, among them His saying: ﴿And for Allah is upon the people the pilgrimage to the House﴾ [[Mahmud said: "There are kinds of emphasis in the speech, among them His saying: ﴿And for Allah is upon the people﴾, meaning upon their necks, from which they are not released..." Ahmad said: his statement that "the intended meaning of whoever disbelieves is one who abandons the Hajj, and it is expressed as disbelief as a harshening upon him" is open to examination, for the principle of the People of the Sunnah requires that one who abandons Hajj does not become a disbeliever by mere abandonment, by unanimous opinion; so the verse must be read as referring to one who abandons Hajj while denying its obligation, and then disbelief returns to belief rather than to mere abandonment. As for al-Zamakhshari, he permits that, because one who abandons Hajj by mere abandonment leaves the bond of faith, its name, and its rulings, since in his view he is not a believer and is eternally abiding like the disbelievers. According to the principle of the Sunnah, what we have mentioned must be adopted, if what is meant by "whoever disbelieves" is one who abandons Hajj. It is also possible that it is a new statement of threat to the disbeliever, and it remains on its apparent meaning, and Allah knows best.]]. It means that it is a right obligatory upon the people, owed to Allah, from which they are not released until they discharge it and come out of its obligation. Among them is that He mentioned "the people," then substituted for it "whoever is able to it, a way," and in this are two kinds of emphasis: first, that substitution is a repetition and reiteration of the intended meaning; second, that clarification after ambiguity and detail after generality is presenting it in two different forms. Among them is His saying: ﴿and whoever disbelieves﴾ in place of "and whoever does not perform Hajj," as harshening upon the one who abandons Hajj; and for this the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies without performing Hajj, let him die, if he wishes, a Jew or a Christian" [[Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it from the narration of Hilal ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bahili: Abu Ishaq told us, from al-Harith, from 'Ali, raised: "Whoever owns provision and a mount that would carry him to the House of Allah, and does not perform Hajj, it is no matter for him to die a Jew or a Christian." He said: it is strange, and its chain has disputed points. Hilal ibn 'Abd Allah is unknown. al-Harith is weak. al-Bazzar transmitted it through this route and said: we do not know it from 'Ali except through this route. Ibn 'Adi and al-'Uqayli transmitted it in the biography of Hilal, and both related from al-Bukhari that he is a munkar al-hadith. al-Bayhaqi said in al-Shu'ab:]].

Hilal alone transmitted it. It has a supporting report (*shahid*) from the hadith of Abu Umamah, which al-Darimi narrated with the wording: «Whoever is not prevented from the Hajj by an evident need, an oppressive ruler, or a restraining illness, and dies without having performed the Hajj, let him die either as a Jew or as a Christian, if he wishes.» He narrated it through the transmission of Shurayk, from Layth ibn Abi Sulaym, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, from him (Abu Umamah). Al-Bayhaqi also narrated it through this same channel in *al-Shu'ab*. Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated it from Abu al-Ahwas, from Layth, from Abd al-Rahman, as a *mursal* report, without mentioning Abu Umamah. Ibn al-Jawzi included it among the *mawdu'at* (fabricated reports), through the channel of Ibn Adi. Ibn Adi included it in *al-Kamil* in the biography of Abu al-Mahzum Yazid ibn Sufyan, from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), and similar to it. Al-Fallas is reported to have called Abu al-Mahzam a liar, but this is an error on the part of Ibn al-Jawzi in his handling of the matter, because the chain to Abu Umamah does not include anyone accused of lying, let alone one who is known to have lied.

[[And similar to it, in the strong warning: «Whoever abandons the prayer deliberately has disbelieved.»]] [[Al-Daraqutni narrated it in *al-Ilal*, through the transmission of Abu al-Nadr Hashim ibn al-Qasim, from Abu Ja'far al-Razi, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Anas, who said: Ali ibn al-Ja'd narrated it from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', as a *mursal* report, and this is closer to the correct version. Al-Bazzar narrated it from the hadith of Abu al-Darda', who said: "Abu al-Qasim (ﷺ) enjoined me that I should not associate anything with Allah even if I am burned, and that I should not abandon a prescribed prayer deliberately. Whoever abandons it deliberately has disbelieved. And I should not drink wine, for it is the key to every evil." He narrated it through the transmission of Rashid al-Hananni, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, and said: Rashid is a Basran with nothing wrong with him, and Shahr is well known. The hadith is found in al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ahmad, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim, from the hadith of Buraydah, without the phrase "deliberately," and its wording is: "The covenant between us and them is the prayer, so whoever abandons it has disbelieved." It was already mentioned in al-Baqarah the hadith of Jabir in Muslim: "Between a servant and disbelief is the abandoning of the prayer." Al-Tirmidhi narrated through the channel of Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, who said: "The companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not consider the abandoning of any act to be disbelief except the prayer," and its chain is sound. Al-Hakim (narrated it) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

Among the [forms of] emphasis is the mention of Allah's being independent of [the worlds], which indicates abhorrence, wrath and abandonment. Another is His saying "from the worlds" though He did not say "from Him," and the indication within it of His independence, which is evident, since if He is independent of the worlds, independence from them necessarily encompasses it (i.e., His independence from all). Also, it indicates complete independence, so it is more expressive of the great wrath that the expression refers to.

It is reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: it was revealed concerning the Jews, for they said: "The Hajj to Makkah is not obligatory." It is also reported that when Allah's saying was revealed: ﴿And for Allah is the duty upon mankind toward the House, the pilgrimage to it﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered all the people of the religions and addressed them, saying: "Allah has prescribed upon you the Hajj, so perform it." One community believed in it, namely the Muslims, while five communities disbelieved in it and said: "We do not believe in it, we do not pray toward it, and we will not perform its pilgrimage." Then Allah revealed: ﴿And whoever disbelieves...﴾. [[Al-Tabari narrated it through the channel of Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, who said: "When it was revealed—" and so he mentioned it. This is a *mu'dal* report (one with two or more consecutive omitted narrators). Juwaybir is abandoned in narration and worthless.]]

It is also reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): «Perform the Hajj before you are prevented from it, for the House has been destroyed twice and will be raised up a third time.» [[Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated: "Yazid ibn Harun informed us, from Humayd, from Bakr ibn Abd Allah al-Muzani, from Abd Allah ibn Umar, who said: 'Benefit from this House, for it—'" and so he mentioned it as a *mawquf* report (traced to a Companion). It has also been narrated as *marfu'* (traced to the Prophet), by Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani through the channel of Sufyan ibn Habib, from Humayd, with this same wording.]]

And it has been narrated: «Perform the Hajj before you are prevented from it; perform the Hajj before righteousness is barred from its side.» [[I have not seen it in this form. What is in al-Daraqutni, at the end of the book of Hajj in his *Sunan*, through the transmission of Abd Allah ibn Isa al-Jundi, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet: «Perform the Hajj before you are prevented from it." They said: "What is the matter with the Hajj, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Its Bedouins will do it upon the backs of their valleys, and none will reach the Hajj." Abd Allah and Muhammad are both unknown, as al-Uqayli said.]]

It is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud: "Perform the pilgrimage to this House before a tree grows in the desert that no animal can eat from without dying." [[I have not found it.]] And from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "If people were to abandon the Hajj for a single year, they would not be given rain." [[I have not found it. In the *Musannaf* of Abd al-Razzaq, through the transmission of Salim ibn Abi Hafsah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "If people were to abandon visiting this House for a single year, they would not be given rain." It is *munqati'* (with a break in its chain).]]

It has also been read as *hijj al-bayt* with a kasra (on the *ha'*).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 96–97 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾ is a qualifier of the House, and the one who established it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is indicated by the reading of those who read (wuḍi'a lil-nās) in the passive form with the agent named, which is Allah. The meaning of Allah establishing a House for mankind is that He made it a place of worship for them, as if He had said: "Indeed, the first place of worship for mankind is the Ka'bah." It is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he was asked about the first mosque established for mankind, and he said: "The Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram), then the Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem)." He was asked how far apart they were, and he said: "Forty [[Agreed upon (muttafaqun 'alayh), from the hadith of Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the first mosque established for mankind. He said: The Sacred Mosque. I said: Then which? He said: Bayt al-Maqdis. I said: How far apart are they? He said: Forty years. Then, wherever the prayer overtakes you, pray, for the whole earth is a mosque for you."]] years." It is narrated from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that a man said to him: "Is it the first house?" He said: "No, there were houses before it, but it is the first house established for mankind, blessed, containing guidance, mercy and blessing." The first to build it was Ibrahim; then a people of the Arabs, from Jurhum, built it; then it was demolished, and the 'Amalaqah built it; then it was demolished, and Quraysh built it. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: it is the first house to be pilgrimaged to after the Flood. It was said: it is the first house to appear above the surface of the water at the creation of the heavens and the earth; it was created two thousand years before the earth, and it was a white foam upon the water, and the earth was spread out beneath it. It was said: it is the first house Adam built on the earth. It was said: when Adam was sent down, the angels said to him: "Circumambulate this House, for we circumambulated it two thousand years before you." There had been at its place, before Adam, a house called al-Ḍurāḥ, which was raised during the Flood to the fourth heaven, where the angels of the heavens circumambulate it. ﴿At Bakkah﴾: the House that is at Bakkah. Bakkah is a name for the Sacred City, and Makkah and Bakkah are two dialects regarding it, like their saying al-Nabīṭ and al-Numayṭ, as the name of a place in al-Dahnā', and like their saying, from interchange: amr rātib and rātim, and ḥummá maghmaṭah and maghbaṭah [[His words "ḥummá maghmaṭah and maghbaṭah": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ: aghmaṭat 'alayhi al-ḥummá, a dialectal form of aghbaṭat, meaning it persisted. (ʿ)]]. It was said: Makkah is the city, and Bakkah is the place of the mosque. It was said: its derivation is from "bakka," meaning to crowd, because of the crowding of people in it. It is narrated from Qatadah: "People crush one another (yabukku), men and women, and some pray in front of others; this is not suitable except in Makkah, as it was named Bakkah, which means crowding." He said:

"When the drinking companion is seized by ill temper (al-akkah), leave him until he is pressed (yabukka bakkah)."

[[He means: when the "akkah," which is bad temper, seizes the drinking companion who drinks with you, or who waters his camels with you, as if it has possessed him and taken hold of him; "leave him" means let him be, until he takes a portion of water, or until he crowds with his camels at the water once, from crowding. This is an exhortation to noble character, forbearance at anger, and generosity.]]

It was also said: it crushes the necks of tyrants, i.e., it breaks them. No tyrant intended it except that Allah, exalted, struck him down. ﴿Blessed﴾, abundant in good for what is gained by those who make pilgrimage to it, perform the 'umrah, remain devoted at it, and circumambulate it, of reward and expiation of sins. Its being in the accusative is as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from the pronoun concealed in the adverbial phrase, since the estimate is "the one who is at Bakkah is," and the governing element in it is the implied verb of stability (fi'l al-istiqrār) in the adverbial phrase. ﴿And a guidance for the worlds﴾, because it is their qiblah and place of worship. ﴿The station of Ibrahim﴾ is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to His saying ﴿clear signs﴾.

If you say: how is the explanation of a plural by a singular valid? I say: there are two aspects. The first is that he is made, alone, equivalent to many signs, because of the prominence of his matter and the strength of his indication of Allah's power and of Ibrahim's prophethood, from the impression of his foot on hard rock, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed Ibrahim was a nation﴾. The second is that it comprises signs: the impression of the foot in the solid rock is a sign; its sinking into it up to the ankles is a sign; the softening of some of the rock and not the rest is a sign; its preservation, apart from the other signs of the prophets, peace be upon them, is a sign specific to Ibrahim; and its preservation, despite the great number of his enemies among the polytheists, the People of the Book, and the heretics, for thousands of years, is a sign. It is also permissible that what is meant is: in it are clear signs: the station of Ibrahim, and the security of whoever enters it, for two is a kind of plurality like three and four. It is also permissible that these two signs are mentioned and the mention of others is omitted, to indicate the abundance of signs, as if it were said: in it are clear signs: the station of Ibrahim, and the security of whoever enters it, and many others besides them. A similar omission is in the verse of Jarir:

"Ḥanīfah were divided into thirds: a third of them were slaves, and a third were their clients."

[[Jarir says: this tribe was divided into thirds; a third of it were slaves, and a third were freedmen of the tribe or freedmen of the slaves. Accordingly the idafah is in the sense of "min" (of), and the third part is not mentioned, because it is known that only the noble chiefs remained, by the evidence of the division into thirds and the progression from slaves to freedmen. This may imply dispraise, that only a third of the tribe are noble and the rest base; and it may imply praise, that their servants among the slaves are many.]]

From this is his peace be upon him saying: "Three of your worldly things have been made dear to me: perfume, women, and the coolness of my eye in prayer [[It has been mentioned earlier, at His saying ﴿and indeed it is heavy except upon the humble﴾, in abridged form. It was earlier noted that al-Nasa'i transmitted it through the route of Sayyar ibn Hatim from Ja'far ibn Sulayman, and through the route of Salam ibn Miskin, both from Thabit from Anas.
Through the route of Sayyar, it was related by Ahmad in al-Zuhd and by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak. Through the route of Salam, Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Sa'd, al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la, and Ibn 'Adi in al-Kamil transmitted it, and he gave it a defect; and al-'Uqayli in al-Du'afa' likewise. al-Daraqutni said in his 'Ilal: it was related by Abu al-Mundhir Salam, Salam ibn Abi al-Ṣahbā' and Ja'far ibn Sulayman, who related it from Thabit from Anas, but Hammad ibn Zayd opposed them, relating it from Thabit as a mursal. Likewise Muhammad ibn Thabit al-Basri related it. The mursal is closer to correct. 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad related it in the additions to al-Zuhd from other than his father, through the route of Yusuf ibn 'Atiyyah, from Thabit as a mursal too, and Yusuf is weak. It has another route, defective, in al-Tabarani's al-Awsat, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Hadrami, from Yahya ibn 'Uthman al-Harbi, from al-Haqal ibn Ziyad, from al-Awza'i, from Ishaq ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Talhah, from Anas, the like of it. I say: in none of its routes is the word "three"; rather, its beginning in all of them is "Women have been made dear to me of your worldly things," and the addition of "three" corrupts the meaning. However, the Imam Abu Bakr ibn Furak explained it in a separate treatise with its inclusion, and likewise al-Ghazali cited it in the Ihya', and it became widespread on people's tongues.]]."

Ibn 'Abbas, Ubayy, Mujahid, and Abu Ja'far al-Madani in the transmission of Qutaybah read: ﴿clear sign﴾, in the singular. In this there is evidence that the station of Ibrahim is itself an explicative apposition. If you say: how did you permit the station of Ibrahim and the security to be an explicative apposition of the signs, when His saying ﴿and whoever enters it is secure﴾ is a new independent sentence, either initial or conditional? I say: I permitted it from the standpoint of meaning, because His saying ﴿and whoever enters it is secure﴾ indicates the security of the one who enters; so it is as if it were said: in it are clear signs: the station of Ibrahim and the security of its entrant. Do you not see that if you said: in it is a clear sign, whoever enters it is secure, it would be correct, since it has the meaning of your saying: in it is a clear sign, the security of whoever enters it.

If you say: how was the cause of this impression? I say: there are two views. The first is that when the building of the Ka'bah rose and Ibrahim was too weak to lift the stones, he stood on this stone, and his feet sank into it. It was also said: he came visiting from Syria to Makkah, and Ismail's wife said to him: "Descend so that your head may be washed," but he did not descend; so she brought him this stone and placed it under his right side, and he placed his foot upon it until one side of his head was washed; then she moved it to his left side until the other side was washed, and the impression of his feet remained on it.

The meaning of ﴿and whoever enters it is secure﴾ is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a sanctuary secure, while people are snatched away from around them?﴾ and that was by the supplication of Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿My Lord, make this city secure﴾. A man who committed every crime and then took refuge in the Sanctuary was not pursued. It is narrated from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Even if I found the slayer of al-Khattab in it, I would not touch him until he came out of it." [[Narrated by 'Abd al-Razzaq in the Book of Hajj of his Musannaf, and Abu al-Walid al-Azraqi in the History of Makkah through his route from Ibn Jurayj, who heard Ibn Abi Husayn from 'Ikrimah ibn Khalid, who said: 'Umar said this. This report is disconnected (munqati').]] According to Abu Hanifah: whoever is liable to be killed outside the Sanctuary, for retaliation, apostasy, or fornication, and takes refuge in the Sanctuary, is not molested, except that he is not sheltered, fed, given drink, or sold to until he is compelled to leave.

It was also said: secure from the Fire. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever dies in either of the two sanctuaries will be raised on the Day of Resurrection secure." [[Ishaq said: 'Isa ibn Yunus told us, Thawr ibn Yazid told us, a shaykh told me, from Anas, with it. al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab related it through Ibn Abi Fudayk from Sulayman ibn Yazid al-Ka'bi from Anas, with it, and added: "Whoever visits me in Madinah seeking reward, will be in my neighbourhood on the Day of Resurrection." Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi related it in full from the hadith of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, with a weak chain, in which there is an unknown narrator. 'Abd al-Razzaq said in his Musannaf: Yahya ibn al-'Ala' and others told us, and Ghalib ibn 'Ubayd Allah raised it, and he mentioned it. Yahya and Ghalib are extremely weak. al-Daraqutni related it from the narration of Harun ibn Abi Qaza'ah, from a man of the family of Hatib, from Hatib in full, and it is defective. al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and al-Saghir related it by two routes from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mu'ammal, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir, without the addition. Ibn 'Adi mentioned it in the biography of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mu'ammal. al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab and al-Tabarani related it from the hadith of 'Abd al-Ghafur ibn Sa'id al-Ansari, from Abu Hashim al-Rummani, from Zadhan, from Salman. al-Bayhaqi said: 'Abd al-Ghafur is weak, and it has been related with a better chain than this one, then he mentioned the route of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mu'ammal. Ibn al-Jawzi included it in al-Mawdu'at through the route of 'Abd al-Ghafur, and cited Ibn Hibban as saying: he used to fabricate hadith. I say: this is an error of Ibn al-Jawzi in his handling, for it is not restricted to 'Abd al-Ghafur.]] secure."

And from him, peace be upon him: "Al-Hajun and al-Baqi' are taken by their edges and scattered into Paradise [[I have not found it.]]," and they are the two cemeteries of Makkah and Madinah. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood at the ridge of al-Hajun, and there was no cemetery there at that time, and he said: "Allah will raise from this spot and from this whole Sanctuary seventy thousand whose faces are like the full moon, who will enter Paradise without reckoning, and each of them will intercede for seventy thousand, whose faces are like the full moon [[I have not found it.]]." And it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever endures the heat of Makkah for an hour of a day, Hell will be removed from him the distance of two hundred [[Thus Abu al-Walid al-Azraqi mentioned it in the History of Makkah, but without a chain. Al-'Uqayli related it in al-Du'afa' in the biography of al-Hasan ibn Rashid from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, raised: "Whoever endures the heat of Makkah for an hour, Allah will remove from him Hell by seventy autumns." He said: this is false, without basis, and al-Hasan ibn Rashid transmits strange reports. Abu Shuja' cited it in al-Firdaws from the hadith of Anas, with the wording: "Hell will be removed from him the distance of a hundred years, and Paradise will draw near to him a hundred years."]] years."

﴿Whoever is able﴾ (man istaṭā'a) is a substitution from "people." It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained "ability" as provision and mount. This is also related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar, and most scholars hold it. It is narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr: it is according to the measure of strength. The school of Malik holds that if a man trusts his strength, it is binding on him. And from him: it is according to the measure of capacity; one may find provision and mount and yet be unable to travel, and one may be able to travel without provision or mount. From al-Dahhak: if one is able to hire himself out, he is able. He was asked about this and said: If some of them had an inheritance in Makkah, would he leave it? Rather, he would set out for it even crawling; so likewise the Hajj is obligatory upon him. The pronoun in ﴿to it﴾ refers either to the House or to the Hajj. Every means of reaching a thing is a path to it. In this statement there are kinds of emphasis and intensification, among them His saying: ﴿And for Allah is upon the people the pilgrimage to the House﴾ [[Mahmud said: "There are kinds of emphasis in the speech, among them His saying: ﴿And for Allah is upon the people﴾, meaning upon their necks, from which they are not released..." Ahmad said: his statement that "the intended meaning of whoever disbelieves is one who abandons the Hajj, and it is expressed as disbelief as a harshening upon him" is open to examination, for the principle of the People of the Sunnah requires that one who abandons Hajj does not become a disbeliever by mere abandonment, by unanimous opinion; so the verse must be read as referring to one who abandons Hajj while denying its obligation, and then disbelief returns to belief rather than to mere abandonment. As for al-Zamakhshari, he permits that, because one who abandons Hajj by mere abandonment leaves the bond of faith, its name, and its rulings, since in his view he is not a believer and is eternally abiding like the disbelievers. According to the principle of the Sunnah, what we have mentioned must be adopted, if what is meant by "whoever disbelieves" is one who abandons Hajj. It is also possible that it is a new statement of threat to the disbeliever, and it remains on its apparent meaning, and Allah knows best.]]. It means that it is a right obligatory upon the people, owed to Allah, from which they are not released until they discharge it and come out of its obligation. Among them is that He mentioned "the people," then substituted for it "whoever is able to it, a way," and in this are two kinds of emphasis: first, that substitution is a repetition and reiteration of the intended meaning; second, that clarification after ambiguity and detail after generality is presenting it in two different forms. Among them is His saying: ﴿and whoever disbelieves﴾ in place of "and whoever does not perform Hajj," as harshening upon the one who abandons Hajj; and for this the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies without performing Hajj, let him die, if he wishes, a Jew or a Christian" [[Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it from the narration of Hilal ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bahili: Abu Ishaq told us, from al-Harith, from 'Ali, raised: "Whoever owns provision and a mount that would carry him to the House of Allah, and does not perform Hajj, it is no matter for him to die a Jew or a Christian." He said: it is strange, and its chain has disputed points. Hilal ibn 'Abd Allah is unknown. al-Harith is weak. al-Bazzar transmitted it through this route and said: we do not know it from 'Ali except through this route. Ibn 'Adi and al-'Uqayli transmitted it in the biography of Hilal, and both related from al-Bukhari that he is a munkar al-hadith. al-Bayhaqi said in al-Shu'ab:]].

Hilal alone transmitted it. It has a supporting report (*shahid*) from the hadith of Abu Umamah, which al-Darimi narrated with the wording: «Whoever is not prevented from the Hajj by an evident need, an oppressive ruler, or a restraining illness, and dies without having performed the Hajj, let him die either as a Jew or as a Christian, if he wishes.» He narrated it through the transmission of Shurayk, from Layth ibn Abi Sulaym, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, from him (Abu Umamah). Al-Bayhaqi also narrated it through this same channel in *al-Shu'ab*. Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated it from Abu al-Ahwas, from Layth, from Abd al-Rahman, as a *mursal* report, without mentioning Abu Umamah. Ibn al-Jawzi included it among the *mawdu'at* (fabricated reports), through the channel of Ibn Adi. Ibn Adi included it in *al-Kamil* in the biography of Abu al-Mahzum Yazid ibn Sufyan, from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), and similar to it. Al-Fallas is reported to have called Abu al-Mahzam a liar, but this is an error on the part of Ibn al-Jawzi in his handling of the matter, because the chain to Abu Umamah does not include anyone accused of lying, let alone one who is known to have lied.

[[And similar to it, in the strong warning: «Whoever abandons the prayer deliberately has disbelieved.»]] [[Al-Daraqutni narrated it in *al-Ilal*, through the transmission of Abu al-Nadr Hashim ibn al-Qasim, from Abu Ja'far al-Razi, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Anas, who said: Ali ibn al-Ja'd narrated it from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', as a *mursal* report, and this is closer to the correct version. Al-Bazzar narrated it from the hadith of Abu al-Darda', who said: "Abu al-Qasim (ﷺ) enjoined me that I should not associate anything with Allah even if I am burned, and that I should not abandon a prescribed prayer deliberately. Whoever abandons it deliberately has disbelieved. And I should not drink wine, for it is the key to every evil." He narrated it through the transmission of Rashid al-Hananni, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, and said: Rashid is a Basran with nothing wrong with him, and Shahr is well known. The hadith is found in al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ahmad, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim, from the hadith of Buraydah, without the phrase "deliberately," and its wording is: "The covenant between us and them is the prayer, so whoever abandons it has disbelieved." It was already mentioned in al-Baqarah the hadith of Jabir in Muslim: "Between a servant and disbelief is the abandoning of the prayer." Al-Tirmidhi narrated through the channel of Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, who said: "The companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not consider the abandoning of any act to be disbelief except the prayer," and its chain is sound. Al-Hakim (narrated it) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

Among the [forms of] emphasis is the mention of Allah's being independent of [the worlds], which indicates abhorrence, wrath and abandonment. Another is His saying "from the worlds" though He did not say "from Him," and the indication within it of His independence, which is evident, since if He is independent of the worlds, independence from them necessarily encompasses it (i.e., His independence from all). Also, it indicates complete independence, so it is more expressive of the great wrath that the expression refers to.

It is reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: it was revealed concerning the Jews, for they said: "The Hajj to Makkah is not obligatory." It is also reported that when Allah's saying was revealed: ﴿And for Allah is the duty upon mankind toward the House, the pilgrimage to it﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gathered all the people of the religions and addressed them, saying: "Allah has prescribed upon you the Hajj, so perform it." One community believed in it, namely the Muslims, while five communities disbelieved in it and said: "We do not believe in it, we do not pray toward it, and we will not perform its pilgrimage." Then Allah revealed: ﴿And whoever disbelieves...﴾. [[Al-Tabari narrated it through the channel of Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, who said: "When it was revealed—" and so he mentioned it. This is a *mu'dal* report (one with two or more consecutive omitted narrators). Juwaybir is abandoned in narration and worthless.]]

It is also reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): «Perform the Hajj before you are prevented from it, for the House has been destroyed twice and will be raised up a third time.» [[Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated: "Yazid ibn Harun informed us, from Humayd, from Bakr ibn Abd Allah al-Muzani, from Abd Allah ibn Umar, who said: 'Benefit from this House, for it—'" and so he mentioned it as a *mawquf* report (traced to a Companion). It has also been narrated as *marfu'* (traced to the Prophet), by Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani through the channel of Sufyan ibn Habib, from Humayd, with this same wording.]]

And it has been narrated: «Perform the Hajj before you are prevented from it; perform the Hajj before righteousness is barred from its side.» [[I have not seen it in this form. What is in al-Daraqutni, at the end of the book of Hajj in his *Sunan*, through the transmission of Abd Allah ibn Isa al-Jundi, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet: «Perform the Hajj before you are prevented from it." They said: "What is the matter with the Hajj, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Its Bedouins will do it upon the backs of their valleys, and none will reach the Hajj." Abd Allah and Muhammad are both unknown, as al-Uqayli said.]]

It is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud: "Perform the pilgrimage to this House before a tree grows in the desert that no animal can eat from without dying." [[I have not found it.]] And from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "If people were to abandon the Hajj for a single year, they would not be given rain." [[I have not found it. In the *Musannaf* of Abd al-Razzaq, through the transmission of Salim ibn Abi Hafsah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "If people were to abandon visiting this House for a single year, they would not be given rain." It is *munqati'* (with a break in its chain).]]

It has also been read as *hijj al-bayt* with a kasra (on the *ha'*).

Allah is Witness. The waw is for the circumstantial clause (wāw al-ḥāl). The meaning: "Why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah, which point you to the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ), while Allah is witness over your deeds, and will therefore requite you for them?" This circumstance requires that you not dare to disbelieve in His signs.

Al-Ḥasan read tuṣaddūn (from aṣadda), "you turn away," meaning: from aṣadda ʿan sabīl Allāh, "to turn away from the way of Allah," that is, from a true religion which you know to be the way of Allah, which He commanded to be followed, namely Islam. They would afflict the believers, scheme to turn them away from it, and, with all their effort, prevent whoever wished to enter it.

It is also said: the Jews came to the Aws and the Khazraj and reminded them of the enmities and wars that had existed between them in the Jahiliyya, so that they would return to the like of it.

Tabghūnahā ʿiwajan: "you seek for it crookedness," that is, you seek crookedness in it, and deviation from the straight path and uprightness.

[Commentary of Aḥmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) on al-Zamakhsharī's remark (qāla Maḥmūd: "ay tabghūnahā iwajan ... ilakh"): In his taqdīr of the preposition together with the object pronoun, when he said "you seek for it crookedness," there is a diminishing of the meaning. More complete than its i'rab is to make the hā' the direct object, and ʿiwajan a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), in which the verbal noun ʿiwaj stands in the place of a noun. In this i'rab there is an intensification: they seek that the straight way itself be crookedness, following the pattern of hyperbole in "rajul ṣawm" (a man who fasts constantly). This makes their reproach and rebuke more forceful. And Allah knows best.]

And you are witnesses that it is the way of Allah, which no one turns away from except one who is astray and misleads others. Or: "and you are witnesses" among the people of your religion, upright men whom they trust in your statements and whom they consult in their gravest matters, namely the rabbis (aḥbār).

Wa-mā Allāhu bi-ghāfilin: a warning (waʿīd). The position of tabghūnahā is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).
