It is said that Shas ibn Qays, a Jew, passed by a group of Ansar from the Aws and the Khazraj who were sitting together in a gathering and talking. [[Al-Tabari narrated it with its wording through Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la, from Ibn Wahb, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father. Ibn Ishaq also narrated it in al-Maghazi, by the route of al-Tabari, saying: "The trustworthy narrator told us, from Zayd ibn Aslam, at length." Ibn Hisham mentioned it but did not mention Ibn Ishaq's chain. He added at its end: "On that day Hudayr ibn Simak, the father of Usayd, was in command of the Aws, and Amr ibn al-Nu'man al-Bayadi was in command of the Khazraj, and both were killed. And Allah revealed concerning Shas: ﴿O you who have believed, if you obey a party of those who were given the Scripture...﴾ [3:100], the verse." Al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi mentioned it in their book on the occasions of revelation (asbab al-nuzul), from Zayd ibn Aslam, without a chain.]] He was a man of great disbelief, extremely harsh in his attacks upon the Muslims, and extremely envious of them. It angered him that they had come together in harmony, after the enmity that had existed between them in the Jahiliyya (the Age of Ignorance). He said: "We have no peace with them when they gather." So he ordered a young Jew to sit with them, remind them of the Day of Bu'ath [[The phrase "the Day of Bu'ath": Bu'ath, with a dammah, is a day of battle between the Aws and the Khazraj. (A)]] and recite to them some of the poetry that had been composed about it. It was a day on which the Aws and the Khazraj had fought, and victory on it had gone to the Aws. He did so. The people then quarrelled, boasted against one another, grew angry, and said: "Arms! Arms!" News of this reached the Prophet (ﷺ), so he went out to them with those of the Muhajirun and the Ansar who were with him, and said: "Do you call to the Jahiliyya [[The phrase "Do you call to the Jahiliyya": in al-Shihab's commentary on al-Baydawi, it is claimed that this is a distortion, and that the correct reading is "Abda'wa al-Jahiliyya," meaning "Do you take it up?" (A)]] while I am among you, after Allah has honored you with Islam, cut off from you the affairs of the Jahiliyya, and joined your hearts together?" The people then recognized that this was a prod from Satan and a scheme of their enemy. They threw down their weapons, wept, and embraced one another. Then they departed together with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). There was never a day whose beginning was more evil and whose end was better than that day.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verse 101:

وَكَيْفَ تَكْفُرُونَ: The interrogative here carries the sense of denunciation and astonishment, and the meaning is: from where could disbelief reach you, when the signs of Allah, which is the Qur'an as a miraculous proof, are recited to you (تُتْلى عَلَيْكُمْ) upon the tongue of the Messenger, fresh and tender [[The commentary on the phrase "upon the tongue of the Messenger, fresh and tender": in al-Sihah, "ghadd" means something fresh, i.e., tender, and every flourishing thing is "ghadd", such as youth and other things. And there is something "tari", i.e., "ghadd", between tenderness. (ʿ)]], and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is among you, admonishing you, advising you, and removing your doubts? وَمَنْ يَعْتَصِمْ بِاللَّهِ: and whoever holds fast to Allah, that is, whoever adheres to His religion. It is also permissible that this be an exhortation to them to take refuge in Him in repelling the evils and schemes of the disbelievers. فَقَدْ هُدِيَ: then he has certainly been guided, meaning guidance has without doubt been attained for him, just as you say: "If you come to so-and-so, you have certainly prospered," as if the guidance has already been attained, so he speaks of it as already accomplished. The sense of expectation in "qad" is clear, because the one who holds fast to Allah is expecting guidance, just as the one who seeks the generous man is expecting prosperity from him.

*Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 102–103:*

﴿as He truly deserves to be feared﴾: its due fear of Him, and what is truly due from it, which is performing the obligations and avoiding the prohibitions. Similar to this is ﴿so fear Allah as much as you are able﴾, meaning: go to great lengths in piety, so that you do not leave any part of what is within your ability. And from ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud):

It is that He is obeyed and not disobeyed, thanked and not denied, and remembered and not forgotten. [[The author said: "It was transmitted as a marfuʿ (traced back to the Prophet)." End. As for the mawquf (ending at a Companion) version, al-Hakim recorded it through the chain of Masʿar from Zayd from Murrah from him, and likewise ʿAbd al-Razzaq recorded it, and through him al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani. Abu Nuʿaym said in the biography of Masʿar in al-Hilyah: "Sulayman ibn Ahmad told us, namely al-Tabarani," and then he mentioned it. Then he said: "This is how people transmitted it from Zayd as a mawquf. Al-Nadr raised it from Muhammad ibn Talhah from Zayd, and then he related it as marfuʿ. Ibn Mardawayh recorded it through Ibn Wahb from Sufyan al-Thawri from Zayd, also as marfuʿ. It has a witness from Ibn ʿAbbas as marfuʿ, recorded by al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab from the narration of Ibn Jarir from ʿAta' from Ibn ʿAbbas. But it is from the copy of ʿAbd al-Ghani ibn Saʿid al-Thaqafi from Musa ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sanʿani, and that copy is discarded."]] It was also transmitted as marfuʿ. And it was said:

It is that the blame of any blamer does not stop you from [doing] Allah's [command], and that you establish justice even if it is against yourself, your son or your father. And it was said: a servant does not fear Allah as He truly deserves until he guards his tongue. And taqah (fear) is from ittaqa, like tuʾdah (deliberateness) is from ittaʾada.

﴿and do not die﴾: its meaning is: do not be in any state other than the state of Islam when death overtakes you. This is like when you say to someone whom you ask to help you in meeting the enemy: "Do not come to me except while you are on a horse." You are not forbidding him from coming, but you are forbidding him from departing from the condition you stipulated to him at the time of coming.

As for ﴿and hold fast to the rope of Allah﴾: it may be a metaphor for relying on Him and trusting in His protection, like a person hanging from a high place who holds on to a strong rope that he trusts will not break. It may also be that "the rope" is a metaphor for His covenant, and "holding fast" refers to trust in the covenant. Or it is an elaboration (tarshih) of the metaphor of the rope by something suitable to it. The meaning is:

Be united in seeking Allah's help and in trusting in Him, and do not scatter away from Him. Or: be united in adhering to His covenant with His servants, which is faith and obedience, or to His Book, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Qur'an is the firm rope of Allah. Its wonders never cease, and it does not wear out through much repetition. Whoever speaks by it speaks truly, whoever acts by it is rightly guided, and whoever holds fast to it is guided to a straight path." [[Recorded by al-Tirmidhi in the Book of the Virtues of the Qur'an, from the hadith of al-Harith al-Aʿwar from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, at length, containing a story. He said: "Gharib (strange); we do not know it except from the hadith of Hamzah al-Zayyat." And its isnad is unknown. End. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ishaq, al-Darimi and al-Bazzar also recorded it through al-Harith. Al-Bazzar said: "We do not know it except through ʿAli, and we do not know anyone transmitting it from him except al-Harith." End. It has a witness from Muʿadh ibn Jabal, recorded by al-Tabarani from the narration of ʿAmr ibn Waqid from Yunus ibn Maysarah from Ibn Idris, with the wording: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned the trials and made them severe. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'What is the way out of them?' He said: 'The Book of Allah,'" and then he related the hadith in full. Al-Hakim also transmitted it as marfuʿ from the hadith of Ibn Masʿud: "This Qur'an is the rope of Allah and the clear light, and an intercessor, a protection for whoever holds fast to it... " the hadith. He recorded it through Salih ibn ʿUmar from Ibrahim al-Bahri from Abu al-Ahwas from him. And Ibrahim is weak.]]

﴿and do not be divided﴾: do not separate from the truth by falling into disagreement among yourselves, as the Jews and Christians disagreed. Or, as you were divided and turning away from one another in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance), with each of you being hostile to and warring against the other. Or: do not introduce anything that would lead to division and dispel the unity and harmony you have, which is contrary to what your Gatherer and the one who unites you (Allah) desires, namely following the truth and holding fast to Islam.

They were in the Jahiliyyah with enmities, grudges and continuous wars among them, and then Allah united their hearts through Islam, cast love into them, so they loved one another, reconciled and became ﴿brothers﴾, compassionate and sincere toward one another, united upon one matter that organized them and removed the disagreement, which is brotherhood in Allah. It was also said: they are the Aws and Khazraj. They were two brothers of the same father and mother, but enmity arose between them and wars were prolonged for one hundred and twenty years, until Allah extinguished that through Islam and united them through the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿and you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire﴾: and you were about to fall into the fire of Hell because of the disbelief you were upon, ﴿so He saved you from it﴾ through Islam. The pronoun (in "from it") refers either to the pit, or to the Fire, or to the brink. [[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "The pronoun refers to the brink (shafa), which is masculine, but he made it feminine because of the annexation (idafah)..." etc. Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: It is permissible for the pronoun to refer back to the pit (hufrah), so there is no need for the interpretation mentioned, just as you say: "I honored the boy of Hind, and I was kind to her." The meaning when it refers back to the pit is more complete, because it is the pit from which one is actually favored with being saved. As for being favored with being saved from the brink, it does not necessarily imply being on the brink, from which one falls into the pit; so saving from the brink is saving from the pit into which one is expected to fall. Therefore, attributing the favor to saving from the pit is more eloquent and effective. Moreover, acquiring the feminine gender from the annexed noun was counted by Abu ʿAli in al-Taʿaliq as a necessity of poetry. (This is contrary to his opinion in al-Idah, transmitted by Ibn Yasʿun.) What led al-Zamakhshari to return the pronoun to the brink is only that it is what they were upon; they were not in the pit so that He would favor them with saving them from it. We have explained, in the course of this discussion, what justifies the favor of saving them from the pit, because they were most likely heading toward it were it not for the divine rescue. Do you not see the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The one who grazes around the protected pasture is about to fall into it," and His (Exalted) saying: ﴿Is one who founded his building on the edge of a crumbling cliff, and it collapsed with him into the Fire of Hell?﴾ Observe how He made the building's being on the edge a cause leading to its collapse into the Fire of Hell, with that confirmed by His saying "crumbling." And Allah knows best.]] And the feminine form was used only because it is in construct with the pit, and he (the brink) is part of it, as the poet said:

*"As the spear's chest was stained with blood"* [[*"Even if you were in a well eighty cubits deep, and you climbed the ladders of the heaven with a ladder,*

*The speech would certainly lure you until you bray, and you would know that I am not one who is silenced among you,*

*And you would choke on the speech which I have spread, as the spear's chest chokes on blood."*

These are by al-Aʿsha, Maymun ibn Qays. In it there are two interpretations. The first: he describes a man for disclosing secrets, and that if he had tried to conceal it, he would not have been able to. That is, even if you had exerted yourself in concealment as though you were in a deep well, and then you climbed from its bottom and reached the ladders of the heavens, meaning its gates. His saying "with a ladder" is an exaggeration of the comparison, as if he had literally climbed on a ladder. "Would lure you" (with a light nun), meaning: would bring you down, the speech bringing you down from the sky step by step to the bottom of the well as you were, and spoil your scheming. So you "bray," i.e., you speak. The "daraja al-sabiyy" is when a child comes close to walking with his steps; "daraja al-qawm" is when some of them die one after another. "Harra al-kalb harīran" is when a dog barks, and in this there is a hint of comparing him to a barking dog. "You would know," i.e., I answer your speech so that you would know that I am not unable to respond among you. The reading "ʿankum" (from you) instead of "ʿindakum" (with you) is also found, and they are the same. Then he returned to explaining how speech is drawn out from him, and said: "And you would choke on the speech which I have spread," i.e., which I have disseminated and published about you.

"Shariqa" means to choke on one's saliva or the like. "Dhāʿa al-khabar dhayʿan wa dhuyūʿan" means the news spread. "Adhāʿahu" means to publish it. That is, you would not be able to swallow and conceal it, just as the spear's chest does not reach the blood on the slain. He likened the speech which he could not conceal to the thing which could not be swallowed, so he used "shariqa" as a metaphor for the inability to conceal, in an explicit metaphor. He compared the first choking to the second to imply that his speech is like blood, to emphasize the impossibility of concealing it. The second interpretation: its meaning is that if you were distant from me, as though you were at the bottom of a well, and you climbed from it to the sky, the speech would draw you closer to me little by little until you bray, i.e., you dislike it and hate it, and you would know that I am not unable to speak which brings you close to me, and you would choke on the speech that I have spread about you. The "ta'" here is for the speaker, i.e., you would not be able to hear it and enter your ear, just as the spear's chest could not swallow the blood. "Ṣadr al-qanāh" is masculine, but it acquired the feminine from the annexed noun, so its verb was feminine and he said "sharqat." It was said that "al-qanah" here means the water channel, and how far is that from blood.]]

And "shafā al-ḥufrah" and "shafatuhā" mean its edge (ḥarfuhā), both masculine and feminine, and its final radical is waw, except that in the masculine it is inverted (maqlūbah) and in the feminine it is deleted. Similar to "shafā" and "shafah" is "janib" and "janibah" (both meaning side). If you ask: how did they make the edge of a pit to be on the edge of the Fire? I say: if they had died in the state they were in, they would have fallen into the Fire. So their life, after which falling into the Fire was expected, is depicted as sitting on its edge, about to fall into it.

﴿Thus﴾, like this eloquent explanation, ﴿Allah makes clear to you His signs, that you may be guided﴾, desiring that you increase in guidance.

Al-Hakim also transmitted it as marfuʿ from the hadith of Ibn Masʿud: "This Qur'an is the rope of Allah and the clear light, and an intercessor, a protection for whoever holds fast to it... " the hadith. He recorded it through Salih ibn ʿUmar from Ibrahim al-Bahri from Abu al-Ahwas from him. And Ibrahim is weak.]]

﴿and do not be divided﴾: do not separate from the truth by falling into disagreement among yourselves, as the Jews and Christians disagreed. Or, as you were divided and turning away from one another in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance), with each of you being hostile to and warring against the other. Or: do not introduce anything that would lead to division and dispel the unity and harmony you have, which is contrary to what your Gatherer and the one who unites you (Allah) desires, namely following the truth and holding fast to Islam.

They were in the Jahiliyyah with enmities, grudges and continuous wars among them, and then Allah united their hearts through Islam, cast love into them, so they loved one another, reconciled and became ﴿brothers﴾, compassionate and sincere toward one another, united upon one matter that organized them and removed the disagreement, which is brotherhood in Allah. It was also said: they are the Aws and Khazraj. They were two brothers of the same father and mother, but enmity arose between them and wars were prolonged for one hundred and twenty years, until Allah extinguished that through Islam and united them through the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿and you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire﴾: and you were about to fall into the fire of Hell because of the disbelief you were upon, ﴿so He saved you from it﴾ through Islam. The pronoun (in "from it") refers either to the pit, or to the Fire, or to the brink. [[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "The pronoun refers to the brink (shafa), which is masculine, but he made it feminine because of the annexation (idafah)..." etc. Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: It is permissible for the pronoun to refer back to the pit (hufrah), so there is no need for the interpretation mentioned, just as you say: "I honored the boy of Hind, and I was kind to her." The meaning when it refers back to the pit is more complete, because it is the pit from which one is actually favored with being saved. As for being favored with being saved from the brink, it does not necessarily imply being on the brink, from which one falls into the pit; so saving from the brink is saving from the pit into which one is expected to fall. Therefore, attributing the favor to saving from the pit is more eloquent and effective. Moreover, acquiring the feminine gender from the annexed noun was counted by Abu ʿAli in al-Taʿaliq as a necessity of poetry. (This is contrary to his opinion in al-Idah, transmitted by Ibn Yasʿun.) What led al-Zamakhshari to return the pronoun to the brink is only that it is what they were upon; they were not in the pit so that He would favor them with saving them from it. We have explained, in the course of this discussion, what justifies the favor of saving them from the pit, because they were most likely heading toward it were it not for the divine rescue. Do you not see the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "The one who grazes around the protected pasture is about to fall into it," and His (Exalted) saying: ﴿Is one who founded his building on the edge of a crumbling cliff, and it collapsed with him into the Fire of Hell?﴾ Observe how He made the building's being on the edge a cause leading to its collapse into the Fire of Hell, with that confirmed by His saying "crumbling." And Allah knows best.]] And the feminine form was used only because it is in construct with the pit, and he (the brink) is part of it, as the poet said:

*"As the spear's chest was stained with blood"* [[*"Even if you were in a well eighty cubits deep, and you climbed the ladders of the heaven with a ladder,*

*The speech would certainly lure you until you bray, and you would know that I am not one who is silenced among you,*

*And you would choke on the speech which I have spread, as the spear's chest chokes on blood."*

These are by al-Aʿsha, Maymun ibn Qays. In it there are two interpretations. The first: he describes a man for disclosing secrets, and that if he had tried to conceal it, he would not have been able to. That is, even if you had exerted yourself in concealment as though you were in a deep well, and then you climbed from its bottom and reached the ladders of the heavens, meaning its gates. His saying "with a ladder" is an exaggeration of the comparison, as if he had literally climbed on a ladder. "Would lure you" (with a light nun), meaning: would bring you down, the speech bringing you down from the sky step by step to the bottom of the well as you were, and spoil your scheming. So you "bray," i.e., you speak. The "daraja al-sabiyy" is when a child comes close to walking with his steps; "daraja al-qawm" is when some of them die one after another. "Harra al-kalb harīran" is when a dog barks, and in this there is a hint of comparing him to a barking dog. "You would know," i.e., I answer your speech so that you would know that I am not unable to respond among you. The reading "ʿankum" (from you) instead of "ʿindakum" (with you) is also found, and they are the same. Then he returned to explaining how speech is drawn out from him, and said: "And you would choke on the speech which I have spread," i.e., which I have disseminated and published about you.

"Shariqa" means to choke on one's saliva or the like. "Dhāʿa al-khabar dhayʿan wa dhuyūʿan" means the news spread. "Adhāʿahu" means to publish it. That is, you would not be able to swallow and conceal it, just as the spear's chest does not reach the blood on the slain. He likened the speech which he could not conceal to the thing which could not be swallowed, so he used "shariqa" as a metaphor for the inability to conceal, in an explicit metaphor. He compared the first choking to the second to imply that his speech is like blood, to emphasize the impossibility of concealing it. The second interpretation: its meaning is that if you were distant from me, as though you were at the bottom of a well, and you climbed from it to the sky, the speech would draw you closer to me little by little until you bray, i.e., you dislike it and hate it, and you would know that I am not unable to speak which brings you close to me, and you would choke on the speech that I have spread about you. The "ta'" here is for the speaker, i.e., you would not be able to hear it and enter your ear, just as the spear's chest could not swallow the blood. "Ṣadr al-qanāh" is masculine, but it acquired the feminine from the annexed noun, so its verb was feminine and he said "sharqat." It was said that "al-qanah" here means the water channel, and how far is that from blood.]]

And "shafā al-ḥufrah" and "shafatuhā" mean its edge (ḥarfuhā), both masculine and feminine, and its final radical is waw, except that in the masculine it is inverted (maqlūbah) and in the feminine it is deleted. Similar to "shafā" and "shafah" is "janib" and "janibah" (both meaning side). If you ask: how did they make the edge of a pit to be on the edge of the Fire? I say: if they had died in the state they were in, they would have fallen into the Fire. So their life, after which falling into the Fire was expected, is depicted as sitting on its edge, about to fall into it.

﴿Thus﴾, like this eloquent explanation, ﴿Allah makes clear to you His signs, that you may be guided﴾, desiring that you increase in guidance.

And let there be among you a community (ummah) who invite to good and enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. [ "Min" is partitive (lil-tab'id). Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: In this partitive sense, and in the indefiniteness of "ummah," there is an alert to the fewness of those who act on this, and that it is addressed only to the elite. From this style is His saying, ﴿Be mindful of Allah, and let every soul look to what it has sent forward for tomorrow﴾ [59:18]. The address is directed at an indefinite "soul" to alert that few look to their return. Likewise His saying, ﴿and an attentive ear will retain it﴾ [69:12], until it is reported in the tafsir that the intended meaning is one specific ear, namely the ear of Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.]

because enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong are communal obligations (fard kifaya, an obligation which is discharged when some perform it), and because only one who knows what is right and what is wrong is fit for it, and who knows how to arrange the enjoining in its implementation and how to carry it out. For the ignorant may forbid what is right and enjoin what is wrong; he may know a ruling according to his own school and be ignorant of it according to another's, so he forbids what is not wrong. He may be harsh where gentleness is called for, and gentle where harshness is called for, and he may denounce one whose denunciation only increases his persistence, or one for whom denunciation is pointless, such as denouncing the jailers (al-ma'sir, i.e., the prison) and the executioners and their like. [Al-ma'sir is the plural of ma'sir, meaning the prison, as stated in al-Sihah. (Ibn al-Munayyir?)]

It is said that "min" is explanatory (lil-tabyin), meaning: "and be a community who enjoin," as in His saying, ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind; you enjoin what is right﴾ [3:110].

﴿And those are the successful﴾ — they are the ones specially deserving of success, not others.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he was asked while on the pulpit, "Who is the best of people?" he said: "The one who most enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong, and is most mindful of Allah, and keeps the ties of kinship most." [Related by Ahmad, Abu Ya'la, al-Tabari and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, from the narration of Sharik, from Simak, from Abdullah ibn Umayra, from the wife of Durrah bint Abi Lahab, who said: "I was with Aisha when a man was brought to the Prophet (ﷺ), who had called out to him while he was on the pulpit. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, who among people is best?' and so on."]

And from him, peace be upon him: "Whoever enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong is the caliph (khalifah) of Allah on His earth, and the caliph of His Messenger, and the caliph of His Book." [Related by Ibn Adi in al-Kamil in the biography of Kadih ibn Rahmah, from his narration, from Ibn Lahi'a, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, from Muslim ibn Jabir, from Ubadah ibn al-Samit. Kadih is discarded (saqit). It has a corroborating mursal report related by Ali ibn Mabad in the Book of Obedience, from Baqiyyah, from Hassan ibn Sulayman, from Abu Nadrah, from al-Hasan al-Basri. It is also related by al-Tha'labi through this route.]

And from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "The best jihad is enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, and hating the wicked; whoever hates the wicked and is angry for Allah's sake, Allah will be angry for his sake." [Abu Nu'aym related it in al-Hilyah in the biography of Ali at length, from the narration of Khallas ibn Amr, who said: "We were sitting with Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, when a man from Khuza'ah came to him and said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, did you hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) describe Islam?' He said: 'I heard him say: Islam is built upon four pillars: patience, certainty, jihad, and justice'..." and so on, until he said: "Jihad has four branches: enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, truthfulness in times of patience, and hatred of the wicked. So whoever enjoins what is right strengthens the back of the believer; whoever forbids what is wrong humbles the nose of the disbeliever; whoever is truthful in times of patience secures his religion and fulfils what is upon him; whoever hates the wicked has been angry for Allah's sake; and whoever is angry for Allah's sake, Allah is angry for his sake." It is through the route of Ishaq ibn Bishr from Muqatil, and both are discarded. He said: And the narration of al-Ala ibn Abd al-Rahman from Qabisah ibn Jabir from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him.]

And from Hudhayfah: "There will come upon people a time when the carcass of a donkey will be dearer to them than a believer who enjoins them what is right and forbids them what is wrong."

And from Sufyan al-Thawri: "When a man is beloved among his neighbours and praised among his brothers, know that he is a flatterer (mudahin)."

Enjoining what is right follows what is enjoined: if it is obligatory, then it is obligatory; if it is recommended (nadb), then it is recommended. As for forbidding what is wrong, it is entirely obligatory, because abandoning all wrong is obligatory, given its ugliness.

If you ask: What is the way to establish the obligation? I say: The two shaykhs disagreed about it. According to Abu Ali [al-Jubba'i], it is revelation and reason; according to Abu Hashim [al-Jubba'i], it is revelation alone.

If you ask: What are the conditions for forbidding? I say: That the one who forbids knows that what he denounces is ugly, for if he does not know, he cannot be secure that he may denounce what is good; that what he forbids is not already committed, for what has already occurred is not fitting to forbid, rather what is fitting is to blame for it and forbid its like; that he does not think it likely that the one forbidden will increase in his wrongs; and that he does not think it likely that his forbidding will have no effect, for that would be pointless.

If you ask: What are the conditions for it being obligatory? I say: That he thinks it likely that the disobedience will occur, such as seeing a drinker preparing to drink wine by readying its implements; and that he does not think it likely that, if he denounces, a grave harm will befall him.

If you ask: How is denunciation to be carried out? I say: He begins with the gentle, and if it does not benefit, he advances to the harsh, because the aim is to stop the wrong. Allah the Exalted says, ﴿make peace between them﴾ [49:9], then He says, ﴿fight﴾ [49:9].

If you ask: Who carries it out? I say: Every Muslim who is able to do it and who meets its conditions. They have agreed that whoever sees another neglecting the prayer must denounce it, because its ugliness is known to everyone. As for denunciation by fighting, the imam and his deputies have priority, for they know statecraft best and possess its means.

If you ask: Who is to be enjoined and forbidden? I say: Every accountable person. And one who is not accountable, when he intends harm to another, is prevented, such as children and the insane; children are forbidden from the prohibited things so that they do not become accustomed to them, just as they are made to pray so that they become trained in it.

If you ask: Is it obligatory for one who commits a wrong to forbid what he himself commits? I say: Yes, it is obligatory upon him, because abandoning its commission and denouncing it are both obligatory upon him; so abandoning one of the two obligations does not remove the other obligation from him. It is related from the early generation (al-salaf): "Enjoin good even if you do not do it yourselves." And it is related that al-Hasan heard Mutarrif ibn Abd Allah say: "I do not say what I do not do." He said: "And which of us does what he says? The Devil would love to gain this from you, so that no one would enjoin what is right or forbid what is wrong."

If you ask: How is it said, ﴿they invite to good and enjoin what is right﴾ [3:104]? I say: Inviting to good is general in the duties, of acts and abstentions, while enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong is specific; so the general is mentioned first, then the specific is coordinated with it, as a notice of its excellence, as in His saying, ﴿and the middle prayer﴾ [2:238].

[(Continuation of his words.) He said: "His saying, ﴿they invite to good and enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾, the mention of inviting to good first..." and so on. Ahmad said: Coordinating the specific with the general indicates, without doubt, extra attention to the specific when it singles out some of what the general includes, as in His saying, ﴿whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and messengers, and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [2:98], and His saying, ﴿therein are fruits, and palm trees and pomegranates﴾ [55:68], and His saying, ﴿Guard the prayers and the middle prayer﴾ [2:238], and the like, because singling out what is mentioned separately serves to distinguish it from the rest of what the general includes. But in this verse, after the general, all that it includes has been mentioned, since the good to which one is invited is either an enjoined act or a forbidden abstention, and it goes beyond neither of these two, so that its specification would not distinguish it from the rest of what the general includes. Rather, the better way to put it is: the benefit of this specification is to mention the invitation to good in general and then in detail. And as for the alert that mention in two ways conveys what is no secret of care, and Allah knows best. Unless a usage is established that restricts enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong to some kinds of good, in which case the intent of al-Zamakhshari would be complete; but I do not see this usage as established, and Allah knows best.]

It is general in the obligations, of acts and abstentions, and enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong is specific; so the general was mentioned, then the specific was coordinated with it, as a notice of its excellence, like His saying, ﴿and the middle prayer﴾ [2:238].

The Qur'anic verses 105–107 of Surah Al ʿImran appear here as quoted within al-Zamakhshari's commentary.

"Like those who split and differed, after clear proofs had come to them." That is, the Jews and the Christians, after the clear proofs (al-bayyinat) had come to them, which necessitated agreement upon one word, the word of truth. It was said: they are the innovators of this community, namely the Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists), the Mujbirah (determinists) and the Hashwiyyah (literalist traditionalists), and those like them. ﴿On the day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black﴾: this is in the accusative as an adverbial complement of the time (zarf), governed by its terror, or by the implied verb "remember" (udhkur). It is also read as "tabyaddu" and "taswaddu" with the prefixed letter of the imperfect vowelled with kasra, and as "tabyaaddu" and "taswaadd", with the whiteness being of light and the blackness being of darkness. Whoever was of the people of the light of truth is marked with whiteness of complexion, brightness and radiance; his record becomes white and radiant, and light runs before him and on his right. Whoever was of the people of the darkness of falsehood is marked with blackness of complexion, dullness and gloom; his record becomes black and dark, and darkness surrounds him from every side. We seek refuge in Allah and in the vastness of His mercy from the darknesses of falsehood and its people.

﴿As for those whose faces turn black, [it will be said to them]: "Did you disbelieve after your belief?"﴾ So it is said to them: "Did you disbelieve?" The interrogative particle (hamzah) is for rebuke and for expressing wonder at their condition.

The apparent meaning is that they are the People of the Book, and their disbelief after belief is their denial of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after acknowledging him before his coming. It is reported from ʿAṭāʾ: the faces of the Muhajirun and the Ansar turn white, and the faces of Banu Qurayzah and al-Nadir turn black. It was said they are the apostates. It was said they are the people of innovation and desires. It is reported from Abu Umamah that they are the Kharijites. When he saw them on the steps of Damascus, his eyes welled with tears, and then he said: "The dogs of the Fire are these; the worst of the slain beneath the canopy of heaven, and the best of the slain beneath the canopy of heaven are those whom these have slain." Abu Ghalib said to him: "Is this something you say from your own opinion, or something you heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?" He said: "Rather, I heard it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) more than once."

He said: "Then what is the matter with you, that your eyes have welled with tears?" He said: "Out of mercy for them, for they were of the people of Islam and they disbelieved." Then he recited this verse, and then he took his hand and said: "Indeed in your land there are many of them, so may Allah protect you from them."[Takhrij note: this report is cited by al-Tha'labi through ʿIkrimah ibn ʿAmmar from Shaddad from Abu Umamah in this form; al-Hakim also narrated it by this route. al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Yaʿla and al-Tabarani all narrated it in full through Abu Ghalib. It has another chain narrated by al-Tabarani from Shahr ibn Hawshab from Abu Umamah.]

It was said they are all the disbelievers, for their turning away from what the acknowledgment obliged, when He made them witness against themselves: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said: ﴿Yes﴾. ﴿Then as for those in the mercy of Allah﴾: that is, in His blessing, which is the everlasting reward. If you say: how is the placement of His words ﴿they will abide therein eternally﴾ after ﴿in the mercy of Allah﴾? I say: it is in the position of a resumptive statement, as if it were said: "How will they be therein?" So it is said: "They will abide therein eternally, never departing from it and never dying."

This is the commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 3, verses 108–109:

﴿Those are the verses of Allah, which we recite to you in truth. And Allah does not desire injustice toward the worlds.﴾ The verses referred to are those concerning promise and threat, which we recite to you, combined with truth and justice, that is, the requital of the good-doer and the evil-doer according to what each deserves. ﴿And Allah does not desire injustice﴾, so that He would seize anyone without sin, or increase the punishment of a sinner, or diminish the reward of a good-doer. The word "injustice" (ظلما) is indefinite, and He said ﴿for the worlds﴾, meaning: He does not desire any kind of injustice toward any of His creation. So glory be to the One who forbears toward the one who attributes to Him the desire of abominations and approval of them.[[His saying "so glory be to the One who forbears toward the one who attributes to Him the desire of abominations" means the people of the Sunna, who say: "Whatever Allah wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be," as the predecessors (al-salaf) agreed. (Ibid.)]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 110–111:

"Kāna" (kāna) expresses the existence of a thing in a past time in an indefinite manner, and there is no indication in it of prior non-existence or of a sudden interruption. From it is His saying, ﴿And God has ever been Forgiving and Merciful﴾. And from it is His saying, ﴿You are the best nation⦆ (kuntum khayra ummatin). It is as if it were said: "You were found to be the best nation." It was also said: "You were, in the knowledge of God, the best nation." And it was said: "You were, among the nations before you, mentioned as being the best nation, described with it." ﴿Brought forth﴾ means "made manifest." His saying ﴿you enjoin﴾ (ta'murūna) is a resumptive sentence (kalām mustaʾnaf) that explains their being the best nation, just as you would say, "Zayd is generous; he feeds people, clothes them, and attends to what sets them right." ﴿And you believe in God﴾ (wa tu'minūna bi-llāh): the belief is made to comprise belief in everything that must be believed in, as belief in God, because whoever believes in some of what must be believed in, such as the Messenger, the Book, resurrection, reckoning, punishment, reward, or other things, his belief is not counted, and so he is as one who does not believe in God. ﴿And they say: We believe in some and disbelieve in others, and they desire to take a way between that. Those are truly the disbelievers﴾. The proof of this is His saying, ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed, along with their belief in God, it would have been better for them﴾.

"It would have been better for them" means that belief would have been better for them than what they are upon, because they only preferred their religion over the religion of Islam out of love for leadership and for gathering the common people as followers. Had they believed, they would have had from leadership, followers, and worldly portions what is better than what they preferred the religion of falsehood for. Together with attaining what they were promised for belief, namely the giving of their reward twice. ﴿Among them are the believers﴾, such as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and his companions. ﴿And most of them are the defiant﴾ (al-fāsiqūn), those who persist in disbelief. ﴿They will not harm you except with some harm﴾ (illā adhan), meaning only a harm limited to injury, by speech, by one who slanders the religion, or by threat, or the like. ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you﴾ (yuwallūkumu al-adbār), routed, and they will not harm you by killing or capturing. ﴿Then they will not be helped﴾ (thumma lā yunṣarūn): then there will be no help for them from anyone, and they will not be protected from you.

In this there is reassurance for those among them who had embraced Islam, because they used to cause them harm by mockery, by reproach, by misleading them, and by threatening them, saying that they could not go beyond injury by words to any harm that would matter. Yet He promised them dominance over them, and vengeance upon them, and that the outcome of their affair would be humiliation and abasement.

If you say: why was the conjoined word in His saying ﴿then they will not be helped﴾ not put in the jussive? [Maḥmūd said: "If you say, why was the conjoined in His saying 'then they will not be helped' not put in the jussive…?" Aḥmad said: This is an ascent in the promise from what is lower to what is higher, for they were promised turning their backs when they fight, then the promise ascended to what is more complete in success, that these people will not be helped at all. This ascent is strengthened by the use of thumma (then) rather than wa (and), for it is here borrowed to denote a distance in rank, not in time, as if he said: "Then here is what is higher in favor and more generous in degrees of kindness, which is that these are a people who will not be helped at all. And God knows best."] I say: He turned it from the judgment of the conditional to the judgment of a fresh statement, as if it were said: "Then I inform you that they will not be helped." If you say: what difference is there in meaning between its being nominative and its being jussive? I say:

If it were jussive, the negation of help would be restricted to their fighting, as turning their backs. But when it is nominative, the negation of help is an unrestricted promise, as if he said: "Then their state and their story, which I inform you of and give you good news of after the turning of backs, is that they are forsaken, with help and strength negated from them; they will not rise after it with any wing, and their affair will not be set right." And it happened as He informed: concerning the state of the Banū Qurayẓa, al-Naḍīr, Banū Qaynuqāʿ, and the Jews of Khaybar. If you say: what is it that this statement is conjoined to? I say: the conditional and its consequent sentence, as if it were said: "I inform you that if they fight you, they will be routed; then I inform you that they will not be helped." If you say: what is the meaning of the delay in thumma? I say: the delay is in rank, because the information about the imposition of abasement upon them is greater than the information about their turning their backs. If you say: what is the position of the two sentences, I mean ﴿among them are the believers﴾ and ﴿they will not harm you﴾? I say: they are two statements coming by way of digression, when the mention of the People of the Book is brought up, as the speaker says: "And in mentioning so-and-so, indeed his affair is such-and-such," and therefore they came without a conjunction.

In the Qur'anic text, "bi-habl min Allah" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), with the implied sense: "except holding fast to a rope from God" (mu'tasimin, mutamassikin, or multabisin bi-habl min Allah). This is an exception from the most general category of circumstances. The meaning is: humiliation has been imposed upon them in all circumstances, except in the state of holding fast to a rope of God and a rope of the people, meaning the protection (dhimmah) of God and the protection of the Muslims. That is to say, they have no honour at all except this one case, namely their seeking refuge in the dhimmah after accepting the jizyah (poll tax).

"Wa baw bi-ghadabin min Allah" means they have incurred a wrath from God that they deserved. "Wa duribat 'alayhimu al-maskanah" means that poverty was imposed upon them as a tent-pole or house is struck upon its people, so they dwell permanently in poverty and do not move away from it. They are the Jews, upon whom be the curse and wrath of God.

"Dhalika" is a reference to what was mentioned: the imposition of humiliation and poverty, and their returning with the wrath of God. That is, this occurs because of their disbelief in the signs of God and their killing of the prophets. Then He said: "Dhalika bi-ma 'asaw," meaning this occurs because of their disobedience to God and their transgression of His limits, so that it may be known that disbelief alone is not the cause for deserving the displeasure of God, and that the displeasure of God is deserved by committing sins just as it is deserved by disbelief. A similar case is His saying: "Mimma khati'atihim ughriqu" (because of their sins they were drowned), and His saying: "Wa akhdhihimu al-riba wa qad nuhu 'anhu wa akliham amwal al-nas bi-al-batil" (and their taking of usury though they were forbidden from it, and their consuming of people's wealth wrongfully).

The pronoun in "laysu" (they are not) refers to the People of the Book, meaning: the People of the Book are not equal. His saying "Among the People of the Book is a community standing (upright)..." is a resumed statement explaining his saying "They are not equal," just as his saying "enjoining what is right" came as an explanation of his saying "You are the best community."

Ummah qa'imah: upright and just, from your saying "aqamtu al-'ud fa-qam," meaning it stood straight (istaqama). They are those among them who embraced Islam. He described their nightly worship, reciting the Qur'an during the hours of the night while prostrating, because this is clearer regarding what they do and more indicative of the good form of their affair. It was also said that it refers to the 'Isha' prayer, because the People of the Book do not perform it.

On the authority of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him): The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) delayed the 'Isha' prayer, then went out to the mosque and found people waiting for the prayer. He said: "Indeed, among the followers of other religions, there is no one who remembers Allah at this hour except you," and he recited this verse. [[Narrated by al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban, Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Ya'la and al-Bazzar, all through the narration of 'Asim from Zirr.]]

His saying "yatlouna" (they recite) and "yu'minuna" (they believe) are in the nominative position as two descriptions of ummah, meaning: an upright community, reciting and believing. He described them with the qualities that were not found among the Jews: reciting the verses of Allah at night while prostrating; and faith in Allah, because their belief in Him is not true belief, since they associated 'Uzayr with Him and disbelieved in some of the books and messengers but not others; and faith in the Last Day, because they describe it contrary to its reality; and enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, because they were hypocrites (mudahinun); and hastening to good deeds, because they were slow to them, unwilling and not desiring them. Hastening to good (al-musara'ah fi al-khayr) is the intense desire for it, because whoever desires a matter hastens to take it up and to carry it out, and prefers promptness over delay.

"Ula'ika" (those): those described with what they were described with are among the righteous (al-salihin), those whose conditions are upright with Allah, whom He is pleased with, and who deserve His praise for them.

It is permissible that by "the righteous" is meant the Muslims. "Falan yukfarouhu" (they will not be denied it): since Allah, Mighty and Exalted, is described as Grateful (shakur) in His saying, "And Allah is Grateful and Forbearing," its meaning is that He will fully reward them, and the opposite of that is negated from Him. If you ask: why does it take two objects, while shakara and kafara are only transitive to one object, as you say "shakara al-ni'mah" and "kafarahā"? I answer: it has been given the sense of deprivation, so it is as if it was said: "you will not be deprived of it," meaning "you will not be deprived of its reward." It was also read as "yaf'alu" and "yukfarūhu," with ya' and ta'. "Wallahu 'alimun bil-muttaqin": a glad tiding to the God-fearing of abundant reward, and an indication that none will succeed with Him except the people of taqwa.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verse 117:

al-Ṣarr: the cold wind [[Maḥmūd said: "al-Ṣarr is the cold wind..." etc. Aḥmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: All of these are sound and well-founded views, and this last one is the best and most sound. However, al-Zamakhshari did not explain the aspect of zarfiyya (the sense of a container or locus) in the examples he mentioned, so we will explain it. We say: if you say, for example, "If my property is entrusted to Zayd, then in ʿAmr after Allah is sufficient," then your saying "sufficient" affirms an indefinite (munkar) predicate stripped of the specifying and particularizing restrictions. Then you make the specific person, who is ʿAmr, a locus for it, and so you individualize that unrestricted indefinite by this meaning. This is a valid zarfiyya, since every restricted (muqayyad) item is a container for its unrestricted (muṭlaq) counterpart, because the unrestricted is part of the restricted. So be alert to this nuance, for it is subtle. And Allah is the Granter of success.]] like ṣarṣar (a violent, freezing wind). He said:

"Do not let the strangers (atāwiyyīn) be equated with them: a violent wind (nakbāʾ ṣirr) striking the people of the encampments."

[[al-Atāwī: the strange, distant one, as if it were derived from al-atāwa, which is a bribe or fee, because he may pay it for residing in a land not his own. al-Nakbāʾ: the violent wind. al-Ṣirr: the hot wind, and it was said: the cold wind. al-Zajjāj said: the sound of fire in the wind. It was said: the sound of the wind. It was said: the atmosphere. It was said: the cold. On this basis, if it is narrated with the genitive (al-jarr) by way of idāfa (annexation), it would be sound. al-Maḥallāt: it was said these are the household implements, such as the axe, the cooking pot, the sieve, and the bucket. It is also permissible that they are the dwellings, namely the shade within a house. He means: do not make the strangers equal to the owners of the houses. It is narrated: "lā yaʿdilanna atāwiyyūn" with the passive form, and what follows it is the deputy subject. al-Jawharī narrated it with the active form and said: meaning, the strangers do not equate anyone with the owners of the encampments, so the object is omitted, which is "madān" (one who is given), and he interpreted al-maḥallāt as all household implements, because the stranger borrows them from their owners. In any case, the nūn here is for emphasis.]] as Layla al-Akhiliyya said:

"He did not overcome the fierce adversary, nor fill the bowls with fat meat on the day of a violent, freezing wind (nakbāʾ ṣarṣar)."

[[Like the one who was the champion of champions, Tawba, who never camped in Najd nor rose out of the lowland. And he did not overcome the fierce adversary, nor fill the bowls with fat meat on the day of a violent, freezing wind.

Layla al-Akhiliyya composed this lamenting her companion Tawba ibn al-Ḥumayyir, recalling his conditions and enumerating his virtues. Fatā al-fityān: meaning he is the young man among them, and they are not youths in comparison to him, even though they are youths in themselves. Tawba is a substitute (badal). lam yanakh: from anākha his camel, the predicate of kaʾanna, meaning as if he had not made his camel kneel in an elevated place. It is narrated: "lam yasir bi-Najd," and "lam yaṭlaʿ" from aṭlaʿa meaning ṭalaʿa, or "lam yaṭlaʿ bi-ʿīrihi min al-mutaghawwar" as a passive participle, i.e. the lowland place in which there is nothing. As if he had not overcome the severe adversary. It is narrated "al-khaṣm al-ṣiḥāḥ" with a fatḥa on the ṣād, meaning the sound one. He means that he used to do all that, and then, as if he does not do it today, because he has died.]]

If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying: ﴿a wind in which is a freezing cold (ṣirr)﴾?

I say: there are several aspects. The first: ṣirr in the description of the wind means "cold," so the description is applied to the cold, meaning in it is the coldness of freezing cold, just as you say "cold cold" for emphasis (mubālagha, hyperbole). The second: that ṣirr is originally a verbal noun meaning cold, so it has been used in its original form. The third: that it comes from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed you have in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example﴾ [33:21], and from your saying: "If so-and-so abandons me, then in Allah is a sufficient guardian and protector." He said:

"And in the Most Merciful is a sufficiency for the weak."

[[Dhanīya... for the poem's verses, it is attributed to Abū Khālid al-Khārijī. It was also said: to Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Azdī. It was said: to ʿImrān ibn Ḥiṭṭān. It was also said other than this: that Qaṭarī ibn al-Fujāʾa blamed him for staying away from the war, so he excused himself with this.

"It has increased life to me, love for my daughters, for they are among the weak. I dread that poverty will see them after me, and that they will drink turbid water after clear. And that they will go naked if the girls are clothed, and the eye turns away from a generous, lean one. Were it not for them, I would have readied my mount, and in the Most Merciful is a sufficiency for the weak."

Banātī is the subject of zāda. Uḥādhir means I fear. I fear that poverty will overtake them after my death, and he expressed that by their seeing him, as an exaggeration, because if he fears their seeing him, he fears their being reached. It is narrated: "makhāfat an yadhuqna al-bu's," meaning hardship, so he compared it to food by way of a metaphor (makniyya), and "tasting" is an imaginative extension (takhyīl). Ranaq the water: it became turbid, and tarannaqa: became turbid, and raṭṭaqahu and arraqahu: made it turbid, and al-ranaq with a vowel on the second letter is a verbal noun like kadar, then it is made sukūn, and by it is intended turbid water. It is narrated "zīfan," meaning adulterated and turbid, and the meaning is one. So the troubled life is compared to it, and the pleasant life is compared to clear water, by way of explicit statement (taṣrīḥ), and "drinking" is an extension (tarshīḥ). Kusiya, on the pattern of faraḥ, is intransitive, the opposite of ʿuriya. It is also permissible here to read it in the passive, from the transitive kusā, like duʿiya. In for the conditional, free of doubt, or with the sense of idh (when). Tanbū: they are removed, a metonymy (kināya) for not marrying them. The generosity (karam) with a sukūn, and it is said with a kasra: an adjective from generosity, applying to the singular and plural, masculine and feminine. It is narrated "ʿan rimm," meaning worn out, and it is more fitting to the context. al-ʿIjāf is the plural of ʿajfāʾ, meaning emaciated, i.e. they are not looked at though they are noble, because of their thinness and wretched condition. Sawaytu mahrī: I put the instruments of war upon it and prepared it and readied it for them. It is narrated "qad samawtu mahrī," and perhaps it is with a lightened mīm, meaning I mounted it and rode it. It was also said: meaning I put upon it the marks of war, so perhaps it is a metathesis. "Sumtu" and it is narrated as sawwamtu with shadda, and this is what fits the meaning that I made marks of war upon it, not that. The one who is with Allah, mighty and majestic, is a sufficient person, and there is no hindrance in hyperbole, especially among the Arabs. In it there is a kind of return to Allah, entrusting oneself to Him, and reliance upon Him, and that He is the Provider, Possessor of strength, the Firm.]]

It likens what they used to spend of their wealth for noble deeds, boasts, seeking praise and good repute among people, not seeking thereby the face of Allah, to a crop struck by frost which was reduced to chaff. It was said: it is what they used to draw near to Allah with, despite their disbelief. It was said: it is what they spent in hostility to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, and it was lost to them, because they did not achieve by their spending what they spent for it. And it likens it to the crop of a people who wronged themselves, ﴿so it destroyed it﴾, as a punishment for their sins, because destruction out of anger is more severe and more emphatic.

If you say: the purpose is to liken what they spent, in its lack of benefit, to a crop of a people who wronged themselves, and its being lost through the crop struck by the cold wind, and the speech does not correspond to the purpose, since it made what they spend likened to the wind.

I say: this is from the compound simile (al-tashbīh al-murakkab) which passed in the explanation of His saying: ﴿like the example of one who kindled a fire﴾ [2:17]. It is also permissible that what is intended is: the likeness of the destruction of what they spend is like the likeness of the destruction of a wind, or the likeness of what they spend is like the likeness of a destroyer, a wind, which is the crop. And it was read: "tunfiqūna" with the letter tāʾ. ﴿And Allah did not wrong them﴾.

The pronoun refers to the spenders, in the sense: Allah did not wrong them by not accepting their expenditures, but they wronged themselves in that they did not bring them in a state deserving acceptance. Or it refers to the owners of the crop who wronged themselves, that is: Allah did not wrong them by destroying their crop, but they wronged themselves by committing what made them deserving of punishment. And it was read "wa-lākin" with the shadda, meaning but they themselves wrong their own souls. It is not permissible to intend: "wa-lākin anfusahum yaẓlimūn," with the omission of the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), because that is only permissible in poetry.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 118–119:

"Bitanat al-rajul" (the inner lining of a man) and "walijatuhu" (his close confidant): his special companion and intimate, to whom he confides his secrets [[On his phrase "bi-shaqurihi": in al-Sihah, al-shaqur (with a damma) means the matters that cling to the heart and are important to it; its singular is shaqr.]] and whom he trusts. He is likened to the lining of a garment, as one says: "So-and-so is my shi'ar" (the garment next to the skin). It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Ansar are the shi'ar (inner garment) and the rest of the people are the di'thar (outer garment)" [[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn 'Asim al-Mazini, within a long hadith whose beginning is: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Junayn, he distributed the spoils."]].

"Min dunikum" (from other than you): from outside your own kind, meaning the Muslims. It is permissible for it to be linked to "la tattakhidhu" (do not take), or to "bitanah" as a qualifier, meaning: a lining that is from outside you, distinct from you. "La ya'lunakum khabalan" (they do not fall short of corrupting you): one says "alla fi al-amr ya'lu" when one falls short in it. It was then used with two objects in their saying "la a'lduka nasihan" (I do not withhold from you sincere advice) and "la a'lduka juhdan" (I do not withhold from you effort), by way of tadmin (implicit meaning). The meaning is: I do not withhold from you sincere advice and I do not diminish it for you. Khabal means corruption.

"Wadda ma 'anittum" (they wish for your distress): wadda your suffering, with "ma" being a verbal noun (masdariyyah). Al-'anat means severe harm and hardship; its root is the re-breaking of a bone after it has been set, meaning they wish that you be harmed in your religion and your worldly affairs with the most severe and complete harm. "Qad badati al-bagda'u min afwahihim" (hatred has already appeared from their mouths): because they cannot contain themselves, despite their self-control and their forcing of themselves, what reveals their hatred of the Muslims slips from their tongues.

It is related from Qatadah: "Hatred has appeared to their allies among the hypocrites and the disbelievers, because some of them inform one another of it."

In the reading of Abdullah: "qad bada al-bagda'" (hatred has appeared).

"Qad bayyanna lakumu al-ayat" (We have made the signs clear for you): the signs indicating the obligation of sincerity in religion, loyalty to the friends of Allah, and enmity toward His enemies. "In kuntum ta'qilun" (if you understand): what has been made clear to you, so that you act upon it.

If you ask: what is the grammatical position of these clauses? I answer: it is permissible that "la ya'lunakum" be a qualifier of "bitanah," and likewise "qad badati al-bagda'u," as if it were said: a lining that does not fall short of corrupting you, whose hatred is manifest. As for "qad bayyanna," it is a new independent statement, and it is better and more eloquent that all of them be resumed clauses, giving the reason for the prohibition of taking them as a lining, as an alert.

"Antum" is the subject (mubtada'), and "ula'" is its predicate: that is, you are those who err in befriending the hypocrites of the People of the Book. His saying "tuhibbunahum wa la yuhibbunakum" (you love them, but they do not love you) explains their error in befriending them, in that they lavish their love upon those whose hearts are full of hatred.

It is said that "ula'" is a relative pronoun, and "tuhibbunahum" is its relative clause. The "wa" in "wa tu'minun" is for the state (hal), and its accusative position is from "la yuhibbunakum": that is, they do not love you while you believe in their whole Book, and they, despite that, hate you. So why do you love them when they do not believe in any part of your Book? This contains severe rebuke: that in their falsehood they are firmer than you are in your truth. Compare His saying: "They suffer as you suffer, but you hope from Allah what they do not hope for" [Q. 4:104].

The one who is enraged or regretful is described as biting the fingertips, the fingers, and the thumbs. Al-Harith ibn Zalim al-Muri said:

"So I kill wretched, base peoples who bite the heads of the thumbs out of rage."
[[Said by al-Harith ibn Zalim al-Muri. Biting the fingertips from rage is a metaphor for its intensity. He mentioned "al-abahim" (the thumbs) and intended all fingers, by way of majaz mursal, since there is no purpose in a specification contrary to what usually occurs. It may also be taken literally.]]

"Qul mutu bighaythikum" (Say: die in your rage): a supplication against them that their rage increase until they perish by it. What is meant by the increase of rage is the increase of what enrages them of the strength of Islam and the honour of its people, and what they have of humiliation, disgrace and destruction in that. "Inna Allaha 'alimun bi-dhat al-sudur" (Indeed Allah knows what is in the breasts): He knows what the hypocrites harbour of rage and hatred, and what occurs from them when some are alone with others. This statement is either within the scope of what is said or outside of it.

If you ask: what is its meaning on both views? I answer: if it is within the scope of what is said, its meaning is: inform them of what they conceal of biting their fingers in rage when they are alone, and say to them that Allah knows what is more hidden than what you conceal among yourselves, namely the inner secrets of the breasts, so do not think that any of your secrets is hidden from Him. If it is outside, its meaning is: say that to them, O Muhammad, and do not be surprised at My informing you of what they conceal, for I know what is more hidden than that, namely what they hold in their breasts and did not reveal by their tongues.

It is also permissible that there is no speech here at all, and that "qul mutu bighaythikum" be a command to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to have good cheer, strong hope, and rejoicing in Allah's promise that they will perish of rage through the exaltation of Islam and their humiliation by it, as if it were said: convince yourself of this.

Al-Hasanah: prosperity, fertility, victory, booty, and similar benefits. Al-sayyi'ah: whatever is the opposite of that.

This is an explanation of the extreme degree of their enmity, in that they envy you for the good that reaches you and gloat over you for the hardship that befalls you. If you ask: how is al-hasanah described with "touching" (mass) and al-sayyi'ah with "striking" (isabah)?

[Mahmud said: "If you ask: how is al-hasanah described with touching and al-sayyi'ah with striking... etc." Ahmad said: It may be said: touching is less firm than striking, and it is as if it were its lowest degree. So the meaning, and God knows best, is: if a good thing touches you at its slightest, it grieves them and they envy you for it; and if striking reaches you and the matter arrives at the point where the gloater pities you, they do not pity you and do not cease from their envy, nor in this state either; rather they rejoice and are delighted. And God knows best.]

I say: "Touching" is used figuratively for the meaning of striking, so the meaning is one. Do you not see His saying: ﴿If a good thing befalls you, it grieves them, and if an affliction befalls you﴾ [Q. 3:120], ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾ [Q. 4:79], ﴿When evil touches him he is anxious, and when good touches him he is withholding﴾ [Q. 70:20–21].

And if you endure against their enmity and fear God, by avoiding what you have been forbidden of allying with them. Or: and if you endure the obligations of the religion and its hardships, and fear God by avoiding His prohibitions, you will be under God's protection, and their scheming will not harm you. It is read ﴿لا يَضُرُّكُمْ﴾ (la yadurrukum) from ḍārahu, yaḍīruhu. And yaḍurrukum with a ḍammah on the rāʾ to follow the ḍammah on the ḍād, like your saying madda yā hādhā. Al-Mufaḍḍal related from ʿĀṣim: ﴿لا يَضُرُّكُمْ﴾ with a fatḥah on the rāʾ. This is an instruction from God and a guidance that one should seek help against the enemy's scheming through patience and piety. The wise have said:

If you wish to vex one who envies you, increase in excellence within yourself.

﴿Indeed God, of what they do﴾, of patience, piety and other things, ﴿is All-Encompassing﴾, so He will deal with you according to what you deserve. It is read with yāʾ, meaning that He knows what they do in their enmity against you, so He will punish them for it.

﴿And remember when you set out at dawn from your family in Medina to position the believers for battle﴾. That was his going out to Uhud from the chamber of ʿAʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her. It is related that the polytheists (al-mushrikun) descended upon Uhud on Wednesday. The Prophet (ﷺ) consulted his companions and summoned ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, whom he had never summoned before that occasion, and consulted him. ʿAbd Allah and most of the Ansar said:

"O Messenger of Allah, remain in Medina and do not go out to them. By Allah, we have never gone out from it to an enemy without them inflicting harm upon us, nor have they entered it against us without our inflicting harm upon them. How much more so when you are among us. Leave them: if they remain, they remain in a wretched confinement; if they enter, the men will fight them face to face, and the women and children will pelt them with stones; and if they return, they return defeated."

Some of them said: "O Messenger of Allah, lead us out to these dogs, so that they do not think we have shrunk from them." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have seen in my dream cows being slaughtered around me, and I interpreted them as good. I saw a notch in the edge of my sword, and I interpreted it as defeat. And I saw as if I had put my hand into a strong coat of mail, and I interpreted it as Medina. So if you see fit, remain in Medina and let them be." Some men among the Muslims, who had missed Badr and whom Allah had honoured with martyrdom on the day of Uhud, said: "Lead us out to our enemies." They kept at him until he went in, put on his armour. When they saw him wearing his armour, they regretted it and said: "Evil is what we have done: we advised the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while revelation was coming to him." They said: "Do as you see fit, O Messenger." He said: "It is not fitting for a Prophet, once he has put on his armour, to take it off until he has fought."

He went out on Friday after the Friday prayer, and in the morning of Saturday, the fifteenth of Shawwal, he was at the ravine (al-shiʿb) of Uhud. He walked on foot and began arranging his companions for battle, as if he were straightening them as one straightens an arrow (al-qidh). If he saw someone come forward beyond the line, he would say: "Fall back." His encampment was on the slope of the valley (ʿudwat al-wadi), and he placed his back and his camp toward Uhud. He appointed ʿAbd Allah ibn Jubayr over the archers and said to them: "Shoot arrows to keep them away from us, so that they do not come at us from behind."

[[Ibn Ishaq related it in al-Maghazi, saying: Muhammad ibn Shihab, ʿAsim ibn ʿUmar, Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hibban, al-Husayn ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman and others among our scholars related to me, all of them transmitting about the battle of Uhud. Among their narration they said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the Muslims on the day of Uhud: "I saw cows and interpreted them as good, and I saw a notch in the edge of my sword," and he mentioned the hadith at length. In it: a man of the Ansar called Malik ibn ʿAmr died on that day. And in it: a mention of the Ummah and other things. It was also transmitted through Ibn Ishaq by al-Bayhaqi in al-Dalail, and al-Tabari quoted a part of it through this route. ʿAbd al-Razzaq related it from Maʿmar from Ibn Shihab from ʿUrwa at length. al-Tabari related it from the narration of Asbat from al-Suddi, with the wording of the author up to his words "and he was at the ravine," and the rest of it is from the speech of Ibn Ishaq. His words in it, "until the arrows are straightened," occur in the narration of al-Waqidi from the nephew of al-Zuhri from ʿUrwa from al-Miswar ibn Makhrama, and al-Waqidi related it at length with this chain.]]

﴿He positions the believers at their stations﴾: he settles them in their places. ʿAbd Allah (ibn Masʿud) read "li-l-mu'minin" (for the believers), meaning he arranges for them and prepares for them. ﴿Stations for battle﴾: places and positions. The words qaʿada (sit) and qama (stand) have been extended until they function as ṣāra (become). The words maqʿad (seat) and maqam (station) are used in the sense of place. "I say to it when it recoils and stirs: 'Stay where you are, you will be praised, or you will rest.'"

To the point that Muʿawiya said: "Hold on to memorizing poetry, for I almost put my foot in the stirrup on the day of Siffin, and what kept me firm was only the saying of ʿAmr ibn al-Atabba." Had it been a firm resolve, the protection (al-wilaya) would not have remained with them, and Allah, Exalted is He, says: ﴿And Allah is their Protector﴾. It is also possible that it means: "Allah is their helper and the one who manages their affair, so why should they lose heart and not rely upon Allah?"

If you ask: what is the meaning of what is related, that some of them said when this verse was revealed: "By Allah, it does not gladden us that we did not have the intention we had, when Allah has informed us that He is our Protector?" I say: the meaning of that is an excess of joy at the honour they had attained through the praise of Allah and His sending down a verse about them that clearly states the validity of the protection, and that this intention, which was not taken to account because it was not a firm resolve or determination, was the cause of its revelation.

Al-fashal: cowardice and feebleness. ʿAbd Allah read: "wa-Allahu waliyyuhum" (and Allah is their Protector), like His saying: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight one another﴾.

﴿And remember when you set out at dawn from your family in Medina to position the believers for battle﴾. That was his going out to Uhud from the chamber of ʿAʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her. It is related that the polytheists (al-mushrikun) descended upon Uhud on Wednesday. The Prophet (ﷺ) consulted his companions and summoned ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, whom he had never summoned before that occasion, and consulted him. ʿAbd Allah and most of the Ansar said:

"O Messenger of Allah, remain in Medina and do not go out to them. By Allah, we have never gone out from it to an enemy without them inflicting harm upon us, nor have they entered it against us without our inflicting harm upon them. How much more so when you are among us. Leave them: if they remain, they remain in a wretched confinement; if they enter, the men will fight them face to face, and the women and children will pelt them with stones; and if they return, they return defeated."

Some of them said: "O Messenger of Allah, lead us out to these dogs, so that they do not think we have shrunk from them." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have seen in my dream cows being slaughtered around me, and I interpreted them as good. I saw a notch in the edge of my sword, and I interpreted it as defeat. And I saw as if I had put my hand into a strong coat of mail, and I interpreted it as Medina. So if you see fit, remain in Medina and let them be." Some men among the Muslims, who had missed Badr and whom Allah had honoured with martyrdom on the day of Uhud, said: "Lead us out to our enemies." They kept at him until he went in, put on his armour. When they saw him wearing his armour, they regretted it and said: "Evil is what we have done: we advised the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while revelation was coming to him." They said: "Do as you see fit, O Messenger." He said: "It is not fitting for a Prophet, once he has put on his armour, to take it off until he has fought."

He went out on Friday after the Friday prayer, and in the morning of Saturday, the fifteenth of Shawwal, he was at the ravine (al-shiʿb) of Uhud. He walked on foot and began arranging his companions for battle, as if he were straightening them as one straightens an arrow (al-qidh). If he saw someone come forward beyond the line, he would say: "Fall back." His encampment was on the slope of the valley (ʿudwat al-wadi), and he placed his back and his camp toward Uhud. He appointed ʿAbd Allah ibn Jubayr over the archers and said to them: "Shoot arrows to keep them away from us, so that they do not come at us from behind."

Badr is the name of a water source between Makkah and Madinah. It belonged to a man called Badr, and it was named after him.

﴿So fear God﴾ in steadfastness alongside His Messenger, ﴿that perhaps you may be thankful﴾, meaning that by your piety you may give thanks for the blessing of His support. Or it means: ﴿perhaps God will bestow upon you another blessing which you may thank Him for﴾. Here gratitude is placed in the position of bestowing, because it is the cause of it.

﴿When you said﴾: this is a temporal clause governing your victory, on the reading that He said this to them on the day of Badr. Alternatively it is a second substitute for ﴿when you set out in the morning﴾, on the reading that He said it to them on the day of Uhud.

If you ask: how can it be right that He said this to them on the day of Uhud, when the angels were not sent down on that day? I answer: He said it to them on the condition of patience and piety, but they did not remain patient regarding the spoils, nor were they pious, since they opposed the command of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Therefore the angels were not sent down. Had they fulfilled the condition set for them, the angels would have been sent down. He mentioned the promise of the angels' descent first in order to strengthen their hearts, so that they would resolve to stand firm and trust in God's victory.

The meaning of ﴿Will it not suffice you?﴾ is a denial that the reinforcement of three thousand angels would not suffice them. The particle *lan*, which is for emphasising negation, is used to signal that, because of their paucity, their weakness and the multitude and might of their enemy, they were as those who despair of victory. *Balā* is an affirmation of what follows *lan*, meaning: ''Rather, the reinforcement with them will suffice you.'' So He affirmed sufficiency, then said: ﴿if you are patient and pious, He will reinforce you with more than that number, marked for battle﴾. ﴿And they will come upon you﴾, meaning the polytheists, ﴿immediately (*min fawrihim*)﴾. This is from your saying: ''He returned from his raid and set out on another raid immediately (*min fawrihi*)'', and ''So-and-so came and returned immediately.'' From this is the statement of Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him: ''The command is immediate (*ʿalā al-fawr*), not delayed (*ʿalā al-tarākhī*).'' The word is a verbal noun from *fārat al-qidr*, when the cooking pot boils over; it was then borrowed for speed, and then the state in which there is no delay, and no turning aside to anything by its doer, was called by it. So it is said: ''He went out from his immediate state,'' just as you say ''He went out at that very moment,'' without delay. The meaning is: if they come upon you at this very moment, ﴿your Lord will reinforce you with angels﴾ at the time of their coming, their descent not being delayed after their arrival. He intends: God hastens your victory and facilitates your triumph if you are patient and pious.

It is read *munzalīn* with doubling of the *zāy*, and *munzilīn* with a kasra on the *zāy*, meaning ''causing the victory to descend.'' *Musawwimīn* is read with a fatha and with a kasra on the *wāw*, meaning ''marked'', that is, ''marking themselves or their horses''. Al-Kalbi said: ''marked with yellow turbans let down over their shoulders.'' From al-Dahhak: ''marked with white wool on the foreheads and tails of the animals.'' From Mujahid: ''the tails of their horses were cut short.'' From Qatadah: ''they were on piebald horses.'' From ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr: ''al-Zubayr's turban on the day of Badr was yellow, and the angels descended in the same manner.'' And from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said to his companions: ''Mark yourselves, for the angels have marked themselves.''
