not from the fighters when they are many, nor from the angels and tranquillity. Rather, these are means by which God strengthens hope for victory and the longing for mercy, and by which He fortifies the hearts of the fighters in the cause of God. ﴿The Mighty﴾, whom none can overpower in His command, ﴿the Wise﴾, who gives victory and withholds it as He sees the benefit.

﴿That He may cut off a part of those who disbelieved﴾: that He may destroy a group of them by killing and capture. This is what happened on the day of Badr: seventy were killed and seventy captured, from the leaders and chieftains of Quraysh. ﴿Or humble them﴾, that is, disgrace them and enrage them with defeat, ﴿so that they turn back frustrated﴾, not having attained their aim.

Similar to this is His saying: ﴿And God turned back those who disbelieved in their rage; they gained no good﴾. It is said *kabatahu*, meaning he struck his liver (*kabid*) when he struck it with rage and burning. The verse of Abu al-Tayyib was interpreted:

*Take your time, O noble king, and be patient,*
*and let your patience be a favour to which we are indebted,*
*Your generosity by remaining, even if little,*
*for in what you bestow there is no little.*
*To enrage an envier and to see an enemy*
*as if they were your farewell and your departure.*

You are only a servant sent to warn them and to strive against them.

Then "an yatūba" has the status of a noun conjoined by "aw" (or) to "the affair" or to "anything." Or: you have no part in their affair, or in God's relenting toward them, or in their punishment.

Do not devour usury, doubling and redoubling (it). He forbade usury together with a rebuke for what they used to do of multiplying it. A man among them, when his debt reached its due term, would extend the term, and the slight addition would swallow up the wealth of the debtor. [[His words "مال المديون" (the wealth of the debtor): perhaps it is "المدين" (the debtor), or it is an irregular usage. (Ṭ)]]

﴿And guard against the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers.﴾ Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, used to say: it is the most frightening verse in the Qur'an, since Allah threatened the believers with the Fire prepared for the disbelievers if they do not guard against Him by avoiding His prohibitions. He reinforced this with what follows it: the hope of the believers in His mercy, linked to their devotion to His obedience and the obedience of His Messenger. Whoever reflects on this verse and its like will not entertain vain desires or wishful thinking about Allah, the Exalted. And in His mention, exalted is He, of "la'alla" (perhaps) and "'asā" (it may be) in such contexts, despite what people have said, lies what is not hidden from the perceptive knower: the subtlety of the path of taqwa (God-consciousness), the difficulty of attaining the pleasure of Allah, and the rarity of reaching His mercy and reward.

And in His mention, exalted is He, of "la'alla" (perhaps) and "'asā" (it may be) in such contexts, despite what people have said, lies what is not hidden from the perceptive knower: the subtlety of the path of taqwa (God-consciousness), the difficulty of attaining the pleasure of Allah, and the rarity of reaching His mercy and reward.

In the codices of the people of Madina and Syria it is read "sari'ū" (hasten) without the waw. The rest read it with the waw ("wa sāri'ū"). The reading of Ubayy and ʿAbd Allah supports it: "wa sāyiqū" (and vie with one another).

The meaning of hastening toward forgiveness and Paradise is: turning toward what would earn them, through which, "whose breadth is the heavens and the earth" (﴿عَرْضُهَا السَّمَاوَاتُ وَالْأَرْضُ﴾), that is, its breadth is like the breadth of the heavens and the earth, as in His saying: ﴿عَرْضُهَا كَعَرْضِ السَّمَاءِ وَالْأَرْضِ﴾. The intended meaning is describing it with vastness and expanse, so it is compared to the widest and most extensive of creation that people know.

Breadth is singled out because it is usually less than length, for emphasis, as in His saying: ﴿بَطَائِنُهَا مِنْ إِسْتَبْرَقٍ﴾. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "like seven heavens and seven earths joined one to another." ﴿فِي السَّرَّاءِ وَالضَّرَّاءِ﴾: in a state of ease and prosperity, and in a state of hardship and difficulty. They do not fail to spend, in both states, whatever they are able to give, whether much or little, as is related of some of the early generations (salaf) that he would give charity with an onion. From ʿAisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she gave a single grape as charity.[[Related by Ibn Saʿd: Yazid ibn Harun informed us, Fudayl ibn Marzuq informed us, from Zabya bint al-Muʿallal, who said: "I entered upon ʿAisha and a beggar came, and she gave him a grape. Then she looked at us and said: Are you surprised at this? In it there are indeed many atoms' weights."]] Or, in all conditions, since no one is free from a state of joy or of harm; neither a state of happiness and gladness nor a state of trial and affliction prevents them from doing good. Whether one of them is at a wedding or in prison, he does not abandon kindness. Spending is mentioned first because it is the hardest thing on the self and the strongest proof of sincerity, and because at that time it was the greatest of deeds, given the need for it in fighting the enemy and aiding the poor Muslims.

﴿الْكَاظِمِينَ الْغَيْظَ﴾: "kaẓama al-qirba" means when he filled it and tied its mouth; "kaẓama al-baʿīr" means when he did not chew the cud. From it comes "kaẓm al-ghayẓ" (suppressing anger), which is to hold back what is in oneself of it through patience and not show any sign of it. From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever suppresses anger while he is able to act upon it, Allah will fill his heart with security and faith."[[Related by Abu Dawud, from the narration of Ibn ʿAjlan from Suwayd ibn Wahb from a man from among the sons of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), from his father. Ibn Tahir said: this Companion is Muʿadh ibn Anas, and his son is Sahl. ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ahmad also narrated it from him, and al-ʿUqayli through his chain. He said: Dawud ibn Qays informed us from Zayd ibn Aslam from a man of the people of Syria called ʿAbd al-Jalil, from a man of his, from Abu Hurayra with it. ʿAbd al-Jalil is unknown.]] And from ʿAisha, may Allah be pleased with her: that a servant of hers angered her, and she said: "By Allah, how excellent is piety! It has left no cure for one who is angry."

﴿وَالْعَافِينَ عَنِ النَّاسِ﴾: those who pardon people when someone wrongs them, they do not hold them to account. It was narrated: "On the Day of Resurrection a caller will call out: Where are those whose reward is with Allah? None will rise except the one who pardoned."[[Related by al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Iman, from the narration of al-Mubarak ibn Fudala from al-Hasan from ʿImran ibn Husayn, raised to the Prophet: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will call from the depths of the Throne: Let those whose reward is with Allah rise. None will rise except the one who pardoned." In its chain is the story of Ibrahim ibn Mahdi with al-Ma'mun. al-Tabarani narrated it from the narration of Mahriz Abu Raja' from al-Hasan who said: "It is said on the Day of Resurrection: Let rise whoever had a right with a people. None will rise except a person who pardoned," then he recited: ﴿وَالْعَافِينَ عَنِ النَّاسِ وَاللَّهُ يُحِبُّ الْمُحْسِنِينَ﴾. Abu Shuja' mentioned it in al-Firdaws from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him.]] And from Ibn ʿUyayna that he narrated it to al-Rashid when he was angry with a man, and he released him.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Such people are few in my Ummah, except those whom Allah protects, and they were many in the nations that passed before."[[al-Tha'labi mentioned it from Muqatil ibn Hayyan who said: "It has reached us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ... " and so he mentioned it. Its chain to Muqatil is at the beginning of the book, and in al-Firdaws from Anas there is something similar at the beginning of the preceding hadith.]]

﴿وَاللَّهُ يُحِبُّ الْمُحْسِنِينَ﴾: the lam may be for the category (jins), so it encompasses every doer of good, and these mentioned are included under it; or it may be for specific reference (ʿahd), so it points to these people.

﴿وَالَّذِينَ﴾ is coordinated with "the God-fearing," meaning: it was prepared for the God-fearing and for the repentant. His saying ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ refers to both groups. It is permissible that "those who" is the subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾.

﴿فَاحِشَةً﴾: an act of increasing ugliness; ﴿أَوْ ظَلَمُوا أَنْفُسَهُمْ﴾: or they wronged themselves, that is, they sinned with any sin for which they are held accountable. It was said: "fāḥisha" is fornication, and "wronging oneself" is what is less than it, such as kissing and touching and the like. It was also said: "fāḥisha" is a major sin, and "wronging oneself" is a minor sin.

﴿ذَكَرُوا اللَّهَ﴾: they remembered His punishment, His threat, or His prohibition, or His great right and majesty which requires awe and modesty before Him. ﴿فَاسْتَغْفَرُوا لِذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾: they repented from them, regretting their ugliness and resolving [[His saying "ʿāzimīn" perhaps means resolved not to return. (ʿA)]].

﴿وَمَنْ يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ﴾: a description of His essence with vastness of mercy and nearness of forgiveness; that the one who repents from sin is with Him as one who has no sin; that there is no refuge for sinners except His grace and generosity; and that His justice requires forgiveness for the penitent, because when the servant comes in apology and disavowal with the utmost of what he can, pardon and overlooking become obligatory.[[His saying "when he comes with the utmost he is able to, pardon becomes obligatory": by revelation this is by consensus, and by reason it is so according to the Mu'tazila only. (ʿA)]] This brings comfort to the hearts of servants, encourages repentance, urges it, and deters from despair and hopelessness, and that sins, however great, His pardon is greater and His generosity more immense. The meaning is that He alone has the means that make forgiveness valid.

﴿وَلَمْ يُصِرُّوا﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the coordinated and what it is coordinated with: they did not persist, did not remain upon the ugliness of their deed without seeking forgiveness. From the Prophet (ﷺ): "One who seeks forgiveness does not persist, even if he returns to it seventy times in a day."[[Related by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la and al-Bazzar, through ʿUthman ibn Wafid from Abu Nusayra from a mawla of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him. al-Tirmidhi said: gharib, and its chain is not strong. al-Bazzar said: we do not know it except from the hadith of Abu Bakr by this route. Abu Nusayra and his shaykh are not known. I say: it has a witness related by al-Tabarani in al-Du'a from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas.]] And it was narrated: "There is no major sin with seeking forgiveness, and no minor sin with persistence."[[Related by Ishaq ibn Bishr Abu Hudhayfa in al-Mubtada' from al-Thawri from Hisham ibn ʿUrwa from his father from ʿAisha, and Ishaq's narrations are munkar. al-Tabarani narrated it in Musnad al-Shamiyyin from the narration of Makhul, from Abu Salama, from Abu Hurayra, and he added at its end: "Blessed is the one who finds in his record much seeking of forgiveness." In its chain is Bishr ibn ʿAbd al-Warith, who is matruk. al-Tha'labi and Ibn Shahin in al-Targhib narrated it through Bishr ibn Ibrahim from Khalifa ibn Sulayman from Abu Salama from Abu Hurayra with it.]]

﴿وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) of the act of persisting, and the negation particle governs both of them together. The meaning: they are not among those who persist in sins while knowing their ugliness, the prohibition against them, and the threat upon them, because one who does not know the ugliness of the ugly may be excused.

In these verses there is a decisive explanation that those who believe are in three categories: the God-fearing, the repentant, and the persisting; and that Paradise is for the God-fearing and the repentant among them, not for the persisting.[[His saying "and the repentant among them, not the persisting" means that persistence is a major sin and the doer of a major sin abides forever in the Fire, but this is according to the Mu'tazila, and Ahl al-Sunna disagreed, since he is a believer in their view and a believer does not abide in it; its verification is in the science of tawhid. (ʿA)]] Whoever disagrees on this has contradicted his intellect and opposed his Lord.

He says: ﴿أَجْرُ الْعَامِلِينَ﴾ after His saying ﴿جَزَاؤُهُمْ﴾, because the two have one meaning. He varied the wording only to add emphasis that this is a reward due for a deed, and a wage owed for it, not as the falsifiers say.[[His saying "a wage owed for it, not as the falsifiers say" means Ahl al-Sunna, who said nothing is obligatory upon Allah. (ʿA)]]

It is narrated that Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed to Musa: "How little shame has he who hopes for My Paradise without works! How can I be generous with My mercy to one who withholds obedience to Me?" From Shahr ibn Hawshab: seeking Paradise without deeds is a sin among sins, awaiting intercession without cause is a kind of delusion, and hoping for mercy from one who is not obeyed is folly and ignorance. From al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him: Allah the Exalted says on the Day of Resurrection: "Cross the Sirat by My pardon, enter Paradise by My mercy, and divide it by your deeds."

From Rabi'a al-Basriyya, may Allah be pleased with her, that she used to recite:

*You hope for salvation but you have not taken its paths;*
*Indeed, the ship does not sail on dry land.*[[Ma bal nafsika tarda an tudanisaha / wa thawbu nafsika maghsulun min al-danas. / Tarju al-najata wa lam tasluk masalikaha / inna al-safina la tajri ʿala al-yabas. (Attributed to Imam ʿAli, may Allah honor his face; also said to be by Abu al-ʿAtahiya.) "Al-bal" means affair and self; it is permissible that it means the essence, and the garment is on its literal sense. It is permissible that it means the spirit, and the garment is a metaphor for the body, since it is to the spirit what a garment is to the body; i.e., it is not fitting to soil the contained while cleaning its container. The variant "ma bal dinika" is also reported. The second line is a circumstantial clause (jumla hāliyya). "Tarju al-najāt" is with the interrogative particle of reproach omitted, presented in the form of a statement to depict its ugliness; the causes that lead to salvation are likened to the traveled roads by way of metaphor, "wa lam tasluk" being an elaboration. "Inna al-safina" is an illustration of the state of one who hopes for a thing without taking up its causes, like a sailor who wants to move a ship over hard ground with no water in it; within it is affirmed the reproach that the interrogative conveyed.]]

The term of praise is elided; its estimate is: "and excellent is the reward of the doers," meaning the forgiveness and the gardens.

﴿قَدْ خَلَتْ مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ سُنَنٌ﴾: he means what Allah established among the nations who denied, of His events, as in His saying: ﴿وَقُتِّلُوا تَقْتِيلًا سُنَّةَ اللَّهِ فِي الَّذِينَ خَلَوْا مِنْ قَبْلُ﴾ ﴿ثُمَّ لَا يَجِدُونَ وَلِيًّا وَلَا نَصِيرًا﴾, ﴿سُنَّةَ اللَّهِ الَّتِي قَدْ خَلَتْ مِنْ قَبْلُ﴾.

In the codices of the people of Madina and Syria it is read "sari'ū" (hasten) without the waw. The rest read it with the waw ("wa sāri'ū"). The reading of Ubayy and ʿAbd Allah supports it: "wa sāyiqū" (and vie with one another).

It is permissible that it means the spirit, and the garment is a metaphor for the body, since it is to the spirit what a garment is to the body; i.e., it is not fitting to soil the contained while cleaning its container. "Tarju al-najāt" is with the interrogative particle of reproach omitted, presented in the form of a statement to depict its ugliness; the causes that lead to salvation are likened to the traveled roads by way of metaphor, "wa lam tasluk" being an elaboration. The term of praise is elided; its estimate is: "and excellent is the reward of the doers," meaning the forgiveness and the gardens.

﴿قَدْ خَلَتْ مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ سُنَنٌ﴾: he means what Allah established among the nations who denied, of His events, as in His saying: ﴿وَقُتِّلُوا تَقْتِيلًا سُنَّةَ اللَّهِ فِي الَّذِينَ خَلَوْا مِنْ قَبْلُ﴾ ﴿ثُمَّ لَا يَجِدُونَ وَلِيًّا وَلَا نَصِيرًا﴾, ﴿سُنَّةَ اللَّهِ الَّتِي قَدْ خَلَتْ مِنْ قَبْلُ﴾.

This is an elucidation for mankind, a clarification of the evil outcome of the state they are in of denial, meaning: it urges them to reflect upon the evil consequences for those who denied before them, and to take warning from what they witness of the traces of their destruction. "And a guidance and an admonition for those who are mindful of God" — meaning that although it is an explanation and an alert for the deniers, it is additionally a reinforcement of firmness and an admonition for those among the believers who have been mindful of God.

It is also permissible that His saying, "Indeed there have passed before you ways [of those who denied]" (qad khalat), is a parenthetical sentence (jumla mu'tariḍa) spurring [them] to faith and to that which merits the reward mentioned for those who act [righteously]; and His saying, "This is an elucidation" (hadha bayan), refers to what has been summarized and explained concerning the matter of the mindful, the repentant, and the persistent [in sin].

"And do not weaken, nor grieve" — a consolation from God, glorified is He, to His Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, and to the believers, concerning what afflicted them on the day of Uhud, and a strengthening of their hearts. Meaning: do not grow feeble in jihad because of what has struck you; that is, let it not bring upon you weakness and cowardice, and do not concern yourselves with it, and do not grieve over those among you who were killed or wounded.

"And you will be the superior ones" — and your state is that you are higher than them and more victorious, because you struck them on the day of Badr more than they struck you on the day of Uhud. Or: "and you are the superior ones in rank," because your fighting is for God and for the exaltation of His word, while their fighting is for Satan, for the exaltation of the word of disbelief; and because your slain are in Paradise and their slain are in the Fire. Or it is a glad tidings to them of superiority and victory, meaning: and you will be the superior ones in the outcome. "Indeed Our host, they are the victorious" (inna jundana lahumu al-ghalibun).

"If you are believers" (in kuntum mu'minin) is connected to the prohibition, in the sense: "do not weaken, if your faith is sound," since soundness of faith entails firmness of heart, trust in God's disposition, and little concern for His enemies. Or it is connected to "you will be the superior ones," meaning: if you are truly affirming what God promises you and gives you glad tidings of, namely victory.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 140–141:

The word ﴿qarḥ﴾ is read with a fatḥah (a) and with a ḍammah (u) on the qāf, and these are two dialects, like ḍaʿf and ḍuʿf. It is said that with the fatḥah it means the wounds, and with the ḍammah it means the pain of them. Abū al-Simāl read it as ﴿qaraḥ﴾ with two fatḥahs. It is also said that qarḥ and qaraḥ are like ṭard and ṭard.

The meaning is: if they inflicted wounds on you on the day of Uḥud, then you had already inflicted them on the day of Badr before that. Yet this did not weaken their hearts or deter them from returning to fight you. So you are more deserving not to become weak. A parallel is ﴿Indeed they feel pain as you feel pain, and you hope from God what they do not hope for﴾. It is also said that this refers to the day of Uḥud, when they had inflicted wounds on you before they disobeyed the command of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

If you ask: how can it be said ﴿a wound like it﴾, when the wound of the disbelievers on the day of Uḥud was not like the wound of the believers?

I say: yes, it was like it. Indeed, a large number of the disbelievers were killed that day. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God had indeed fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission, until you lost courage, disputed about the matter, and disobeyed after He had shown you what you love﴾.

﴿And those days, We alternate them among the people.﴾ ﴿Tilka﴾ (those) is the mubtada' (subject of the nominal sentence), and ﴿al-ayyām﴾ (the days) is its ṣifah (qualifier). ﴿Nudāwiluhā﴾ (We alternate them) is the khabar (predicate). It is also permissible that ﴿tilka al-ayyām﴾ be both the subject and the predicate, as you say: ﴿hiya al-ayyām tablā kulla jadīd﴾ (they are the days that wear out every new thing). The meaning of ﴿al-ayyām﴾ is the times of victory and defeat. ﴿Nudāwiluhā﴾ means: We turn them among the people, so that sometimes it is in favour of these and sometimes in favour of those, as in the verse which is one of the verses of the Kitāb (of Sībawayh), where he said:

Fa-yawman ʿalaynā wa-yawman lanā
wa-yawman nusāʾu wa-yawman nusarr

[Fa-lā wa-abī al-nāsi lā yaʿlamūna
fa-lā al-khayru khayrun wa-lā al-sharru sharr
Fa-yawmun ʿalaynā wa-yawmun lanā
wa-yawmun nusāʾu wa-yawmun nusarr]

These are by al-Namir ibn Tawlab, and they are from the verses of the Kitāb. The ﴿lā﴾ (no) is superfluous before the oath, because it is generally used for negating something. It is also said that it indicates the clarity of the matter sworn to and that it does not need an oath; but this appears only in a verse such as ﴿So I do not swear﴾, where it is presented in the familiar form of negation. The word ﴿al-nās﴾ (the people) is the mubtada', whose khabar is ﴿lā yaʿlamūn﴾ (do not know). Then he explained this by saying: the good that they claim is good is not good as they claim, and the evil that they claim is evil is not evil as they claim. Or: good is not always good, and evil is not always evil. ﴿Fa-yawmun ʿalaynā﴾ means a day when we are forsaken. ﴿Wa-yawmun lanā﴾ means a day when we are victorious. ﴿Wa-yawmun nusāʾu﴾ means a day when we are grieved. ﴿Wa-yawmun nusarr﴾ means a day when we are made glad. It is also narrated with the accusative on ﴿yawm﴾. The meaning then is: one day the cycle turns against us, and one day the rule is ours; a day we are grieved, and a day we are glad. Each of these two clauses is in the position of explanation of what precedes them. In the second verse there is ﴿laff wa-nashr﴾ (a wrapping and spreading, i.e. a rhetorical pairing) arranged in order, and that is good.

Among the proverbs of the Arabs: ﴿war is sijāl﴾ (war is alternating, i.e. victory and defeat change hands). It is narrated from Abū Sufyān that he climbed the mountain on the day of Uḥud, remained there for a while, and then said: "Where is the son of Abū Kabshah? Where is the son of Abū Quḥāfah? Where is the son of al-Khaṭṭāb?" ʿUmar said: "This is the Messenger of God (ﷺ), this is Abū Bakr, and here I am, ʿUmar." Abū Sufyān said: "A day for a day, and the days are turns, and war is sijāl." ʿUmar (may God be pleased with him) said: "Not equal. Our dead are in Paradise, and your dead are in the Fire." He said: "You claim that, then we have indeed failed and lost." [Narrated by Aḥmad, al-Ḥākim, al-Ṭabarānī and al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalāʾil, through the narration of Ibn Abī al-Zinād from his father from Ibn ʿAbbās that Abū Sufyān said on the day of Uḥud what was mentioned. I say: its origin is in the Ṣaḥīḥ from another route, without this context.] The word ﴿al-mudāwalah﴾ (alternating) is like ﴿al-muʿāwarah﴾ (exchanging). And he said:

Yaridu al-miyāha fa-lā yazālu mudāwilā
fī al-nāsi bayna tamaththulin wa-samāʿi

[Fa-la-ahdayanna maʿa al-riyāḥi qaṣīdatan
minnī muḥabbaratan ilā al-qaʿqāʿi
Tarudd al-miyāha fa-lā tazālu tadāwulā
fī al-nāsi bayna tamaththulin wa-samāʿi]

The muḥabbarah (adorned) means the excellent one. Al-Qaʿqāʿ is the name of the one praised, and originally it means the dry, hard thing. That poem goes to the waters; he specified the waters because of the many people who gather there and because they entertain themselves with poetry there. That is, it goes to the places of water and is not still circulated among the people, or it is subject to circulation, or it keeps circulating among the people, moving between recitation, meaning that people quote it as proverbs for their situations, and between listening to it for its excellence. It is also narrated: ﴿yaridu al-miyāha fa-lā yazālu mudāwilan﴾ etc., and he mentioned the pronoun of the poem because it means poetry.

It is said: ﴿dāwaltu baynahum al-shayʾa fa-tadāwalūhu﴾ (I made the thing alternate among them, so they passed it around).

As for ﴿wa-liyaʿlama Allāhu alladhīna āmanū﴾ (and that God might know those who believed), there are two interpretations. The first is that the cause (ʿillah) is omitted, and its meaning is: and that those who stand firm in faith among you may be distinguished from those who are wavering. We did that, and this is from the category of ﴿tamthīl﴾ (figurative expression), meaning: we acted as one acts who wants to know which of you is firm in faith and which is not; otherwise God, mighty and majestic, has always known things before they happen. It is also said that the meaning is: that He may make them know with a knowledge on which reward depends, namely that He makes them know that firmness exists in them. The second is that the cause is omitted and this clause is coordinated with it, meaning: we did that so that such and such would happen, and so that God would know. It was omitted to show that the benefit in what He did is not one, to console them about what befell them, and to make them see that a servant is distressed by the calamities that befall him, and does not realise that God has in this benefits of which he is unaware. ﴿Wa-yattakhidha minkum shuhadāʾ﴾ (and that He may take witnesses from among you) means: and that He may honour some of you with martyrdom, meaning those who were martyred on the day of Uḥud. Or: and that He may take from among you those who are fit to be witnesses over the nations on the Day of Resurrection, by the hardships with which your patience is tested, from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾. ﴿Wa-Allāhu lā yuḥibbu al-ẓālimīn﴾ (and God does not love the wrongdoers) is a parenthetical statement between part of the reason and part of it. Its meaning: God does not love those who are not among these steadfast believers, who strive in the way of God, and who are purified of sins. ﴿Tamḥīṣ﴾ (purification) means cleansing and refining. ﴿Wa-yamḥaqa al-kāfirīn﴾ (and that He may destroy the disbelievers) means: and destroy them. The meaning: if the victory is for the believers, it is for distinguishing, for martyrdom, and for purification, and other things that are better for them; and if the victory is for the disbelievers, it is to annihilate them and erase their traces.

**أم منقطعة** (*munqati'a*, "disjunctive" ﴿am﴾) [[The statement "am munqati'a" means it is the one explained by *bal* and the hamza. (A)]] and the meaning of the hamza in it is denial. **﴿Wa-lamma ya'lami Allahu﴾** means "and Allah has not yet known," i.e., "and you have not yet struggled (*tujahidu*)," because knowledge is related to the known. [[Mahmud said: "*And you have not yet struggled*, because knowledge is related to the known... etc." Ahmad said: Expressing the negation of the known by the negation of knowledge is specific to the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted. For it follows that if His knowledge does not relate to the existence of something, that thing does not exist, since nothing escapes His knowledge due to the comprehensiveness of its relation. Thus it is correct to express the negation of a thing by the negation of the eternal knowledge's relation to its existence, which justifies the implication. This is not the case with the knowledge of individual created beings, for one does not express the negation of a thing by the negation of created beings' knowledge of it, because that thing may exist without being known to created beings.

Al-Zamakhshari's words appear to hold this expression valid absolutely and believe the mentioned implication to be general. Therefore, he said regarding the words of Pharaoh ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ that he expressed the negation of the known by the negation of knowledge, because it is among its implications. It will come that al-Zamakhshari erred in this place; otherwise he is too exalted to fall into such a thing in belief. And Allah knows best. Pharaoh only expressed it that way to deceive his chiefs and to complete his false claim of divinity, that nothing escapes his knowledge. So if there were another god besides him, according to his claim, his knowledge would relate to it. This is considered among Pharaoh's follies and empty claims. And Allah is the Granter of success.]] So the negation of knowledge is placed in the position of the negation of its object, because the object is negated by the negation of the knowledge. A man says: "Allah does not know any good in so-and-so," meaning: "there is no good in him that Allah would know."

**Wa-lamma** means *lam* (not yet), except that it carries a degree of expectation, so it indicates the negation of struggle in the past and the expectation of it in the future. You say: "He promised me that he would do such-and-such, *wa-lamma*" (and not yet), meaning he has not done it, and I am expecting him to do it.

It was read as **﴿wa-lamma ya'lama Allahu﴾** with a fatha on the *mim*. It was also said that the intended reading is the light nun: *wa-lamma ya'lamanna*, then it was dropped.

**﴿Wa-ya'lama al-sabirin﴾** is in the accusative by the implicit *an* (*bi-idmar an*), and the *waw* carries the sense of combining, like your saying: "Do not eat fish and drink milk." Al-Hasan read it in the jussive, as a conjunction (*'atf*). It was narrated by Abd al-Warith from Abu 'Amr as **﴿wa-ya'lamu﴾** with a damma, on the basis that the *waw* is for the circumstantial state (*hal*), as if it were said: "*And you have not yet struggled while you are patient.*"

And you used to wish for death before you met it. This was addressed to those who had not witnessed Badr, who wished to attend an engagement with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) so that they might obtain the honour of martyrdom that the martyrs of Badr had attained. They were the ones who pressed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to go out against the polytheists [[His words "in the going out" are perhaps "and their opinion was in going out." (ʿA.)]], while his opinion was to remain in Medina. I answer: the one who wishes for martyrdom intends only to attain the honour of the martyrs, and this implication does not occur to his mind, just as one who drinks the medicine of a Christian physician intends the hoped-for cure, and it does not enter his mind that in it there is a benefit and kindness to the enemy of Allah and a promotion of his profession.

"But I ask the Most Merciful for forgiveness
and a blow with a wide wound that throws out foam,
or a thrust with the two hands of a thirsty man [for blood], dispatching [the enemy],
with a spear that pierces the bowels and the liver,
so that when they pass by my grave they will say:
'May Allah guide you, O warrior, for you have been guided.'"

When Abdullah ibn Qami'ah al-Harithi struck the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with a stone, breaking his front tooth and wounding his face, he advanced intending to kill him. Mus'ab ibn Umayr, who was the standard-bearer on the day of Badr and on the day of Uhud, defended him (ﷺ) until Ibn Qami'ah killed him, believing him to be the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said: "I have killed Muhammad."

A crier cried out: "Verily, Muhammad has been killed." It was said that the crier was Satan, and the news of his killing spread among the people, and they turned back. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began calling out, "To me, servants of Allah!" until a group of his companions gathered to him. He rebuked them for their flight, and they said: "O Messenger of Allah, may we be ransomed by our fathers and mothers, the news of your death reached us and our hearts were terrified, so we turned back in flight." Then it was revealed.

It is narrated that when the crier cried out, some of the Muslims said: "Would that Abdullah ibn Ubayy might obtain safe-conduct for us from Abu Sufyan." Some of the hypocrites said: "If he were a prophet he would not have been killed. Return to your brethren and to your religion." Anas ibn an-Nadr, the paternal uncle of Anas ibn Malik, said: "O people, if Muhammad has been killed, the Lord of Muhammad is living and does not die. What will you do with life after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? Fight for what he fought for, and die upon what he died upon." Then he said: "O Allah, I apologise to You for what these say, and I disavow to You what these have brought." Then he charged with his sword and fought until he was killed. And [it is narrated] from one of the Muhajirun: that he passed by an Ansari who was writhing in his blood, and said, "O so-and-so, do you know that Muhammad has been killed?" He said, "If he has been killed, he has conveyed [the message]. Fight for your religion."

Kitāban (kitāban) is an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu’akkid), because the meaning is: God prescribed death as a decreed writ (kitāban), a term fixed for a known appointed time that cannot be advanced or delayed.

﴿And whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him from it﴾: this is an allusion (ta‘rīḍ) to those whom the spoils of war distracted on the day of Uhud. "From it" means from its reward (min thawābihā).

﴿And We will reward the grateful﴾: the reward is left general (al-jazā’ al-mubham), and the grateful are those who acknowledged God's blessing, so nothing distracted them from jihad.

It is also read as yu’tihi and sayajzī, with the yā’ (y) in both places.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 146–148:

It is read *qātala* (qātala, "fought"), *qutila* (quṭila, "was killed"), and *qutilla* (quttila, "was killed"), with shadda. The subject (fā'il) is *rabbiyyūn* (rabbiyyūn, "companies of devout men"), or the pronoun referring to the Prophet. *Ma'ahu ribbiyyūn* is a ḥāl (ḥāl, circumstantial clause) relating to him, meaning: "he was killed while there were with him rabbiyyūn." The reading with shadda supports the first aspect (wajh).

From Sa'id ibn Jubayr (raḥimahu Allāh): "We have never heard of a Prophet being killed in battle."

*Rabbiyyūn* means *rabbāniyyūn* (rabbāniyyūn, "devoted worshippers of God"). It is read with all three vowels: the fatḥa is according to the regular pattern, while the ḍamma and kasra are alterations of the relative form (nisba).

It is also read *fa-mā wahanū* (fa-mā wahanū, "so they did not weaken") with a kasra on the hā'.

The meaning: *fa-mā wahanū* ("so they did not weaken") at the killing of the Prophet, *wa-mā ḍa'ufū* ("nor were they weakened") in jihad after him, *wa-mā istakānū* ("nor did they submit") to the enemy. This is an allusion to the weakness and breakdown that afflicted them at the rumour of the killing of the Messenger of God (ṣallā Allāh 'alayhi wa-sallam), and to their feebleness at that time in striving against the polytheists and their submission to them, when they wished to seek support from the hypocrite 'Abd Allāh ibn Ubayy in seeking security from Abu Sufyan. *Wa-mā kāna qawlahum illā hādhā al-qawl* ("and their words were only this statement"), namely attributing their sins and excesses to themselves, despite being rabbāniyyūn, out of humbling themselves and regarding them as small. Seeking forgiveness from them is placed before asking for firmness of foot in the places of war and victory over the enemy, so that their request to their Lord comes from purity, cleanliness and humility, and is nearer to being answered. *Fa-ātāhum Allāh thawāb al-dunyā* ("so God gave them the reward of this world"): victory, booty, honour and good repute. The reward of the Hereafter is specified as "the good" to indicate its excellence and precedence, and that it is the one reckoned of worth with Him. (*Turīdūna 'araḍ al-dunyā wa-Allāhu yurīdu al-ākhira*, "You desire the goods of this world, while God desires the Hereafter.")

This is an allusion to the weakness and breakdown that afflicted them at the rumour of the killing of the Messenger of God (ṣallā Allāh 'alayhi wa-sallam), and to their feebleness at that time in striving against the polytheists and their submission to them, when they wished to seek support from the hypocrite 'Abd Allāh ibn Ubayy in seeking security from Abu Sufyan. *Wa-mā kāna qawlahum illā hādhā al-qawl* ("and their words were only this statement"), namely attributing their sins and excesses to themselves, despite being rabbāniyyūn, out of humbling themselves and regarding them as small. Seeking forgiveness from them is placed before asking for firmness of foot in the places of war and victory over the enemy, so that their request to their Lord comes from purity, cleanliness and humility, and is nearer to being answered. *Fa-ātāhum Allāh thawāb al-dunyā* ("so God gave them the reward of this world"): victory, booty, honour and good repute. The reward of the Hereafter is specified as "the good" to indicate its excellence and precedence, and that it is the one reckoned of worth with Him. (*Turīdūna 'araḍ al-dunyā wa-Allāhu yurīdu al-ākhira*, "You desire the goods of this world, while God desires the Hereafter.")

If you obey those who disbelieved... ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: it was revealed concerning the statement of the hypocrites to the believers at the time of the defeat: "Return to your brothers and enter into their religion." And from al-Ḥasan (may Allah be pleased with him): "If you seek counsel from the Jews and the Christians and accept from them, because they used to mislead them and cast doubts about the religion upon them, saying: 'If he were a true prophet, he would not have been defeated, and what befell him and his companions would not have befallen them. He is only a man whose condition is like that of other people: a day for him and a day against him.'" And from al-Suddī: "If you submit to Abū Sufyān and his companions and seek their safe-conduct, they will return you to your religion." It was also said that it is general, applying to all disbelievers, and that the believers must keep away from them, must not obey them in anything, must not submit to their judgment or their counsel, lest they draw them into agreeing with them.

Rather, Allah is your Mawlā (protector and helper), i.e., your helper; you do not need the help or patronage of anyone along with Him. It was recited in the accusative (naṣb), on the reading: "Rather, obey Allah, your Mawlā."

"We will cast" (sanulqī) is read with nūn and with yā'. "Terror" (al-ruʿb) is read with a sukūn on the ʿayn and with a ḍamma on it.

It was said: Allah cast fear into the hearts of the polytheists on the day of Uhud, so they fled to Mecca without any cause, though they had strength and dominance. It was also said: they went off to Mecca, and when they were part of the way they said: "We have accomplished nothing. We killed some of them, then left them while we were fāhirūn [[The editor's note: the phrase "fāhirūn" is perhaps "fāriḥūn." Al-fāriḥ means one skilled at a thing, as the Ṣiḥāḥ states. (ʿ)]]. Return and wipe them out." When they resolved on that, Allah cast terror into their hearts and they held back.

Because of what they associated (bi-mā ashrakū): that is, the cause of Allah casting terror into their hearts was their association of partners with Him, for which He sent down no authority (mā lam yunazzil bihi sulṭānan): gods for whose association with Allah He sent down no proof.

If you say: "Was there a proof, so that He would send it down, and so that association would be valid for them?" I say: he did not mean that there was a proof except that it was not sent down to them, because shirk cannot stand on any proof. The intention is the negation of both the proof and its sending down together, like his saying:

*The hare is not startled by its terrors,*
*nor does the lizard dart into its burrow there.*

This is by Ibn Aḥmar. He means: the hare is not frightened by the terrors of that desert, that is, there is no terror in it that would alarm it. So the line is a metaphor for that, like his saying: "nor do you see the lizard in it entering its hole," that is, there is no lizard in it that dives into its burrow. "Yanjaḥir" is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) if *tarā* is visual, and a second object if it is cognitive. It is also permissible that the meaning is: there is no hare in it that its terrors frighten, just as there is no lizard in it that enters its hole, so both are negated. This is more fitting to what precedes.

And God certainly fulfilled His promise to you ﴿وَلَقَدْ صَدَقَكُمُ اللَّهُ وَعْدَهُ﴾, namely that God would give them victory on condition of patience and God-consciousness, in His words: ﴿If you are patient and conscious of God, and they come at you suddenly from this very direction, your Lord will reinforce you﴾. It is also possible that the promise is His words: ﴿We will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾, so that when they [the believers] faltered and disputed, He did not allow the terror to overcome them.

It is said: when they returned to Medina, some of the believers said, "How did this befall us when God had promised us victory?" So this was revealed. The reason was that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) placed Uhud behind his back, faced Medina, and stationed the archers at the mountain, ordering them to hold their position and not leave it, whether the state was in favour of the Muslims or against them. When the polytheists advanced, the archers began shooting at their horses, while the rest struck them with swords, until they were routed and the Muslims were on their heels, ﴿killing them﴾, that is, slaying them with a devastating slaughter.

﴿Until when you faltered﴾. Faltering (al-fashal) means cowardice and weakness of judgment. ﴿And disputed﴾: some of them said, "The polytheists have been routed, so what is our position here?" Others said, "We will not disobey the command of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." Among those who held their position was ʿAbd Allah ibn Jubayr, commander of the archers, with a small group fewer than ten. They are the ones meant by His words: ﴿and among you are those who desire the Hereafter﴾. And a group of them went after the spoils, ﴿plundering﴾, and they are the ones who desired this world. So the polytheists charged back at the archers, killed ʿAbd Allah ibn Jubayr (may God be pleased with him), and advanced upon the Muslims. The wind turned to the west wind (dabur), though it had been the east wind (sabaʾ), until they routed them and killed whoever they killed. This is His words: ﴿Then He turned you away from them to test you﴾, to examine your patience in the face of calamities and your steadfastness in faith at that moment. ﴿And He had already pardoned you﴾, for He knew of your remorse over what had preceded from you of disobedience to the command of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). ﴿And God is bountiful to the believers﴾, bestowing on them pardon. Or He is bountiful to them in all circumstances, whether they were granted victory or defeated, because trial is a mercy just as victory is a mercy.

If you say: where is the complement of ﴿until when﴾? I say: it is omitted, its implied sense being: "until, when you faltered, His help withheld from you." It is also possible that the meaning is: God fulfilled His promise to you up to the time of your faltering, ﴿when you were climbing﴾.

This is in the accusative case, governed by ﴿He turned you away﴾, or by His words ﴿to test you﴾, or by the implied verb "remember". The verb "al-iṣʿād" means going away into the land and moving far off within it. It is said: "He ascended the mountain" (ṣaʿida fi al-jabal) and "he went far into the land" (aṣʿada fi al-arḍ). It is said: "We went up from Mecca to Medina" (aṣʿadnā min Makkah ilā al-Madīnah).

Al-Hasan (may God be pleased with him) recited ﴿tasʿadūn﴾, meaning "climbing the mountain." The recitation of Ubayy supports the first reading: ﴿when you were climbing into the valley﴾. Abu Haywah recited ﴿tasʿadūn﴾ with a fatha on the tāʾ and a shaddah on the ʿayn, from taṣaʿʿada fi al-sullam ("he climbed the ladder"). Al-Hasan (may God be pleased with him) recited ﴿tulūna﴾ with a single waw, and we have already mentioned its explanation. It was also recited as ﴿yuṣʿidūn﴾ and ﴿yalūn﴾ with the letter yāʾ.

﴿And the Messenger was calling you﴾. He would say: "To me, servants of God! To me, servants of God! I am the Messenger of God. Whoever turns back, for him is Paradise." ﴿In your rear﴾, that is, in your rearguard and your other, later body, which is the one at the back. It is said: "I came at the end of the people and their last part (akhrāhum)," just as you say "at their front and their first part (awwalihim and ūlāhum)," the first meaning the front and the first group.

﴿Then He recompensed you﴾ is coordinated with ﴿He turned you away﴾, meaning: so God requited you with grief when He turned you away from them and tested you. The grief was a cause (bi-sabab) of grief which you caused the Messenger of God (ﷺ) through your disobedience to him, or a doubled grief, grief upon grief, and grief following grief. It arose from the anxiety caused by the rumour of the killing of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the wounds and deaths, the victory of the polytheists, the loss of the spoils and the victory. ﴿So that you would not grieve﴾: so that you would train yourselves to swallow sorrows and endure hardships, so you would not grieve afterwards over any benefit that escaped you or any harm that befell you.

It is also possible that the pronoun in ﴿Then He recompensed you﴾ refers to the Messenger, meaning: he shared your grief (fa-ʾāsākum fi al-ightimām). [[His statement "fa-ʾāsākum fi al-ightimām" (he shared your grief) is perhaps: fa-ʾāsākum, i.e. he became your exemplar (uswatukum), as stated in al-Sihah (al-Jawhari's lexicon). (ʿ)]] And just as what befell him of the breaking of his molar and the wound to his face and other injuries grieved him, what befell you grieved him too. So He recompensed you with a grief which he felt on your account, in return for a grief you had caused him, and He did not reproach you for your disobedience and opposition to his command. God only did this to console you and relieve you, so that you would not grieve over what escaped you of God's help, nor over what befell you of the enemy's victory.

God sent down security upon the believers and removed from them the fear that had been with them, until they became drowsy and sleep overcame them. Abu Talhah (may God be pleased with him) said: "Drowsiness overtook us while we were in our battle line, so the sword would fall from the hand of one of us, and he would take it, then it would fall again and he would take it. There was not one of us but was swaying beneath his shield."

[[Al-Bukhari transmitted it from the narration of Qatadah from Anas with this wording, but the end of it, "There was not one of us but was swaying beneath his shield," is not in it. It is complete in al-Hakim. Likewise al-Tabari transmitted it from the narration of Thabit from Anas (may God be pleased with him).]]

And from Ibn al-Zubayr (may God be pleased with him): "I saw myself with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when fear grew intense upon us, and God sent sleep upon us. By God, I was hearing the words of Muʿattib ibn Qushayr while drowsiness was covering me: 'If we had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here.'"

[[Ibn Ishaq transmitted it in al-Maghazi: Yahya ibn ʿAbbad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr narrated to me from his father, from ʿUbayd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, from his father, with it. It was also transmitted by Ishaq, al-Bazzar, al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nuʿaym and al-Bayhaqi, all through this chain.]]

"Al-amanah" means security (al-amn). It has also been read as ﴿amnah﴾ with the letter mīm sukun, as if it were the single instance of security. ﴿Drowsiness﴾ (nuʿāsan) is a substitute (badal) for ﴿security﴾. It is also possible that it is the object, and ﴿security﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) preceding it, as in your saying: "I saw a rider on foot," or it is an object of purpose meaning "you were overcome with drowsiness as security." It is also possible that it is a circumstantial clause from the addressees, meaning "possessors of security," or it is the plural of āmin, like ṣaḥāb and barrah.

﴿Covering﴾ (yaghshā) has been read with yāʾ and with tāʾ, in response to ﴿drowsiness﴾ or to ﴿security﴾.

﴿A group of you﴾: these are the people of sincerity and certainty. ﴿And a group﴾: these are the hypocrites. ﴿Concerned only with themselves﴾ (qad ahammathum anfusuhum): their concern was nothing but themselves, neither the religion nor the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the Muslims. Or it means: their own selves brought them into anxieties and sorrows, and so they were in complaint and mutual recrimination.

﴿Other than the truth﴾ is in the position of an absolute object (ḥukm al-maṣdar). Its meaning: they harbour thoughts about God other than the true thought that ought to be held about Him.

﴿The thought of ignorance﴾ (ẓanna al-jāhiliyyah) is a substitution (badal) from it. It is also possible that the meaning is: "they harbour the thought of ignorance about God." ﴿Other than the truth﴾ is an emphasis for ﴿they harbour thoughts﴾, as when you say: "this statement is other than what you say," and "this statement is not your statement." ﴿The thought of ignorance﴾ is like your saying: "Hatim is generosity" and "a man of truth," meaning the thought specific to the pagan community. It is also possible that what is meant is the thought of the people of ignorance, that is, no one holds such a thought except the polytheists who are ignorant of God.

﴿They say﴾ to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), asking him: ﴿Is there anything for us in the matter?﴾ Its meaning: "Is there for us, the community of Muslims, any share in God's affair at all?" They mean victory and manifest triumph over the enemy. ﴿Say: indeed, the matter belongs entirely to God﴾, and to His friends, the believers. It is victory and dominance, ﴿God has decreed: I and My messengers will surely prevail﴾, and ﴿indeed Our soldiers, they will be the victorious﴾.

﴿They conceal within themselves what they do not reveal to you﴾. Its meaning: they say to you in what they show: "Is there for us anything in the matter?" This is the question of believers seeking guidance. But in what they conceal, they are upon hypocrisy. They say within themselves, or some of them say to others, denying your statement to them that the matter belongs entirely to God: ﴿If there were anything for us in the matter﴾, that is, if the matter were as Muhammad says, that the matter belongs entirely to God and to His friends, and that they are the victors, ﴿we would never have been slain﴾, and those of the Muslims who were killed in this battle would not have been killed.

﴿Say: even if you had been in your houses﴾, meaning: whoever God knew would be killed and fall in these battlegrounds, and it was recorded in the Preserved Tablet, there was no escape from its occurrence. So even if you had sat in your houses, ﴿those for whom killing had been decreed would have come forth to their resting places﴾, which are their places of falling, so that what God knew would happen would occur. The meaning is that God wrote in the Tablet the killing of whoever among the believers would be killed, and wrote alongside it that they are the victors, because He knew that the final outcome lies in victory for them, that the religion of Islam will prevail over all religions, and that what afflicts them at some times is a purification for them and an encouragement to martyrdom. Their eagerness for martyrdom incites them to struggle, and so victory is attained. It has been said: the meaning is "Is there for us any part in the planning?", meaning: "You had no control over any of the planning when you went out from Medina to Uhud, and it was incumbent upon us to remain and not depart, as was the opinion of ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and others. Had we possessed any control over planning, we would not have been killed in this battle." ﴿Say: indeed the planning belongs entirely to God﴾, meaning that God, mighty and majestic, has planned the affair as it came to pass. Even if you had remained in Medina and not come out of your houses, none of you who were destined for killing would have escaped it.

It has been read as ﴿kutiba ʿalayhimu al-qitāl﴾ (fighting was prescribed for them) and ﴿kutiba ʿalayhimu al-qatl﴾ (killing was prescribed for them), with the verb in the active voice. And ﴿wa-liyubarraza﴾ with shaddah and a ḍammah on the bāʾ.

﴿And that God might test what is in your breasts and purify what is in your hearts﴾: that He might examine the sincerity that is in your breasts and purify what is in your hearts of the whisperings of Satan. He did this, or did this for many purposes, and for trial and purification.

If you ask: how do the clauses after His words ﴿and a group﴾ stand in relation to it? I say: ﴿concerned only with themselves﴾ is a description of ﴿a group﴾. ﴿They harbour thoughts﴾ is another description, or a circumstantial clause meaning: "their own selves had concerned them, harbouring thoughts." Or it is a resumptive clause explaining the preceding clause. ﴿They say﴾ is a substitution for ﴿they harbour thoughts﴾.

If you ask: how is it correct that what is a question about the matter should be a substitution for a report about a thought? I say: their question arose from a thought, and therefore it is permissible for it to be a substitution for it. ﴿They conceal﴾ is a circumstantial clause of ﴿they say﴾. ﴿Say: indeed the matter belongs entirely to God﴾ is an interjection between the circumstantial clause and the one it describes. ﴿They say﴾ is a substitution for ﴿they conceal﴾, and it is better that it be a resumptive new clause.

[[Mahmud said: "If you say, how is it correct that what is a question about the matter should be a substitution...?" Ahmad says: this consideration is noted in His words about the angels: ﴿Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?﴾, the verse. This question is an interrogative, and an interrogative is not described by truth or its opposite as a report is. Nevertheless, His words addressed to them are: ﴿Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful﴾, meaning in your statement: "Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?" So their question was treated as a report, because it implies the report that this human kind is not protected from corruption and bloodshed, except those whom God protects from them. And God knows best.]]

It is said: when they returned to Medina, some of the believers said, "How did this befall us when God had promised us victory?" So this was revealed. Istazallahum: he sought to make them slip and invited them to the lapse. Bi-ba'di ma kasabu: through some of what they had earned of their sins. The meaning is that those who fled on the day of Uhud were caused to turn away because they had obeyed Satan and committed sins, so for that reason He withheld from them support and the strengthening of their hearts, until they turned away. It was also said: the slipping of them by Satan is the turning away itself, and he invited them to it through sins that had already preceded in them, because sin drags on to sin, just as obedience drags on to obedience and becomes a means of grace (lutf) toward it. Al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him) said: He made them slip by their acceptance of what Satan adorned for them of flight. It was also said: (bi-ba'di ma kasabu) is their abandoning of the position (markaz) where the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had commanded them to stand firm. That led them to flight.

It was also said: the recollection of those sins made them dislike meeting Allah with them, so they postponed the jihad until they would set their affairs right and fight in a state that is pleasing (to Allah). If you ask: why was it said (bi-ba'di ma kasabu)? I say: it is like His saying, exalted is He, (and He pardons much). And indeed Allah has pardoned them for their repentance and their apology. Indeed Allah is Forgiving of sins, Forbearing, who does not hasten punishment.

[Translation of the passage from al-Zamakhshari's al-Kashshaf on Q. 3:156–158]

"And they say to their brothers" — i.e., on account of their brothers, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it."﴾ The meaning of "brotherhood" is sharing a kind (jins) or a lineage (nasab).

"When they travel through the earth" — when they journey in it and go far away for trade or other purposes, "or they are raiders" — plural of ghāzin (one who raids), like ʿāf and ʿafā (the plural of ʿāf, "one who is desolate"), as in the poet's line: "ʿafā al-ḥiyāḍ ajūn" [note: "The desolate pools, stagnant"]. [Note on the verse: In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: al-ʿafā is the plural of ʿāf, meaning the effaced one. And al-ājin is water that has changed in taste and colour. And the plural of ājin is ajūn, like rākiʿ and rukūʿ, and shāhid and shuhūd. (ʿ)]

It is also read with the zāy lightened, dropping the tāʾ from ghuzāh (raiders).

If you ask: how is "when they travel" (iḍā ḍarabū) used with "they say" (qālū)? I answer: it is the narration of a past situation, as when you say "whenever they travel through the earth."

If you ask: what does "that God may make it" (liyajʿala) depend on? I answer: "they said" — that is, they said that and believed it, "so that it may be a regret in their hearts," the lām being like it in: ﴿So that it might become for them an enemy and a sorrow﴾. Or [it depends on] "do not be," in the sense: do not be like them in uttering that saying and believing it, so that God may make it a regret in their hearts alone, and guard your hearts from it.

If you ask: what is the meaning of ascribing the action to God, Exalted is He? I answer: its meaning is that when they hold that false belief, God, Mighty and Majestic, places grief and regret in their hearts and constricts their breasts as a punishment. Their believing is their action, and what arises from it of grief, regret and constriction of breast is the action of God, Mighty and Majestic, like His saying: ﴿He makes his breast narrow and constricted, as though he were climbing up into the sky﴾. It is also permissible that this refers to what the prohibition implies, i.e. do not be like them, so that God makes your not being like them a regret in their hearts, because opposing them in what they say and believe, and contradicting them, is what distresses and enrages them. "And God gives life and causes death" — a rebuttal of their saying: the matter is in His hand; He may give life to the traveller and the raider, and cause death to the resident and the one who sits, as He wills.

It is reported from Khālid ibn al-Walīd, may God be pleased with him, that he said at his death: "There is no spot of a hand's breadth on me without a blow or a thrust in it, and here I am dying as a camel dies. May the eyes of the cowards not sleep." "And God is Seeing of what you do" — so do not be like them.

It is read with the yāʾ, meaning: those who disbelieved. ﴿Surely forgiveness﴾ is the answer to the oath, and it stands in place of the answer to the condition; likewise ﴿Surely to God you will be gathered﴾.

He first refuted the disbelievers' claim that whoever of their brothers travelled or raided would not have died had he been in Medina, and he forbade the Muslims from this, because it is a cause of holding back from jihad. Then he said to them: "And if you are killed or die in the way of God, the forgiveness and mercy you attain thereby is better than what they gather of the world and its benefits even if you had not died."

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both: "better than the earth filled with red gold" [note: In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: ṭalāʿ al-arḍ means its fullness; and dhahba is a piece of gold. (ʿ)]. It is read with the yāʾ, meaning: the disbelievers are gathered. ﴿To God you will be gathered﴾ — to God, the Merciful, the Vast in mercy, the Bestower of great reward; you will be gathered. The placing of God's name in this position, with its being fronted and the lām attached to the preposition connected to it, is no hidden matter.

It is read ﴿mutum﴾ with the mīm vowelled with a damma and with a kasra, from "māta yamūtu" and "māta yamātu."

"Mā" is extra (zā'idah) for emphasis, and to indicate that his gentleness toward them was only through mercy from Allah, like His saying: ﴿So for their breaking their covenant, We cursed them﴾. The meaning of "mercy" is that He steadied his heart and enabled him to be gentle and kind toward them, until He rewarded them with grief upon grief and consoled them with a return to them after they had opposed him, disobeyed his command, fled, and abandoned him. ﴿And had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you﴾: they would have dispersed from you, so that no one of them would remain around you. ﴿So pardon them﴾ in what concerns you personally, ﴿and ask forgiveness for them﴾ in what concerns the right of Allah, completing the compassion for them. ﴿And consult them in the matter﴾, meaning in the matter of war and similar matters on which no revelation has come down to you, so that you may seek support in their opinion, and because of what it contains of comforting their hearts and raising their status.

It is related from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, "Allah already knew that he had no need of them, but He wished that he should set a precedent for those after him." And from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace: "No people ever consulted together but they were guided to the most rightful course of their affair" [[Al-Hasan's statement is repeated in the commentary on Surat al-Shura, and it is the preserved version. Al-Tabari narrated it through his chain.]]. And from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: "I have never seen anyone consult more than the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace" [[This text contains a distortion. The correct wording is "from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to his Companions." Al-Shafi'i narrated it from Ibn 'Uyaynah from al-Zuhri from him, and it is disconnected (munqati'). It is an abridgement of the long hadith about the story of al-Hudaybiyah and the conquest campaign, which Ibn Hibban narrated through the transmission of 'Abd al-Razzaq from Ma'mar from al-Zuhri from 'Urwah from al-Miswar and Marwan. In it al-Zuhri said: "Abu Hurayrah used to say," and then he mentioned it. Likewise 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated it in his Musannaf, and it is found with Ahmad and Ishaq. Al-Tirmidhi alluded to it at the end of the chapter on jihad, saying: "It is related from Abu Hurayrah," and then he mentioned it.]]. It is also said: when the chiefs of the Arabs were not consulted on a matter, it grieved them, so Allah commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to consult his Companions, so that his independent decision without them would not burden them.

It is recited: ﴿And consult them in some of the matter﴾. ﴿So when you have resolved﴾, meaning when you have settled your opinion on something after consultation, ﴿then rely upon Allah﴾ in carrying out your decision toward what is most right and most beneficial, for what is best for you is known only to Allah, not to you or to anyone you consult. It is also recited ﴿fa-idha 'azamtu﴾ with a damma on the tā', meaning: when I have resolved for you upon something and guided you to it, then rely upon Me, and do not consult anyone after that.

If Allah helps you, no one can overcome you; but if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him? So in the believers let them put their trust. This is an alert that the whole matter belongs to Allah, and that trust in Him is obligatory. Similar to it is: ﴿Whatever mercy Allah grants to people, none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, none can release after Him.﴾ "After Him" means after His forsaking you. Or it is like your saying: "There is no one who does good to you after so-and-so," meaning, when he has passed away. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read: "wa-in yakhdhulkum" (if He forsakes you), from akhadhahu, when he made him forsaken. It contains encouragement to obedience and to that which earns them Allah's help and support, and a warning against disobedience and that which makes them deserving of punishment by forsaking. ﴿And upon Allah﴾: let the believers single out their Lord for trust and reliance, because they know that there is no helper besides Him, and because their faith requires this and necessitates it.

It is said: "Ghalla shay'an min al-maghnam ghulūlan, wa-aghalla ighlālan" (he took something from the spoils of war), when he took it secretly. It is said: "aghalla al-jāzir" (the butcher), when he stole some meat along with the hide. And al-ghull is the resentment lodged in the breast. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever We send on a task and he embezzles something will come on the Day of Resurrection carrying it on his neck." [Narrated by Ibn Majah from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Unays, that he and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab once discussed charity, and 'Umar said: "Did you not hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he mentioned the embezzlement of charity: that whoever embezzles a camel or a sheep will bring it on the Day of Resurrection." 'Abdullah ibn Unays said: "Yes."] And in the two Sahihs, from Abu Humayd al-Sa'idi: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) employed an official, and the official came when he had finished his work. The hadith continues: and in it, 'By Him in whose hand is Muhammad's soul, none of you does any work but he comes with it on the Day of Resurrection carrying it on his neck.'" And his (ﷺ) saying: "Gifts to rulers are embezzlement." [Narrated by Ahmad, al-Bazzar, and al-Tabarani from the hadith of Abu Humayd al-Sa'idi with the wording "gifts to officials," and it is from the narration of Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash from Yahya ibn Sa'id from 'Urwa from him. Al-Bazzar said: Isma'il erred in its chain and its text. He only meant the hadith of al-Zuhri from 'Urwa, from Abu Humayd, with the wording mentioned above. Likewise Ibn 'Adi counted it among the munkar narrations of Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash. And 'Abd al-Razzaq said: Sufyan al-Thawri narrated to us from Aban ibn Abi 'Ayyash from Abu Nadra from Jabir, with the wording "Gifts to the commanders are embezzlement." Ishaq narrated it: Waki' informed us, Sufyan narrated to us from one who narrated to him from Abu Nadra, with the same. Al-Bazzar said: Aban is abandoned. Then he (al-Bazzar) cited it from the narration of Qays ibn al-Rabi' from Layth ibn Abi Sulaym, from 'Ata', from Jabir, with the same. Ibn 'Adi also recorded it in the biography of Ahmad ibn Mu'awiya al-Bahili, from his narration, from al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, from Ibn 'Awn, from Ibn Sirin, from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him). And he said: This is a false hadith. Al-Tabarani mentioned in al-Awsat that Ahmad ibn Mu'awiya was alone in narrating it.] And from him (ﷺ): "There is no liability on the borrower other than the one who embezzles." [Narrated by al-Bayhaqi from the narration of 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father from his grandfather, and he added: "And there is no liability on the depositary other than the one who embezzles." Al-Bayhaqi said: This is weak, and what is preserved is that it is a saying of Shurayh.] And from him (ﷺ): "No looting, no tampering, and no embezzlement." [Narrated by Abu Dawud and Ahmad from the narration of al-Zuhri from 'Urwa from al-Miswar and Marwan in a hadith. Al-Darimi, al-Tabarani, and Ibn 'Adi narrated it from the narration of Kathir ibn 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn 'Awf from his father from his grandfather, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "No plunder, no tampering, no embezzlement, and whoever embezzles will come with what he embezzled on the Day of Resurrection." Ibn Zanjawayh narrated it in al-Amwal, and Ibrahim al-Harbi in al-Gharib, from the narration of Musa ibn 'Ubayda from Aban ibn Salama from his father. And Musa is weak.] It is said: "aghallahu" means when he found him to be a ghall (embezzler), like your saying: "abkhaltuhu" (I found him stingy) and "afhamtuhu" (I found him unable to speak). [His saying "like your saying abkhaltuhu and afhamtuhu": In al-Sihah: afhamtuhu means I found him unable to compose poetry. (Ε)]

﴿It is not for a prophet to embezzle﴾: it is not right for him, and it is not sound for him to do so. The meaning is that prophethood is incompatible with embezzlement. Likewise, whoever reads it in the passive form (yughalla) refers back to the first meaning, for its meaning is: it is not sound for him that he be found an embezzler, and he is not found an embezzler except if he is one.

In this there are two interpretations. The first: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) be cleared and exonerated from that, and that his infallibility be emphasized, by stating that prophethood and embezzlement are mutually exclusive, lest anyone suspect him of any of it or doubt him. As it is narrated that a red woolen cloak was lost on the day of Badr, and some hypocrites said: "Perhaps the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took it." [Narrated by al-Tirmidhi from the hadith of Khusayf from Miqsam from Ibn 'Abbas with the wording "some people said," and he said it is good. He said: It was narrated from Miqsam without mentioning Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Tabarani, Abu Ya'la, Ibn 'Adi, al-Tabari, and al-Wahidi all narrated it through this route. Ibn 'Adi faulted it because of Khusayf.]

And it is narrated that it was revealed concerning the spoils of Uhud [Al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi mentioned it in his Asbab, from al-Kalbi and Muqatil, who said: "It was revealed concerning the spoils of Uhud when the archers left their post..."], when the archers left the post and sought booty, and said: "We fear that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) will say: 'Whoever takes something, it is his,' and that he will not distribute the spoils as he did not distribute them on the day of Badr." So the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Did I not charge you not to leave the post until my command reaches you?" They said: "We left behind our brothers standing." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Rather, you thought that we would embezzle and not distribute to you."

The second: that it is an intensification of the prohibition addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), according to what is narrated: that he sent out scouts, and they gained spoils, and he divided them but did not give a share to the scouts, so this was revealed. Meaning: it is not for a prophet to give to one people and withhold from others; rather he must distribute equally. And the deprivation of some warriors was called "ghulul" as an exaggeration and a disparagement of the matter's appearance. Had it been read ﴿an yughalla﴾ from aghalla in the sense of ghalla, it would be permissible to read ﴿ya'ti bima ghalla yawma al-qiyama﴾ (he will come on the Day of Resurrection with that which he embezzled), meaning he will come with the very thing he embezzled, carrying it, as in the hadith: "He comes on the Day of Resurrection carrying it on his neck." [Its beginning was mentioned six hadiths earlier.] [His saying: "He comes on the Day of Resurrection carrying it on his neck": perhaps its beginning is: "Whoever embezzles something." (Ε)] And it is narrated: "Let me not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with a camel that bellows, or a cow that lows, or a sheep that bleats, calling out: 'O Muhammad, O Muhammad!' and I will say: 'I possess nothing for you against Allah; I have conveyed it to you.'" [Narrated by 'Ali ibn al-Madini in al-'Ilal, and Abu Ya'la and al-Tabari from the narration of Hafs ibn Humayd from 'Ikrima from Ibn 'Abbas from 'Umar with this in a long hadith; its origin is in the two Sahihs from Abu Zur'a ibn 'Amr ibn Jarir from Abu Hurayra with the wording: "Let me not find any one of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with a camel on his neck that bellows..." the hadith.]

And it is related that one of the rude Bedouin Arabs stole a musk pouch, and the verse was recited to him, and he said: "Then I will carry it, fragrant of scent and light in its load." It is permissible to mean: he will come with what he bore of its burden, its consequence, and its sin. If you say: Why not say "then every soul will be paid in full for what it earned," so that it is connected to it? I say: A general term was brought which encompasses every earner, the embezzler and others, and so it is connected to it in meaning; and it is more eloquent and more emphatic, for when the embezzler knows that every earner, whether good or evil, will be recompensed and his reward paid in full, he knows he cannot escape from among them despite the magnitude of what he has earned. ﴿And they will not be wronged﴾: that is, He will be just among them in recompense, each receiving his reward according to the measure of his earnings.

It is also said that *dhawu darajat* ("those possessing degrees") is meant. The meaning is the difference between the abodes of those among them who are rewarded and the abodes of those who are punished, or the difference between reward and punishment.

Among what Abu Talib said when he gave a sermon at the marriage of Khadija (may Allah be pleased with her), when the Banu Hashim and the leaders of Mudar were present:

"Praise belongs to Allah, who made us among the offspring of Ibrahim, the seed of Isma'il, the root of Ma'add and the stock of Mudar. Verses 3:165–168 of the Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf)

﴿When a calamity afflicted you﴾, meaning what befell them on the day of Uhud, the killing of seventy of them, ﴿though you had inflicted twice as much﴾, on the day of Badr, the killing of seventy and the taking of seventy captive. The *lamma* (when) is in the accusative, governed by *qultum* (you said). The phrase ﴿afflicted you﴾ is in the genitive position, since *lamma* is prefixed to it, and its implied sense is: "Did you say when a calamity afflicted you?" The *anna* (how/whence) in ﴿How is this?﴾ is in the accusative because it is the object of speech, and the hamza is interrogative, for affirmation and rebuke.

If you ask: "To what does this conjunction (wa) attach this clause?" I say: it attaches to what preceded in the story of Uhud, from His saying ﴿Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you﴾. It is also permissible that it be attached to an elided clause, as if it were said: "Did you do such and such, and did you then say such and such? How is this?", meaning: from where is this? Like His saying, ﴿From where is this for you?﴾, in reference to His saying ﴿From yourselves﴾ and His saying ﴿From Allah﴾. The meaning is: you are the cause of what befell you, by your choice to leave Madinah, or by your abandoning the position.

*Fa-ja'a bi-jalmūdin lahu mithla ra'sihi*
