The phrase ﴿afflicted you﴾ is in the genitive position, since *lamma* is prefixed to it, and its implied sense is: "Did you say when a calamity afflicted you?" The *anna* (how/whence) in ﴿How is this?﴾ is in the accusative because it is the object of speech, and the hamza is interrogative, for affirmation and rebuke.

If you ask: "To what does this conjunction (wa) attach this clause?" I say: it attaches to what preceded in the story of Uhud, from His saying ﴿Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you﴾. It is also permissible that it be attached to an elided clause, as if it were said: "Did you do such and such, and did you then say such and such? How is this?", meaning: from where is this? Like His saying, ﴿From where is this for you?﴾, in reference to His saying ﴿From yourselves﴾ and His saying ﴿From Allah﴾. The meaning is: you are the cause of what befell you, by your choice to leave Madinah, or by your abandoning the position.

From Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "By your taking ransom from the captives of Badr before permission was given to you." ﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent﴾, that is, He is capable of granting victory and of withholding it, and of afflicting you at one time and afflicting them at another. ﴿And what befell you on the day the two armies met﴾, the day your host and the host of the polytheists met, was ﴿by permission of Allah﴾, that is, by His allowing it, He used *idhn* (permission) metaphorically for His leaving the disbelievers free, and that He did not prevent them from you in order to test you, because the one who grants permission leaves the one given permission free to achieve his aim. ﴿And that He might know﴾, and it occurred so that the believers and the hypocrites might be distinguished, and so that the faith of these and the hypocrisy of those might become manifest. ﴿And it was said to them﴾ is part of the relative clause, coordinated with *nafaqu* (they were hypocritical). It did not say *fa-qalu* (so they said) because it is an answer to a question prompted by the believers' summons to them to fight, as if it were said: "What did they say to them?" And it was said: "They said, 'If we knew fighting, we would surely follow you.'" It is also permissible that the relative clause be restricted to *nafaqu*, and that ﴿And it was said to them﴾ be an independent statement, which made the command binding upon them: either to fight for the sake of God as the believers fight, or, if they were not concerned with the cause of the religion*, to repel the enemy in defense of themselves, their families, and their property. But they refused to fight and utterly denied their capacity for it, because of their hypocrisy and corruption. This is what is reported: that Abdullah ibn Ubayy withdrew with his allies, and it was said to him, and he said that. It was also said: "Or repel the enemy by increasing the numbers of the fighters, even if you do not fight, for the multitude of numbers terrifies the enemy and weakens him." From Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi, when his sight had failed: "If I were able, I would sell my house and join a frontier post of the Muslims, and I would be between them and their enemy." It was said: "How, when your sight has gone?" He said: this is because of His saying ﴿or repel﴾; he meant: increase their numbers.

Another interpretation: their saying ﴿If we knew fighting﴾ means: if we knew that what you are doing could properly be called fighting, ﴿we would surely follow you﴾. They meant that what you are engaged in, because of the error of your opinion and your deviation from the right course, is nothing, and that such a thing is not called fighting; it is only casting oneself into destruction, because the opinion of Abdullah was to remain in Madinah and he did not consider the going out to be correct.

﴿They were, that day, nearer to disbelief than to faith﴾, meaning: before that day they used to display faith, and no sign had appeared from them indicating their disbelief. But when they withdrew from the army of the believers and said what they said, they distanced themselves by that from the faith that had been presumed of them, and drew near to disbelief. It was also said: they were nearer to the disbelievers in support than to the believers, because their reducing the numbers of the Muslims by withdrawal was a strengthening of the polytheists.

﴿They say with their mouths﴾: their faith does not go beyond their mouths and the points of articulation of the letters, and their hearts do not comprehend anything of it. The mention of the mouths together with the hearts is a depiction of their hypocrisy, that their faith exists in their mouths and is absent from their hearts, contrary to the attribute of the believers, whose hearts agree with their mouths.

﴿And Allah knows best what they conceal﴾, of hypocrisy, and of what passes between some of them and others of disparagement of the believers, of ascribing them ignorance, of judging their opinion to be wrong, of gloating over them, and other things, because you know some of that in a general way from signs, while I know all of it with comprehensive knowledge of its details and modes.

﴿Those who said﴾ has several possibilities in its i'rab (grammatical analysis): that it be in the accusative, as a censure, or as a reply to ﴿those who were hypocritical﴾; or in the nominative, meaning "they are those who said"; or in the substitution of the waw of *yaktumun* (they conceal). It is also permissible that it be in the genitive, as a substitute for the pronoun in *bi-afwahihim* (with their mouths) or *qulubihim* (their hearts), like the poet's saying:

"On his generosity, Hatim would be stingy with water."

*Fa-lamma tasafanna al-adawatu ajhashat*
*ila ghudūni al-'anbari al-jarāḍimi*

*Fa-ja'a bi-jalmūdin lahu mithla ra'sihi*
*li-yashraba ma'a al-qawmi bayna al-sarā'imi*

*Ala ḥālatin law anna fil-qawmi ḥātaman*
*'ala jūdihi la-ḍanna bil-māi ḥātimu*

This is by al-Farazdaq, excusing what happened to him on a journey with his guide Asim al-Anbari, when they lost the way. *Al-tasafun* is the sharing of little water by means of a *sifn* (a small vessel for ablution and the like). *Al-adawa* is the vessel for water, its plural being *adawā*. Attributing the sharing to it is a rational metaphor (*majaz 'aqli*), because it is the place where the water they shared was contained. Closer to this is that it is a metonymic metaphor (*majaz mursal*) for what is in it. *Al-jahsh* and *al-ijhash* is a person's supplicating to another and preparing himself to weep before him, like a child before its mother. *Ghudūn al-jild* are the creases of the skin; it is also narrated as *'uyūn*. Attributing the *ijhash* to it is a rational metaphor, because it is the place where its effect appears. *Al-jarāḍim* is one with a wide belly who eats much. The intended *jalmūd* is a large hard vessel, like his head, that is, the head of al-'Anbari, and in it is an allusion to his foolishness, since excessive largeness of the head is a sign of dullness; hardness too is an allusion to that. *Li-yashraba* means: so that he might take the water of the people between *al-sarā'im*, the plural of *sarīma*, which is the cut-off part of the sand, or a herd of camels. It alludes to their being in a desert with no water, in a straitened condition, so that if Hatim were among the people with his well-known generosity, he would have been stingy with the water. *'Ala* here means *fi* (in). This is supported by the narration of al-Mubarrad in his *Kāmil*: "'ala sā'a" (in an hour). *Ḥātim*, in the genitive, is an apposition to the pronoun in *jūdihi* (his generosity). In it is a mention of the name Hatim, namely Hatim ibn Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn al-Hashraj.

﴿For their brothers﴾, that is, because of their brothers, of the kind of the hypocrites slain on the day of Uhud, or their brothers by lineage and by sharing the dwelling. ﴿And they sat back﴾, that is, they said, having sat back from fighting: "If our brothers had obeyed us in what we commanded them, which was to sit back, and had agreed with us in it, they would not have been killed, just as we were not killed." ﴿Say: Then avert from yourselves death, if you are truthful﴾. Its meaning: say, if you are truthful in claiming that you found a way to ward off being killed, which is sitting back from fighting, then strive to find a way to ward off death. The intent is that such warding off is of no benefit to you, because if you ward off being killed, which is one of the causes of death, you will not be able to ward off its other scattered causes, and some of them must inevitably come upon you.

It is reported that seventy hypocrites died on the day they uttered this saying.

If you say: "They were truthful in that they warded off being killed by sitting back, so what is the meaning of His saying ﴿if you are truthful﴾?" I say: its meaning is that deliverance from being killed may have as its cause sitting back from fighting, and it may have another cause, because the causes of deliverance are many. A man's fighting may be the cause of his deliverance, and had he not fought he would have been killed. So what tells you that the cause of your deliverance is sitting back, and that you are truthful in your claim? What prevents you from thinking the cause is something else?

Another interpretation: ﴿if you are truthful﴾ in your saying: "If they had obeyed us and sat back, they would not have been killed." The meaning is that if they had obeyed you and sat back, they would have been killed sitting back just as they were killed fighting.

And His saying ﴿Then avert from yourselves death﴾ is a mockery of them, that is: if you are men who ward off the causes of death, then ward off all its causes so that you do not die.

﴿And do not let those who are killed in the way of Allah be thought dead﴾. The address ﴿do not think﴾ (wa la tahsabanna) is directed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone.

It was also recited with the yā' (ya), as: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) should not think" (wa la yahsabanna Rasulu-llahi (ﷺ)), or "let no thinker think" (wa la yahsabanna hasib).

It is permissible for ﴿those who were killed﴾ (alladhina qutilu) to be the subject (fā'il), and the sense would then be: "Let not those who were killed think them dead," meaning: "Let not those who were killed in the way of Allah think themselves dead."

If you ask: how is the first object (al-maf'ul al-awwal) omitted? I answer: it is originally a subject (mubtada'), so it was omitted just as the subject is omitted in His words ﴿alive﴾ (ahya'). The meaning is: "They are alive," which the context indicates.

It was also recited: wa la tahsabanna with a fatḥa on the sīn, and qutilu with the shadda (intensive form). And ﴿alive﴾ (ahya') is in the accusative, in the sense of: "Rather, consider them alive," ﴿with their Lord, provided for﴾ (ʿinda rabbihim yurzaqun), meaning: they are brought near to Him and have high rank with Him, as in His words: ﴿those who are with your Lord﴾ (fa-alladhina ʿinda rabbika).

﴿They are provided for﴾ (yurzaqun) like the provision of all other living beings, eating and drinking. This is an affirmation of their being alive and a description of their condition, which is the enjoyment of Allah's provision.

﴿Rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾ (fariḥina bima atahumu-llahu min fadlihi), namely the success in martyrdom, what has been brought to them of honour, and their preference over others, by being alive and brought near, with the provision and bliss of Paradise hastened for them.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When your brothers were struck at Uhud, Allah placed their spirits in the bodies of green birds, which roam in the rivers of Paradise, eat from its fruits, and take refuge in lamps of gold suspended in the shade of the Throne."

[Narrated by Abu Dawud, Ibn Abi Shayba, al-Hakim, Abu Ya'la and al-Bazzar, all from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, and more complete than it.

Al-Daraqutni said: Muhammad ibn Ishaq alone transmitted it from Isma'il ibn Umayya, and its origin is in Muslim from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), with the wording: "Their spirits are in the bodies of green birds which have lamps suspended from the Throne, roaming in Paradise wherever they wish," and so on.]

﴿And they rejoice﴾ (wa yastabshirun) in their brothers the fighters (al-mujahidin), ﴿in those who have not yet joined them﴾ (bi-alladhina lam yalhaqu bihim), that is, who have not been killed so as to join them, ﴿from behind them﴾ (min khalfihim). He means: those who are behind them have remained after them, while they have gone ahead of them.

It was said: ﴿have not joined them﴾ means: they have not attained their merit and rank.

﴿That there is no fear upon them﴾ (alla khawfun ʿalayhim) is a substitute (badal) for ﴿those﴾ (alladhina). The meaning is: they rejoice at what has become clear to them about the condition of those whom they left behind among the believers, namely that they will be raised up secure on the Day of Resurrection. Allah gave them this glad tidings, so they rejoice in it.

Mentioning the condition of the martyrs and their rejoicing over those left behind is an incitement to those who remain after them to increase in obedience, to strive earnestly in jihad, to desire attaining the ranks of the martyrs and obtaining their merit, and it is an encouragement for one who sees himself in good to wish the same for his brothers in Allah. It is also glad tidings to the believers of success in the final return.

He repeated ﴿they rejoice﴾ (yastabshirun) in order to attach to it what explains His words ﴿that there is no fear upon them, nor do they grieve﴾ (alla khawfun ʿalayhim wa la hum yahzanun), namely the mention of the blessing and bounty, and that this is a reward for them for their faith, which must, by the justice and wisdom of Allah, come to them and not be lost.

It was recited: ﴿and that Allah﴾ (wa anna-llaha) with a fatḥa, in conjunction (ʿatf) with ﴿the blessing and the bounty﴾. And with a kasra, as a new sentence (ibtida') and as a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ). This is the recitation of al-Kisa'i, and it is supported by the recitation of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud).

﴿And Allah does not waste﴾.

The one who answered the call of God and the Messenger, after the wound had struck them, is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is (for those who did good). Alternatively, it is a qualifier (sifah) of "the believers," or it is in the accusative (nasb) as an expression of praise.

It is narrated that when Abu Sufyan and his companions turned back from Uhud and reached al-Rawha', they regretted it and resolved to return.[[Ibn Ishaq narrated it in al-Maghazi from his shaykhs, and through his chain al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il mentioned it at length.]] This reached the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he wished to frighten them and show them the strength of himself and his companions. So he called his companions to set out in pursuit of Abu Sufyan, and said: "None shall go out with us except those who were present with us yesterday." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) set out with a group until they reached Hamra' al-Asad, which is eight miles from Madinah. His companions were still suffering from their wounds, but they forced themselves on so that they would not miss the reward. God cast terror into the hearts of the polytheists, and they departed. Then this was revealed.

The "min" in ﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا مِنْهُمْ﴾ (for those among them who did good) is explicative (li-l-tabyin), like it is in His saying: ﴿God has promised those among them who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness﴾.[[Qur'an 48:29.]] This is because those who answered the call of God and the Messenger all did good and were mindful of God, not just some of them.

It is narrated from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr that Aisha, may God be pleased with her, said to me: "Your two parents are indeed among those who answered the call of God and the Messenger."[[Agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim), and al-Hakim erred and included it in his al-Mustadrak.]] She meant Abu Bakr and al-Zubayr.

The one to whom the people said: ﴿Indeed the people have gathered against you﴾. It is narrated that Abu Sufyan called out when he was turning away from Uhud: "O Muhammad, let our appointment be the season of Badr next year, if you wish." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If God wills." When the following year came, Abu Sufyan went out with the people of Makkah until he camped at Marr al-Zahran. God cast terror into his heart, and it occurred to him to turn back. He met Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i, who had come to perform 'umrah, and said: "O Nu'aym, I made an appointment with Muhammad to meet at the season of Badr. This is a year of drought, and only a year in which we graze on the trees and drink milk would suit us. It has occurred to me to turn back, but if Muhammad goes out and I do not go out, that will make him bold. So go to Madinah and dissuade them, and I will give you ten camels." Nu'aym went out and found the Muslims preparing. He said to them: "This is not the right opinion. They came to you in your homes and dwellings, and not one of you escaped except as a fugitive. Do you want to go out when they have gathered against you at the season? By God, not one of you will escape."

It is also said: a caravan of the 'Abd al-Qays passed by Abu Sufyan, heading to Madinah for provisions, and he promised them a camel-load of raisins if they would dissuade the Muslims. The Muslims disliked going out. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, I will certainly go out, even if no one goes out with me." So he went out with seventy riders.[[Ibn Sa'd narrated it through Ibn Ishaq, Musa ibn 'Uqbah and others. al-Waqidi also narrated it in al-Maghazi, saying: "al-Dahhak ibn 'Uthman, 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far, Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Muslim, Ibn Abi Habib and others told me," and they said: "When Abu Sufyan wanted to turn back from Uhud," and mentioned it at length. As for his saying "It is also said that it is the word that Abraham said when he was thrown into the fire," al-Bukhari narrated it through Abu al-Duha from Ibn 'Abbas.]] They were saying: ﴿God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾. It is also said that this is the word Abraham, peace be upon him, said when he was cast into the fire.

So they reached Badr and remained there for eight nights. They had merchandise with them, which they sold, and they gained good profit. Then they returned to Madinah safe and victorious. Abu Sufyan returned to Makkah, and the people of Makkah named his army "the army of the sawiq" (the army of the parched grain), saying: "You only went out to drink sawiq."

So the first "people" are the dissuaders, and the others are Abu Sufyan and his companions.

If you ask: how is it said "the people" when Nu'aym alone was the one who dissuaded?

The Shaytan is the predicate (khabar) of "dhalikum," meaning: "That [one] who discourages you is only the Shaytan." The clause "He frightens his allies" (yukhawwifu awliyā'ahu) is a resumed clause (jumla mustaʼnafa) explaining his satanic nature. Alternatively, al-Shaytan is an attribute (ṣifa) of the demonstrative noun (ism al-ishara), and "yukhawwif" is the predicate. By "al-Shaytan" is meant Nu'aym, or Abu Sufyan.

It is also permissible that there is an omitted possessive element (al-muḍāf al-maḥdhūf), meaning: "That is only the speech of the Shaytan," that is, the speech of Iblis, may Allah curse him: ﴿He frightens his allies﴾, that is, he frightens you [with] his allies, who are Abu Sufyan and his companions. This is supported by the reading of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud: "yukhawwifukum awliyā'ahu" (he frightens you with his allies). And [support is found in] His saying: ﴿So do not fear them﴾.

It was also said: "He frightens his allies," meaning those who stayed behind from going out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). If you say: To what does the pronoun in ﴿So do not fear them﴾ refer according to this interpretation? I say: To the people, in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the people have gathered against you﴾. So: ﴿do not fear them﴾, lest you stay back from fighting and become cowardly, ﴿but fear Me﴾, so strive alongside My Messenger and hasten to what he commands you, ﴿if you are believers﴾. That is, faith requires that you prefer the fear of Allah over the fear of people. ﴿And they fear none but Allah﴾.

**﴿Those who race to disbelief﴾**: they fall into it quickly and desire it with the greatest eagerness. They are the hypocrites among those who stayed behind. It is also said: they are a people who apostatized from Islam.

If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿And let them not grieve you﴾? Is it not right for the Messenger to grieve over the hypocrisy of the hypocrites and the apostasy of the apostates?

I answer: its meaning is, "They should not grieve you out of fear that they might harm you or aid against you." Do you not see His saying ﴿Indeed, they will not harm Allah at all﴾? That is, by their racing into disbelief they harm none but themselves, and the consequence of that does not return to others. Then He explains how its consequence returns to them, by His saying ﴿Allah intends not to give them any share in the Hereafter﴾, that is, any portion of reward, ﴿and for them is a great punishment﴾ in place of reward. This is the most emphatic way in which a person can harm himself.

If you ask: why was it not said, "Allah will not give them a share in the Hereafter"? What is the benefit of mentioning intention (irada)?

I answer: its benefit is to indicate that the motive for depriving them and punishing them has become so pure that no deterrent remains, at the time they raced into disbelief. This alerts us to their persistence in transgression and their reaching its utmost limit, to the point that the Most Merciful of the merciful intends not to show them mercy.

﴿Indeed, those who have bought disbelief in exchange for faith﴾: this may be a repetition of their mention, for emphasis and for recording against them what has been attributed to them. Or it may be general, referring to the disbelievers, while the first refers specifically to the hypocrites among those who stayed behind, or to those who apostatized from Islam, or the reverse.

*Shay'an* (anything) is in the accusative because it functions as a *maṣdar* (verbal noun), since the meaning is "any harm at all" or "some harm."

Likewise, the increase in sin is made a cause for the delay and a reason for it.

I answer: since it was in the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah that they would increase in sin, the granting of respite occurred on account of it and because of it, by way of metaphor.

Yahya ibn Wathhab read with *kasr* (kasra) on the first *inna* and *fatḥ* (fatha) on the second. Its meaning is: "Our granting of respite is better for their souls if they act upon it and recognize Allah's favor to them in lengthening the term and withholding immediate punishment."

I answer: its meaning is: "Do not suppose that Our granting of respite is for the increase of sin and for punishment." The *wāw* (and) is for the circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), as if it were said: "So that they may increase in sin, while there awaits them a humiliating punishment."

**﴿Those who race to disbelief﴾**: they fall into it quickly and desire it with the greatest eagerness. They are the hypocrites among those who stayed behind. It is also said: they are a people who apostatized from Islam.

If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿And let them not grieve you﴾? Is it not right for the Messenger to grieve over the hypocrisy of the hypocrites and the apostasy of the apostates?

I answer: its meaning is, "They should not grieve you out of fear that they might harm you or aid against you." Do you not see His saying ﴿Indeed, they will not harm Allah at all﴾? I answer: its benefit is to indicate that the motive for depriving them and punishing them has become so pure that no deterrent remains, at the time they raced into disbelief. This alerts us to their persistence in transgression and their reaching its utmost limit, to the point that the Most Merciful of the merciful intends not to show them mercy.

The lam is for emphasizing the negation, regarding your present condition of mixing, the sincere believers with the hypocrites, ﴿until He distinguishes the wicked from the good﴾, meaning until the hypocrite is separated from the sincere believer. It is read as ﴿yamīza﴾ (from *mayyaza*), and in a transmission from Ibn Kathir it is read as ﴿yumīza﴾ (from *amāza*, which has the same meaning as *mayyaza*).

If you ask, to whom does the address in ﴿antum﴾ refer? I say: it refers to all those who affirm the faith, both the sincere and the hypocrites. It is as if it were said: God would not leave the sincere among you in the state you are in, mixed with one another, and your sincere ones cannot be recognized from your hypocrites because you all agree on affirming (the faith), until He separates them from you through revelation to His Prophet and by informing him of your conditions. Then He said: ﴿And God would not disclose to you the unseen﴾, that is, God would not grant any one of you knowledge of the unseen matters. So do not imagine, when the Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, informs (them) of a man's hypocrisy and another's sincerity, that he knows what is in the hearts with God's knowledge, so that he reports their disbelief and their faith. ﴿But God chooses of His messengers whom He wills﴾, so He sends the Messenger and reveals to him, informing him that in the unseen there is such-and-such, and that so-and-so has hypocrisy in his heart and so-and-so has sincerity in his heart. Thus he knows that from God's information, not from knowing the unseen matters himself.

It is permissible that it is meant: He will not leave you mixed until He distinguishes the wicked from the good, by imposing on you the difficult obligations which only the sincere ones whose hearts God has tested can endure, such as sacrificing lives in jihad and spending wealth in the way of God. He makes that a measure of your beliefs and a witness to your inner selves, so that some of you know what is in the heart of others by way of inference, not by standing upon the secrets of the breasts and knowing them, for that is among the things God has kept to Himself.

And God would not make any one of you aware of the unseen and the hidden matters of hearts, until He distinguishes the sound from the corrupt, making them aware of it. ﴿But God chooses of His messengers whom He wills﴾, so He informs him of some of the unseen matters. ﴿So believe in God and His messengers﴾, by estimating Him as He truly deserves, and knowing Him alone as the One who knows the unseen, and by placing them in their proper ranks, by knowing them as servants whom He has chosen, who know only what God has taught them, and who report only what God has informed them of the unseen, and who have no share in knowledge of the unseen whatsoever.

It is related from al-Suddi that he said: The disbelievers said, "If Muhammad is truthful, let him tell us who among us will believe and who will disbelieve." So this was revealed.

(And let not those who are stingy think) — whoever reads it with the ta' (tahsabanna, "you think") supposes an omitted modifier (mudaf), meaning: "And let not you think that the stinginess of those who are stingy is good for them." Likewise whoever reads it with the ya' (yahsabanna, "they think") and makes the subject of yahsabanna the pronoun of the Messenger of Allah, or the pronoun of someone [else]. Whoever makes its subject "those who are stingy," then the first object (al-maf'ul al-awwal) in his view is omitted, its estimated form being: "And let not those who are stingy think their stinginess is good for them" (wa la yahsabanna alladhina yabkhaluna bukhlahum huwa khayran lahum). What permitted its omission is the indication of "yabkhaluna" (they are stingy) upon it, and [the word] huwa is a separator (fasl).

Al-Aghmash read it without huwa: sa-yutawwaqunа ma bakhilu bihi [this is an explanation of His saying: "it is evil for them" (huwa sharrun lahum)], i.e., they will be bound by the consequence of what they were stingy with, like the binding of a collar (ilzam al-tawq). In their proverbs: "Taqqaladaha tawq al-hamama" (she wore it, the collar of the dove), said when someone comes with a blemish by which he is reviled and blamed.

It is also said: what they were stingy with of zakat will be made into a serpent which they will have around their necks on the Day of Resurrection; it will bite them from horn to foot, peck at their head, and say: "I am your wealth."

From the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning one who withholds zakat: "He will be collared with a bald, venomous serpent (shuja' aqra')" [agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, raised (marfu'): "Whoever Allah gives wealth but he does not pay its zakat, his wealth will be made, on the Day of Resurrection, into a bald serpent with two black spots over its eyes, which will be put around his neck as a collar."] And it is narrated as "shuja' aswad" (a black serpent).

From al-Nakha'i: "They will be collared with a collar of fire."

And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth (wa lillahi miratha al-samawati wa al-ard): i.e., to Him belongs what is in them of what their people inherit, of wealth and other things. So why do they stingily withhold from Him His own possession, and not spend it in His cause? A similar statement is His saying: "And spend of that in which He has made you successors (mustakhlafin)."

It is also read: "bi-ma ta'malun" with the ta' and with the ya'. The ta' is according to the manner of iltifat (the shift of address), and it is more forceful in warning; the ya' is according to the apparent (zahir) sense.

The Jews said this when they heard Allah, Exalted, say: ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan?﴾ Either they said it out of genuine belief in it, or out of mockery of the Qur'an. Whichever it was, the statement is grave and comes only from those who are persistent rebels in their disbelief. The meaning of Allah's hearing it is that it was not hidden from Him, and that He has prepared for it its due punishment. ﴿We shall record what they have said﴾ in the scrolls of the recording angels. Or it means: We shall preserve it and fix it in Our knowledge, never forgetting it, just as what is written down is fixed.

If you ask: how can He say ﴿Allah has certainly heard﴾ and then say ﴿We shall record﴾? Why not say, "And We have recorded"? The answer: He first mentioned the fact of hearing, emphasised by an oath, and then said ﴿We shall record﴾ as a warning, meaning that their recording and documenting will never escape Us, just as their killing of the prophets will never escape Us. He linked their killing of the prophets to this statement to indicate that the two are brothers in gravity, that this is not the first of the monstrous things they have committed, that they are deeply rooted in disbelief and have precedents in it, and that one who killed the prophets is not far from daring to say something like this.

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent with Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) a letter to the Jews of Banu Qaynuqa', inviting them to Islam, to establishing the prayer, to giving zakat, and to lending Allah a goodly loan. [This was recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim through the route of Ibn Ishaq: "Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad related to me from Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas," and he mentioned it at length.] Then Finhas the Jew said: "Indeed Allah is poor, since He asks us for a loan." Abu Bakr struck him in the face and said: "Were it not for the covenant between us and you, I would strike off your neck." Finhas complained of him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and denied what he had said, so this verse was revealed.

A similar statement is their saying ﴿The hand of Allah is chained﴾. As for ﴿And We shall say, "Taste"﴾, it means We shall take vengeance on them by saying to them on the Day of Resurrection: ﴿Taste the punishment of the Blaze﴾, just as you made the Muslims taste anguish. It is said to one who is being avenged upon: "Feel it, and taste it" (ahiss wa dhuq).

Abu Sufyan said to Hamzah (may Allah be pleased with him): "Dhuq, 'aqq" [This was mentioned by Ibn Ishaq in al-Maghazi, who said: al-Julays ibn Zabban al-Kinani, the chief of the Ahabish, passed by Abu Sufyan while he was striking the jaw of Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib with the butt of a spear and saying "Dhuq, 'aqq." It is also recorded through Ibn Ishaq's route by al-Daraqutni in al-Mu'talif.] Regarding his words "to Hamzah (may Allah be pleased with him): Dhuq, 'aqq": in al-Sihah it is said: 'aqq and 'aqqa, like 'amir and 'umar. "Dhuq 'aqq" means: taste the requital of your deed, you disobedient one. (ʿ)

Hamzah read ﴿سيكتب﴾ with the ya', in the passive form, and ﴿ويقول﴾ with the ya'. Al-Hasan and al-A'raj read ﴿سيكتب﴾ with the ya' and with the active subject. Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿ويقال ذوقوا﴾.

The mention of the hands is because most actions are carried out by them. So every deed is treated as if done by the hands, by way of prevalence (al-taghlib, a figure of speech in which a part stands for the whole or one term dominates another). If you ask: why is His words ﴿and that Allah is not unjust to His servants﴾ conjoined to ﴿what your hands have sent before﴾, and how is His not being unjust to the servants made a partner to their committing evil deeds in deserving punishment? The answer: the meaning of His not being unjust to the servants is that He is just toward them, and it is part of justice that He punish the evildoer among them and reward the one who does good.

It is also recorded through Ibn Ishaq's route by al-Daraqutni in al-Mu'talif.] Regarding his words "to Hamzah (may Allah be pleased with him): Dhuq, 'aqq": in al-Sihah it is said: 'aqq and 'aqqa, like 'amir and 'umar. "Dhuq 'aqq" means: taste the requital of your deed, you disobedient one. (ʿ)

Hamzah read ﴿سيكتب﴾ with the ya', in the passive form, and ﴿ويقول﴾ with the ya'. Al-Hasan and al-A'raj read ﴿سيكتب﴾ with the ya' and with the active subject. Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿ويقال ذوقوا﴾.

The mention of the hands is because most actions are carried out by them. So every deed is treated as if done by the hands, by way of prevalence (al-taghlib, a figure of speech in which a part stands for the whole or one term dominates another). If you ask: why is His words ﴿and that Allah is not unjust to His servants﴾ conjoined to ﴿what your hands have sent before﴾, and how is His not being unjust to the servants made a partner to their committing evil deeds in deserving punishment? The answer: the meaning of His not being unjust to the servants is that He is just toward them, and it is part of justice that He punish the evildoer among them and reward the one who does good.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verses 183–184:

He (Allah) "commanded us" (ʿahida ilaynā): He enjoined on us and instructed us in the Torah, "that we should not believe in any messenger until he brings us this particular sign," namely that he show us a sacrifice (qurbān) which fire descends from heaven and consumes. This was the sign of the prophets of the Children of Israel: one would bring the offering, the prophet would stand and supplicate, and fire would descend from heaven and consume it. But this claim is baseless and a fabrication against Allah, because the fire consuming the offering did not oblige belief in the messenger who brought it, except insofar as it was a sign and a miracle. Thus it is, and all other signs are equal, so it is not permissible for Allah, exalted is He, to single it out from among the signs. Allah has held them to account: their prophets came to them with many clear proofs which made belief in them obligatory, and they also came to them with this very sign they had demanded. So why did they kill them, if they were truthful that belief becomes binding upon them through bringing it?

It is also read as "bi-qurbānin" with two dammas (bi-qurbānin with ḍammatayn). Its counterpart is "al-sulṭān" (the authority/proof).

If you say: What is the meaning of His words "and with what you have said" (wa-bi-alladhī qultum)? I say: its meaning is "and with that which you have said," i.e., with the content of your saying: "a sacrifice which fire consumes."

Its import is like His words: "then they return to what they said" (thumma yaʿūdūna li-mā qālū), i.e., to the meaning of what they said.

In the codices of the people of Syria: "wa-bi-l-zuburi" (and with the scriptures), and the zubur are the leaves (ṣuḥuf). "And the illuminating Book" (wa-l-kitāb al-munīr) is the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms.

This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the denial of his people and the denial of the Jews.

Al-Yazidi read ذائِقَةُ الْمَوْتِ according to the original form. Al-A'mash read (ذائقة الموت) by dropping the tanwin with the accusative, as in the verse:

وَلَا ذَاكِرَ اللَّهَ إلّا قَلِيلَا

﴿Then I reminded her, and rebuked her with a gentle rebuke and kind words.
So I left her, not seeking to be pleased, and not remembering Allah except a little.﴾

These lines are by Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali. He used to sit at the courtyard of a beautiful woman in Basra, and she said to him: "Would you like to marry me? I have praiseworthy qualities, such and such." He said: "Yes," and he married her from her family. He found her to be the opposite of what she had claimed, so he rebuked her and addressed her family with poetry containing that, then divorced her in front of them. He referred to her with the masculine pronoun out of modesty. The meaning: I reminded her of what she had said and rebuked her for what she had done, with a good rebuke, but I found her not accepting my rebuke. The word Allah is in the accusative governed by ذاكر, and its tanwin was dropped although it is not in a construct state, by analogy with dropping the light emphatic nun before a following unvocalised letter. Or it is the tanwin of a proper name qualified by ابن placed in apposition to a name. ذاكر is conjoined to مستعتب.

The "لا" is extra, to emphasise the negation. ذاكر was not made to be construct to Allah, so that it remains purely indefinite like the one before it, and so that the negation is more emphatic, because the construct form may suggest that his habit is remembrance, so one might imagine that the negation is of the habit and not of the act of remembrance itself.

If you say: how is His saying ﴿and you will only be paid your rewards in full on the Day of Resurrection﴾ connected to what precedes? I say: its connection is that all of you will die, and death is unavoidable for you, and you will not be paid your rewards for your obedience and disobedience immediately after your death, but you will be paid them on the day you rise from the graves. If you say: this seems to negate what is reported, that the grave is a garden from the gardens of Paradise or a pit from the pits of the Fire [narrated by al-Tirmidhi from the hadith of Abu Sa'id, and it is weak. Al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Awsat in the biography of Mas'ud ibn Muhammad al-Ramli with its chain to Abu Hurayra, and said: only Ayyub ibn Suwayd narrated it from al-Awza'i; alone in it was his son Muhammad from him. I say: and it is weak.]. I say: the word "payment" removes this illusion, because the meaning is that the full payment and completion of rewards occurs on that day, and what occurs before that is some of the rewards. Al-zahzahah: removing and distancing, the intensive form of al-zahh, which is pulling quickly. ﴿So he has indeed succeeded﴾ means he has achieved absolute success, encompassing everything by which one can succeed, and there is no goal of success beyond salvation from the wrath of Allah and the everlasting punishment, and attaining the pleasure of Allah and everlasting bliss. O Allah, grant us success in what will let us attain success before You in the return.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever loves to be distanced from the Fire and admitted into Paradise, let his death find him believing in Allah and the Last Day, and let him treat people as he loves to be treated" [narrated by Muslim from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As in a long hadith]. This includes preserving both the rights of Allah and the rights of people.

The worldly life is likened to goods by which a buyer is deceived and misled until he buys them, and then it becomes clear to him that they are defective and worthless. The Shaytan is the deceiver, the great deluder. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr: this applies only to one who prefers it over the Hereafter; but as for one who seeks the Hereafter through it, it is a provision for a time. The believers were addressed with this so that they would prepare themselves to bear the harms and hardships they will meet, and to be patient with them, so that when they encounter them they meet them prepared, and they are not overwhelmed as one is overwhelmed when hardship strikes him suddenly, so he rejects it and his soul recoils from it.

The affliction in the souls: killing, captivity, wounds, and whatever kinds of fear and calamities befall them.

And in the wealth: spending in the way of good, and whatever blights befall it. And what you hear from the People of the Book [[His words "and what you hear from the People of the Book" – what you hear from those who associated partners (with God) remains. (ʿA.)]] of insults against the upright religion, and the turning away of those who wish to believe, and the faulting of those who have believed, and what came from Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf in his satire of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his incitement of the polytheists, and from Finḥāṣ, and from the Banu Qurayẓa and the Naḍīr. Indeed, that (﴿فَإِنَّ ذَلِكَ﴾ "indeed, that") — "patience and piety are among the steadfast matters of affairs" (﴿مِنْ عَزْمِ الْأُمُورِ﴾), i.e., among the matters that are resolved upon, meaning: among the things that must be resolved upon, or among what God has resolved should be. The meaning is that this is one of God's firm resolutions; you must certainly be patient and mindful of God.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verse 187:**

﴿And when Allah took the covenant﴾: remember the time when Allah took the covenant of the People of the Book. ﴿you shall make it clearly known﴾: the pronoun refers to the Book.

He emphasized on them the obligation to explain the Book and to avoid concealing it, just as one emphasizes to a man who has resolved on something and been told: "By Allah, you must do it!"

﴿They threw it behind their backs﴾: they cast aside the covenant and its emphasis, meaning they did not observe it and paid it no heed. Throwing something behind the back is an idiom for discarding it and ceasing to regard it. Its opposite is to place it before one's eyes and cast it between one's eyes. This is sufficient proof that it is binding on scholars to make clear to people what is true and what they know, and not to conceal any part of it for a corrupt purpose, such as facilitating matters for oppressors, pleasing their inclinations, seeking their favor, obtaining some benefit or worldly gain, or out of fear (taqiyya, dissimulation of one's belief under threat of harm), for which there is no evidence or sign; or out of stinginess with knowledge, or out of reluctance that others be credited with it.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever conceals knowledge from its people, he will be bridled with a bridle of fire."
[[Related by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah from the narration of Ali ibn al-Hakam al-Bunani from ʿAtaʾ from Abu Hurayrah with the wording: "Whoever is asked about knowledge and conceals it, Allah will bridle him with a bridle of fire." Abu Dawud related it from the narration of Hammad ibn Salamah, and the other two from the narration of ʿAmmarah ibn Zadhan, both from ʿAli, and the men in Abu Dawud's chain are trustworthy. But it has a defect. ʿAbd al-Warith related it from ʿAli ibn al-Hakam from a man from ʿAtaʾ. It is said that this unnamed man is Hajjaj ibn Artah, and in Ibn Majah's narration there is an explicit statement of ʿAli ibn ʿAtaʾ's hearing it.

However, ʿAmmarah is weak. The hadith of Abu Hurayrah has another route, which Ibn al-Qattan graded as sound, and he mentioned it from the narration of Qasim ibn Asbagh from Abu al-Ahwas, who is al-ʿUkbari, from Ibn al-Sarri from Muʿtamir from his father from ʿAtaʾ with the same wording. Ibn Abi al-Sarri has confusions, and it seems a hadith entered into another hadith for him. Al-Tabarani related it in al-Awsat through the route of Jabir al-Ju'fi from al-Shaʿbi from ʿAtaʾ, and Jabir is weak. It has many routes from Abu Hurayrah, which Ibn al-Jawzi listed in al-ʿIlal al-Mutanahiyah. On this subject there is also a report from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, related by Ibn Hibban in his Sahih and al-Hakim through the route of Ibn Wahb from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas from his father from Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Hubuli from him. From Ibn ʿAbbas it was related by al-Tabarani and al-ʿUqayli, and in its chain is Maʿmar ibn Zaʾidah. Al-ʿUqayli said: "No one follows him in this." There is another route, which Abu Yaʿla mentioned: Zuhayr related to us, Yunus ibn Muhammad related to us, Abu ʿAwanah related to us from ʿAbd al-Aʿla from Saʿid ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas with it. Ibn al-Jawzi related it through two other routes and weakened them. From Anas: Ibn Majah related it through the route of Yusuf ibn Ibrahim, who said: "I heard Anas" with it. Ibn al-Jawzi related it through two other routes and also weakened them. From Ibn Masʿud and Talq ibn ʿAli, both in al-Tabarani. From Jabir and ʿAʾishah, both in al-ʿUqayli. From Ibn ʿUmar in Ibn ʿAdi. From Abu Saʿid al-Khudri in Abu Yaʿla. Their chains are all weak. From ʿAmr ibn ʿAbasah, Ibn al-Jawzi related it with the wording "then he has been cleared of Islam," and its chain is also weak. Imam Ahmad said: "Nothing authentic has been transmitted on this subject."

(Note) None of its routes contains the words "from its people."]]

It is also related from Tawus that he said to Wahb: "I see that Allah will surely punish you for these books." And he said: "By Allah, if you were a prophet and concealed knowledge as you conceal it, you would see that Allah would punish you."

It is related from Muhammad ibn Kaʿb: "It is not lawful for any scholar to remain silent about his knowledge [[His words "about his knowledge" — perhaps after it there is a missing part, its estimated meaning being "until he teaches it." (Ghayn)]], and it is not lawful for an ignorant person to remain silent about his ignorance until he asks."

It is related from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him: "Allah did not take a covenant from the ignorant that they should learn until He took a covenant from the learned that they should teach."
[[Related by al-Harith ibn Abi Usamah: ʿAbd al-Wahhab al-Khaffafi told us, al-Hasan ibn ʿUmarah told us, al-Hakam ibn ʿUyaynah told me from Yahya ibn al-Jazzar: I heard ʿAli say the above. Al-Hasan is abandoned. Through al-Harith's route it was related by al-Tha'labi, and we have related it in the Juz' al-Dhira'. He said: "al-Harith ibn Usamah wrote" the above, and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr mentioned it in al-ʿIlm, saying: "It is narrated from ʿAli." The author of al-Firdaws also mentioned it from ʿAli. So it seems he (al-Harith) stopped at it as a Marfuʿ (attributed to the Prophet).]]

It has been read: ﴿ليبيننه﴾ and ﴿ولا يكتمونه﴾ with the ya' (third person), because they are absent (third person). And with the ta' (second person), as a relation of their address, like His saying: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Scripture: you will surely cause corruption...﴾

This is an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The first object of the verb is ﴿those who rejoice﴾ (alladhīna yafrahūna), and the second is ﴿with a place of safety﴾ (bi-mafāzah). His words ﴿so do not think them﴾ (fa-lā taḥsabannahum) are an emphatic repetition, with the implied meaning: ﴿do not think them﴾ successful.

It is also recited as ﴿لا تحسبن﴾ and ﴿فلا تحسبنهم﴾ with a ḍamma on the bāʾ, addressing the believers. It is recited as ﴿ولا يحسبن﴾ and ﴿فلا يحسبنهم﴾ with a yāʾ and a fatḥa on the bāʾ in both places, so that the verb refers to the Messenger. Abū ʿAmr recited it with a yāʾ and a fatḥa on the bāʾ in the first place and a ḍamma in the second, so that the verb refers to ﴿those who rejoice﴾. In that reading the first object is omitted, meaning: ﴿those who rejoice﴾ should not think themselves successful, and ﴿فلا يحسبنهم﴾ is an emphatic repetition.

The phrase ﴿بِمَا أُوتُوا﴾ (bimā ūtū) means "by what they did." The verbs atā (أتى) and jāʾa (جاء) are used in the sense of "did." Allah says: ﴿إِنَّهُ كانَ وَعْدُهُ مَأْتِيًّا﴾ ("His promise was ever fulfilled") and ﴿لَقَدْ جِئْتِ شَيْئاً فَرِيًّا﴾ ("You have certainly come up with a terrible thing"). This meaning is supported by the recitation of Ubayy: ﴿يفرحون بما فعلوا﴾ ("rejoice in what they did"). It is also recited as ﴿آتوا﴾, meaning "gave." ʿAlī (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhu) recited ﴿بما أوتوا﴾.

The phrase ﴿بِمَفازَةٍ مِنَ الْعَذابِ﴾ means "safe from the punishment," that is, delivered from it.

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked the Jews about something in the Torah, and they concealed the truth and informed him of the opposite.[[Agreed upon (by al-Bukhārī and Muslim) from the narration of Ḥumayd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān that Marwān said to his doorkeeper: "O Rāfiʿ, go to Ibn ʿAbbās and say to him: 'If any one of us rejoices in what he has been given and loves to be praised for what he has not done, he will be punished, and we will all be punished.'" Ibn ʿAbbās (raḍiyallāhu ʿanhumā) said: "This verse was only revealed about the People of the Book. The Jews came to him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) asked them about something, and they concealed it..." [the hadith continues].]] They showed him that they had confirmed him, sought his praise, and rejoiced in what they had done. Allah informed His Messenger of this and consoled him with what He revealed of their threat. The meaning is: do not think that the Jews who rejoice in what they did, namely their deception of you, and who love that you praise them for what they did not do, namely your telling the truth about what you asked them, will be saved from the punishment.

The meaning of ﴿يَفْرَحُونَ بِمَا أَتَوْا﴾ is "in what they were given of the knowledge of the Torah." It has also been said that it means they rejoice in what they did, namely concealing the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and love to be praised for what they did not do, namely following the religion of Ibrāhīm (ʿalayhi al-salām), since they claimed that Ibrāhīm was a Jew and that they were upon his religion.

It has also been said that they were a group who stayed behind from the expedition with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When he returned, they made excuses to him, claiming they had seen benefit in staying behind, and they sought his praise for not going out.

It has also been said that they are the hypocrites, who rejoice in what they achieved by displaying faith to the Muslims and by their hypocrisy, through which they reached their aims, and who seek praise from them for a faith they did not truly hold, since they concealed disbelief.

It is also permissible for the verse to include everyone who does a good deed and then rejoices in it with self-admiration, and loves that people praise him and commend him for piety and asceticism, and for qualities he does not have.

And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. So He governs their affairs, and He is over all things Competent—so He is able to punish them. Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth are signs, clear proofs, of the Maker, of His great power and His dazzling wisdom, for those of understanding (li-ulil-albab), those who open up their insights to contemplation, inference, and reflection, and who do not look upon them with the gaze of beasts, heedless of the wonders of their natural constitution.

And in the "Small Admonitions" (al-Nasa'ih al-Saghar): Fill your eyes with the adornment of these stars, and let them be counted among these wonders, reflecting on the power of their Determiner and contemplating the wisdom of their Governor, before fate carries you away and you are prevented from looking.

And from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both: I said to 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her: "Tell me of the most wondrous thing you saw from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." [Ibn Hibban narrated it through the chain of 'Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Sulayman from 'Ata': "I, Ibn 'Umar and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr entered upon 'A'isha, and she said: 'It is time that you visited us.' He said: 'I say what the first one said: Visit occasionally, and you will increase in love.' She said: 'Leave us from this idleness of yours.' Then Ibn 'Umar said to 'A'isha: 'Tell us of the most wondrous thing you saw from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)...' the hadith in full." 'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Tha'labi and others also narrated it through Abu Janab al-Kalbi from 'Ata': Ibn 'Umar said to her: "Tell me..." and he mentioned it.] She wept at length, then said: "All of his affairs were wondrous. He came to me on my night, entered under my blanket until his skin touched my skin, then said: 'O 'A'isha, will you permit me tonight to worship my Lord?' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I love your nearness and I love what pleases you; I have given you permission.' So he rose to a waterskin in the house and performed ablution, not pouring much water, then stood to pray and recited from the Qur'an, and began to weep until the tears reached his lap. Then he sat, praised Allah and extolled Him, and continued weeping; then he raised his hands and wept until I saw his tears had wet the ground. Then Bilal came to call him to the dawn prayer and saw him weeping, and said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, do you weep when Allah has forgiven you your past and future sins?' He said: 'O Bilal, should I not be a grateful servant?' Then he said: 'And why should I not weep, when Allah has revealed to me tonight: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth...﴾ Woe to him who recites it and does not reflect upon it.'" It is also reported: "Woe to him who chews it between his jaws and does not contemplate it."
[Narrated by Ibn Mardawayh in the tafsir of Surat al-Rum, through Abu Janab from 'Ata' from 'A'isha, who said: "When this verse was revealed: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your tongues and your colors﴾, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Woe to him who chews it between his jaws and then does not reflect upon it.'"]

And from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he rose at night, would use the siwak, then look at the sky and then say: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth...﴾
[Narrated by al-Tha'labi through the route of Hammad from Hajjaj from Habib ibn Abi Thabit from Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Abi Talib from 'Ali; its origin is in the agreed-upon (Bukhari and Muslim) hadith from Ibn 'Abbas.]

It is related that a man from the Children of Israel, whenever he worshipped Allah for thirty years, a cloud would shade him. A youth from among their youths worshipped and was not shaded. His mother said to him: "Perhaps some lapse occurred from you during your period?" He said: "I do not recall." She said: "Perhaps you once looked at the sky and did not take heed?" He said: "Perhaps." She said: "You were only afflicted by that."

﴿Those who remember Allah, standing, sitting, and lying on their sides﴾: they remember Allah constantly, in every state they are in—standing, sitting, or lying down—not neglecting remembrance in most of their conditions. It is related from Ibn 'Umar, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr and a group that on the day of the 'Id they went out to the musalla and began to remember Allah. Some of them said: "Did not Allah the Exalted say: ﴿remembering Allah standing and sitting﴾?" So they stood and remembered Allah on their feet.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever wishes to frolic in the gardens of Paradise, let him increase his remembrance of Allah."
[Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ishaq and al-Tabarani from the hadith of Mu'adh; its chain includes Musa ibn 'Ubayda, who is weak. Al-Tha'labi narrated it in the tafsir of al-'Ankabut, and Ibn Mardawayh in the tafsir of al-Waqi'a.]

It is also said: its meaning is that they pray in these states according to their ability. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to 'Imran ibn Husayn: "Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; if you cannot, then on your side, making gestures (tumi' ima'an)."
[Narrated by al-Bukhari and the authors of the Sunan from the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn, who said: "I had hemorrhoids," and mentioned the hadith; the end "making gestures" is not in it. Sahib al-Hidaya cited it as al-Zamakhshari did.]

This is evidence for al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, regarding laying the sick person on his side as in the grave-niche (lahd). According to Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, he is laid on his back, and when he finds relief, he sits up.

The place of ﴿'ala junubihim﴾ is an accusative of circumstance (hal), conjoined (ataf) to what precedes it, as if it were said: standing, sitting and lying on their sides. ﴿And they contemplate the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ and what the creation of these great bodies indicates, the perfection of their craftsmanship, and what is arranged within them, with wonders whose details the intellects fall short of grasping, on account of the greatness of the Maker's majesty and the magnificence of His dominion. It is related from Sufyan al-Thawri that he prayed two rak'ahs behind the Maqam, then raised his head to the sky; when he saw the stars, he fainted, and he would pass blood in his urine from the length of his grief and reflection.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "While a man was lying on his bed, he raised his head and looked at the stars and the sky, and said: 'I bear witness that You are a Lord and Creator. O Allah, forgive me.' Allah looked at him and forgave him."
[Narrated by al-Tha'labi through the route of Zayd ibn Aslam from 'Ata' ibn Yasar from Abu Hurayra; its chain includes one who is not known.]

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no worship like reflection."

If you ask: how could they ask God to fulfill what He promised, when God does not break the promise? I answer: its meaning is a request for success in what preserves for them the means of fulfilling the promise; or it is a form of seeking refuge in God and submitting to Him, as the prophets, peace be upon them, used to seek forgiveness while knowing they were forgiven, intending by that humility before their Lord and supplication to Him, and the seeking of refuge which is the mark of servanthood.

Then You have indeed disgraced him; that is, You have utterly disgraced him. This is like His saying, ﴿then he has indeed succeeded﴾. A similar expression in their speech is: "Whoever reaches the pasture of al-Samman has indeed reached (it), and whoever overtakes so-and-so has indeed overtaken him." [[His saying "whoever reaches the pasture of al-Samman": in al-Sihah, a place beside a stretch of sand called ʿAlij. And ʿAlij: a place in the desert with sand. (ʿA)]]

﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾: the lam here indicates those who enter the Fire, and it informs that whoever enters the Fire has no helper, neither through intercession nor otherwise. [[His saying "has no helper, neither through intercession nor otherwise": this is the view of the Mu'tazilah. As for the People of the Sunnah, a believer who enters the Fire will be brought out by intercession or by pardon, as is verified in its proper place. (ʿA)]] You say:

"I heard a man say such-and-such, and I heard Zayd speaking." You attach the verb to the man and omit the thing heard, because you have described him by what is heard, or made him a circumstantial qualifier of it, so that mention of it is dispensed with. Without the description or the circumstantial qualifier, it could not be omitted, and one would say, "I heard the speech of so-and-so, or his words."

If you ask: what is the benefit of combining "one who calls" (al-munadi) and "is called" (yunadi)? I answer: the calling is mentioned absolutely and then restricted by faith, to magnify the status of the one who calls, for there is no caller greater than one who calls to faith. A similar expression is: "I passed by a guide who guides to Islam." For when the caller is mentioned without qualification, the mind goes to one who calls to war, or to quench a strife, or to relieve one in distress, or to meet some calamity, or to some benefit; likewise the guide may be understood as one who guides to the road, or who guides to sound judgment, and other things. So when you say "calls to faith" and "guides to Islam," you have elevated and magnified the status of the caller and the guide.

It is said: "He called him to such-and-such (li-kadha) and to such-and-such (ila kadha)," and "he invited him to it (li-hi) and to it (ilayhi)." Similarly: "He guided him to the road (lil-tariq) and to it (ilayhi)," because the meaning of the end-point (intiha' al-ghayah) and the meaning of specification (al-ikhtisas) both occur together. The caller is the Messenger: ﴿Call to God﴾ and ﴿Call to the way of your Lord﴾. From Muhammad ibn Ka'b: it is the Qur'an.

﴿That believe﴾: that is, "believe," or "that they should believe."

﴿Our sins﴾: our major sins. ﴿our misdeeds﴾: our minor sins. ﴿and make us die with the righteous﴾: specially associated with them in their company, counted among their number. The "abrar" (righteous) is the plural of barr or barr (pious), like rabb and arbab, and sahib and As'hab.

﴿upon Your messengers﴾: this phrase is connected to the promise, as in your saying: "God promised Paradise upon obedience." The meaning is: what You promised us upon affirming Your messengers. Do you not see how He followed the mention of the one who calls to faith, who is the Messenger, with their saying "we believed," which is the affirmation? It is also permissible that it be connected to an omitted element, meaning: what You promised us descending upon Your messengers, or conveyed upon Your messengers, because the messengers are charged with that (﴿but upon him is what he is charged with﴾). It is also said: "upon the tongues of Your messengers." The promised thing is the reward. It is also said: the victory over the enemies.

If you ask: how could they ask God to fulfill what He promised, when God does not break the promise? I answer: its meaning is a request for success in what preserves for them the means of fulfilling the promise; or it is a form of seeking refuge in God and submitting to Him, as the prophets, peace be upon them, used to seek forgiveness while knowing they were forgiven, intending by that humility before their Lord and supplication to Him, and the seeking of refuge which is the mark of servanthood.

It is said: istajaba lahu and istajabahu (he responded to him).

*Wa-dāʿin daʿā yā man yuhību ilā al-nadā... fa-lam yastajibhu ʿinda dhāka mujību*
*(And a caller called out, "O you who summons to generosity..." but no one answered him at that moment.)*

*Fa-qultu: udʿu ukhrā wa-irfaʿi al-ṣawta jahratan... laʿalla abī al-mughwāri minka qarību*
*(So I said: "Call again, and raise your voice aloud; perhaps my brother al-Mughwar is near you.")*

It is by Kaʿb ibn Saʿd al-Ghanawī, lamenting his brother Harim, whose kunya was Abū al-Mughwār. *Jahratan* is an absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*) serving as emphasis. *Abī* is in the genitive after *laʿalla*, which is the dialect of the tribe of ʿUqayl. Using *laʿalla*, which normally expresses hope and nearness, for something remote shows the intensity of his longing and his treating the distant as if it were near. It is also transmitted as *laʿalla Abā al-Mughwār*, in the standard usage. The meaning is: many a caller summons to noble deeds and no one answers him. So I said to him, "Call once more with raised voice; perhaps my brother is near and will answer you as is his custom, for he often seeks lofty matters." This is an image and imaginative depiction, since in reality there is no caller.

﴿That I do not waste the work of any worker among you﴾ is read with the fatha, with the ya' elided, and with the kasra, to indicate "saying." It is also read *lā uḍayyiʿu* with shaddah (intensive form).

﴿Male or female; you are of one another﴾: the phrase *min dhakarin aw unthā* explains the agent. *Baʿḍukum min baʿḍin* means that your males and females share one origin, so each of you is from the other, that is, from his origin, or as if he were from him because of the intensity of your connection and unity. It is said that the meaning is the bond of Islam. This is a parenthetical sentence (*jumla iʿtirāḍiyya*) through which the equal share of women with men in what Allah promised His righteous servants is clarified.

It is related that Umm Salama said: "O Messenger of Allah, I hear Allah mention men in migration and not mention women." (Reported by al-Tirmidhī, from the narration of ʿAmr ibn Dīnār: Salama, a man of the descendants of Umm Salama (may Allah be pleased with her), informed me that she said.) Then ﴿So those who emigrated﴾ was revealed. It is a detailed explanation of the deed of the worker among them, in order to magnify and exalt it, as if He said: "Those who performed these exalted noble deeds, namely emigrating from their homelands fleeing to Allah with their religion from the abode of trial, and were compelled to leave their homes in which they were born and raised, bearing what the polytheists had inflicted upon them of humiliation (*al-khasf*)." [Regarding his words "bi-mā sāmahum" (what they had inflicted upon them): in al-Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: sāmahu al-khasf, and sāmahu khasfan, and khasfan also with a ḍamma, meaning: he caused him to suffer humiliation. (ʿ)] ﴿and were harmed in My way﴾, that is, for His sake and because of Him, meaning the path of religion; ﴿and fought and were killed﴾, that is, fought the polytheists and were martyred. It is read *wa-quttilū* with shaddah. Also *qatalū wa-qātalū* with the first verb in the active form, read with and without shaddah. *Qutilū wa-qutilū* with the first active and the second passive. *Qutilū wa-qātalū* with both in the active.

﴿A reward﴾ is in the position of an emphatic verbal noun (*maṣdar*) meaning "a recompense" or "a bestowal of reward." ﴿From Allah﴾: because His saying "I will surely remove from them their misdeeds… and I will surely admit them" has the meaning of "I will surely reward them." ﴿And with Him﴾ is like saying that the reward is specific to Him and to His power and grace; no other can reward, nor has any other power over it, just as a man says, "With me is what you desire," meaning it is specific to him and to his possession, even if it is not in his presence. This is Allah's instruction on how one should supplicate and beseech Him humbly. The repetition of ﴿Our Lord﴾ is part of supplication, and an announcement of what necessitates a good response and a good reward: enduring hardships in the religion of Allah, patience in the difficulty of its obligations, cutting off the hopes of the lazy who wish for wishes against Him, and a rebuke to those who do not see reward as attainable through deeds, through ignorance and dullness. (The phrase "a rebuke to those who do not see reward" intends the people of the Sunna, who hold that it is permissible for Allah to grant favor to the servant without deed, and that He is not obliged to reward the worker. This is established in its proper place. (ʿ))

It is related from Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq (may Allah be pleased with him): "Whoever is afflicted by a matter and says 'Our Lord' five times, Allah will save him from what he fears and give him what he desires," and he recited this verse. From al-Ḥasan: Allah related of them that they said "Our Lord" five times, then informed that He responded to them. However, He followed that with the raising of the supplication and what it is answered by, so it is necessary to put it forward before the supplication.

(لا يَغُرَّنَّكَ) The address is to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, or to every person. That is: do not look at what they have of abundant provision, of movement and of quick gain, and of reaching the shares of this world, and do not be deceived by the outward appearance of what you see of their spreading out in the land and their moving about in the lands, earning and trading and ﴿wealthy and comfortable﴾ [[Al-Zamakhshari's words "ويتجرون ويتدهقنون" mean: they grow full and enjoy the softness of food and the goodness of drink. This is stated by al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari), under the root دهق and the root دهقن. What agrees better with what is in al-Sihah is يتدهمقون, since he said: Al-Asma'i said: al-dahmaqah is the softness of food, its goodness and its fineness. And the hadith of ʿUmar: "If I wished that ﴿food﴾ be made soft for me, I would have done it, but Allah blamed a people and said: ﴿You used up your good things...﴾ [the verse]," but he did not explicitly mention al-dahqanah with this meaning. (ʿ)]]. It was reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: they are the people of Makkah. It was said: they are the Jews. It was narrated that some of the believers used to see what they were in of fertility and ease and softness of life, and they would say: The enemies of Allah, in what we see, are in goodness, while we have perished from hunger and hardship. If you say: How was it permissible for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to be deceived by that, so that he was forbidden from being deceived by it? I say: In this there are two aspects. The first is that the leader and foremost of a people is addressed with something, and his address stands in place of addressing all of them, so it is as if it were said: ﴿Do not let them deceive you.﴾ The second: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was not deceived by their condition, so he was emphatically charged to remain as he was and to hold firm to his commitment, like His saying: ﴿And do not be among the disbelievers﴾, ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾, ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾. And this, in prohibition, is like His saying in command: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, ﴿O you who believe, believe﴾. The prohibition is apparently directed at the turning about, while in meaning it is directed at the addressee. This is from assigning the cause the status of the effect, because if the turning about were to deceive him, he would have been deceived by it, so the cause was prevented in order that the effect be prevented. It was read: لا يغرنك with the light nun. مَتاعٌ قَلِيلٌ is the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: that is a little enjoyment, and it is the turning about in the lands. He meant its smallness in comparison with what they have of the bliss of the Hereafter, or in comparison with what Allah has prepared for the believers of reward, or he meant that it is little in itself because it ends, and everything that passes away is little. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The likeness of this world in the Hereafter is only like one of you dipping his finger into the sea; let him see what it returns with." [Reported by Muslim from the hadith of al-Mustawrid ibn Shaddad.] وَبِئْسَ الْمِهادُ: and wretched is the resting place, that is: wretched is what they have prepared for their souls.

That is: do not look at what they have of abundant provision, of movement and of quick gain, and of reaching the shares of this world, and do not be deceived by the outward appearance of what you see of their spreading out in the land and their moving about in the lands, earning and trading and ﴿wealthy and comfortable﴾ [[Al-Zamakhshari's words "ويتجرون ويتدهقنون" mean: they grow full and enjoy the softness of food and the goodness of drink. [Reported by Muslim from the hadith of al-Mustawrid ibn Shaddad.] وَبِئْسَ الْمِهادُ: and wretched is the resting place, that is: wretched is what they have prepared for their souls.

The *nuzl* and *nuzul* (provision for a guest): it is what is prepared for the one who arrives as a guest. Abu al-Shu'ara' al-Dabbi said:

*"When a tyrant came upon us with his army as a guest, we made lances and keen swords his nuzl."* [[From Abu al-Shu'ara' al-Dabbi. *al-Jabbar* is the obstinate king. *Dayfahu yadifuhu* means he alighted with him as a guest, that is, when the tyrant alighted among us with his army in the manner of a guest. There is mockery in this, since he came as a fighter, and the poet likened him to one who comes seeking kindness. What supports this comparison is that he made the spears and the keen, sharpened swords his nuzl, which is the food prepared for a guest.]]

Its accusative case (*nasb*) is either as a *hal* (circumstantial accusative, a state of the subject) of *jannat* (gardens), since it is specified by the description, and the governing element is the *lam* (the preposition meaning "for" in *lahum*). It may also be a *maṣdar* (verbal noun) that is *mu'akkad* (emphatic, reinforcing the verb's sense), as if it were said: *zarqa'* (blue), or *'ata'* (a gift) *min 'indi Allah* (from God). *Wa-ma 'inda Allah* (and what is with God), of the abundant and lasting, *khayrun lil-abrar* (is better for the righteous), than what the wicked enjoy of the scant and fleeting.

Maslama ibn Muharib and al-A'mash read *nuzulan* with a sukun (a silent letter, not a vowel). Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' read *la-kinna alladhina ittaqu* with the doubled *nun* (the stressed form of *lakinna*).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 3, verse 199:

﴿And indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah, and in that which has been revealed to you and that which has been revealed to them, humbly submissive to Allah, not selling the signs of Allah for a small price.﴾

Mujahid narrated: It was revealed concerning ʿAbdullah ibn Salam and others among the Muslims of the People of the Book. It was also said: concerning forty people from Najran, thirty-two from Abyssinia, and eight from Byzantium, who were upon the religion of ʿIsa (peace be upon him) and then embraced Islam. It was also said: concerning Ashama al-Najashi, king of Abyssinia. The meaning of Ashama is "gift" in Arabic. That is because when he died, Jibril informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of his death, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Go out and pray over your brother who has died in a land other than yours." So he went out to al-Baqiʿ, and the land of Abyssinia was revealed to him, and he saw the bier of al-Najashi, prayed over him and asked forgiveness for him. The hypocrites said: "Look at this one, praying over a Christian serf whom he has never seen and who is not upon his religion." [[Al-Tha'labi mentioned it as a statement of Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada. Its wording is: "He went out to al-Baqiʿ, and the Abyssinian land was uncovered for him from Madina, and he saw the bier of al-Najashi," and the rest is similar. He mentioned its chain of transmission at the end of the book. Al-Wahidi mentioned it without a chain. Al-Tabari and Ibn ʿAdi in the biography of Abu Bakr al-Hudhali, whose name is Salma, and he is weak, narrated it from Qatada from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab from Jabir, without his words "and he looked at the land of Abyssinia and saw the bier of al-Najashi," and he added in it, "and he said takbir four times." Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated it from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam from his father from ʿAta ibn Yasar from Abu Saʿid, who said: "When the death of al-Najashi reached the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: 'Go out and pray over your brother whom we have not seen.' So he went out with us, and the Prophet (ﷺ) went forward and we stood behind him. He prayed and we prayed. When we finished, the hypocrites said: 'Look at this one, praying over a Christian serf whom he has never seen.' Then Allah the Exalted revealed: (And indeed, among the People of the Book...)."]] And so it was revealed. The lam of emphasis was attached to the subject of "inna" in order to separate the adverbial phrase between them, like His saying: ﴿And indeed among you is one who will certainly lag behind﴾. ﴿What has been revealed to you﴾ refers to the Qur'an, and ﴿what has been revealed to them﴾ refers to the two Books. ﴿Humbly submissive (khashiʿin) to Allah﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "yu'minu", because "man yu'minu" carries the meaning of the plural. ﴿Not selling the signs of Allah for a small price﴾, as those of their rabbis and elders who did not embrace Islam do. ﴿For them is their reward with their Lord﴾, i.e., the reward specific to them, which is what He promised in His saying: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾ and ﴿He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾. ﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾, because His action is effective in everything, so He knows what reward each doer deserves. It is also permissible that it means: "What you are promised is coming soon, since the promise has been mentioned."

Be steadfast in the religion and its obligations, and outdo your enemies, the enemies of God, in steadfastness in jihad. That is, surpass them in patience through the hardships of war; do not be less patient or firm than they are. Musabara (outdoing in endurance) is a branch of patience; it is mentioned after patience in general, which is already obligatory, singling it out for its intensity and difficulty. And be stationed (rabitu): establish yourselves on the frontiers, stationing your horses there, watchful and prepared for raiding. God, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And from the stationing of horses, by which you may strike terror into the enemy of God and your enemy﴾.

And from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever stations himself for one day and night in the way of God, it is as the reward of a month's fasting and its night prayer; he fasts without breaking it and stands in prayer without slackening, and he does not turn away from his prayer except for a need." [[Ahmad and Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated it from a hadith of Salman, more complete than this. Ibn Hibban has it from a hadith of Salman: "Stationing for a day and a night in the way of God is better than fasting a month and standing in prayer, continuously fasting and standing without pause." Its origin is in Muslim, and al-Hakim made an error and included it in his al-Mustadrak.]]

And from the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Whoever recites Surah Al 'Imran, he is given a safeguard with every verse of it upon the bridge of Hell." [[Ibn al-Jawzi narrated it in al-Mawdu'at (the fabricated ones) from a hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and it will come at the end of the book. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through another route from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and al-Wahidi in al-Tafsir al-Awsat from a hadith of Abu Umamah, may God be pleased with him.]] And from him, upon him blessings and peace: "Whoever recites the surah in which Al 'Imran is mentioned on Friday, God and His angels bless him until the sun is hidden." [[Al-Tabarani narrated it from a hadith of Ibn Abbas, and its chain is weak.]]
